Wow. I’m not sure if Alicia A is an owner or just has a very different experience, but mine aligns far more with Larry’s: really slow service, subpar food, and outrageous prices. We arrived on a Saturday morning as a party of three and were quoted a 20-minute wait. Thanks to a larger party disappearing, we were seated in about 10 minutes—but the placement was odd: a lonely table in a cavernous, bright orange room that quickly turned into a holding area for the growing crowd. After five minutes, a server appeared to take our order, then vanished again. Drinks eventually showed up, but the portioning felt stingy and the pacing off from the start. Every beverage came in a tiny 6-ounce glass—the kind you’d expect for fresh-squeezed orange juice. Predictably, those glasses sat empty more often than not, and refills were scarce. It set the tone for an experience defined by waiting: waiting for attention, waiting for refills, and waiting for the food. We sat for about 25 minutes before our $8 waffles arrived. Eight dollars—for a single chocolate chip waffle. Not a premium chip in sight, just standard semi-sweets, and not a large, indulgent portion either. The waffle was roughly eight inches in diameter and, worse, it arrived completely alone: no fruit, no whipped cream, no side of bacon or hash browns, nothing to justify the price. Texture-wise, it missed the mark entirely—hard, ultra-crispy, and devoid of the malted tenderness that makes a waffle comforting. It felt like it challenged my teeth more than it pleased my palate. Service didn’t improve after the food landed; long stretches passed without a check-in. The room filled with waiting patrons, adding to an uncomfortable vibe. Most concerning, a pool of yellow liquid under our table remained unaddressed even after we alerted staff. When a breakfast spot struggles this much with value, execution, and basic hospitality, it’s hard to recommend. If you’re nearby, you might be better off heading across the street to The Good Egg. This visit was all cost and no comfort.

Should this actually be a two-star review rather than three? Probably. I’ve eaten here several times over the years and always appreciated the laid-back vibe and once-reliable comfort food. Unfortunately, my recent visits suggest a restaurant on a slow downhill slide, with service quality eroding each time. On this visit, the service was plainly subpar. Our server seemed attentive and energetic—just not at our table. A young woman seated nearby received prompt, enthusiastic attention and extras, while my family struggled to get basics taken care of. When a taco entrée we ordered arrived with two tacos after he’d told us it came with three, we asked for clarification. Instead of fixing the issue, he launched into a speech about how some chefs allow three and others insist on two, and how the kitchen and waitstaff “need to get on the same page.” That may be true, but it’s not the guest’s problem. Inconsistency and inattentiveness usually point to weak management. Too bad. Until the house tightens up, I won’t be back anytime soon.

I’m a subscriber to Blockbuster Online, and the five free in‐store swaps per month are a lifesaver. On a Saturday, after burning through my deliveries, I stopped by this location to trade a couple discs, and the experience was seamless. The associate who helped me was friendly, efficient, and knew the system. The store itself was clean, well‐organized, and stocked far better than I expected. I even snagged two titles that had just been released the day before, which was a pleasant surprise for a weekend—extra star for availability. Between the easy swaps, the tidy shelves, and the convenient location, this branch makes the Online membership feel genuinely valuable. I’ll definitely be returning whenever I need a quick refresh without waiting on the mail. If you’re using the program, this store is exactly what you want for hassle‐free swaps.

My mom and I went here together after work yesterday. Tucked into a small storefront that’s easy to miss if you’re not looking for it, this intimate spot offers a cozy, no-frills setting with a handful of tables and a compact ordering counter. Dine-in guests are looked after at their tables, which adds a personal touch in a space that otherwise feels utilitarian. On our visit, only one front-of-house staffer was working, and while she was attentive and kind, the pace inevitably suffered—ordering, receiving the bill, and general service all took longer than expected. We came excited to try the goat curry, but they were out, so I went with the jerk chicken and my mom chose the brown stewed chicken. Both plates arrived with “rice and peas” (rice and beans) and mixed vegetables. Here’s where the first hiccup appeared: the menu lists side dishes in two lines, and while entrees include two sides, the second line apparently carries a $2.50 upcharge per side. The menu doesn’t clearly distinguish this, and we were surprised to see an extra $5 for our two orders of mixed vegetables. It’s a small cost, but the lack of clarity makes it feel misleading. Once the food hit the table, almost every frustration melted away. The jerk chicken delivered bold island heat without tipping into punishing territory—still very spicy, so consider yourself warned, but deeply flavorful and balanced. Both chicken dishes were incredibly tender and juicy, bathed in those signature runny, savory juices that speak to authentic Caribbean homestyle cooking. My mom appreciated that her brown stewed chicken wasn’t overly salty, a common pitfall that this kitchen avoids. The rice and peas were fragrant, well-spiced, and mercifully not greasy. The mixed vegetables—zucchini, cauliflower, onions, and carrots—were tasty, though less traditionally Caribbean, and they were out of greens that night, which we’d have preferred. If I could break down the experience: Food earns a full 5 stars, Service a fair 3 stars, and Speed a modest 2 stars. With more staff, the latter two would likely rise, because the effort and hospitality are clearly there. Despite the menu confusion and the slower pace, I would absolutely return. I’m eager to try the goat curry when it’s available and have my eye on the Jamaican rum cake for dessert. For adventurous eaters in Pittsburgh seeking authentic flavors, Royal Caribbean is a small but rewarding destination worth finding.

Belch oh wait Belch excuse me pleaae. Just got back from this place and we are feeling quite bloated. We left dinner feeling uncomfortably bloated. The house margarita disappointed; I was glad I’d had a cocktail before my husband drove us over. Chips and salsa were just okay. We both ordered the taco–enchilada combo. The taco was fine—I liked the crisp shell and shredded beef. The enchilada, however, was bland, with weak sauce and what seemed like a half cup of melted cheap cheese; I left it on the plate. Guacamole was decent, service was good, but nothing made us want to return.

Ahhh Vegas..... Our group opted for the Westin this trip, trading an on‐strip address for a calm haven just a short walk away. Pro tip: that walk shrinks fast when you’re in heels—taxis became our best friends. From the moment we stepped inside, the hotel made an impression: a light, lovely scent, abundant floral arrangements, and chic, modern decor setting an elegant tone. Check-in was seamless and genuinely welcoming. Our room was spotless and contemporary, with a killer view stretching across the Strip’s neon glow. What truly elevated the stay was the staff. From the doorman who greeted us by name to the housekeeper who anticipated little needs, every interaction felt warm, attentive, and sincere. We felt comfortable—cared for—throughout. The complimentary happy hour and snack reception were a delightful surprise, perfect for regrouping before the night. The casino, while petite compared with the Strip’s behemoths, delivered its own happy-hour fun without the chaos. And that’s the Westin’s magic: tranquility in the heart of spectacle. It’s peaceful, polished, and refreshingly calm—a counterpoint to Vegas at full throttle. If you crave the energy of the city with a sanctuary to retreat to, the Westin hits the sweet spot. Five stars from us. Viva..... well, you know the rest. We’ll be back next time, absolutely.

This hotel changed my whole perspective on fancy living in Vegas. Palms Place isn’t the first condo-hotel in Las Vegas, but it was my first taste of that style of stay—and it completely reset my expectations. The suite felt more like a chic apartment than a hotel room: two balconies for skyline views, a cozy fireplace, a proper living room, a separate bedroom, and a sleek, modern bathroom. The real game-changer, though, was the dining room and fully equipped kitchen. An empty fridge and freezer (no overpriced mini-bar traps), microwave, stovetops, and a complete set of dishes and silverware made the place feel instantly livable. We could have moved in for the weekend—honestly, we practically did. That kitchen proved invaluable when my friends returned triumphantly with more than 100 leftover hot wings from a $0.25 special. Reheating late-night bounty without hunting for plastic cutlery or paying room service prices felt like luxury of the practical kind. While Palms Place sits off the Strip, that never felt like a drawback. In Vegas, you’re cabbing or ridesharing regardless—whether you’re at Mandalay Bay heading to XS, or hopping between mid-Strip spots like Bellagio. The little extra distance actually works in your favor: prices are consistently lower than comparable on-Strip properties, yet the quality competes with (and often exceeds) many mid-tier, three-star hotels there. That stay spoiled me in the best way. Since then, a microwave and an empty fridge have become must-haves when I book a room. I’ll make an exception for Wynn or Encore, but Palms Place set a new bar for what “luxury” should feel like—thoughtful, spacious, and livable. For anyone open to a slightly off-Strip address with on-point amenities and value, Palms Place delivers a refined Vegas experience without sacrificing comfort or convenience.

Sun Asian Kitchen has a name that promises flavor, and for South Phoenix locals, the location is convenient. The standout is its happy hour: budget-friendly bites and booze, like six generously filled crab puffs for just $3. Still, the kitchen’s output lands only a notch above fast food, and the ambiance suffers. Cheesy decor and three blaring TVs on different channels can make dining feel chaotic—especially if Animal Planet’s gross-out clips are playing while you eat. On the plus side, the staff is attentive and lightning-quick, though their rapid-fire chatter might catch you off guard. If you’re nearby and craving something easy without a long drive, it’s a decent, value-forward stop; just don’t expect a serene, high-end experience.

Bask Balances Community Spirit, Cozy Ambience, and Craft Cocktails We visited Bask with a LivingSocial deal and unexpectedly found the restaurant hosting an Autism Awareness fundraiser. The house offered a complimentary drink, and profits were donated to Autism Services of Mecklenburg County—a thoughtful touch that set a welcoming tone. This event recurs the last Wednesday of each month from 5 to 8 p.m., and while most guests seemed to be there for it, the room never felt crowded. Only one server appeared to be on duty, yet she was attentive and kept our glasses filled without missing a beat. The space itself is beautiful: polished but not pretentious, equally suited to dressy attire or a casual night out. The menu is concise rather than expansive, but it covers a range of tastes and budgets, with salads and sandwiches under $10 and entrées peaking near $28. You can preview the offerings on their website. We started with the crab dip, a rich, creamy spread partnered with house-made potato chips. The chips were thick and sturdy enough to scoop generously, and while the dip looked modest in size, it was hearty and generously studded with crab. For mains, the vegetable lasagna skips pasta altogether, layering vegetables, tomato sauce, and cheese into a comforting, flavor-forward bake. It sounds austere, but it’s delicious—and after the appetizer, the modest portion was plenty. The trout arrived as a fairly large fillet over green beans, topped with crunchy sweet potato sticks. It was tasty, if not particularly memorable. Dessert brought a wedge of bread pudding set over what tasted like vanilla sauce, dotted with chocolate chips and thoroughly satisfying. I had hoped to try the Guinness ice cream, but it wasn’t available that evening. Bask’s cocktail list is a highlight, mixing old-school standards with inventive house creations. Between the community-minded events, attentive service, balanced menu, and smart drinks program, we’ll definitely be back. A few notes: reservations may be wise on event nights, though we were seated promptly. Portion sizes lean sensible rather than oversized, which suits the menu’s refined feel. Pricing felt fair for the quality, and the overall experience—particularly the cocktails—makes Bask easy to recommend.

Okay, I've never been to Mexico, so I can’t vouch for authenticity, but I can vouch for flavor. El Toro delivers variety in spades, from reliable tacos and burritos to more adventurous specialties. The Milaneza has become a personal favorite, and the Burrito Loco is a delicious, belly-busting challenge. Their salsa is bright and excellent, the kind that keeps you reaching for another chip. My family loves this place—whether we’re dining in or grabbing takeout, El Toro is an easy yes. The only drawback to takeout is missing out on their Golden Margaritas, preferably the huge ones that make the evening. Friendly staff, prompt service, and very reasonable prices seal the deal. Consistently fantastic. Ambiance is casual, comfortable, and welcoming too.

I’ve eaten here twice, which says more about the bleak C gate options than this place’s charms. The food isn’t awful: my chicken quesadilla arrived crisp, with genuinely fresh salsa, and that’s more than you can say for some fat-city specials nearby (looking at you, Pizza Gut). But the service is chaotic. I sat at a dirty table for fifteen minutes while servers buzzed past, and when I finally flagged someone, I got a shruggy “this isn’t my table.” Okay then. In an area starving for decent choices, this spot survives by default. Add basic attentiveness—and maybe a Nathan’s counter—and it could be tolerable enough.

Cooper’s Tavern promises more than it delivers. After a long wait, you’re met with a solid beer list but food that rarely rises above mediocre. Menu descriptions sound enticing, yet dishes arrive bland and forgettable. In a square brimming with stronger options, Cooper’s struggles to stand out. For drinks, it’s fine; for dinner, look elsewhere unless you’re patient and not picky, or craving something memorable.

never been to a marc by marc jacobs before and this one was so pretty and I was very happy:) the layout is really organized and it's easy to find something if you're looking for something specific (like I was). the men's to the left, the women's to the right, the back wall for the purses. As a first-time visitor, I was pleasantly surprised by how intuitive the store feels. The clear layout made it easy to beeline for what I wanted: the Latin-inscribed rings I’d been eyeing online. They actually had my size (6), and at $4 each the price was extremely reasonable—dare I say cheap—yet still charming. Staff were friendly and helpful. They guided me and kept things upbeat. The only downside was checkout. Their card machine was broken, so purchases were being manually entered on a laptop. Buying two rings took about ten minutes, which felt far too long and cost a star. Still, for organization, selection, and value, I left happy with my new rings.

Think of this spot as my personal Cheers—regulars will get the reference. I drop in three to four times a week because it nails the essentials: better-than-average bar food, downright awesome drink prices, and a staff that’s unfailingly friendly and hustles to make every visit enjoyable. With 15 big flat-screens wrapping the room, it’s a go-to for catching any game without sacrificing value, vibe, or service.

I went in to Excellent Nails for a fill. I visited Excellent Nails for a simple fill and left baffled. After the usual question about colors, I requested pink and white with one finger in a different acrylic color. When I asked if that was doable, the technician said yes but seemed annoyed. She brought over the acrylics, and when I said I wasn’t picky—just a fall shade like orange, red, or brown—her irritation became obvious. She rifled through the box, tossing containers, then abruptly told me she doesn’t know how to do fills and that I should come back later. I don’t understand why the interaction turned so unpleasant. My request wasn’t exotic, and I was flexible about color. If the salon doesn’t offer fills or if certain staff aren’t trained, that should be communicated clearly and courteously. Instead, I felt dismissed and embarrassed. Everyone has bad days, but professionalism matters, especially in a service industry. Based on this experience, I won’t be returning, and I can’t recommend Excellent Nails to others seeking reliable, respectful nail care today.

Old-school Mexican spot with traditional vibes and solid food. No beer offered, and the A/C struggled, so visit when it’s cooler. Not a chain atmosphere—authentic, simple, and enjoyable. I’ll return soon.

So the first time I went here, I don't remember a thing. Did I have a good time? I think I did. Rok delivers a decent club experience, especially if you aren’t paying cover. The music is usually on point and keeps the energy high, though the bar service can be painfully slow. Compared with other Vegas clubs, it’s not my top pick, but it’s far from a miss. If you can get in free or cheaply, it becomes a worthwhile stop; otherwise, temper expectations and consider other options.

Millie’s is a little slice of Puerto Rican heaven. As a Puerto Rican, I was blown away by the authentic flavors, generous portions, and the warmth that greets you at the door. The staff’s genuine friendliness makes it feel like going home for a meal. The cozy, small space adds to its charm, creating an intimate, welcoming vibe. I gladly drive two hours to eat here—it’s absolutely worth the trip every time. If you’re on the fence, go. You’ll be very pleasantly surprised and leave smiling.

This place seems pretty cool. I visited during the day, and even on St. Patrick’s Day it felt relatively manageable, with a festive buzz but not the shoulder-to-shoulder crush you might expect. There’s plenty to like—energy, music, and people-watching—but a few caveats are worth noting. Some street vendors use very aggressive tactics: they’ll pull you into a pitch, stall for time, and then escort you straight to a card reader as if the sale were a foregone conclusion. Don’t be shy about declining and walking away; a firm “no, thanks” saves time and money. More concerning was an encounter with an individual behaving erratically who deliberately bumped me after I passed. It was unsettling and could have turned worse. Keep your head on a swivel, give people space, and trust your instincts. The area can be fun, but situational awareness matters. Overall, I’d return during daylight for the atmosphere, but I’d go with friends, keep valuables secure, and set boundaries with hawkers. With a little vigilance, you can enjoy the scene without getting drawn into hassles.

One of the worst cities my career has brought me to. This city has been a disappointment: subpar schools, reckless drivers—worse than LA—and sky-high costs. Everything looks identical, from cookie-cutter houses to indistinguishable people. I’m counting the days until I leave and won’t return. For gambling, I’ll go to Lake Charles, Louisiana, next door.

Definitely a weird dining experience. The food showed some potential, but I stopped halfway, worried I might get sick, and my boyfriend barely touched his. The restaurant had a strong odor, and the furniture felt old and outdated, which didn’t help the ambiance. On the bright side, our server was kind and attentive, earning a tip. Unfortunately, the experience was uncomfortable, and we won’t be returning.

After five years in Pittsburgh, I can say with confidence that Belvedere’s is one of my favorite places in the city and a cornerstone of why I love living in Lawrenceville. From the moment you walk through the door, a playful “You Are Beautiful” hand stamp sets the tone, and the affection continues in the form of wallet-friendly specials. On Thursday 80’s Night, Pabst Blue Ribbon pounders are just a dollar before midnight, rising to a still-gentle two bucks afterward, with $3 well drinks and rotating deals that keep the tab light. What truly makes Belvedere’s shine is its radically welcoming atmosphere. Come with an open mind and you’ll find an eclectic crowd and an even broader spectrum of dancing styles. Judgment is checked at the door, respect is a given, and joy is the default. If you need a breather from the dance floor, there are couches for lounging, pool tables and darts for casual play, and a separate bar in a quieter room where conversation can actually happen. Programming is a blast: Thursdays are for the 80’s, the first through third Saturdays celebrate the 90’s, and the fourth Saturday brings roller derby night’s raucous energy. Behind the bar, staff are consistently friendly and surprisingly conscientious, often asking about your plan for a safe ride home before pouring the next round. Even the bathroom attendants—casual, chatty, and genuinely helpful—add to the quirky charm. While I don’t go for the food, the kitchen delivers pleasant surprises; a friend’s plate of French fries loaded with black beans, peppers, and onions was downright addictive. Ultimately, Belvedere’s hipster-punk vibe, diverse clientele, and inclusive spirit make it a spot where you practically have to try to have a bad time. One caveat: expect to carry the smoky perfume of the night with you for days. If you can handle the haze, you’ll find a singular, lovable dive that feels like home. It’s the rare bar where nostalgia, kindness, and affordable drinks meet to create unforgettable nights and lasting neighborhood loyalty.

My wife and I finally decided to buy a house. We searched for almost 4 months and had Dave inspect 3 houses for us. He was fast, professional and completely honest about the houses. After four months of house hunting, we relied on Dave to inspect three different properties, and his professionalism stood out every time. We fell in love with a home in Mesa, but Dave’s thorough evaluation changed our minds. He didn’t just flag immediate issues—we appreciated how he explained potential future problems we hadn’t even considered, giving us a clearer picture of long-term ownership. Another property appeared solid except for a roof concern. A roofer quoted $6,500 for repairs before Dave visited. While Dave isn’t a roofer, his careful inspection found no evidence of the damage claimed and concluded the required work was negligible. That saved us from a likely unnecessary expense and reinforced our trust in his integrity and judgment. Although we ultimately passed on that house for unrelated reasons, his insights were invaluable. We ended up buying a brand-new home that didn’t require a formal inspection, but we were grateful for Dave’s guidance throughout the process. He was consistently prompt, thorough, and candid—qualities that helped us avoid costly mistakes. If you want a home inspector who prioritizes your best interests, communicates clearly, and delivers honest, actionable feedback, Dave is the person you want on your side.

We were not at all impressed! Our Monday night visit to this buffet was a lesson in frustration and lowered expectations. Despite the room not being particularly busy, we waited nearly 45 minutes just to be seated. Adding insult to injury, an “Express Line” lets anyone skip ahead for an extra $5 per person, so we watched multiple parties breeze past while we stood idle near the front. By the time we sat down, patience—and goodwill—had worn thin. We came for the crab legs, but they were a serious disappointment: batches swung between undercooked and overcooked, shells stubbornly clamped on, and the meat was scarce. The prime rib fared no better—cold and excessively fatty. On the brighter side, the spaghetti with Alfredo sauce was surprisingly comforting, the carved ham was passable, and the dessert selection offered plenty of variety to end the meal on a sweeter note. Value is another sticking point. At the regular price of $19.99, this experience falls short; with a buy-one-get-one-free coupon, it felt marginally acceptable at roughly $10 per person. Even so, the long wait, pay-to-skip seating, and uneven food quality overshadowed the few redeeming bites. We won’t be returning—and we suggest you skip the crab legs. Overall, this buffet missed the mark.

Late-Night Comfort Food with Lightning-Fast Service We dropped in around 1 a.m., found the room lively yet snagged a table immediately, and were impressed from the first pour of water. Service was friendly and incredibly fast: our plates arrived just 2–3 minutes after ordering, with steady check-ins, refills, and timely clearing—never rushed, always considerate. I split the diner stack—a hearty plate of hash browns, a biscuit, eggs over easy, and sausage, all generously smothered in gravy. The pepper was noticeable but balanced, adding depth without overpowering the dish. At roughly $8.25, it’s among the priciest items, but absolutely worth it; most other menu options sit in the $6 range, making this spot a solid value for late-night comfort food. Friends were equally pleased with crisp fries, a nostalgic root beer float, and a bowl of chili that skewed salty—possibly thanks to the added crackers—though still satisfying. The combination of speed, warmth, and consistency makes this place stand out, especially at an hour when good service can be hard to find. For anyone craving hearty fare and great service after midnight, this diner delivers. Highly recommended.

The food was fabulous - vegan, gluten free, organic. I visited this spot in Montreal and ordered the Om Burger—an inspired patty of mushroom, sun-dried tomato, flaxseed, and mixed vegetables, served on chapati and piled with tomato, red onion, lettuce, mustard, ketchup, and a caper aioli. Each bite delivered complex flavors and satisfying texture. For dessert, the brownie proved irresistible; I meant to save half, but couldn’t stop. With six days in town, I’m planning a return visit to explore more entrées from this delicious menu.

Great Convenience Stop with Stellar Service As a regular commuter, this store is a reliable, clean, and well-organized stop. Shopping in the early morning avoids crowds, and the experience is consistently smooth. Customer service stands out—friendly, courteous, and seasoned staff who have been here for years. Their professionalism and genuine care exemplify true customer service, making each visit quick, pleasant, efficient, and convenient.

Dr Chung is a great guy, very professional, which is the only reason I continue to use him. Unfortunately, it's absolutely horrible with wait times. Dr. Chung’s professionalism keeps me coming back, and his team is courteous. That said, the wait times are excessive. An 11:00 appointment often means being seen around 12:30 or even 1:00, after sitting in an exam room for over an hour. This has happened multiple times, and I’ve heard similar complaints from Culinary Insurance patients. The care is solid, but the scheduling and patient flow need serious improvement. Great staff—please prioritize reducing delays to match the quality of service.

I did not have a great experience. In the past, ultrasound techs have made me feel welcome, but not here. I was told it was fine to bring my 18-month-old, yet when he wandered the room, the tech quipped, "Are you sure you want another one?" That’s not a joke any pregnant woman wants to hear. She completed the ultrasound, but the appointment felt rushed and transactional, with little warmth or patience. I won’t be returning. I’m giving two stars only because I did get to see my baby and find out the sex.

I really want to like this place They have a lot going for them: cool staff, decent food, good location, and a solid beer selection. Unfortunately, my friends and I have had nights derailed by a small but persistent crowd of obnoxious patrons. On multiple visits, we’ve encountered loud, creepy, drunk guys hooting at women and ignoring clear signals to back off. One even tried to pick a fight with a female friend after she calmly told him his approach was inappropriate. This isn’t on the staff—they’re friendly and attentive—but the vibe suffers when harassment goes unchecked. A couple of trained bouncers on busier nights could make a real difference, setting boundaries and protecting the experience. I want to love Baer’s Den; fix the crowd and it could be great.

Service 5 stars Service is flawless—five stars. Atmosphere varies: outside is a beautiful five; inside, with the open wall to the mall, feels like a three. For a $$$$ spot in a mall, that’s really hard to get used to. Definitely wait the 20 minutes for an outdoor table. Food earns four stars: the fig flatbread is good, but the crab risotto is great. Portions are generous and satisfying.

I guess I got what I paid for..... Very mediocre at BEST. Ordered delivery to save over hotel room service, and I regret it. Calamari and fries were limp and bland; the app combo was outright gross; chicken Alfredo was just okay. The only redeeming dish was the spaghetti and meatballs. Fried items were a total miss and left me with a sour stomach. If you’re at a hotel, skip this delivery and stick to real room service. Ew.

Replacing the old LongHorn Steakhouse, this new Mexican spot feels familiar in all the expected ways—but not always in the best. The menu is the standard lineup of tacos, enchiladas, and combo plates, with few surprises. Complimentary chips arrive warm, crisp, and unfortunately on the salty side. I ordered a pork-with-green-chile entrée (the exact name escapes me), which came with a straightforward vegetable soup. The soup was startlingly over-salted—my partner agreed—and the main dish followed the same heavy-handed approach. I enjoy bold seasoning and generally crave salt, often favoring food saltier than most, yet this was overwhelming to the point of distraction. It tasted as if every component had been seasoned twice. With moderation, the flavors could shine; dialed-back salt would transform this from passable to pleasant. As it stands, it’s an average Mexican joint hampered by a pervasive salt problem. Until the kitchen reins it in, I’ll steer toward Abuelo’s for a more balanced meal right now.

Visited only for the lunch buffet. It’s consistently packed, with a small dining area and tightly arranged tables, making it feel cramped. The food is good and flavorful, but I’ve enjoyed other buffets more. I plan to return for dinner to compare the experience and see differences.

So we were in Phoenix for the day and had a lot of plans. Thanks to all the places I'd read up on, I thought we’d have a full slate of activities. I’d penciled in a quick pop-in to IKEA—and we ended up spending the bulk of our time there. Here’s our reality: we’ve been in our house a few months, we have a million plans for it, and we don’t have a lot of leftover money to make them happen. For us, IKEA is a lifesaver. No, you’re not buying heirloom pieces here; if that’s what you’re after, look elsewhere. But if you want a stylishly decorated place on a reasonable budget, IKEA is a must. Even if you walk out empty-handed, you leave with ideas. I was practically drooling over their organization solutions—pantries, closets, entryways—every vignette sparks a “we could do that” moment. Families, bring the kids. There’s a supervised play area if you want to shop solo, but my kids were thrilled just exploring the second floor. They pretended each room was theirs, hosting imaginary dinners, meetings, and parties. It turns a shopping trip into playtime and makes the whole experience surprisingly fun. I also appreciate the restaurant’s model of lower prices because you clear your own table. Honestly, I’d love to see that everywhere. Give me a discount and I’ll happily bus mine and anyone else’s. A $0.99 kids plate and $0.50 coffee? Sign me up. And yes, the Swedish meatballs have earned cult status in our house—my son now claims they only taste right with the little flag on top. We had a whole negotiation about returning just for the flags! Overall, I loved it. My husband joked that he felt like “sheeple” for a moment, swept along by the crowd and the maze of showrooms, but I don’t care. I’ll take inexpensive, simple, and stylish anytime. I even like paying for plastic bags; it nudges you toward reusable options, and I wouldn’t mind seeing that become standard policy. If you’re staring down a long home to-do list with a modest budget, IKEA Phoenix is easily a day well spent—equal parts inspiration, practicality, and a bit of Scandinavian comfort food to carry you through.

Sandbar, you provided me amazingly lame service tonight..... Royally lame. My night at Sandbar lasted one glorious minute, and it was epic in the worst way. I was invited out at the last minute and showed up around 11 p.m. wearing my LA Galaxy Herbalife soccer jersey. I distribute Herbalife products, so the branding makes sense, and while I don’t usually wear a jersey for a night out, it was a spontaneous plan and changing wasn’t in the cards. As I approached the door, the college-aged bouncers looked at each other and said, “No go, bro. You can’t wear athletic gear in.” I was stunned. I’ve never been denied entry to a bar, and there was nothing obscene, revealing, or aggressive about what I had on. It was a soccer jersey, not a tank top, not a hoodie, not a bandana. If there’s a dress code, fine—but explain it clearly and treat people with respect. The bouncers had no answer beyond the blanket “no athletic gear” line, and the tone made it worse. The strangest part was what came next: one of them asked the women in our group, “Does he have anything under the shirt, maybe?” So after denying me, they were probing for a workaround while I was already walking away. Why would I want to eat or drink there after that? It felt arbitrary, dismissive, and frankly clueless about customer service. They lost out on at least $75 in business from our group, and they’ll lose more, because I won’t be back. What frustrates me most is that I chose Sandbar after reading positive reviews and expecting a fun, easy night. Instead, I was turned away for “athletic gear” without any posted notice or reasonable accommodation. Dress codes are a choice, but if you insist on them, post them clearly at the entrance and train your staff to communicate with courtesy. Offer options—suggest a loaner layer, or politely explain the policy without attitude. A little common sense goes a long way. I don’t plan to attempt giving Sandbar my business again, and I doubt anyone will message or call to make it right—but the invitation stands. I’ll spend my time (and money) at bars that value guests and apply policies with consistency and respect. My minute at Sandbar was memorable, just not in a good way.
Do not buy here! You’ve been warned. Seriously. They double-charged us for a wedding cake. Bookkeeping looked sloppy—scribbles in a ragged notepad. Based on our experience, stay away.
Best dim sum I've ever had—better than any NYC spot I've tried. Every dish dazzles, consistently fresh and flavorful. My must-do in Vegas; I never skip it. Culinary happiness, every visit.

What I'm basing my review on: Tom yun kung, Red curry “native Lao spicy,” and good beers at good prices If you crave heat with real flavor, this place is a standout. I kicked off with the Tom yun kung at spicy level 4 (native Laotian), the highest they offer. It delivered a bold, clean punch that opened my sinuses without drowning the delicate, savory-sour character of the broth and its plump shrimp—an energizing start to the meal. The red curry, also at level 4 “native Lao spicy,” balanced fire and richness beautifully: creamy, aromatic, and assertive without tipping into harshness. With that intensity, ice-cold beers at genuinely good prices were the perfect pairing and value add. The vibe suits a casual hang with a friend, and the menu rewards spice enthusiasts. Five stars for taste, experience, and price—an absolute must-try for lovers of real heat.

This show is amazing—an uproarious blend of laughter, talent, and nonstop excitement. Be aware: the humor leans heavily on sexual vocabulary, so choose your companions accordingly. After seeing nearly every Vegas show, this is the only one I’d eagerly revisit—again and again. The two hosts are hilarious and unforgettable, leaving you laughing for days. If you want the best night out in Vegas, don’t miss this electrifying spectacle. Enjoy!

Service isn't the greatest here. After a recent visit, Service truly needs improvement. We had just placed our order when another server dropped a bowl of pho at our table less than a minute later. When I explained we’d just ordered, he replied, “Yeah, it comes out quick,” even though our server was still entering the order into the POS. The food didn’t redeem it: the boba pearls were too hard and chewy, under-soaked, and the pho lacked the fragrant aroma I’ve come to expect elsewhere. On my last trip, the herb and sprout plate was tired—brown and wilting—not the fresh brightness pho deserves. To be fair, the overall draw here is convenience; grabbing a bowl late at night can hit the spot. But with better service and fresher accompaniments, it could be more than a midnight stop.

Concerns about transparency and safety at The Drip Room Our pharmacy heard about The Drip Room when a patient asked about IV vitamins and found the lounge online. We called to ask what’s in the “Extreme Party Drip.” The staffer couldn’t name specific medications, describing only anti-nausea, anti-inflammatory, and pain components. When we asked where their IV bags and drugs are sourced, he cited “internationally renowned compounding pharmacies” but offered no names. We also asked about past fungal meningitis outbreaks tied to compounding pharmacies; he said he’d never heard of them. Confidence wasn’t helped by vague credentials: we were told naturopathic doctors and nurses give the IVs, with paramedics “on staff.” The sales pitch claimed people can “never get enough vitamins” from diet or supplements—only 30% absorption—and that IV delivery is superior, followed by injections and sublingual. Regardless of one’s view on IV vitamin therapy, transparency and safety should be non-negotiable. Clients deserve ingredient lists, dosages, named sources and accreditations, and staff who can answer basic safety questions. Without that, trusting anyone to infuse “vitamins” or medications is risky. Until The Drip Room shares verifiable details on products, sourcing, sterilization, and oversight, we recommend caution and consultation with a licensed physician before considering elective IV treatments. Clear, evidence-based information builds trust; vague assurances do not.

Just finished a takeout order from KST as part of my ongoing Dan P mission of Thai restaurant reviews, and it was a rollercoaster of expectation versus reality. Before calling, I combed through the online menu and couldn’t help getting excited: multiple salmon lunch specials—Salmon Basil, Salmon with Garlic, Three Taste Salmon—plus brown rice options. It felt like I’d discovered a new go-to for healthier midday meals. Love at first menu review, truly. Then came the first speed bump. I called to place the order and was told, “We don’t have salmon anymore.” A letdown, but fair enough—menus change. I pivoted to Chicken Basil, requested at a 7/10 spice level, consoling myself with the promise of brown rice and a satisfying lunch special. Walking into KST, I was surprised by how large and bustling it was—packed, energetic, clearly popular. I even queued behind a couple being seated before clarifying I was there for takeout. The waiter who helped me was terrific: friendly, fast, and efficient. I was in and out in about two minutes, impressed by the front-of-house rhythm. Back at the office, the disappointments began stacking up. Inside the bag was just the takeout container—no napkins, no plasticware, no sauces. For a busy restaurant, these omissions might be understandable once or twice, but basic takeout essentials should be standard. Then I opened the container and realized what else was missing. The website lists lunch specials as served with steamed or fried rice, egg roll, wonton, salad, and soup of the day (with soup excluded for to-go orders). My order included none of those extras—no egg roll, no wonton, no salad—just the entrée and rice. The container itself was about two-thirds full, making me suspect the missing third was meant to house the sides. The brown rice I’d been looking forward to? Also missing. Instead, regular steamed white rice. Texture-wise, it leaned toward separated grains rather than the slightly sticky style I prefer—closer to an Uncle Ben’s sort of feel than typical Thai rice. Here’s the twist: what I did receive tasted good. The chicken was nicely ground, and the overall flavor of the basil dish was vibrant and satisfying. The spice level landed hotter than I usually expect for a 7, but not unpleasant—just a notch above my typical comfort zone. If the rest of the order had matched the promise, this could’ve been a solid midday win. Ultimately, the gap between online menu expectations and the actual takeout execution was too wide to ignore. Friendly, efficient service couldn’t offset the missing sides, lack of basic takeout supplies, and the bait-and-switch on brown rice. All told, it’s a 2 out of 5. If they’d delivered what was advertised, it would have been a firm 3. Brown rice, I hardly knew you.

I’m thrilled with my haircut. The stylist was courteous, punctual, and respectful of my tight schedule. The cut is easy to style and looks absolutely adorable. I also loved the high-quality products used, which left my hair feeling healthy and shiny. Highly recommended salon experience. Professional service overall.

What’s a girl to do when she turns 30? Have a spa day and live it up. For my milestone birthday, I kicked off my third decade in style with my favorite trio: wine, chocolate, and the spa. A few days ahead, I booked a relaxation massage and a spa pedicure and convinced a girlfriend to take the day off to unwind with me. From the moment we arrived, we were greeted by smiling faces and handed menus to choose a spa lunch. After a quick tour of the expansive facilities, we slipped into full-on pampering mode. I kept wondering why I hadn’t taken advantage of this local gem sooner. The relaxation massage was exactly what my busy workweek body needed—gentle, thorough, and deeply calming. Just as I resurfaced, lunch appeared: a generous spread of salad, bread, fresh fruit, and a cookie. The portions were surprisingly large; I couldn’t finish it all. Next, we ventured into the steam room. Ten minutes in and my skin felt years younger—plump, smooth, and glowing. I’m now convinced I need a steam shower at home. After a few hours of lounging, we wrapped the day with pedicures. The staff is polished and professional, and the products are top-notch. I can’t do bargain nail salons with harsh lotions that irritate my skin, so having ambiance, quality products, and fair pricing in one place feels like a luxury worth repeating. I’ll definitely be back, and I’m eyeing their first-Wednesday-of-the-month special. If you’re local and haven’t been, stop putting it off—your future, well-rested self will thank you. Consider it the perfect reset between hectic weeks.

I was just here the other night, and this place keeps getting better. Service was awesome. The ribeye? Incredible. The gnocchi? Fuhgettaboutit—pure bliss. And the s'mores were out of this world. Guilty pleasure sentence: death by gnocchi.

Fun place for a few beers? Absolutely. Come hungry? Maybe not yet. This spot shines where it matters to hop-heads: the tap list is broad and engaging, even if a couple of the more adventurous pours were sold out on my visit. There were still plenty of interesting beers to keep everyone at the table happy, and prices were refreshingly reasonable. The kitchen feels stuck in neutral. Expect safe, predictable boards and flatbreads—easy to share, unlikely to offend, but hardly memorable. Nothing was bad; it was uninspired, the kind of bites you forget as soon as the glass hits the table. Service landed in the “fine under pressure” category. Our server hustled with good attitude, and the room clearly was still working through opening-week kinks. I’m optimistic it will tighten up. The soundtrack slaps: a blend of kicky, 80s and current alt that sets a lively tone. The music curation feels thoughtful. The space is a winner—playful design, comfy lounge clusters that feel like a Vig patio transplanted indoors. Though parking will be a headache until they add valet. Come for the beer; nibble if you must.

I've heard about this place for years and finally made my way down the stairs! Choosing a spot between Arcadia and Union Hills, we passed on Dick’s Hideaway and Bomberos, and mourned Richardson’s, before landing at the Rokerij. The staff was friendly, attentive, and on it from the moment we arrived. Downstairs holds only three dining tables, so we waited happily by the fireplace, lounging on a sofa with ESPN’s Tour recaps looping and music at a perfect volume. We nibbled stuffed mushrooms and bacon-wrapped shrimp—both excellent—and sipped a crisp New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc that paired beautifully with the apps. The room wasn’t crowded, the vibe was cozy yet lively, and service never missed a beat. For a tucked-away evening with great bites and polished hospitality, Rokerij delivers. Great experience overall—I’ll return.

Though this Vietnamese hot spot has a strong reputation, I’d call the food solid rather than standout. It’s good, but not definitively the best in town, especially given comparable options nearby. For convenience and space, I prefer Ben Thanh on Central: it’s larger, easier to get a table, and there’s rarely a wait, making it my go-to over the buzzier name.

Stephanie is exceptional to work with. I saw her for back pain and she helped me tremendously. She’s kind, attentive, and pleasant. I even referred a client to her; he echoed my experience, praising her skill and care. Highly recommended for compassionate, effective treatment.

I love Mexican food, so I hold it to high standards, but this spot fell short. Even before stepping inside, a harsh, urine-like odor lingered outside, and someone was asking for change by the entrance—an unfortunate first impression. I ordered a super carne asada burrito (rice, meat, sour cream, etc.), an al pastor taco, and a horchata. The burrito was passable, filling but forgettable; I’ve had far better elsewhere. Surprisingly, the taco outshone the burrito, with better seasoning and texture, though still not outstanding. The horchata disappointed most, thin and lacking flavor. Service was fine, yet the overall experience didn’t redeem the flaws. With many better Mexican options around, I wouldn’t recommend this place. Ambiance inside was ordinary, and prices felt average for the area overall.

Great food. Horrible service. Stopped in with a friend, excited to try the menu. The food, once it arrived, was tasty, but everything else disappointed. When my friend asked for a recommendation, the cashier snapped, “I’m too busy—read the menu.” Our order came with no forks, plates, or napkins. The server said he was off the clock and bringing the food was a favor. Good flavors, but astonishingly rude, indifferent service ruined the visit.

I am blessed to have a lovely boyfriend from Andhra Pradesh who is an EXCELLENT cook. Everyone flips out when he cooks and begs him to cook again. Honestly, I can't stand most Indian food, but he is a magical unicorn in the kitchen. Anyway...the man was starving last night and he wanted to take me to Woodlands. Woodlands set the stage with attractive plates and a polished presentation; at first glance, everything looked delicious and thoughtfully prepared. Service, however, faltered early. My boyfriend tried to order an item he’d seen on the online menu, but our server seemed unfamiliar with it and responded in a dismissive way. While not the worst service I’ve encountered, the tone chipped away at the experience and left us feeling brushed off. We started with idli and vada. The vada was fine—crispy and passable—but the idli felt too dense for my taste. The sambar missed the mark, lacking the depth and balance that make it comforting. The coconut chutney, unfortunately, disagreed with me so strongly that I felt queasy afterward, which made it hard to keep eating even though I tried to push through. On the brighter side, the dosa was the highlight: crisp, flavorful, and satisfying. The veggie uthappam was serviceable, with a pleasant chew and well-cooked toppings, though it didn’t rise to the level of the dosa. A practical warning: if you plan to take leftovers home, be prepared—the aroma intensifies once the food cools. We ended up tossing ours during the drive to spare the car. I’m open to giving Woodlands another shot, perhaps with different dishes or on a less rushed night. That said, my boyfriend’s home cooking sets a sky-high bar, and nothing we had quite matched the magic he brings to South Indian flavors. Overall impression: likely solid for many diners, but uneven for me—three stars, minus one for the service.

A Legit NY Slice in Scottsdale As a native of the NYC area who lives off pizza, I’m thrilled this Scottsdale spot nails true New York style. The crust is thin, foldable, with a crisp bite and gentle chew. The sauce leans savory with a hint of sweetness, and the cheese is rich and clean—bonus points for using Grande Cheese instead of cutting corners. It’s the kind of slice that satisfies at any hour, and the late-night hours are clutch when cravings hit after midnight. Consistency across the menu seals it. Calzones, knots, and heroes show the same attention to quality, making it more than a pizza-only destination. If you judge pizza by chain standards, you’ll miss why this place stands out; California Pizza Kitchen has its fast-food lane, but this tastes like the real NYC deal. Two thumbs up for honest ingredients, skilled execution, and an authentic slice far from the five boroughs.

A small place with nice decor and seating outside. This cozy spot nails the essentials: inviting decor, a few outdoor tables, and friendly staff who greet you on arrival and send you off with thank-yous. I ordered the steak Philly with wiz—OMG, it’s a winner—and my food was ready in minutes, with the room half full at 2 p.m. Expect this place to get busy, because quality and speed are hard to beat. I appreciated the to-go containers of fry sauce and jalapeños, perfect for customizing each bite. One quibble: three digital menu monitors feel excessive when prices and items rarely change; a printed board could save energy without sacrificing clarity. The bright screens aren’t necessary. Rant aside, this is a great spot for a memorable Philly, service, and warm hospitality. It’s my new favorite sandwich place in town, and I’m planning a return visit.

I love Two-Finger Soup! (see story below) Da Vang delivers consistently flavorful, affordable Vietnamese staples. My go-tos: pho, rice with grilled pork; sides: crisp egg rolls, fresh spring rolls; steamed buns to-go. While I’ve sipped more complex broths in SoCal, the pho here is satisfying and portions generous. Service is utilitarian—order by number, food lands in about five minutes, pay and go—which is exactly what I want in a busy pho joint. One caveat: on a couple of visits I’ve noticed servers hustling bowls to the table with fingers a bit too close to the rim—my sister jokingly nicknamed it “Two-Finger Soup.” Consider a gentle reminder if you’re particular about presentation. The atmosphere is lively, with a genuinely diverse crowd of regulars that speaks to the place’s broad appeal. It’s the kind of neighborhood spot where newcomers and seasoned pho fans share tables, slurp quietly, and leave happy. Bottom line: tasty comfort food, great prices, lightning-fast turnaround. Not the absolute best pho around, but reliably good and easy to love—especially when the craving hits.

With an ambiance on par with un Hardee's or--if I'm feeling generous--un Country Kitchen El Pescador doesn't start off with a bang. Arriving late, my two coworkers and I were seated immediately—a perk of the hour rather than host polish. After one companion’s needlessly convoluted drink order, I chose an orange-hued, allegedly lime-flavored margarita on the rocks. Not exceptional, not awful; a serviceable, forgettable sip that set a modest tone. Food arrived astonishingly fast—before we’d finished our first drinks. I led with chimichangas, a choice my coworkers promptly echoed. Two long, slender chimis landed, draped in lettuce, tomato, sour cream, and guacamole, flanked by reliable refried beans. Ever-demanding, my tablemates requested extra guacamole and sour cream, and both appeared without fuss. The chimichangas were excellent: deep-fried to the familiar crackle, served in a mild red sauce, and undeniably satisfying. The beef outshone the chicken, but neither disappointed. The guacamole, almost pure avocado, was lush and delicious. Indifferent service and a non-existent vibe can dull an evening, yet El Pescador’s kitchen redeems things with speed and competence. It won’t jump to the top of my list, but for a straightforward, fast, and tasty plate—especially those chimichangas—I’d likely return to go fish at El Pescador again, on a weeknight when crowds thin.

One of the Best Breakfasts in Madison I'd heard they serve one of Madison's best breakfasts, and I agree. The experience is an adventure: a tiny, bustling space with cramped tables and convivial communal seating that enhances the charm. The atmosphere is warm and lively, and the food arrives fresh, hot, and delicious, comforting classics done right. Highly recommended for breakfast lovers.

The one-star ranking is for Bare Pool Lounge. Total rip-off: $30 to enter, $100 just to sit, and $400 for a bed lounger. As a guy, I expected decent scenery, but it was about 90 dudes and maybe eight women. Overpriced, overcrowded, underwhelming. Save your money and skip this spot. Do not go. Huge disappointment and poor value.

A Grease-Laden Breakfast That Misses the Mark I’ve eaten here and at the sister spot on the Strip several times, hoping each visit might redeem the last. It hasn’t. Breakfast shouldn’t be a slog through grease and sugar, yet that’s the prevailing theme. Eggs routinely arrive swimming in fat, leaving the bottom of the plate an oil slick. Potatoes—something that can shine with crisp edges and seasoning—are weighed down by excess oil. Pancakes are thin but heavy, saturated with butter and grease, the kind you’d halve and save for dessert rather than start your day with. What’s missing is care and finesse. Quality ingredients, handled simply—less fat, less sugar, proper seasoning—can sing. Here, the volume is cranked to ten, and the flavors blur into richness for richness’s sake. The water is unpleasant and likely drags the coffee down with it; a filtration system would be an easy, meaningful fix. Within the Pittsburgh breakfast landscape, this may rank among the better-known options, which says as much about the regional scene as it does about the kitchen. If you’re intent on eating out for breakfast in the ’Burgh, Deluca’s consistently does a more thoughtful job. I love breakfast—it’s my favorite meal—and I want to root for places that treat it with respect. Too often here I leave feeling sorry I got sucked in again. Dial back the grease, invest in better ingredients, filter the water, and let straightforward technique and seasoning take the lead. Until then, it’s a heavy, disappointing start to the day.

I have given this place three chances. Why I will never know. Each time has been unpleasant Despite its convenience to my workplace, this spot keeps letting me down. On my latest visit, with only three tables occupied, I ordered a BBQ Chicken Salad to-go expecting a quick turnaround. Instead, I waited 10–15 minutes—surprising given the light crowd. Back at my desk, the disappointment deepened: the chicken looked gray and unappetizing, the greens were soggy, and the dressing tasted mismatched. I couldn’t finish it. At $9.50, it felt like money wasted. They also asked whether I wanted a roll; I said yes, but it never made it into the bag. I’ve had fresher, better-balanced salads from fast-food chains, which says a lot about quality control here. After three chances and three unpleasant experiences, I’m done. Timelier service, properly cooked protein, crisp produce, and accuracy with to-go items would be the minimum needed to regain trust. Until then, I can’t recommend this place, and I won’t be returning—lunchtime is too short to gamble on another disappointing bowl.

As a first-time parent at the youth run, I’m happy to report this event delivers on safety, organization, and pure kid-centric fun. Important note: my review covers the youth run only. Security is truly top notch. Every child receives a bib with a unique number, and each parent is given a matching bib clearly labeled “parent.” Organizers will not release a child unless the parent is present and the numbers match, and this protocol was consistently and carefully enforced. That peace of mind set the tone for a stress-free day. Operationally, packet pickup was quick and straightforward, and parking was plentiful and close. The race experience itself was a blast for the kids, capped by the thrilling moment of sprinting into the stadium—an adrenaline rush my daughter won’t soon forget. She loved it so much she’s already talking about doing the 5K next year. For $12, the value is excellent. My daughter received a t-shirt, a string backpack, and useful coupons, and the post-race spread included mac and cheese, cookies, Fruit Gushers, and water. It felt generous and well thought out. Staff and volunteers were visible, helpful, and friendly throughout, keeping lines moving and answering questions. The only blemish on an otherwise stellar experience was the wait between age-group heats. It did take a long time to cycle through, and we even got rained on—though the weather is out of the organizers’ control. In hindsight, the pauses made sense: staff were clearly prioritizing accounting for every child before starting the next group. Overall, a well-run, family-friendly event I would gladly return to, with safety as the undeniable standout.
I always stick to pho ga and spring rolls here, and they’re decent. I haven’t explored the rest of the menu. The dining area feels a bit dirty, but prices are low and service is quick.

I usually eat at the original R&T’s at MC85/Litchfield, but this location delivers the same quality and comfort. The homemade red enchilada sauce is, hands down, the best I’ve had in Arizona—rich, vibrant, and unmistakably made from scratch, not the flat, canned taste you find elsewhere. My undisputed favorite is the Sonoran Enchiladas, a distinctive, hard‐to‐find dish that keeps me coming back; I like to add pico de gallo and sliced avocado on the side for extra freshness and texture. The table salsa is bold and spicy, which I enjoy, but I wish they’d also offer a mild or even medium option. A broader heat range would welcome more diners without compromising flavor. Consistently satisfying, R&T’s remains a standout for overall value.

We just got back from Bill’s Gambling Hall, and it reminded us why it’s our go-to spot. Service was attentive and friendly, and our room was clean, comfortable, and—crucially—bed-bug free. The casino’s generous comps kept the party going with Jäger shots and more than enough beers, so the vibe stayed lively well into the morning. The only hiccup was a room assignment with one king bed instead of two queens; after coming home around 7 a.m. each day, we barely noticed. On the floor, the dealers were outstanding—professional, personable, and they dealt us a weekend of wins. It’s always nicer to be taking than laying, and this trip delivered. We’ve been coming here since the mid-90s, back when it was the Barbary Coast, and the combination of price, value, and selection continues to hit the sweet spot. If you’re particular about the social scene, bring your own crew; the crowd includes lots of longtime regulars. Overall, Bill’s Gambling Hall is a dependable, spirited hangout that pairs nostalgia with solid hospitality. We love this place and plan to keep returning.

Matthew delivered exceptional service with fast communication. He handled our soccer team uniforms flawlessly and on time, making the entire process effortless. His reliability and efficiency meant no one had to manage laundry, freeing us to focus on the game and priorities. Highly recommended.

This spot nails authentic BBQ: tender meats, smoky flavors, and friendly, attentive service. Casual, no-frills atmosphere, fair prices, and a standout value with half-price appetizers make it an easy, satisfying go-to.

As a Mexican food expert, I’d give this spot a solid four stars. It’s not exactly authentic, but flavors are satisfying, ingredients feel high-quality, and the ambiance is genuinely cool. The salsa is standout, and the carne al carbón is especially flavorful. Portions run large; trimming serving sizes could improve balance. Overall, it’s a welcome addition to the neighborhood and an easy recommendation for good, reliable Mexican-inspired fare today.

Stay far away from this buffet. I got food poisoning after eating here. For the high price, the selection was disappointing, and the quality subpar. Save your money and health; choose another place instead.

The views are undeniably stunning, but the food and service didn’t justify the price. My swordfish arrived overcooked, the lamb was disappointingly bland, and the lemon cake was dry. Our waitress praised our selections, yet seemed inattentive—she mixed up our bill twice and didn’t appear to remember what we ordered. Pricing felt steep: Bud in a bottle was $8 and that lackluster cake was $15. You can find comparable vistas by driving or hiking without the markup. Overall, the meal we got wasn’t worth it, and I left very disappointed. Save your money and appetite.

Terrible customer service and misleading policies. The “all you can eat” menu felt deceptive: our server said the bean soup and steamed egg were limited to one per table, despite the menu saying “unlimited.” Communication was a major issue; staff had limited English, and they seemed to prioritize Korean-speaking customers, making it difficult for others to order or clarify questions. I left frustrated and disappointed. Unless you’re fluent in Korean or patient, expect a challenging experience. I won’t be returning.

I've never lived in Chicago, but sometimes I sure miss Chicago Dogs. And though there are some places to get a reasonable interpretation of a Chicago Dog, none of them really hit it right in every single way...until now! Uncle Al’s finally nails what I’ve been craving. They use their own franks, and the care shows with a proper casing that snaps when you bite—exactly how a Chicago dog should be. Skinless is available for those who prefer it, but the snap is the soul. The menu lists a dozen other styles, yet for purists, the Chicago is the only correct choice. Ketchup on a hot dog? No thanks. Uncle Al’s gets the details right, and that fidelity keeps me coming back. They offer sandwiches and burgers, but if you’re smart, you come for the dogs. Pair them with the fries: real potatoes, a touch limp, oddly irresistible. I’ve tried the coleslaw twice and regretted it both times. Stick to the dogs and those imperfect-but-addictive fries, and you’ll leave happy—and already planning your next visit.

If you're looking for a fancy steakhouse in Vegas, Delmonico is your go-to. Not being a huge fan of Emeril Lagasse, my preconceptions were flipped after one dinner in this magnificent room. Nothing here is shy of stellar: the food is precisely executed, the service anticipatory yet warm, and every detail polished to a high sheen. The steaks are the main event. Ask for an extra char and you’ll still cut into a warm medium-rare center—juicy, intensely beefy, and seasoned to sing in every bite. The sides aren’t afterthoughts; they’re confident co-stars that could pass as mains, each one delivering bold flavor and flawless textures. Dessert seals the deal. I’ve had Emeril’s banana cream pie at MGM, but Delmonico’s warm chocolate brioche bread pudding is something else entirely—like birthdays, Christmas, New Year’s, all the holidays, and the birth of your first child in a single spoonful. It’s so good it could bring you to tears. For a flawless steak dinner in Las Vegas—where impeccable cooking meets gracious, detail-driven hospitality—Delmonico is the place you’ll recommend before you’ve even paid the check. Make a reservation and be impressed.

During three years at Capri on Camelback, I found a few redeeming features, but far more frustrations. On the plus side, the gym is decent for an apartment complex, and the Wi‐Fi center is serviceable, though nothing special. There’s an onsite convenience store, but I rarely used it—frankly, there are plenty of better spots around Phoenix for a quick sandwich. The downsides dominated daily life. The leasing office often felt unprofessional and the maintenance team was slow and inconsistent. The community skewed toward loud, party‐heavy nights and unsupervised kids running around, and resident screening seemed lax. I dealt with repeated bug issues (cockroaches and mosquitos), pet waste left on the grounds, odd hallway odors, and constant noise amplified by thin walls. More than once, someone pulled fire alarms in the middle of the night. Appliances were prone to problems, and I witnessed enough theft incidents to feel unsafe. Marketing claims that Capri “redefines excellence” don’t match reality. In my experience, it struggled to rise above mediocrity. If quiet, reliable, and respectful living conditions matter to you, do yourself a favor and look elsewhere. I would not rent here again.

The hair stylist was great and friendly, delivering an awesome cut and experience. Unfortunately, the front desk soured the visit: the receptionists were curt and rude, and the salon’s cash-only policy felt outdated and inconvenient. To make matters worse, their on-site ATM adds a $2.50 fee just to pay. Despite the talent in the chair, the poor customer service up front means I’m unlikely to return.

I am a firm believer: if you can complain, you should also praise. We returned to Chelsea’s for lunch on the patio under cooling misters. Our server was attentive, drinks arrived right away, and our food was exactly as ordered. The fries are among the best anywhere—crisp and perfectly seasoned—and the Rare French Dip is amazing, tender, and flavorful. I’m so glad I went back; this felt like the Chelsea’s I know and love. Thank you, Allison, for encouraging me to try again. With solid service, relaxing ambiance, and standout dishes, Chelsea’s has won me over. I will definitely be back.

You're not going to find a better deal on the Strip than Earl of Sandwich at Planet Hollywood. With sandwiches around $6, it’s a budget-friendly gem in Vegas without sacrificing flavor. My go-to orders are the Best BLT, crisp and satisfying, and the Montague, loaded with hot roast beef and turkey. Service is quick, and the sandwiches come out hot and fresh. Bonus: Fat Tuesday sits right next door, so you can pair your meal with a yard-long 190 Octane. Hot sandwiches and icy drinks—Vegas perfection.

After two visits, I left underwhelmed. The fish didn’t taste as fresh as at other spots, and the rolls lacked tightness and creativity—Sakana easily outshines it. In this neighborhood, sushi options are scarce, so convenience is its main appeal. Fine for a quick fix when cravings hit, but not somewhere I’d choose for a date or a special night out. Overall, consistency needs improvement, and the experience falls short of making it a go-to destination.

I went here after hearing about it on a tour. I didn't eat anything but had a drink, so my review will be mainly on the atmosphere and service. It’s dark, intimate, and has a moody vibe that suits date nights or a quick stop for a drink. I can see it getting loud if it’s packed, but on my visit the crowd was just right. Service was fast and personable; the bartender chatted briefly. Overall, a great spot—nothing groundbreaking, but I’d happily return.

I wasn't planning on having my baby there..... but I did and it ended up being great. I wasn’t planning to deliver at Mountain View, but a 38‐week appointment changed everything. With high blood pressure and protein in urine, my doctor sent me to the hospital and recommended Mountain View for its nursing staff—and I can see why. I arrived at 4 p.m. Thursday, was induced by 6 p.m., and had a C‐section at 8 a.m. Friday. As a first-time mom, I was amazed by how little pain I felt and how consistently kind, attentive, and professional the team was. Communication was clear, environment calm, and my baby and I were cared for from admission through recovery. The only downside was billing: duplicate charges went to collections, hurting my credit. Five-star clinical care, but administrative billing needs improvement.

I'm sorry. I like Zen for what it is and all, it is good, better than the other places I've tried in Vegas however it just seems too plain for me to be a fan of. Is it more that curry, rice, and fried stuff!? Zen delivers a straightforward curry experience that’s clean, efficient, and reliably satisfying, but it may not excite those seeking bold thrills. The menu is refreshingly simple: choose your curry base (original, vegetable, or spinach), select a spice level (1–5 free; 6–10 for an extra $0.20), pick your rice (plain or brown), and add a fried protein or two—think pork or chicken katsu, tofu katsu, pork or chicken tenders, shrimp, sausage, and more. I’ve stuck with the original curry, dialing the heat anywhere from 5 to 10 depending on the mood. The flavor is solid and comforting, and yes, it can make you sweat, but even with the table spices, it never quite reaches the fire-breathing intensity I crave. Perhaps the aim here is balance over burn. The plates come as hearty half-and-half compositions—rice on one side, curry on the other. The kurobuta sausages are a highlight, offering a nice snap and richness; the fried items, while competently done, are fairly standard. Portions are decent but may feel modest if you’re a bigger eater—you might leave a bit peckish unless you load up on add-ons. Just note that extras can push the price up quickly. Pro tip: ask for a smaller spoon or a fork; the default spoon is oversized and a little awkward. The space itself is bright, tidy, and pleasant. It can get busy, so expect occasional waits and some weaving between tables. Service is consistently friendly and efficient—drinks get refilled, food arrives in a reasonable timeframe, and the check is handled without fuss. Bottom line: Zen is good—better than many curry options in Vegas—yet it leans safe and simple. I wouldn’t steer anyone away; I’d happily return if friends suggest it. Just don’t expect fireworks, especially if your palate chases serious heat or more adventurous variety.

I’ve been to this hybrid coffeehouse-bar twice: once on a bar-hop-fueled night that ended in drunken chess, and once for a sober rematch. Both visits revealed a place that’s less about culinary revelations and more about a laid-back, communal vibe that rewards lingering. On the late-night visit, after bouncing from Beauty Bar to Griffin and devouring what I insisted was “the greatest hot dog of my life” at the stand outside—inebriation is a generous editor—we headed in. The door guy did his job and carded me; after 7 p.m., it’s 21+ when the beer comes out. We grabbed a table, split a sandwich I can barely remember for obvious reasons, and dove into three rounds of chess. I lost them all. Not the food, not the beer, not the night’s highlight: it was the simple pleasure of sitting over a board with pieces clicking and the room humming. On the return trip, clear-headed and caffeinated, I ordered a large iced white mocha. Size-wise, it skewed closer to a Starbucks “grande” than a true large, which might irk volume seekers, but I appreciated the restraint with the ice. The drink was sweet and serviceable—pleasant, not a must-repeat. As with the sandwich, the coffee didn’t aim to impress so much as accompany the experience. And maybe that’s the point here. Games are the quiet heartbeat of the space. Up front you’ll find chess and a scatter of other donated, well-loved board games. There are easy places to sit, plugs for laptops, and enough room to talk in a low murmur without feeling like you’re intruding on anyone’s concentration. In back, bins of vinyl wait to be flipped through; at the counter, a record spins and sets the tone. It’s analog in a way that feels sincere rather than curated for effect. The crowd is a slice of the city: students with chargers snaking to wall outlets, business suits on late coffees, cops grabbing a break, the obliging drunk or two, even an older guy in Dr. Dre Beats headphones watching YouTube with monk-like focus. Label it hipster and you’ll miss the mix. It’s chill, not performative. A plea to fellow players: return the games up front and put the pieces back when you’re done. My poor white pawn and bishop went missing. Verdict: I got my revenge in the sober rematch—best two out of three—and left feeling the same way both times. The food and coffee won’t wow you, but this is a fantastic place to hang out, play a game, and watch a little slice-of-life unfold. Not my Central Perk, maybe, but definitely somebody’s.

Best Chinese food I have had in Arizona that is not dim sum George & Son Chinese & Asian Cuisine has landed in North Phoenix next to the AMC Deer Valley movie theater, bringing the same recipes locals know from its Scottsdale sister restaurant. I stopped in for lunch and left impressed by both flavor and value. I tried the Mongolian Beef ($7.95) and Shrimp with Walnuts (Honey Walnut Shrimp) ($8.95) lunch platters. Each comes with a salad, crab puff, vegetable roll, lo mein, and steamed rice—a generous spread for the price. The only miss was the salad arriving warm; it should be colder. Everything else, however, delivered bold, satisfying flavors. The Mongolian Beef was notably tender, with a sauce that balanced savory and sweet and plenty of scallions for brightness. The Honey Walnut Shrimp was crisply breaded, tossed in a creamy, craveable sauce, and studded with fresh, crunchy walnuts. Portions were abundant without feeling heavy, making the lunch combos a standout deal. The menu covers the staples—Egg Foo Young, six varieties of Fried Rice, Moo Shu Pork, and Ma Po Tofu—alongside broader Asian favorites like Hong Kong Style Ribs, Pad Thai, and Salt & Pepper Shrimp. It’s the kind of lineup that suits both traditionalists and those looking to mix it up. Service is notably warm; hosts and servers are friendly and actively seek feedback, bordering on over-friendly in the best way. The space is modern, clean, and appears to have a full bar, making it a comfortable spot for casual lunches and group dinners alike. If other eateries such as Shangri-La draw four stars, George & Son feels like a six. Still, I’ll give it 4.5 stars as the best non–dim sum Chinese I’ve had in Arizona. Come for lunch and the combo value; return for dinner to share plates ($10+ per dish). Address: 3049 W Agua Fria Fwy, Phoenix, AZ 85027, next to the movie theater.

My first visit to Tammie Coe on a Thursday ended in disappointment. As a customer with food allergies, I approached the counter with a few straightforward questions about ingredients. The clerk’s response was disinterested at best; I practically had to beg her to call someone for clarification, and when she finally considered it, she grimaced. At $2.50 per cookie, I expected not only quality but basic courtesy and product knowledge. I’ve had larger, all-natural cookies elsewhere for less, so attentive service would have made the price easier to swallow and likely secured a sale of at least two cookies—plus potential return visits. Instead, the reluctance to assist sent me out the door empty-handed. Oddly, a neighboring shop, Chill Out, showed the same unwillingness to contact their supplier. For businesses that sell food to people with allergies, this lack of responsiveness is troubling. Sadly, I left deciding I won’t return to Tammie Coe again.

The bread basket was amazing—maybe a little too good, because I filled up on it early. I started with the shrimp and tamale, which were really good, and the sauce was excellent. The scallop was cooked to perfection, and the appetizers were generous enough to be a meal. By the time my entree arrived, I was stuffed. The lobster tacos, at $20 for three small tacos, were underwhelming. The real standout: the side of creamed corn—rich, comforting, and a must.

One Word: Pushy In the first five minutes, I was approached four times by sales staff — three different associates, one of them twice — with a constant chorus of "those are on sale!", "great price!", and "everything's discounted!" I don't mind being greeted, just not every minute. Acknowledgement is nice, but I knew what I wanted and needed a moment to consider pairing them with my wardrobe. The relentless pitch derailed my focus and turned browsing into a gauntlet. Ironically, the store's selection is appealing; I was ready to buy. Yet the pressure made me walk out empty-handed, craving courtesy and space. Attentive service should enhance the experience, not overpower it. Three stars for inventory, but management should recalibrate the approach: greet, offer help once, then let shoppers breathe. Peaceful shopping sells more than repeated discounts.

I really don't see the hype with this place. I feel like maybe five years ago it used to be a good spot, but now it’s lacking in every department. From the moment I walked in, an ungodly stench hit me at the door and seemed to drift through half the dining room. I was relieved to be seated in the back, because there was no way I could eat while inhaling that smell. Unfortunately, the food didn’t redeem the experience. I ordered the all-you-can-eat fish and shrimp combo; it arrived promptly, but tasted stale and old. It wasn’t a seasoning issue—the fish and shrimp were dry, lifeless, and unpleasant, with a texture and quality closer to fast food than a sit-down restaurant. Quantity clearly overshadowed quality. The one bright spot was the staff. They were extremely nice, hardworking, and quick, checking in often and keeping things moving. If only the kitchen and upkeep matched their effort.
