Between the pervasive odor and disappointing plates, this place feels past its prime. Unless major changes are made—freshness standards, ventilation, and maintenance—I’ll be skipping this spot. Great service can’t save mediocre food and a dining room that doesn’t smell right.

My last visit with Dalton was disappointing, and this time wasn’t much better. The server never offered an iced tea refill and tried to clear my plate before I finished, then hovered every minute as if rushing me out. To top it off, the garlic fries arrived burnt. The only saving graces were the free Wi-Fi and catching the Steelers on the big screen. With basic hospitality missing, it’s hard to recommend, though the amenities keep it from a two-star rating.

Excellent meal. Good value. We loved the salmon with cream sauce—perfectly cooked and rich without being heavy. The chickpea salad was tasty and interesting, and the dinner salad’s dressing was spot-on. A superb French baguette rounded everything out. Servers were accommodating and attentive, and the ambience matched exactly what we were hoping for tonight overall.

Great area, pretty place. Good atmosphere. We were greeted promptly and seated quickly, which set a positive tone. Unfortunately, about 20 minutes passed without any service until I walked across the restaurant to alert the hostess. When we finally were served, the service felt bored and lazy, turning the experience into a disappointment that genuinely ruined my dinner. The absence of a manager apology, gesture, or even a small discount compounded the frustration. The setting has real promise, and I’m willing to return again to see if this was an anomaly. I hope the next visit matches the ambiance.

I became a fan of this place when I lived in CA for six months- right before they were bought out and started shutting down locations left and right. I gave up hope of ever eating their sweet onion cashews ever again when we moved to LV. And then I randomly drove past one and nearly crashed my car craning my neck to see if they were open or not. Later, I safely drove myself to this location. And hallelujah—the great prices and fresh food are back in my life! Inside, I noticed several signs explaining that clearance products now live in their original departments with fresh pricing stickers instead of being corralled into a single aisle. Whether that’s a staffing solution or a savvy way to boost sell-through, it works. I’m pretty sure every single thing I bought was on clearance: bagged salad kits, taco-chili seasoned chicken breasts, a supreme pizza, a handful of oven- and stove-ready vegetable dishes, and even a baking sheet I’ve needed since our move. The total? A treasure-trove $21. This is exactly why I F&E—smart pricing, solid quality, and the thrill of a good find. There’s also signage out front announcing new 24/7 hours, which is awesome for night owls and early birds alike. The store felt clean, organized, and easy to navigate, with quick checkout and helpful staff. Now I just need to buddy up and learn their markdown schedule. Pro tip: wander every aisle, watch for those stickers, and let the deals inspire your next meal.

Got a mani/pedi for $35 and loved it. My nails looked great, with a nice selection of colors to choose from. Everyone was very friendly, and our appointment started right on time. The atmosphere was relaxing and welcoming. I smudged one finger minutes after leaving, drove back, and they kindly fixed it immediately. Excellent service—I'll definitely be returning. Thank you again!

Good pizza? Yes. Best I've had? No. Pomo came highly recommended, and I walked in with equally high expectations. While the thin-crust style suits me, the pizzas simply didn’t hold their toppings, a problem compounded by truly awkward slicing. Of the three pies we ordered, one arrived cut into off-centered quarters, leaving two giant pieces and two tiny scraps. Another was cut into sixths, with two razor-thin slices and two overly thick wedges, plus only a pair that looked normal. The third, somehow, was cut into fifths—one triangle flanked by four trapezoids. It made sharing messy and uneven. Toppings were just as inconsistently handled. Our vegetarian pizza with roasted vegetables came half eggplant, half zucchini, and a mound of bell peppers dumped in the middle, rather than evenly distributed. Once we spread things around and traded toppings, the flavors were good enough, but the experience felt careless. Pomo serves decent pizza, but execution matters. Between flimsy crusts, erratic cuts, and uneven toppings, the promise didn’t match the hype. Meh. I’d look elsewhere next time.

Breakfast was good, and the staff were great. The wait, however, was long—an hour—so if you’re really hungry, bring a snack; we even ran errands while waiting. I’d go again with people who haven’t been, mostly for the novelty of a famously long breakfast wait overall.

Always a favorite, this Macy’s—once The Broadway—remains as inviting as ever. Abundant parking, including covered garage spaces, is a summer lifesaver. Inside, you’ll find a well-curated selection of clothing, jewelry, cosmetics, and household goods that makes one-stop shopping easy. Customer service consistently shines: helpful, courteous, and efficient. In a retail world that’s constantly changing, this store stays pleasant. I highly recommend it and confidently give it a five-star rating.

Despite the typical Las Vegas price tag, this lunch stood out for its quality and ambiance. We sampled dim sum, an outstanding shrimp wonton soup, and a flavorful noodle dish topped with barbecued pork. Each bite felt carefully prepared and balanced. Service was polished, the dining room elegant yet comfortable, and the overall experience memorable—arguably our favorite meal of the trip.

As an East Valley player, I was thrilled when Guitar Center opened in Mesa—finally a shop close to home, so I wouldn’t have to trek to Milanos. I’ve stopped in several times and even bought a couple of guitars, but the experience keeps falling short, mostly because of the staff. When you’re spending $2,000 or more on an instrument, you expect to work with people who live and breathe guitars. At Mesa, too often I’ve met employees who can’t explain differences between models or confirm basic specs. Asking which pickups were in a Les Paul—were they 57 Classics?—yielded shrugs, and I had to do the research myself. That erodes confidence in a big-ticket purchase. Used gear pricing feels inconsistent, apparently at a manager’s discretion, and frequently higher than other GC locations for the same items. Meanwhile, trade-in offers on my tube amp were so low they felt predatory, which likely discourages sellers. The result seems to be a thin selection on the used wall coupled with markups that don’t make sense. By contrast, the Tempe and Scottsdale stores have stronger inventory and staff who can actually talk shop. Mesa could benefit from training, transparent pricing, and a culture that respects musicians’ knowledge and budgets. Since corporate ownership changes, some stores have felt more transactional and less like a haven for players. I’d love to see Mesa become a place where expertise, fair deals, and passion for instruments lead the way. I’m rooting for this store, because convenience matters, but convenience can’t replace trust, selection, fair pricing, and knowledgeable staff behind the counter every day. Until then, I’m sticking with Tempe and Scottsdale.

Great spot for sampling small plates, with prompt, friendly service and vibe that could pass for Momofuku. Standouts: earthy mushroom ramen, tender lamb, and addictive shrimp beignets. Pork buns are good, but if you’ve had them elsewhere, the price stings. Sweet potato donuts are delightful—I just wish they appeared at breakfast or another venue. Overall, inventive, satisfying, and worth a visit, if you order strategically.

Not sure what all the hype is about!? I visited this spot for the first time after seeing the crowds. On the positive side, the staff were warm and friendly, and the menu offers a wide variety of drinks and juices. Unfortunately, the food didn’t live up to the buzz. I paid $25 for four steak tacos, a piece of corn, and a Coke. The steak was bland and underseasoned, lacking the flavor I’ve experienced in Mexican food across Mexico, Chicago, New Mexico, Texas, California, and Las Vegas. Given the price and the taste, I don’t see myself returning or recommending it—despite the excellent service.

We visited for a company dinner, and though I’m not a meat lover, the fillet mignon was truly mouthwatering and perfectly cooked. The red-hued ambiance was absolutely beautiful, and the cheesecake was extremely good. Service stood out—respectful, attentive, and genuinely polite from every waiter. Overall, an amazing experience that impressed our whole team and left us eager to return back soon.

I first visited Taphouse Kitchen after hearing it was a prime nosh-and-mingle spot. It delivered: warm, inviting vibes, genuinely kind staff, and a menu crafted from scratch. The wings set the tone—crispy, a confident spice blend, and a whisper of sweetness that kept me reaching for another. Two weeks later, I nearly went elsewhere for brunch; thankfully, I didn’t. The brioche French toast was transcendent—pillowy, custardy, and lightly caramelized, the kind of dish that lingers in your thoughts. The eggs Benedict impressed with a smart twist: roasted turkey on sourdough crowned with ultra-fresh guacamole studded with bacon bits. Service stayed upbeat, refills came promptly, and every bite felt thoughtful. Portions are generous without feeling heavy, and the space encourages lingering conversation. It’s deadly good—and absolutely worth every penny.

Here’s the thing: the breakfast here is really good. Think classic, down-home comfort with huge portions and the kind of hearty plates that make you happy you chose breakfast over brunch somewhere else. The kitchen nails the fundamentals, and when you’re in the mood for a satisfying morning meal, this place delivers. Where they stumble is service under pressure. We came as a large group of 14 around 11–11:30 on a Sunday without a reservation—yes, that just happened—and the brunch rush was already in full swing. The staff seemed plentiful, but our assigned server was clearly overwhelmed. Orders lagged, details got lost, and you could feel the strain. Thankfully, Bloody Marys and Mimosas kept spirits high, and we’re not the complaining type; we knew we’d thrown them a curveball. Still, if a restaurant decides to seat a party that size during peak hours, it’s smart to assign multiple servers or have experienced staff tag-team the table. One moment captured the chaos: several of us asked for tortillas instead of muffins or toast, but our plates arrived with rolls. When we reminded the server, she asked for the rolls back—an awkward request that raised eyebrows. She returned later and dropped it, which was a relief, but it spoke to how frazzled things felt. Here’s the bottom line: the food is excellent, the portions are generous, and we’ll absolutely keep coming back. But we’ll avoid bringing a big group on a Sunday morning without a reservation. If you’re rolling in deep, call ahead. If you don’t, be prepared to wait, stay flexible, and maybe order a cocktail to smooth out the bumps. Despite the service wobble, we had a good time, and the breakfast is worth returning for—just with a smarter game plan.

Delicious!!! We detoured from our original plan to eat at Raku and popped in here instead, and I’m so glad we did. The black cod is the undisputed star—silky, caramelized, and addictive. The menu is perfect for grazing; you can sample many plates without getting stuffed. Highlights: garlic yellowtail with yuzu (bright and savory), an off-menu sashimi salad worth asking your server about, and mochi ice cream where mango reigns supreme. The tofu eggplant agedashi hits that comforting, savory note, and the tuna, albacore, and yellowtail sashimi are all top-notch, though the salmon was just okay. Seafood ceviche with kiwi is intriguing but not essential, and the curry sushi is a quirky bite. Filet mignon with citrus soy was fine but not memorable, while the almond yuzu frangipane made a lovely finish. I left happy, eager to return—and spotting Andre Agassi was a fun bonus. Service was friendly and attentive without being intrusive.

I was introduced to this burger spot on a whim by a friend who knows my weakness for a good burger, and wow—what a pleasant surprise. The menu is imaginative, full of craveable combinations that all sounded tempting. I went with the BBQ, Bacon & Cheddar and a side of Smash Fries, those thin, crisp fries tossed with oil and seasoning. After grabbing my drink, I settled in, and the food arrived at the table quickly. The burger was cooked exactly to my requested doneness, juicy rather than dry, with smoky-sweet barbecue sauce, crisp bacon, and melted cheddar coming together in a rich, satisfying bite. Yes, it was a bit greasy—because it’s a burger, not a health food—and that’s part of the pleasure. The Smash Fries were awesome: well-seasoned, aromatic, and hard to stop eating. Service was fast, seating was easy, and the whole experience felt seamless. For anyone craving an indulgent, well-executed burger-and-fries fix, this place delivers. I’m already planning my next visit. Bring an appetite and embrace the delicious mess.

DP Dough..... My first impression wasn’t great. When I picked up my first calzone at the store, the space looked a bit unsanitary, and not everyone wore gloves or aprons. That said, my second experience—delivery—won me over. DP Dough delivers to surprisingly far destinations and operates 24/7, making it a clutch option when hunger hits at 3 a.m. Their menu boasts a wide selection of calzones, but I’ve stuck with the Ranch Buffer a couple of times. It’s consistently tasty, especially after a few beers, with a satisfying balance of flavors and hearty filling. While I hope the in-store cleanliness improves, I still recommend DP Dough for convenient, late-night comfort food. If you’re craving a calzone, give the Ranch Buffer a try.

A Rocky Start on S. Craig After eagerly awaiting this spot’s opening on S. Craig, I stopped in for a simple breakfast sandwich despite hearing from coworkers that early visits were disappointing. Service was friendly and quickly corrected an initial overcharge, which I appreciated. Unfortunately, the food missed the mark: the sausage was so overcooked it was hard and crunchy, suggesting a microwaved patty handled far too long. In week two, growing pains are understandable, but execution matters. Streamlined order accuracy and better kitchen oversight—especially on basic items—could turn things around quickly. I’m willing to give them another chance, and I hope management leans into training and consistency before first impressions harden. If these issues persist, they risk joining the list of short-lived concepts on S. Craig. For now, cautious optimism, but with clear room for improvement.

On a packed Friday night in Las Vegas, when every restaurant quoted waits an hour longer than they should, Marrakech proved a welcome surprise. Tucked into an unassuming strip-mall storefront just off the Strip—neighbors include Ruth’s Chris and a tapas spot—this Moroccan-themed hideaway trades glitz for atmosphere. Step past the plain façade and you’re in a jewel-box room draped in floor-to-ceiling carpeting, staffed by servers in harem pants. Seating is on low couches, dishes are designed to be shared and eaten with your hands, and portions are generous enough to satisfy hungry wanderers. The food is flavorful and the evening builds to a belly-dancer performance that turns dinner into an escape. Unusual, intimate, and fun—Marrakech is a smart detour from the Vegas frenzy.

Great pizza and outstanding service. Our server was wonderful—sweet, attentive, and took time to explain the restaurant’s history and how the pizzas are made. Food arrived quickly and tasted fantastic. The decor is charming, especially the wine-bottle chandelier. Only drawback is the price, a bit steep for pizza, but overall a memorable experience.

Eh...for the price ($10 at dinner with a'rewards card' that you can get for free next to the buffet instead of paying the regular $14) it wasn't bad but I surely won't be running back. Most of the food tasted bland and basic, geared toward quantity over quality. On Monday evening, the line moved quickly—about a 10–15 minute wait—but the spread was unimpressive once inside. I’d rather pay an extra $20–30 for a good downtown buffet. If you’re a local craving cheap, junky eats, this might scratch the itch. The pizza was decent, and the staff were friendly, but overall it’s a forgettable, fill-your-belly stop.

I used to think this was a solid 3 star place. But not anymore. I left the Valley last week and, before I went, I set out to revisit my favorite spots—Chompie’s among them. I hadn’t been back since Adam Richman swung through, but my previous visit in January didn’t prepare me for the sticker shock I felt this time. Prices that were once merely high now feel exorbitant, edging into price-gouging territory. I could forgive a bit of inflation for a great experience, but the service has slipped, too. On this visit, my friend and I were seated promptly by a friendly hostess. A busser dropped off waters, and then..... nothing. Ten minutes ticked by—ten long minutes—while we made eye contact with two servers who never approached. No greeting, no “be right with you,” no acknowledgment at all. We were hungry, we were ready, and we were invisible. Ultimately, we left. It’s a shame, because I was ready to splurge on those sliders I remembered fondly. Instead, Crackers and Co earned our business. The bill was a few dollars lighter, and someone took our order within ten minutes—smiling, attentive, and present. Nostalgia can’t overcome indifferent service and ballooning prices. I hope management takes note, but for now, even three stars feels generous. Not anymore.

I LOOOVE THIS PLACE!!! Its my home away from home! I can’t say enough good things. Yoga One is a beautiful studio with awesome staff and killer workouts. Every class feels like a complete mind, body, and soul experience, and the lavender towel at the end is bliss. The $5 classes and community focus make it accessible and welcoming. I skipped a LivingSocial deal elsewhere because Yoga One delivers everything I need. If you haven’t tried it, go now. They’re absolutely awesome!

Friendly, knowledgeable staff and well-stocked counters make this post office a reliable stop for routine mailing needs. The lobby feels safe thanks to bright lighting, and the abundance of post boxes is a plus. Its location across from the Archdale Lynx station adds convenience for commuters. Be prepared for waits: lines often swell around the lunch hour and just before closing. The “regular” hours—Monday to Friday, 8 a.m.–5 p.m., and Saturday, 9 a.m.–2:30 p.m.—will suit traditional schedules but can be limiting for those who need after‐work access. The biggest drawback is the lack of a self‐service kiosk. There’s only a stamp vending machine, which is of limited use if you need to weigh a package, calculate postage, or pay by credit/debit card. That omission undercuts after‐hours flexibility. At 3.5 miles from my home, it’s farther than I’d like for my designated post office. Still, if your timing aligns, the courteous staff and convenient transit access make it a dependable choice.

Wow, this place has really gone downhill. This used to be a well maintained, fun place to go when I was in high school. We revisited last week and it was a totally different experience. Batting cages were the bright spot, but the nets over them were torn, a real safety concern for anyone parked beyond. $1.50 for 18 pitches felt fair. The driving range looked serviceable, though we didn’t try it. The mini-golf course was a letdown: holes through fake boulders, missing turf, uneven cement, and none of the water features or decorations that once made it charming. By hole five, we were already looking for an exit. Seeking a make-good, we returned to the window. The manager met us with a brusque attitude, refused alternatives, and immediately demanded receipts and cards. Refunds were ultimately issued—which we appreciated—but the interaction left a sour taste. Facilities didn’t help matters: the bathrooms were dirty and clearly neglected. Overall, the property feels abandoned by standards and care. With some investment and attention, this could be the lively, family-friendly spot it used to be. Until then, we won’t be returning.

Stopped by late at this 24-hour spot and was told anything I ordered would be microwaved because the grill had just been cleaned and staff didn’t want to dirty it. That defeats the purpose of being open. Disappointing service and food standards. I left without ordering and won’t be back.

Service was abysmal. The waitress never smiled, was rude, unresponsive, and slow. She didn’t return to check on our order. My beer arrived warm; she took it away, poured it into a chilled glass, and brought it back half full—still warm. The food came out cold, compounding the disappointment. Between the indifferent attitude and the shabby handling of basics, this visit was a total miss. I left a penny tip—and even that felt generous.

5.0 stars for the oxtail soup Available only from 11 p.m. to 11 a.m., this California Hotel late-night gem is worth planning around. Located in downtown Vegas, the cafe draws a loyal late-night crowd. We arrived at 11:30 p.m. and were seated immediately; all four of us ordered the oxtail soup. Each bowl had three generous, fall-off-the-bone pieces in a savory broth, plus a side of white rice and dishes of chopped cilantro and minced ginger—toss them in for a bright lift. Pure comfort. By the time we left at 12:30 a.m., a line of 20-plus had formed, so come early. Parking tip: Main Street casino charges $5, but you can get it refunded at the California Hotel cashier with your restaurant receipt. We meant to return the next night and didn’t, and still couldn’t stop thinking about that soup all the way home.
Unbeatable tacos keep me coming weekly. Fresh fillings, grilled tortillas, zesty salsas. Cozy dive-y vibe adds charm. Friendly staff, quick service, value. My go-to.

Drinks and dessert with the girls in Vegas hit the sweet spot. The warm butter cake with fresh fruit was melt-in-your-mouth amazing; the strawberries paired perfectly, juicy against rich crumb. The only excess? A mountain of fresh whipped cream—fluffy, tasty, but comically huge. Two spoonfuls sufficed. Otherwise, delightful flavors, great vibes, and a lovely end to the night.

Wow, could I have had worse experience. If you’re visiting Mandalay Bay and need to ship something quickly, the on-site FedEx near the expo hall seems convenient—until you actually try to use it. My recent visit turned into a textbook case of poor communication, shifting quotes, and frustrating customer service that wasted time and eroded trust. I arrived needing to send a package and waited while Javier, the associate at the counter, finished with another customer. He weighed my item, asked for the destination zip code, and quoted me $18 for shipping plus a $15 handling fee. Pricey for a basic shipment, sure, but given the location, I accepted. He then spent an unexpectedly long time packaging the item while I watched the clock, already anxious about an upcoming commitment. Once everything was wrapped and back on the scale, the total jumped to $45.50—apparently due to “forgotten” fees. Annoyed but resigned after already investing half an hour, I agreed. I pulled out cash, only to learn Javier couldn’t take it and I’d have to pay at another register. At the second counter, an Assistant Manager finished with another customer, then re-entered all my details from scratch. After more waiting, he announced the total had climbed again—to $59.00. I was stunned. I explained the $45.50 quote I had already agreed to and asked why the price kept changing. Javier had disappeared to the back without so much as a thank-you or apology, and the manager had to go retrieve him. Together they offered vague explanations and additional fees that conveniently pushed the price to the highest number yet. When I asked to pay the amount I’d agreed to moments earlier, the manager said it wasn’t possible and refused to make it right. With no time left and needing the package out that day, I swallowed the cost. But the experience left me questioning whether I’ll use FedEx again—especially locations that layer on arbitrary handling charges and seem to rely on last-minute price changes. This was for three-day shipping, not overnight, and the process should have been straightforward. If the box doesn’t arrive as promised, it will be the final straw. Hidden fees, inconsistent quoting, and dismissive service undermine customer confidence. At a minimum, quotes should be transparent and honored at checkout. Based on this encounter, I recommend avoiding this FedEx in Mandalay Bay. Convenience shouldn’t come at the expense of integrity.

Consistently the slowest service you will find at any Starbucks. This Ballantyne location has a busy drive-through and routinely fields five or six baristas behind the counter, yet waits drag on far beyond reasonable. The store sits in a high-volume area with no nearby alternative, leaving customers a captive audience to sluggish operations. Orders back up, mobile pickups stall, and the line barely moves. If you value your time, skip this exit: continue either direction on I‐485 to the next Starbucks, where the staff is markedly more competent and genuinely efficient.

Shared the classic creole seafood gumbo, shrimp basket, fried okra, and pecan pie with a friend. Hands down the best gumbo I’ve had—super hearty, finished every last drop. Shrimp and okra were fried fresh and delicious. Service was great. Good food all around; don’t miss this spot if you’re in the area.

Stopped in to grab a stick before a dinner presentation across the street and was pleasantly surprised. The shop features a clean, well-stocked walk-in humidor and a friendly owner who offered help without hovering. Pricing is moderate—certainly not the cheapest, but far from pricey. Selection was solid, though oddly the only CAOs on hand were the flavored varieties, surprising given the brand’s popularity. I left with a Padron 2000 maduro at a fair price and plan to return when I have time to linger.

On a recent trip to Charlotte, Lavecchia’s was our designated “fancy” stop, chosen on local word-of-mouth despite the chorus of mixed Yelp takes. The experience landed squarely in the middle: polished in some ways, puzzling in others. The room channels a glossy, retro vibe that reads less timeless than early-’90s Miami—think Miami Vice cosplay more than modern elegance. It’s memorable, if not exactly atmospheric. The house-style lobster showcased solid technique, neatly freed from its shell and cooked competently. It was enjoyable because, well, lobster is hard to dislike, but it never crossed into memorable. Mussels arrived with attractive presentation, yet the batch carried a faint gamey, fishy edge that dulled the appeal; a quick taste test in the kitchen might have caught it. Two dishes truly impressed. The namesake Lavecchia salad, modestly priced, was bright and balanced, its candied walnuts adding a welcome crunch and sweetness. And the oysters with tuna were a small revelation: six briny Blue Points on the half shell, each capped with a slice of tuna sashimi and a honey–rice wine–wasabi glaze. Eaten in one bite, they delivered a refreshing, layered burst—clean, subtly sweet, and gently spicy. Net result: Lavecchia’s is okay overall, but worth a visit for the oysters-and-tuna and that excellent house salad. Otherwise, set expectations to'solid but uneven'.
Delicious food and drinks, but service was slow. Waiters were rude despite the busy crowd. If they dislike serving guests, perhaps they should find new jobs.

Staff here are friendly, but that alone can’t earn another star. I ordered the chicken lunch special and it was a letdown from start to finish. The box was big, yet the portion inside was tiny—more like a kids’ meal. The chicken pieces were so small they added up to about one regular strip, which felt like a rip-off. The gravy had no flavor at all, and the chicken itself was dry, overly breaded, and tasted freezer-burned. I found myself wishing for ranch just to get through it. This will be my last time ordering the chicken here. If I return, it will be only for their soft-serve imitation ice cream when I’m in the mood for an artificial sugar rush. Value and quality weren’t there.

I ordered 20 wings here recently, and they were, without exaggeration, the worst I’ve ever eaten. Each wing was tiny, with barely a bite of meat, soggy instead of crispy, and disturbingly gray in tint. As a cash-strapped student, I forced myself to finish them, grateful only that I didn’t end up sick afterward—that’s the best thing I can say. The flavors were bland and oddly off, edging toward a “gone bad” taste that made them even less appetizing. Beyond quality, the price was shocking: on par with Buffalo Wild Wings, yet nowhere near the size, crunch, or freshness I expect for that cost. If I were the owner, I’d be embarrassed to serve wings like these. I won’t be returning, and I strongly advise others to steer clear. This felt like throwing money away for a subpar, questionable meal—an experience I wouldn’t wish on anyone.

A Jerky Lover’s Mixed Experience with Great Carne Seca and One Problematic Employee A self-described gringo and die-hard beef jerky fan, I’ve been buying carne seca from local carnicerías for years, and this shop quickly became my go-to. Their delivered carne seca is consistently flavorful, with a marinade that hits all the right notes—savory, slightly spicy, and addictive enough that I was picking up a pound to a pound and a half every week. For months, I went primarily to this store because, for the most part, the team behind the counter was welcoming and efficient. Unfortunately, one gentleman regularly undermined that otherwise positive experience. Each interaction with him felt like I didn’t belong there—curt replies, no eye contact, and a vibe of “why are you in this store?” that wore thin despite my best efforts to stay friendly. The breaking point came when he weighed out my usual and suddenly charged $28 a pound, up from the standard $20 I’d paid every visit. When I asked if the price had jumped eight dollars in three days, he simply said yes, offering no context or explanation. Curious, I noted the manufacturer on the case and planned to follow up, but first I returned when he wasn’t working. The price was right back to $20 a pound, and a different, much nicer employee confirmed there had been no increase. That inconsistency, coupled with the poor service from one person, was enough for me to move my weekly jerky runs to other carnicerías that appreciate their customers and charge consistently. I’m leaving two stars rather than one because the rest of the staff has been great and the product itself is excellent. Still, one bad apple can spoil the barrel, and it’s hard to justify loyalty when a single employee makes you feel unwelcome and plays games with the price. Consistency and respect matter as much as flavor, and I’ll happily spend my money where both are guaranteed.

Me and my wife (both chefs) stopped in for a date night. We were craving something different and definitely not a chain, and this locally owned, family-run spot delivered. We kicked things off with fried pickles—my wife is a diehard pickle fan yet had never tried them fried—and they were an outstanding start: crisp, tangy, and addictive. For her entree, she went with the muffaletta and Cajun chips. The chips were thick-cut (a rare treat) and perfectly seasoned, while the sandwich itself was packed with quality meats and a stellar olive mix I could happily eat on just about anything. I ordered the two-meat plate with alligator and shrimp. The alligator had solid flavor, though it leaned a bit chewy; the shrimp, however, were spot-on—lightly breaded and cooked to perfection. Service was equally impressive: friendly, knowledgeable staff who took the time to walk us through all the sauces and made us feel welcome. This is exactly the kind of place we love supporting, and we’re already spreading the word. With thoughtful touches and bold flavors, it made for a memorable, relaxed date night indeed.

Not terrible, but not up to par either. The beer selection is the clear highlight, with plenty to explore—oddly including Guinness on tap but not Bass. That omission showed when a black-and-tan attempt missed the mark. Starters were passable, and the namesake tap haus salad fell flat and bland. We split the daily special, but staff substituted a semi-charred steak without checking, explaining the fish had sold out—unhelpful for my vegetarian wife. The steak itself was just okay and not something I’d choose; this isn’t Durrant’s. Sides arrived mostly cold and underseasoned. Friendly intentions aside, execution in the kitchen lags behind the bar. The robust draft list keeps the place afloat, but the food program needs serious attention.

Spectacle Without Heart: Britney Spears Live Review As a longtime fan, I went in hopeful for a night that married spectacle with intimacy. Production values were top-notch, and the dancers were electrifying, but Britney often seemed disengaged, rushing from number to number with little eye contact or meaningful banter. She covered the stage to give different sections a glimpse, yet sightlines favored the center; from off-center seats, whole sequences felt incomplete. The pit looked like the best way to be immersed, but pricing is prohibitive. I had to stand for most of the show just to catch the choreography. Vocals were largely prerecorded—about 80% appeared lip-synced—undercutting the immediacy you expect from a concert. A moment meant to spotlight a fan onstage felt awkward and hurried, more box-check than genuine connection. The fix seems simple: trim five songs, add breathing room, talk to the audience, share stories behind the hits, and maybe incorporate an intimate unplugged interlude. The production is undeniably polished, but polish without presence can feel hollow. In the end, it was a dazzling show—lights, costumes, dancers firing on all cylinders—yet a disappointing concert in terms of live musical experience and artist-audience rapport. Still, seeing an icon in person carries its own thrill, and for that alone it felt like a once-in-a-lifetime moment. Fans seeking spectacle will leave satisfied; those craving heart may walk away wanting more. I left impressed by scale, but yearning for connection and live vocals.

This place has the best gelato that I’ve ever had. I’m no expert, but these flavors burst with intensity and clarity. The pear tastes more pear-like than the ripest fruit—bright, refreshing, and never cloying. Not every flavor hit my palate, yet the staff happily offers generous samples until you find the ones that blow you away. The texture is silky, sweetness balanced, and the range—from fruit-forward to decadent—keeps every scoop exciting. Friendly service, fair prices, and the lively market setting seal the deal. An absolute must-eat in Montreal’s Jean Talon Market. I’ll be back soon.

My husband and I try to have one or two nice dinners every time we visit Vegas, but I will never come back to this restaurant. The service was abysmal: our waiter kept disappearing, and it took over 30 minutes just to place an appetizer order. Sensing our frustration, the chef sent complimentary fries, but the gesture couldn’t salvage the experience. Our meals took forever to arrive and were unimpressive when they finally did. The waiter remained curt and rude throughout, compounding the disappointment. For the quality and service, the prices are inflated. I don’t understand how this place has four stars.

Pretty much as expected for airport dining, Philips and "lobster" don’t mix. I ordered an entrée salad and opted to add the "lobster" on top. There was some lobster, but it tasted like it had been microwaved, and there were odd bits of meat that seemed more like crab. Not appetizing, so I left most of it. The salad itself was generous, fresh, and satisfying, though, which redeemed the meal. My server was pleasant and attentive, but the constant upselling made me uncomfortable. For a quick airport bite, stick to the basics here. Next time, I’ll skip the "lobster" and just enjoy the salad.
The double stack burger dazzled with juicy layers and perfect balance, while the black and white milkshake was creamy bliss. Better than Five Guys/In-N-Out. Must-try.

On my second visit, the irony struck: a place called “Hand Wash” running assembly-line washers. It’s not truly hand washed; only the drying and detailing—done rather sloppily—are by hand. To their credit, a tech did remove what I thought was a permanent black rubber mark on my door, so there’s some hand effort. Still, the overall experience felt impersonal and rushed. With my Groupon now finished, I don’t see myself returning.

o sole mio..... o sole mio..... This chain restaurant delivers passable fare but leaves no impression. I left unable to recall my meal or drink—telling, perhaps, of its generic menu and forgettable flavors. Service didn’t help: the hostess seemed grumpy, visibly annoyed when our party added one person, despite a nearly empty dining room. Nothing was terrible, yet nothing stood out. If you want an unremarkable, utilitarian meal, it will do; if you seek warmth or character, look elsewhere.

A Disappointing Visit to Minera in Madison Minera promises a broad array of Indian fare, but my recent visit left me more frustrated than fulfilled. In an age when diners research and reserve online, the absence of a working website was the first red flag. Unfortunately, most aspects of the experience—from buffet execution to service—reinforced that uneasy first impression. The lunch buffet felt uninspired, with a spread that seemed strikingly similar to a competitor’s, down to the placement of dishes. Regardless of its source of inspiration, the selection lacked originality and the flavors were forgettable. Dinner didn’t fare better: the food was serviceable at best, never rising above average, and certainly not the kind of cooking you go out of your way for. The space itself is cramped. Four-top tables are better suited for two, and when the buffet line forms, the dining room devolves into congestion and confusion. Ambience details felt overlooked—some two-person dinner tables lacked tablecloths altogether—giving the room a makeshift feel rather than a warm, intentional one. Service was the most troubling issue. Staff seemed unsure of table assignments and ticket flow, leading to mix-ups and awkward moments as dishes arrived at the wrong tables. On the plus side, the kitchen’s turnaround time was quick; when orders did go through, food reached the table promptly. But speed can’t compensate for disorganization. Given Minera’s specialization in South Indian cuisine, we centered our meal on dosas. They arrived without the traditional accompaniments—sambar and chutneys—and we had to request them separately. When they did come, the sides tasted stale, and the sambar had a noticeably gritty texture. A mistaken order compounded the disappointment: a Rava Masala Dosa became an Onion Rava Dosa, and instead of remaking it, the kitchen sent out a small bowl of masala on the side. That shortcut felt careless and undercut the dish. Details like serving appetizers in small Corelle side dishes further diminished the experience. While there’s nothing inherently wrong with simple tableware, the presentation read as cost-cutting rather than casual charm. Minera’s menu ambitiously spans many regional styles, but that breadth appears to dilute execution. A tighter focus on the kitchen’s strengths—paired with staff training, clearer ticket management, improved presentation, and a more thoughtfully curated buffet—could transform the experience. For now, despite the quick kitchen, the combination of cramped quarters, lackluster flavors, and disorganized service makes Minera hard to recommend.

Our party of four enjoyed an outstanding lunch. Three chose cooked salmon, one savored tender lamb; every bite was to die for. The $22 table d'hote - appetizer, main, and dessert - felt like a bargain for such quality. Service was impeccable, with attentive, knowledgeable waiters who elevated the experience. We left delighted, planning our return soon, bringing friends.

We finally caught the show at Mandalay Bay, and the performers were fantastic. I loved the dancing and acrobatics—classic Cirque du Soleil energy with something happening throughout. My husband was a bit disappointed there weren’t live vocalists, but this isn’t a Broadway musical or Jersey Boys; it’s a spectacle driven by movement and visuals. Go in expecting choreography and aerial artistry rather than sung numbers, and you’ll have a great time.

Don't bring your vegetarian friends here! They'll be insulted! Carnivores, rejoice: this spot is a messy, meaty playground. The beef ribs are cartoonishly huge, more Flintstone than fine dining—lots of bone, not tons of meat, but plenty of sticky-finger fun, hence the paper towel rolls on every table. The menu piles it on: pulled pork sandwiches, BBQ chicken, sausages, burgers, pork ribs, beef ribs, chili, fries, and mac ’n’ cheese. You can absolutely stuff yourself silly. Having lived in the States, I won’t pretend it rivals the hallowed smokepits of Tennessee, Texas, or Kansas; the bark, smoke ring, and low-and-slow finesse aren’t quite there. Still, when a barbecue craving hits, Bofinger scratches the itch reliably, with hearty portions, straightforward flavors, and an unapologetic devotion to meat-first indulgence.

Within Champaign, Ambar definitely has the largest selection of dishes Ambar’s well-priced buffet is a standout, with staples like aloo mutter and chicken tikka masala that are consistently excellent. You’ll almost always find savory chicken curry and smoky tandoori chicken, alongside fresh rice and warm naan. Desserts delight: sheera is amaaazing, gulab jamun is comforting, and you can order kulfi or rasmalai—both are outstanding. Owned by a kind Punjabi family, Ambar combines hospitality, convenience, and a cozy ambience into a mouth-watering experience that keeps me coming back. For variety, value, and flavor, it’s one of Champaign’s best dining establishments.

Extremely noisy environment but should be expected from a family location. The noise level was high, as expected for families. Our visit was marred by an hour-long wait for our food. One of the worst feelings is watching tables seated after you get served first; we later learned our ticket was “lost” in the window. The staff comped our drinks—one mimosa and two orange juices—which was appreciated, and our server was kind and tried to salvage the experience. Still, after an hour, the food was subpar and we were exhausted. Two stars, primarily for the server’s effort. Next time, we’ll choose The Cracked Egg down the road—10/10 times.

My son visited over Christmas and decided to get a haircut, finding a $20 deal on Groupon. Unfortunately, it was a disappointing experience from start to finish. The cut looked virtually unchanged when he walked out, and I had to trim it again at home. He’ll now need another appointment when he’s back in Texas to fix it properly. What made it worse was that the stylist openly said she had bronchitis, repeatedly leaving and returning during the service. For a business that serves people, allowing staff to work while clearly sick is unacceptable. The regular price was listed as $40, but even at $20 with the coupon, it felt like a complete waste. Honestly, I wouldn’t have paid forty cents, let alone twenty. We won’t be returning and wouldn’t recommend this place.

Drawn by the promise of a dedicated Latin/Salsa night, I arrived ready to dance. The evening started promisingly: about half a dozen Latin tracks, including a single salsa cut, a few merengue tunes, and some reggaeton. Then the vibe unraveled. As audience requests crept in, the set veered sharply from the advertised theme, culminating in mainstream pop like "#Selfie." The floor thinned, likely because patrons expecting Latin rhythms felt misled. I even slipped the DJ a note reminding them of the night's theme. For the brief moments when the music aligned, it was fun. But unless management enforces the format and curates requests, I probably won't return anytime soon.

From torn upholstery and indifferent service to overpriced drinks, cramped seating, and an incessant din, this venue disappoints at every turn. Comfort is nonexistent, value is dubious, and hospitality absent. I searched for a silver lining and found only one: the glassware appeared clean. Skip it.

Even with a 25% off coupon, this meal felt like a miss—especially in Las Vegas, where every bite should feel special on a quick two-day trip. At best, it was mediocre; at worst, it squandered precious time and appetite. I ordered a club-style sandwich with fries and a bowl of French onion soup. The soup was the biggest letdown: sweeter than dessert, missing the savory backbone and cheesy comfort that define the classic. Imagine French onion soup stripped of salt and depth, then dusted with sugar. The fries arrived cold, despite my sandwich appearing promptly from the open kitchen. If the plate didn’t linger, the only explanation is an old batch of fries tossed on at the last minute. Service was decent—our waiter was friendly and attentive—but hospitality can’t overcome fundamental flaws on the plate. I sat inside because the outdoor area had a longer wait; given the setting in the Venetian’s central thoroughfare, the “outside” ambience probably delivers a livelier experience, but it wouldn’t have rescued the food. With several other restaurants steps away in the same square, I won’t be returning. In Vegas, mediocrity is more than disappointing—it’s a missed opportunity. Save your time and appetite for somewhere else.

Even when I was a Fresher I kinda hated the idea of this. Fresher’s Week markets itself as organized fun, but it often feels like forced mingling and speed-friendship powered by alcohol. I’ve never liked “let’s get to know each other” outings, and I don’t really date, so the scene—meeting drunk people, forgetting them by morning, swapping saliva—never appealed. Potterrow, the hub of it all, tends to reek of snakebite and vomit at the best of times; during Fresher’s Week, the stench seems to bloom. The lineup is a greatest hits of the venue’s blandest events you’ll see all year—The Big Cheese included—wrapped in sleaze and second-hand embarrassment. Pack thousands of 18-year-olds into a tight 500-metre square, and you get predictable chaos: bravado, bad decisions, and theatrics no one wants to remember. If you prefer authenticity over orchestrated revelry, skip the circus and find your own rhythm on campus. If not, dive in; it might be your thing. Your mileage may vary.

I'm disappointed. I wanted to love this place: the English pub décor and cozy lounge are genuinely beautiful, and the vibe on arrival is spot‐on. Unfortunately, the kitchen and service undermine everything the space promises. Across two visits I tried the wings, Firkin burger, Irish nachos, and mac & cheese with ham. Only the wings were decent. The namesake burger arrived undercooked and bland, a letdown for the item that should be the house flagship. Irish nachos tasted plain and felt microwaved rather than freshly prepared. The mac & cheese was, frankly, one of the worst dishes I’ve had—not just in Vegas, but anywhere—gummy, flavorless, and deeply disappointing. Operationally, the reliance on heat lamps shows: texture and temperature suffer. Staff, aside from Kimberly—who was attentive and kind even though she wasn’t our server—seemed uninterested in guests. On the bar side, the beer list aims for craft, and several options were above average, but the DFH 60 Minute tasted old and several listed beers were unavailable. I’ve been to many bars and pubs, and I won’t be returning here. Kimberly and the attempt at craft beer barely earned an extra star this experience doesn’t deserve.

We booked the basic room at PH and were happy with the price paid given the hotel was rated 4 stars. Upon arrival, we waited in line about an hour to check in. I would think perhaps adding one or two more people to assist with the process would make the customers first experience with PH much more positive. The front desk person told us they didn't have any no smoking rooms available even though we had reserved one. They could upgrade us for $20 more per day. What a gimmick! We heard them use the same technique on several others as we were waiting in line. Not wanting a smoking room, we paid the extra $60 plus tax for three nights. At this price point, we would have considered other hotels. Next, we asked the check-in person if we could have a quiet room since I am a light sleeper. She said,'I have assigned you a nice, quiet room on the 30th floor.' Well, our quiet room shared a wall with two elevators. The constant sound of the elevators was extremely loud in our room, so thanks for the nice, quiet room! The room was okay, but rooms at the Luxor Towers, Treasure Island, Mirage, and obviously, Bellagio are all larger and nicer. For about the same price, next visit I would opt for Treasure Island, Luxor, MGM or Monte Carlo!

This is hands down the worst company I have ever dealt with. I’ve called four Phoenix locations and not one answered. On the rare occasion someone picks up, they’re rude and seem unhelpful. Putting a dog on the line might be less frustrating. Our bill jumped from $45 to $110 despite having only HBO with basic cable and no internet. I’d switch to dish or DirecTV, but my apartment doesn’t face the right direction for installation. The service is abysmal, the support nonexistent, and the pricing borderline predatory. I’m convinced a cable company run out of a cardboard box could do better. Service quality simply isn’t there. Save yourself the headache and stay away from this company.

This is an authentic Mexican taco stand operating out of an immobile truck. Everything is cooked to order and tastes great. The spicy green salsa is a standout. Quesadillas are excellent. Tacos cost $1.75, and quesadillas run about $5–$6—great value overall for locals.

Looking for a wallet-friendly Thai spot for date night? Noodlehead in Pittsburgh delivers. On a recent Friday, we slipped into its trendy, bustling space and kept things simple: Street Noodle #1 for me, Pad Thai for my date. Both plates arrived quickly and impressed with clean, satisfying flavors and well-balanced heat, especially considering the modest prices. Noodlehead’s menu leans concise—don’t expect the breadth you’ll find at Thai Cuisine in Bloomfield or Nicky’s Thai Kitchen on the North Side—but what they do offer is executed with confidence. Value is the headline. Our bill stayed strikingly low, making it easy to sample and share. Do note a couple of quirks: it’s cash-only, so plan ahead unless you want an impromptu ATM run, and it’s BYOB, with a refreshingly small corkage of 50 cents per person. Pairing a favorite bottle with spicy noodles is part of the charm. If you’re chasing the absolute pinnacle of Thai dining in the area, the aforementioned spots may edge Noodlehead—at a higher price point. For a relaxed, affordable outing with lively vibes and tasty food, Noodlehead is a win and a smart choice for a cheap date night.

The positives: atmosphere was comfortable and very nice. Mushroom fries were ah- mazing! We loved the comfortable, inviting vibe, and the mushroom fries were truly amazing. Unfortunately, the rest of the night was a letdown. A quoted 30-minute wait stretched to 65 minutes, with “your table is being set up” repeated five times. Once seated, we waited 1 hour and 45 minutes for our meals, which arrived lukewarm. Throughout, different staffers told us our food was “coming next”—a recurring refrain. Communication felt hollow, with assurances repeated but no follow-through. Service felt unprofessional, with servers arguing in front of our table. The low point: a waiter accidentally poured vinegar down a friend’s back, followed by no apology—just a wet towel. In total, the visit consumed about three hours. With slow, inconsistent service overshadowing a comfortable atmosphere and one standout dish, we won’t be back.

Roadrunner Pharmacy makes refills effortless. Exceptional customer service and speedy delivery every time. My cat, Libra, loves the surprise toy included monthly, such a thoughtful touch. Highly recommend! Thank you!

Love this place. HUGE and tons of selection! Snacks, drinks, gifts, furniture, dish wear, candles, lotions, etc. Found the Japanese marble sodas. =) Huge store with an amazing selection—snacks, drinks, gifts, furniture, dishware, candles, lotions, and more. Thrilled to find Japanese marble sodas; a shopping destination!

Very Disappointed! As neighborhood residents, we were eager to welcome this spot, especially given its promise of a wine bar within walking distance. Unfortunately, the experience fell flat. Despite the branding, the ambience and menu skew far more beer-and-burger joint than true wine bar—think Postino or Bombero’s for comparison. We ordered the “garage” meat and cheese plate, and what arrived looked like refrigerator leftovers: scant slices of meat, meager nubs of cheese, and just two tiny pieces of crostini. Portioning was inadequate for even one person, let alone sharing. With two glasses of wine and the board, our tab hit roughly $40, leaving us feeling shortchanged. We left and headed down the street to Postino, where the antipasti board reminded us what thoughtful curation, quality, and value can look like. If this venue aims to compete as a wine destination, the kitchen and management need to recalibrate—upgrade ingredients, rethink portions, and study the local benchmarks. Until then, it’s not a place we’ll return to or recommend.

Jana’s turns out some of the best baked goods in town, the sort that make you plan your day around a pastry run. The only drawback is their limited, occasionally shifting hours; I rarely catch them after work, so call ahead if you’re coming from afar. One of Jana’s underappreciated strengths is authenticity. Cheesecake didn’t start in New York—it came from Eastern Europe, and their version honors that heritage with traditional farmer’s cheese, just like grandma Sofia’s recipe. On a recent lucky visit, I snagged a makowiec, the poppy seed–filled cake. It was exceptional: tender crumb, fragrant filling, and balanced sweetness. Even with the scheduling quirks, Jana’s is worth the effort. I wish they stayed open later.

Yummy but $$ This frozen yogurt spot stands out—rich, creamy, and consistently delicious. I’m addicted, especially to the pistachio flavor. However, some downsides: the brownies used to be great but now taste oddly off, and the generous coupons (BOGO, half-off) have disappeared. With prices feeling steep and fewer deals, it’s harder to justify frequent visits, though the yogurt itself remains excellent.

There was a time when Carson's in Chicago served the best ribs in the country. Now I have discovered Dillons Grand. Dillons Grand delivers ribs that are tender, meaty, and flavorful, with a St. Louis–style sauce that has just enough bite to keep things interesting. The sides shine too: rich beans and creamy mac and cheese that beg for repeat visits. Expect a loud, lively room rather than white tablecloths—it’s barbecue, not fine dining—and enjoy the window views of the golf course and pond. Service, however, lagged. Beer glasses arrived unchilled, staff didn’t take time with the elderly guests at our table, and interactions felt impersonal. The first bite of ribs nearly erased those missteps, but not entirely. On balance, Dillons Grand earns a solid four stars—phenomenal food with room to improve service.

Airport dining often feels like a compromise—pre-made, pricey, and forgettable—but this breakfast stop offered a few pleasant surprises. My fruit-and-yogurt plate came with mostly ripe fruit, a rarity in travel hubs, and a generously sized bowl of yogurt that bordered on too much to finish. My husband’s breakfast burrito, a basic build of tortilla, eggs, sour cream, salsa, and potatoes on the side, tasted better than expected; add-ons for cheese or meat cost extra, which quickly bumps up the bill. Portions overall were ample and flavors solid for an airport venue. The biggest disappointment was the beverage list: no decaf options at all, despite requests for tea, hot chocolate, or decaf coffee—the server said they had none. Service was brisk, if not especially flexible. If you’re looking for a filling, reasonably tasty meal before a flight, this is serviceable, but be prepared for airport-level pricing and limited drink choices.
Leticia’s is a must-visit: Saturday karaoke from 8:30 to close, amazing fried ice cream, and luscious homemade caramel. Fun, delicious, welcoming.

Hands down the best piercing studio in Arizona. The staff is incredibly knowledgeable and welcoming, guiding you through options with clear, thorough information so you can make a confident, informed choice. If anything goes awry, they’re responsive and supportive, helping you troubleshoot. Kat has been exceptionally helpful to me, but every piercer I’ve met inspires trust. No matter who you see, you’ll be in excellent hands.

This is now our favorite Peruvian restaurant. The anticuchos were the best we've ever had, and the parihuela seafood soup was divine. My wife loved the Salteado Vegetariano—an unexpected delight. We brought our own wine; a modest $5 corkage felt fair. We skipped dessert, saving room for next time. Warm service and vibrant flavors—don’t miss this gem; truly memorable.

Three Weeks to Fix a Microwave: A Masterclass in Poor Communication My built-in microwave/oven stopped heating on 9/17. I scheduled service and was told on 9/18 that someone would arrive on 9/19 between 1 and 5. No one showed. When I called, the representative was curt and repeatedly insisted I was wrong and that my appointment was actually for 9/20 between 1 and 5. On 9/20 at about 4 pm, the technician arrived. When I explained the unit wasn’t heating and mentioned an unusual noise, I was told not to speak while he assessed the appliance. After a brief look, he said two parts were needed, neither in stock, and they would be ordered. I was instructed not to ask questions and to call the number on a green card for anything further. Not exactly reassuring. On 9/24, I received an email saying the parts had been delivered and left at the front door—though it wasn’t clear whose door. Calls to clarify went unanswered and unreturned. My warranty company (AHS) confirmed only one part had arrived; the second came on 9/29. We scheduled installation for 10/2, 1–5. At 2 pm on 10/2, I was told one of the parts had arrived broken and needed to be reordered. More delays, more calls, and still little accountability. On 10/6, I was told that 10/7 would finally be the day. To their credit, the technician did arrive on 10/7 and the unit was repaired—nearly three weeks after the initial breakdown. This experience was defined by no-shows, shifting timelines, unanswered calls, vague notifications, and, most troubling, a dismissive attitude toward the customer. Being told not to speak in my own home was outrageous. The appliance is fixed, but the process was exhausting. This company needs major improvements in communication, accountability, and basic respect. Based on this experience, I cannot recommend them.

I've been here twice After two visits, I’m confident this spot isn’t worth the time. The first time, we were seated in a back booth away from the bar and were immediately put off by fruit flies swarming the area—one even landed in my friend’s drink. Service dragged from the start. My wife ordered a wedge salad without onions, but it arrived with onions anyway. She also tried a featured cocktail and had to send it back because it was overloaded with sour mix. My friend’s drink was so poorly made he ended up diluting it with his sweet tea just to make it palatable. Hoping the first visit was a fluke, we returned. Unfortunately, the service was even slower, and the same salad mistake happened again: “no onions” apparently didn’t register. Across both visits, the food and cocktails lacked any standout qualities, and basic execution was inconsistent. When simple requests aren’t honored and drinks are bungled, it’s hard to justify a third chance. Honestly, I’d rather head to the TGI Fridays or Applebee’s across the street than be disappointed here again.

One of my favorite things to do is consignment shop. On a dreary day I decided to look up a few local shops to hit up and my finale trip was to Hey Betty's. Hey Betty’s is a compact consignment boutique that makes smart use of its small footprint. The space is tidy and well curated, avoiding the garage-sale clutter common in secondhand shops. Men’s selections are minimal, but vintage aficionados will find eye-catching hat boxes, distinctive jewelry, and a sense of discovery. Unfortunately, the experience is marred by poor customer service. On my visit, the woman at the counter—presumably the owner—was disengaged and unwelcoming. We initiated the greeting; she stayed absorbed in a magazine, offering no guidance or warmth. Interaction only happened when we pressed for it, and even then, it lacked enthusiasm. For shoppers who value connection and a bit of storytelling with their vintage finds, this indifference is disappointing. Great consignment shopping blends treasure hunting with hospitable guidance. When staff don’t acknowledge customers, it dampens the hunt and makes a return visit unlikely. I’d still point vintage lovers to Hey Betty’s for its appealing inventory and organized presentation. But if attentive service and a friendly atmosphere are priorities, there are better options. In short: strong selection, weak service—worth a look for the goods, not for the experience.

Consistently excellent, G & P delivers across the board. The standout is the BBQ chicken pizza on lavash—smoky, tender, and perfectly crisp. Prices are reasonable, making it a go-to for our office. We love that call-in to-go orders are ready in 10–15 minutes, leaving plenty of lunch-hour breathing room. It’s a healthy, satisfying option without the sticker shock. If you want reliable flavor, speed, and value, you can’t go wrong with their menu.

Food was delicious, service (Srdjan) was atrocious. After he brought the food, he ignored us for 40 minutes. No water refills, no plate clearing, no box, no check until we were finally able to flag him down. I won't go back; too bad, because the calamari was the best I've had! Despite outstanding calamari—the best I’ve had—the experience was marred by atrocious service from Srdjan. After dropping our meals, he vanished for roughly 40 minutes: no water refills, no plates cleared, no to-go box, and no check until we flagged him down. Great kitchen, unacceptable service. Regretfully, we won’t return ever again.

Two stars due to finding a hair in my coleslaw. Our waitress wore her hair loose and kept touching it, which likely caused the issue. For a food service environment, tied-back hair or a bun should be mandatory. On the plus side, the food tasted good, though the kitchen had run out of a couple items we requested. Service was uneven; my father-in-law had to ask for a refill, but he was satisfied with his meal overall. If we return, I hope management enforces stricter hygiene rules to prevent incidents like this.

We’ve visited this fro-yo spot a few times since it opened, and it’s consistently clean, bright, and rarely crowded—definitely a plus. Unfortunately, this visit missed the mark. More than half of the available flavors skewed fruity, which isn’t our preference, leaving non-fruity options surprisingly limited. Toppings and ambiance were fine, but the flavor balance felt off and dampened the experience. With several similar shops nearby, we’ll likely call ahead next time to check flavor lineups before committing. When the selection aligns with our tastes, this location shines; otherwise, it’s a bit of a letdown.

Two of my favorite words are happy hour, and Todd English P.U.B. in Las Vegas doubles down on them with two sessions daily: 3–6 pm and 10 pm–midnight. On our first evening in town, my husband and I slid into two bar stools for the afternoon stretch. After a brief wait, an exceptionally friendly bartender took care of us, guiding us through an impressive beer list that includes Double Jack, one of my personal favorites. The vibe was upbeat, the pours generous, and the value unmistakable. We liked it so much that we returned for the late-night happy hour on Saturday with two friends. The crowd had thinned, making four seats at the bar easy to snag, and service was even snappier. Our friends jumped into the “7 Second Challenge”—chug a pint in seven seconds or less—and nailed it, earning their first drinks free. It’s a playful touch that suits the bar’s lively personality. Food-wise, I sampled the grilled cheese with brie and bacon. While the idea sounded indulgent, the execution leaned too heavily on the bacon, overwhelming the sandwich and leaving the brie underrepresented. I wouldn’t order that particular item again, but the menu holds enough allure that I’d happily try other dishes. Ultimately, Todd English P.U.B. delivers what great happy hours should: quality drinks, welcoming service, and standout deals. I’ll be back on my next Vegas trip for those twice-a-day specials. For current promotions, check their Facebook page for the latest.

Food was not a home run. It was just so so. Actually kind of disappointed. Service was terrible. In a certain way, it felt like a fast food joint. Never coming back again Disappointed by mediocre food and abysmal service. Dishes arrived lukewarm, flavors uninspired, and chaotic vibe felt like a fast-food joint. Prices didn’t match quality. Ambiance lacked warmth. Not worth the trip; won’t return.

This is not the quality that I expected to come of GameWorks. I purchased an all-day pass, but the card failed to read and had to be replaced. The Groupon 24-hour unlimited play capped at about 14 hours. Staff were young and seemed inexperienced with customer service. Many games malfunctioned, with error messages on multiple machines during my three visits. Overall, a disappointing experience that undermines the fun. Proceed with caution until GameWorks improves reliability and honors its advertised offers.

You will have a much better time throwing a couple hundred of your hard earned dollars into a trash bucket on the front porch, dousing it in lighter fluid, and lighting it on fire than eating here! The net result is the same and it will be warmer! This restaurant announces its intentions early with a credit-card-required reservation policy and the threat of a no-show charge. In theory, that signals a high-demand dining room carefully managing seats. In practice, we arrived to a freezing, nearly empty space where no one appeared to be clamoring for our table. The chill wasn’t just atmospheric; it seeped into the entire experience. Service set the tone: brisk, stern, and conspicuously joyless. Whether it was the unbearable cold, a first-day learning curve, or management’s mandate to keep things austere, our server’s demeanor made the evening feel transactional at best. There was no warmth, no playfulness, no hospitality—just orders taken and plates dropped. You will order. You will eat. You will die. Not necessarily in that order. The food, meanwhile, landed firmly in the “fine, I guess” category—and arrived cold, which hardly helped. Portions were meager for the price, and the bill soared past what the execution justified. Yes, some diners will proclaim their steak “cooked to perfection,” but achieving a competent sear and doneness isn’t the pinnacle of culinary achievement. When you’re charging premium Vegas prices, hot plates, generous portions, and balanced seasoning are baseline expectations. Beyond the plates, the misalignment is philosophical. Tucked inside Planet Hollywood on the Strip, this place carries a whimsical name yet behaves as if it’s a solemn temple of gastronomy. The seriousness feels unearned, and the pretentious veneer mistakes austerity for excellence. In a city brimming with memorable meals and genuine hospitality, this experience was cold—literally and figuratively—overpriced, under-portioned, and curiously self-important. If you value comfort, warmth, and a sense that your money bought something more than posture, stroll elsewhere. You’ll find better food, better service, and far better value without needing a lighter.

Not that I have ridiculously high expectations for a laundry mat but I do expect: Parktowne misses the basics. On several visits, the place reeks of pot, the last thing you want when you’re trying to de-odorize clothes. Safety is another concern; doing laundry at night feels uneasy, and the absence of even a part-time attendant doesn’t help. In a city that needs jobs, staffing this space seems like an obvious fix. Most importantly, the machines don’t deliver. Despite using the correct amount of detergent and paying a premium for washers and dryers, loads often come out only half-clean. For a routine chore that’s already a hassle, Parktowne adds frustration instead of convenience. I wish I had laundry in my building, because this spot just isn’t cutting it.

I always drive by this place and decided to see what it's all about. I finally stopped by after driving by countless times and hit the holiday rush. There were fewer than ten people, yet I waited about ten minutes to pay for a single loaf. Having worked retail, it’s frustrating to watch slow, disorganized checkout; quick transactions matter, especially for bread. If I’d waited longer, I might have walked out. That said, the sourdough redeemed the experience: crackling crust, chewy interior, and it stayed fresh for days. On product alone, I’d gladly return and make this my go‐to for bread. Service, though, needs attention. Streamlined cashiering or an express lane would transform the visit. Even a simple pre-order pickup option would help. I’ll try again off‐peak—the baking is excellent. Here’s hoping management tightens checkout efficiency—the quality deserves better.

First visit exceeded expectations. Our waitress was fantastic, food delicious, and prices surprisingly affordable. Friendly service, tasty dishes, unbeatable value—highly recommended. Must-try spot we’ll revisit.

I really like The Potting Shed—quirky, rustic, and wholeheartedly committed to its shed theme. The atmosphere feels cozy and characterful, but what truly shines is the staff. Even when the place was busy and the till went down—a stressful, inconvenient blip—they remained lovely, calm, and helpful. Extra points for customer service. Pricing gets a reputation for being steep, yet the value is there: lunch for £5, or coffee and a generous slice of cake for £3. Choices were a bit limited, but when it’s between chocolate and red velvet, that’s a sweet dilemma.

Well I just moved back to Vegas following a stint in food truck-crazed Los Angeles, so I was kinda excited to see the trucks catching on in LV. I finally got off my lazy butt and tracked down the Slider Truck this week - turns out they were right down the street from my house - sweet! With LA’s food truck scene as a benchmark, I rolled up with high hopes. My husband and I reached the meetup spot around 6:20, just twenty minutes after they opened, and found a modest line of about ten people. “No big deal,” we thought; we’ve patiently queued for Philly steaks, Asian tacos, hot dogs, and barbecue from trucks before. What we didn’t expect was how long everything would take. It was a full 30 minutes before we even placed our order, followed by almost 15 minutes to receive our food. For sliders, that felt excessive. The sign says burgers are cooked to order, and that’s appreciated, but many fast-casual spots cook to order and manage far quicker throughput. With only a short line, the pace inside the truck was puzzling. When the food did arrive, the burgers and fries were solid—juicy, flavorful, and filling. The menu’s lineup of creative slider combinations is genuinely appealing, and the execution is respectable. On taste alone, I’d have landed at 2.5 stars; rounding down reflects the overall experience rather than the bites themselves. Price-wise, it’s fine, but given the setting—a parking lot, no seating or climate control—one might expect a bit more value or speed to justify the tab. Service is where expectations and reality diverged. People rave about the friendly vibe, and yes, the guy at the window offers a cheerful fist pound before you order. It’s a nice touch, but charm doesn’t make up for an extra 40 minutes of waiting when you’re hungry and the line is short. A smile is great; efficiency is better. Bottom line: If you’re craving a fast burger, Fatburger will get you fed sooner. If inventive toppings and variety are your priority, Bachi Burger, Grind, or Burger Bar each offer broader menus and comfortable seating. If price is the driver, In-N-Out undercuts the truck by more than half and delivers consistent speed. The Slider Truck is worth a try if you’re chasing the novelty of eating from a truck and don’t mind the wait. Just go in knowing you’re trading convenience and comfort for the experience—and plan accordingly.

We ended up here after The Steak House was closed, and it turned into the best “second choice” I’ve had in ages. The three of us ordered a feast and everything impressed. Even our pickiest eater was all-in. The pancit was springy and savory, the skewers smoky and satisfying, and the soft-shell crab was downright addictive. My short ribs were so tender a fork slid right through. Both the downstairs and upstairs bars hum with energy yet keep an intimate, date-friendly vibe. Service hiccup at first—our original server was awkward—but a switch to Jerry (or Jared) transformed the night. He was attentive, knowledgeable, and genuinely warm, delivering the best service of our trip. Great food, great ambiance, and hospitality that wins you over. I’d come back in a heartbeat.

Woohoo! This is the most amazing burger you will ever taste!! If you love character, this spot’s got it in spades: a cute, rugged log-cabin vibe like an old Western town, perfectly at home in Arizona’s Wild West spirit. It’s seriously rugged and worn, but warmly inviting. The burgers are charcoal-broiled right in front of you, and the smoky aroma is irresistible. Every bite brings craveable char and a juicy center. Sides are solid if not spectacular—the fries are good, and the onion rings land about the same. Value seals it: about twenty bucks covered two burgers, fries, onion rings, and a cold beer for my boo and me. Simple, satisfying, unforgettable. Go now.

I don't like writing bad reviews, but this place is the worst. The donuts are okay, but for the past month their latte machine has been “down.” How long does it take to fix an essential piece of equipment? For a large franchise, this is unacceptable and suggests poor management and no urgency. Coffee is expected. Until they repair it properly and communicate clearly, I’ll take my mornings—and my money—elsewhere.

I’ve visited this spot twice, both times for lunch, and it delivers a mixed bag. The setting is undeniably cute—trendy interiors and a patio that’s great for lingering—though the occasional waft of sewage along the patio was hard to ignore and puzzling for such a stylish venue. Sushi rolls were decent if unspectacular, the kind you enjoy in the moment but won’t crave later. Service, however, was the standout drawback: hostesses came off curt, and while our servers were pleasant, the pacing was glacial. I had nearly finished a bottle of sake before our food arrived, and the check took just as long. The menu feels overpriced for lunchtime, and the calamari appetizer was a miss. Instead of delicate tempura rings, we received hefty rectangular pieces, heavily battered and deep-fried—a preparation more reminiscent of a sports bar than a Japanese restaurant. It’s a contrast that undercuts the otherwise polished ambiance. Still, with good company and no tight schedule, the slow tempo felt tolerable, even relaxing. For diners on a clock, it could be a deal breaker. Overall, this place is okay: attractive setting, okay sushi, and inconsistent execution. I’ll likely return while I explore the Arizona sushi scene, but I’m still searching for a spot that truly impresses.

The food here is really great. Once our favorite Greek restaurant, this spot consistently served delicious food. Unfortunately, one dinner changed everything. At a nearby table, a patron was smoking hookah and drinking, growing increasingly loud and intoxicated. In full view of the dining room, she eventually vomited all over her table, then went to the restroom and continued. Whether it was the hookah, the alcohol, or both, the spectacle was impossible to ignore and ruined our meal. The staff didn’t resolve it, and the memory lingered. It’s been three years, and although we still miss the flavors and service, we haven’t been able to go back. We wish the ambiance were more controlled; a quieter, more hygienic environment matters. Sadly, the Maryland Parkway location is too far for us to consider as an alternative.

This place is great! I’ve visited on and off for 8–10 years, and the ribs are consistently tender and delicious. The combination meat sampler plate is a perfect introduction for first-timers. Prices run a bit high, but quality BBQ isn’t cheap when done right. I wish they offered coupons, though the daily specials help quite a bit. Overall.

Simple perfection: The Original delivers After reading the hype, I doubted a sandwich could be that memorable—then The Original proved me wrong. Toasted bread with the ideal crunch, a generous layer of divine horseradish cream, and balanced fillings that sing together. My husband ordered the club, which was fine but forgettable; we both agreed The Original easily stole the show. It was so good I found myself eating faster just to avoid sharing another bite. One star off for the mediocre club, but if you’re choosing, skip it and go straight for The Original. Pure, unfussy, craveable goodness, every single time.

title: The food was nothing to write home about, but the Breakfast Club is a conveniently located option for anyone attending a conference or staying at a hotel nearby. Service was quick and good. Unfortunately, my $7 Bloody Mary was too salty and too watery, and I left it unfinished. The $10 mushroom omelette tasted like standard diner fare, but I appreciated the use of shiitake and oyster mushrooms instead of basic button or cremini.

Hosting a milestone celebration at Lindo Michoacan proved nothing short of exceptional. From the moment the private room was booked to the final farewell, the team delivered a flawlessly coordinated 90th birthday party for a family matriarch.
