Great happy hour spot for casual drinks and bites. The baked goat cheese is outstanding, especially with their warm baguettes. Service stayed friendly and efficient despite our large group. Comfortable vibe, value, and a place I’m happy to add to my HH rotation. Definitely returning.

Our whole family are die hard CSI fans, so we wanted to see this exhibit. As longtime devotees of the show, we arrived hopeful that the CSI experience would let us flex our investigative muscles. Instead, it felt more like a small corner of a science museum geared toward very young visitors. The premise is compelling: choose one of three crime scenes, survey the evidence, and work through lab stations to crack the case. We picked Case 3, rumored to be the hardest, and dove in with notebooks ready, eager to apply observation and deduction. That enthusiasm evaporated quickly. After the initial walk-through of the crime scene, the very first station essentially listed every item you were supposed to notice, undercutting any sense of discovery. From there, the labs walk you through pre-digested findings. You don’t analyze materials so much as copy down what the exhibit spoon-feeds you. Rather than feeling like investigators, we felt like stenographers, dutifully recording obvious details already decided for us. The autopsy room continues this pattern: it clearly explains the cause of death, leaving no room for inference or independent thought. At the end, you input your “findings” to solve the case—findings you didn’t actually generate—and then you’re offered a $5 upsell for a CSI agent certificate. We declined, yet our kids later received emails with certificates attached, which raised eyebrows and had us double-checking our credit card statement just in case. The biggest disappointment was the length. Even if you take your time, the entire exhibit wraps in about 30 minutes. If visitors were allowed to work through all three cases, it could stretch closer to an hour and feel more substantial. Why access is limited to only one case remains puzzling, especially for fans who would relish more complexity and replay value. On the positive side, we didn’t pay full price. We used the 3-for-$54 deal at New York-New York (http://www.nynyhotelcasino.com/entertainment/entertainment_3for54.aspx), which brought our per-ticket cost down to $18. Bundling made the day worthwhile because the other attractions were far stronger. The Bodies Exhibit was genuinely amazing and worth full price; the Shark Reef was also very good. In hindsight, we would skip the CSI exhibit and choose the Titanic exhibit or simply ride the roller coaster. As a concept, a hands-on forensic experience is fantastic. In execution, this one assumes the intelligence of a first grader and overexplains to the point of condescension. For CSI fans hoping to think critically, follow leads, and piece together evidence, this exhibit is too shallow and too brief. Had we paid full price, we would have been genuinely upset.

I first stumbled upon AA Bakery while desperately searching for "lo por baang" for my mom. After a quick cry for help on Facebook, I was directed here. How did I not see this place sooner? AA Bakery offers a wide array of Asian-style pastries, breads, and cakes, and on first glance it’s an easy spot to like. The onion bread and custard buns are solid, fresh, and satisfying, but beyond that, the selection didn’t win me over. I picked up an assortment of wife cakes for my mom—nicely packaged, with far more flavors than the usual winter melon—but the texture missed the mark. Instead of that hallmark delicate flakiness, these were dense and a bit odd-tasting, which dulled the nostalgia I was hoping to gift. Service was efficient and friendly, and prices are fair. With so many stronger Asian bakeries around the valley, I don’t see myself becoming a regular. Still, if I’m nearby, I’d gladly swing in for their Hong Kong-style egg tarts.
Ate here yesterday; three fish tacos. Today I'm sick, likely food poisoning. Very disappointed—won't return. Beware the fish tacos here.

All other movie theaters have now been ruined for me! And here is why: After one visit to this luxury cinema, I’m ruined for regular theaters. The plush, solid leather recliners redefine comfort, making two-hour runtimes feel blissfully short. Prices are refreshingly reasonable—about $1.50 more than the usual multiplex—which makes the upgrade an easy yes. Concessions elevate the experience: beer, wine with generous pours, and gourmet sausages that beat standard popcorn fare. Programming is strong, too, with plenty of film choices and a screen perfectly scaled to the room, delivering crisp, immersive viewing. A few tips: reserve seats ahead; even booking a day in advance nearly left us without options. Arrive early, as concession lines can stretch. And be kind to the staff—hospitality is hard work, and a little grace goes a long way. Verdict: worth the hype every single time.

A Disappointing Encounter at Island Style: Communication and Courtesy Absent After years of patronage and introducing friends and relatives to Island Style, our most recent experience left us stunned and deeply disappointed. At 5:45 p.m., we called to confirm they would be open; posted hours are 10 a.m. to 9 p.m., but we were told they sometimes close early if business is slow. Russell, who works for the owner, Gina, assured us they were open and asked how many would be dining. We confirmed seven adults and one child for 7:00 p.m., and he said, “Sure, sure.” We arrived at 7:02 p.m. to a locked door and a CLOSED sign in the window. The interior was dark—lights off, no one inside. We knocked several times and even called twice, but there was no answer. With guests in tow, it was embarrassingly awkward to be left at the door without explanation, especially after confirming our arrival only an hour earlier. After waiting about ten minutes, we left and chose a reliable favorite that consistently delivers good food and respectful service. The next day, we called to share what happened. Russell’s response was shockingly rude and dismissive. He barked, “No can help..... No cook..... I no can cook so I had to close.” He added that the cook had to leave because her baby was sick and that he had to drive her because “she no drive.” Emergencies happen; anyone can understand that. But the lack of communication—no sign explaining the situation, no call back, no attempt to let us know after confirming our party—was unacceptable. When we suggested he could have left a note or notified us, he grew hostile: “Sista, you only making me mad.” There was no apology, no accountability, and no courtesy. We also asked whether Gina could step in; he dismissed that, saying she had her own restaurant to run. The attitude was clear: our plans and our business didn’t matter. That’s not how you run a customer-facing operation. We’ve supported Island Style and brought them new patrons. After this experience, we won’t be returning, and we’ll be telling others about the inconsiderate treatment and unreliable hours. Businesses thrive on trust and communication. If you promise to be open until 9 p.m. and confirm a 7 p.m. party, you owe your customers a minimum of respect—especially when emergencies arise. Courtesy costs nothing. Until management addresses staffing, communication, and basic customer service, we recommend choosing establishments that value their patrons and uphold their posted hours.

Horrible customer service I visited this alterations shop for the first time and was met with standoffish staff. When I returned to pick up my pants, I noticed the zipper was broken. I pointed it out, and they refused to repair the zipper or reimburse me for the fix. The pants were brand new, and there’s no way I would have walked out of the fitting room with the zipper down. It seemed clear the damage occurred in their shop. When I asked to be reimbursed for the tailoring, the owner argued with me for ten minutes. He said he could fix the zipper but, out of principle, would do nothing, and claimed he had many high-end clients and didn’t need my business. The lack of accountability and dismissive attitude were unacceptable. I left disappointed and frustrated. If you value respect and responsibility, consider taking your garments elsewhere. Truly unacceptable experience overall.

I really enjoyed our visit to this unique museum. We scored a better-than two-for-one Groupon deal, which made the outing an easy yes. Plan generously: I strongly recommend allowing at least four hours to take in the full experience—our three-hour visit wasn’t nearly enough to see and savor everything. Throughout, there are clever surprise exhibits that deliver a full-on atomic experience; I won’t spoil them here, because discovery is half the fun. You’ll even receive a special badge for the Area 51 exhibit, a neat little keepsake. Unfortunately, that particular gallery felt amateurish and proved disappointing compared with the rest. The good news: the remainder of the museum is engaging, informative, and exceptionally well done. For value, variety, and memorable moments, this museum is a standout. Go—you won’t be disappointed. Highly recommended.

I'll admit from the get go, I understand Chinese buffets are not where one would go for gourmet chinese but this place wasn't even really GOOD. Expectations were modest going in, because Chinese buffets rarely promise gourmet fare. Even with that mindset, this buffet missed the mark. The selection looked passable, yet vegetarians will find little beyond green beans, desserts, and fruit. The signage touted sushi, but offerings were cooked mussels and shrimp on ice—no rolls whatsoever. As for taste, most dishes fell somewhere between bland and disappointing. The orange chicken lacked any hint of citrus or spice, and the meats were mostly fatty with dull seasoning. I tried to make a meal of the green beans—usually my buffet staple—but they were wrinkled, withered, and ate like bark-covered twigs. After a couple bites, regret set in. Service, however, was a bright spot. We were seated promptly, beverages arrived quickly, and our glasses stayed filled throughout. The dining area seemed clean, though I cannot speak to the restrooms. In sum, efficient service and a tidy room cannot compensate for a buffet that delivers so little in flavor, freshness, and variety. Vegetarians and anyone seeking authentic taste should look elsewhere. Overall, value felt lacking.

Went there for the first time 3 weeks ago As a longtime jazz lover, I’d had this spot on my list for ages—my jazz piano teacher, Tim Whalen, used to perform here weekly—so a friend’s birthday finally gave me the perfect excuse. First impression: it’s pricey. Final verdict: worth every dollar. The room hums with low-lit sophistication and the promise of live music, and the service matches the tone—quick, attentive, and, crucially, well-paced. Courses glide in without that rushed, plate-piling chaos too many upscale places mistake for efficiency. We started with briny, impeccably shucked oysters and a daily special: an ahi tuna concoction that set the night’s theme. For mains, we split the ahi tuna steak and a porterhouse. The kitchen takes a confident approach to tuna—slightly undercooked to spotlight pristine freshness—and absolutely nails it. It’s the best tuna I’ve had in ages: clean, ocean-sweet, and luxuriously tender. The porterhouse drew nothing but praise from the carnivores at the table, seared with authority and juicy to the bone. We skipped dessert, victims of our own enthusiasm for the warm, addictive bread service. No regrets—though next time I’ll pace myself to explore the sweets. Live jazz is more than a backdrop here; it’s part of the identity. The acts are legit, adding warmth and rhythm without drowning conversation. A post-meal chat with the manager revealed their secret: tuna flown in direct from Hawaii every Friday. After that bite, I believe it. Come if you love great food and real jazz—and if you’ve got a bit of extra cash in your pocket. For a special night out, this place delivers on every promise.
Hit or Miss: Often short-staffed, delivery can be slow. Also closes early—before 11—so plan ahead. Service varies; timing makes or breaks the experience.

Despite Scottsdale-level pricing, this North Scottsdale venue feels neglected. Ants swarm the tattered putt-putt courses, and bumper boats need restarting. Poor maintenance and shabby facilities ruin the experience. You’d expect better standards for the cost. Look elsewhere until it’s fixed.

Stopped in for a quick meal before class and revisited their combo menu. I went with wide noodles topped with beef stew, black mushrooms with oyster sauce, and beef balls; you can also have these combos served over rice. The noodle soup arrives as your chosen noodle with the sides layered on top. Flavor-wise, it was decent—comforting if not standout—but the beef balls were enormous, easily the largest I’ve been served anywhere. At $6.50 including tax, it’s a solid budget option. Service was brisk and the portions generous for the price. From past visits, I think their BBQ over rice is the stronger bet, so I’ll be back to explore more from that section, and the Roast Duck Wonton Noodle Soup is high on my list. Note: this is a cash-only operation, so come prepared.

Years ago, I worked at Cookies in Bloom. The pace felt assembly-line, but the decorated cookies were undeniably cute, creative, and delicious. While in Phoenix today, we popped in for a treat, expecting those signature designs. Instead, we were told there were no decorated cookies available—only standard chocolate chip, sugar, and oatmeal raisin. Graduation day had the team focused solely on fulfilling orders. I understand the rush, but walk-in customers shouldn’t be left empty-handed. A small display, pre-made options, or a posted availability calendar would help. Still, I hope the charming, tasty artistry returns for everyday visitors.

Frustrating Experience at a Busy Whole Foods I've shopped at many Whole Foods, and only a few have left me questioning management—this location tops the list. The biggest issue is the checkout bottleneck: express lanes are rarely open, lines crawl, and by the time you pay, hot-bar meals have gone cold. Staff insist things have improved, yet resources clearly feel stretched. Cashiers make frequent mistakes, registers glitch, and management seems convinced they've opened enough lanes when they haven't. Meanwhile, prepared foods sit unattended, drying out, with customers rearranging items to make them look appetizing. For a store with heavy traffic, basics like adequate staffing, functioning systems, and attentive upkeep shouldn't be optional. Leadership needs to acknowledge the gaps and invest in trained people and better execution. Whole Foods, please wake up—your customers notice, and patience is wearing thin.

The Hebrides Bar is exactly what you would expect from a train-station local....very localised! I popped in for a quick tipple with my mum before a London train and walked into a room where everyone seemed to know each other. Conversation dipped, eyes followed us, and we sat under a quiet scrutiny. Neither staff nor regulars made an effort to make us feel welcome, leaving a chilly, uninviting atmosphere. Friends later told me their experiences were quite different—lively weekends, friendly late nights, good craic. Perhaps timing is everything. I plan to return on a weekend to see if the vibe improves, but after that frosty first impression, my expectations are modest.

The prime view! Stepping into the Mandarin Oriental for the first time feels like a discreet passage into calm: a short, cozy elevator ride from the valet deposits you in a lobby that whispers luxury without showing off. We arrived nervously, reservation-free, expecting to be turned away. Instead, gracious hosts found us a table pressed against floor-to-ceiling glass, with the understanding we’d vacate by 3:45 for the next seating—more than an hour to savor Afternoon Tea and the sweep of the Las Vegas skyline. We opted for the Classic English Afternoon Tea. The tea list is thoughtful, and our selections brewed clean and aromatic. Most sandwiches were balanced and fresh; a couple of desserts missed the mark, but the warm, tender scones—served with proper accompaniments—were irresistible and quietly stole the show. Service never faltered: attentive, unhurried, and genuinely welcoming, enhancing an atmosphere tuned to relaxation rather than spectacle. Pricing felt fair for the caliber delivered. A practical tip: arrive with a light meal already in you; the experience shines when you’re not ravenous. And do not skip a detour to the restrooms—the meticulous design continues there, arguably the city’s finest. In a town of excess, this tea is a masterclass in restraint, detail, and, yes, a prime view.

An evening that promised an Italian dinner fell short. The starters—creamy burrata and crisp salads—looked gorgeous and tasted great. Then the entrees arrived and the table went quiet; bland, uninspired, and overpriced, we felt duped. Curiously, the place seems to thrive late at night, more of a scene than a kitchen. Maybe stick to fries and bar snacks after hours. I’ll look elsewhere until consistency and care return to the mains on the plate.

My go-to taco place in Charlotte! On a beautiful Saturday around 1 p.m., we were seated and served fast; our party of four was in and out in about 30 minutes. Check in for the free warm chips—they arrive straight from the fryer—and don’t skip a side of guac. It’s bright, fresh, and so real it browns by the next day at home. Order the tacos auténticos: the steak is nicely seasoned, tender without being chewy, and the fish boasts a crisp exterior with flavorful, flaky meat inside. The self-serve salsa bar is a standout, spanning mild to blazing and even pleasing my mom, whose spice tolerance is off the charts. Friendly, efficient service, quality ingredients, and crowd-pleasing options make this our reliable Charlotte taco fix. Value and flavor deliver on every visit consistently.

To answer the question, "Is this museum appropriate for my preschooler?" Yes, yes it is. I knew it was going to be a good day when, upon entering the Carnegie Science Center, we passed three families leaving with tired kids ages two to six. That set the tone for a visit tailor-made for preschoolers and adults. The top floor is a dedicated early-childhood zone, complete with a pint-size door that delights little visitors. Inside, a bubbling water table, air-powered ball launcher, and an array of blocks and magnet stations invite nonstop, open-ended play. We spent a large share of our time here, and my active preschooler never once looked bored. The third-floor aquarium felt modest to me as an adult, but it more than delivered for my son. He gently petted a soft-shelled crab and used “techno hands” to retrieve “treasure” from a sunken-ship display—pure magic for small hands and big imaginations. The second floor’s miniature railroad is a perennial crowd-pleaser, with intricate scenes that mesmerize kids and parents alike. On the main level, the bungee-assisted trampoline stole the show: safely harnessed, my preschooler bounced and even tried a flip, grinning ear to ear. Beyond our highlights, the Center overflows with hands-on exhibits that encourage touching, tinkering, and discovery. It’s a refreshing alternative to many children’s museums—engaging for little learners yet rich enough to entertain the whole family. Tips: - Plan at least two hours; add more if you’ll visit the planetarium or IMAX. - During the school year, expect large school groups on field trips. - If you belong to a science museum, check the ASTC Travel Passport Program (astc.org) for reciprocal benefits—your admission, parking, and even gift shop purchases may be discounted or free. Bottom line: Carnegie Science Center makes STEM playful, safe, and accessible for preschoolers—fun for parents, too.

Yum—the pitas are delicious, and I keep coming back. However, service feels understaffed and not friendly; interactions have been curt and unengaging. I usually opt for takeout to avoid the wait. With warmer, more attentive staff and better staffing levels, this place could be outstanding.

After a disappointing visit to our old standby, Kabuki, we turned to Yelp and landed at this tucked-away sushi spot. First impressions were quirky: stepping in, there was a faint scent reminiscent of a hair-and-nail salon, though no salon was nearby. A few moments later, the atmosphere shifted to that clean, appetizing sushi aroma—fresh rice and seaweed, not a hint of fishiness. Drinks come with a small caveat: sodas are canned and run $1.50 since there’s no fountain yet, so iced tea felt like the smarter choice. The food, however, is where this place shines. I ordered a Rainbow Roll that was so balanced and fresh—silky fish, perfectly seasoned rice, and a tidy presentation—that I immediately asked for a second. Edamame, usually my go-to, was fine but didn’t impress; it lacked the pop of salt and heat that makes a simple dish memorable. Despite its less-than-ideal location, the restaurant was packed, a good sign that locals know what’s good. Would I return? Definitely—come for the rolls, stay for the consistency.

Absolutely amazing airline! The gate agent boarding Flight 260 to JFK on June 19 was truly wonderful—helpful and upbeat. I’ve never experienced better customer service. I felt genuinely welcomed and excited to board. Virgin America, you nailed it. Keep shining and setting standards.

Waited three hours to match a single quart of paint in an empty store. Staff didn't offer to expedite, even after I added four gallons to the order. Frustrating service. I’ll choose Home Depot next time—no wait there and far more efficient.

After a disappointing attempt at the Bellagio buffet—the line snaked forever—we circled back to Treasure Island, where we were staying, and took a chance on this spot. Good call. I ordered the fettuccine Alfredo and added chicken; my friends went with a Caesar salad and the calamari. Every dish hit the mark: creamy pasta, crisp salad, and tender, lightly fried squid. The only drawback was the price tag. My entrée came out to $26, which felt steep—roughly $20 for the pasta and $6 to add chicken. I was so hungry I didn’t scrutinize the menu, and the meal did make my stomach happy, but the upcharge was a surprise. Still, flavor and portion size delivered, and my friends’ plates were equally solid (I snagged a bite). For convenient, reliable comfort food on the Strip, this place impressed us. I’d definitely go back.

The in-laws were in town this past weekend, so we decided to show them the newly opened Romare Bearden Park. The park was a lot of fun and after checking it out we decided to stroll over to French Quarter for lunch. With a soft spot for Uptown spots and Cajun-inspired dishes, I walked into French Quarter expecting a relaxed, satisfying lunch. Unfortunately, both service and food missed the mark. Our server seemed scattered from the start—forgetting parts of our order, delivering plates without silverware, and then taking several minutes to bring utensils so we could actually eat. Drink refills never arrived, and the whole dining room felt unwelcoming thanks to an arctic blast of air conditioning on what was arguably the nicest day of the year. It couldn’t have been warmer than the mid-60s inside. By the time we finally dug in, our food had cooled off, and the flavors didn’t redeem the wait. The gumbo had a canned, flat quality rather than the depth and warmth you expect from a proper roux, and the mashed potatoes tasted unmistakably instant. Any hope for a turnaround ended with a restroom visit: dirty stalls and no toilet paper sealed the experience with a disappointing final note. It’s a shame, because the location is prime—steps from a vibrant new park and perfect for out-of-town guests. With attentive service, better quality control in the kitchen, and basic maintenance, French Quarter could shine. As it stands, I won’t be returning.

My downtown friend swears by this spot, warning me it’s “very hipster.” He wasn’t wrong—cool vibe, comfy chairs, and all the trappings. Unfortunately, the coffee was bland and the staff seemed indifferent, dulling the experience. Atmosphere alone can’t save it. I’d meet elsewhere next time; there’s little reason to return.

Dropped my Samsung GS4—screen shattered, display black After dropping my Galaxy S4, the screen shattered and the display stayed black even though it powered on. I brought it to Kandel at Smart Fix, and he replaced the screen the same day in about thirty minutes. He also fixed the sound issue caused by the drop. The service was fast, professional, and exactly what I needed. My phone now works perfectly again. I’ll definitely return to Smart Fix for any future phone or computer problems. Thank you, Kandel!!

This was my first time eating Rika Arepa Express and it was BEYOND AMAZING!!! Rika Arepa Express blew me away with flavors and generous portions. I recommend the #2 and one of their fresh fruit drinks—the 20oz juice is vibrant and only $2, an unbeatable deal. Portions are large enough to share if you’re a light eater. The owner is welcoming and helpful, and service is attentive. Whether you’re new to arepas or a devoted fan, this spot delivers great value and hospitality.

Beautiful interior, excellent service, divine food. That is all that I really need to say. However, there are mentionable aspects that set this restaurant apart from others. Carpe Diem is the quintessential date night restaurant. It features romantic lighting, a carved ceiling, and large paintings of flowers—what could be sexier than that? We had reservations and were seated immediately. The wine list offers several thoughtful selections by the glass; while prices run high, the pours are generous enough that a single glass carried each of us through dinner. Warm bread with butter arrived first, and it was irresistible. I rarely eat bread, yet their loaf was so good I polished off a piece and a half without regret. I was thrilled to see Anson Mills products highlighted on the menu and even more impressed by the breadth of vegetarian and vegan choices, including a dedicated vegetarian special for the evening. I chose that special: a rustic tart with a whole-grain crust layered with tomatoes, asparagus, cheese, and a perfectly cooked over-easy egg. Phenomenal. My date ordered Anson Mills rice grits crowned with sea island red peas and Gouda, opting for mushrooms instead of shrimp. Another stellar dish—rich, earthy, and deeply satisfying. With this level of quality, five stars feels skimpy. Carpe Diem earns an entire solar system. Make reservations, savor bread, and let the evening sweep you away.

I work at this store and I've worked at a few other H&M's. This is not the best store nor is it the worst. As someone who has put in time across multiple locations, I can say many complaints you read have kernels of truth—but there are two sides to the story. Retail staffing is a revolving door, and our sales floor is often staffed by new hires. A small core team anchors the operation, but many colleagues don’t stay long enough to master the systems, policies, and product knowledge needed to help every customer quickly. Training takes time, and while we do our best, there will be moments when the learning curve is visible. A frequent criticism is that associates “have attitude.” I genuinely try to go out of my way to help, and so do many of my coworkers. But respect has to go both ways. When garments are tossed at us, when we’re called crude names, or belittled in front of other shoppers, it’s hard to remain endlessly cheerful. That doesn’t excuse any poor service, and I apologize for any interaction that felt less than warm. Still, kindness makes a real difference in a high-pressure, high-traffic environment. Another point of confusion involves promotions and credit-card offers. Different stores sometimes run deals that are unique to their location or require manager approval. Not all managers interpret or authorize the same exceptions, and associates are obligated to follow the rules as written, or risk corrective action. So when one store honors a discount and another can’t, it may look like we’re being difficult, but we’re following policy—often to the letter. If something seems inconsistent, ask us to clarify; we’ll try to find an approved solution or bring in a manager. We truly appreciate the customers who make the job easier: the ones who ask for sizes instead of tearing through freshly folded stacks, who treat staff with basic courtesy, and who understand we’re juggling multiple tasks at once. You’re the reason many of us keep smiling on the busiest days. Most of us are college students or young adults working to cover tuition and rent, not simply clocking in for a store discount. If you have a question or concern, bring it to us before frustration builds—we’ll do our best to help. In short, this store isn’t perfect, but it isn’t terrible either. With patience, clear communication, and mutual respect, we can turn more visits into good experiences for everyone.

It's not that the Earl of Sandwich makes the best food on the Strip -- far from it. What sets Earl of Sandwich apart is how reliably great it is when you need it most. The freshly par-baked bread comes out super hot and soft, with generous fillings that melt together into gooey, satisfying bites—comfort food that delights drunken and sober tastebuds alike. In a city overloaded with medium-expensive spots flaunting fancy-pants menus that rarely deliver, this place earns five stars for being cheap, fast, and genuinely delicious at any hour. It’s the kind of dependable, no-fuss option Vegas sorely needs. At first glance, it looks like a standard fast-food chain: an assembly line of workers, ultra-reasonable prices, and straightforward choices. Don’t be fooled. These sandwiches are the real deal. On my visit, our group split a ham and cheese and an original roast beef. Both were excellent: the ham and cheese popped with a bright mustard tang, while the roast beef offered a gentle horseradish kick that complemented, rather than overwhelmed, the meat. The portions are solid—satisfying for many—but the bigger appetites in our party wanted two each for dinner. At just over $5 a sandwich, doubling up won’t dent your bankroll; you’ll still have plenty left for the slot machines. Service is brisk, the line moves quickly, and the food lands hot in your hands—a huge plus when you’re racing between shows, or staggering out of a club. It’s open late, making it a perfect post-party pit stop. Earl of Sandwich may be an international chain (please open in Los Angeles!), but on the Strip, it’s a refreshingly tasty alternative that nails value, speed, and comfort.

This place was a joke, we went there after making a reservation that they would not honor. After 2 hours in the line, they approved us to get inside. So was it worth the wait, no way. Despite a reservation, we waited nearly two hours in a packed line only to be herded into an even more overcrowded room where moving was impossible. We were shoved repeatedly, and a drunk patron picked a fight after the crush pushed us into him. Security didn’t de-escalate; they sided with the other guy, which felt like favoritism toward those paying for pricey tables that can run up to $5,000 on weekends. The vibe was chaotic, uncomfortable, and unsafe—absolutely not worth the time or money. If you’re considering this spot, be prepared to cough up serious cash or endure a miserable experience. With so many better clubs in Vegas, do yourself a favor and skip this one. Reservations meant nothing.

This review focuses solely on a single cocktail and the service surrounding it, as I didn’t sample the food. While waiting for friends to finish eating, I wasn’t in the mood for much alcohol but decided to order a light cocktail: Chambord with 7-Up. From the first sip, it was clear something was off—the 7-Up was completely flat. With no carbonation, the drink tasted like Chambord diluted with water, which is both unappealing and unacceptable for a nearly $20 cocktail. To make sure I wasn’t imagining it, I asked my boyfriend to taste it; he agreed the mixer was flat. I brought this to the bartender’s attention, expecting a quick check of the soda line or gun and a fresh pour. Instead, she poured some of the liquid out of my glass and topped it off with more of the same flat 7-Up. She then suggested it only seemed uncarbonated because the drink wasn’t diluted enough, a dismissive explanation that ignored the obvious lack of fizz. Carbonation is not subtle—you can taste and see it. I tried the “fixed” drink and, unsurprisingly, it remained flat. Rather than argue, I returned it. A basic standard of service would be to verify the mixer, replace the drink entirely, or offer an alternative. None of that happened. What turned a disappointing cocktail into a truly negative experience was the bartender’s attitude. After I returned the drink, she spoke disparagingly about me to another waitress, who then glared at me. I was polite throughout, and there’s no reason for a guest to be treated that way for raising a legitimate quality issue. In short: poor drink execution and unprofessional service. I can’t speak to the food, but based on this experience, management needs to address staff training on both technical basics—like checking soda carbonation—and guest courtesy. Until then, I’d think twice before ordering a cocktail here.

For a Fairmont, this property was a surprise—though not the kind I hoped for. My experience with the brand has mostly been dining, as I usually stay loyal to another chain or book via Hotwire. This time, a good rate and the need for a two-bedroom ruled out Hotwire, so we gave Fairmont a shot. The hotel was fully booked, and I was offered free breakfast if I accepted a smoking room, which I declined. Our room on the fourth floor carried a noticeable cigarette smell, likely drifting from the smoking rooms on the floor above. Ambiance throughout the hotel was good, but the room itself was minuscule. The traditional, heavy furniture overwhelmed the space, leaving little room to walk or store belongings. The bathroom didn’t fare better: poor layout and a shower that took ages to drain made basic routines frustrating. A friend with Fairmont Platinum status was upgraded to a suite, but even that felt underwhelming for the brand and price point. Service and concierge weren’t used, and parking was not applicable. Location, however, is excellent if you’re traveling without a car: the hotel sits right above VIA Rail and connects directly to STM, making it an ideal transport hub and only a few minutes from the main drag. In the end, while the setting and connectivity were strong, the core experience—room size, layout, and maintenance—fell short of expectations for a luxury chain. Given the combination of cramped quarters and underwhelming amenities, I’m unlikely to stay here again.

We received great service from Luis and others. I liked the vibration of the staff and location. We visited for lunch and ordered off the midday menu. The food was good but short of great—most items were overly sauced, masking flavors. The salsas didn’t hit the mark: options ranged from too sweet to too spicy, without a balanced, chunky, spicy salsa that I prefer. The chips were fresh, but they deserved a brighter, more balanced salsa. I admit I’ve been spoiled by Leticia’s and Juan’s Flaming Fajitas, so my expectations for depth and freshness are high. Attentive service from Luis and the team, plus a lively vibe and convenient location, stood out. On that basis, I would return. One detraction: the restaurant serves Pepsi products exclusively, which I consider a customer service misstep.

Where is the negative 2 stars button? I ordered fish that tasted cheap, limp, and utterly unseasoned, like it had been thawed, mishandled, and tossed straight into old grease that stank up the place. The plate was bland to the point of disbelief, and the experience felt like the kind where the house pockets your cash while your taste buds get nothing. If you crave flavor, look elsewhere. My last visit was accidental; my next won’t happen—ever. Even the alley seemed deserted, which says plenty. They owe me $12 and forty wasted minutes. And to think people complained about Pete’s—this made Pete’s look gourmet. Never again, not even out of curiosity.

This is a wonderful family restaurant with very personal service and attention to quality ingredients. The warmth starts at the bar, where Mark mixes outstanding margaritas—balanced, bright, and mercifully free of the syrupy sweetness so common elsewhere. He’s soft‐spoken, with a wry sense of humor that suits the intimate vibe. Maria provides the spark: outgoing, attentive, and clearly proud of every plate she sends out. After a few visits, this has become my favorite Mexican restaurant in Phoenix. The mole enchiladas are the star. They aren’t served daily; look for mole on Tuesdays and weekends. Rich, complex, and soulful, it’s to die for—among the best moles I’ve had, even compared with trips to Mexico.

It pays to budget at least an hour for a buffet, as I learned at Treasure Island’s breakfast spread. I piled my plate high and found the offerings hit-or-miss. The corned beef hash was a standout—savory and satisfying—while the cheese blintz was a definite miss. The ham was reliably good, but that’s hard to mess up. Overall, the food was just okay. Service, however, shone: drink orders were prompt and attentive. Next time I’m in Las Vegas, I’ll likely sample other breakfast buffets to compare. Prices felt reasonable.

Every HOB is the same, right? Not true. At this House of Blues, the usual all-standing crush downstairs has been reshaped with pockets of “VIP” real estate: roped-off couches, a minder at the gate, and the now-ubiquitous bottle service. In the City of Sin, the bottle game is everywhere, and HOB has joined the party. We rolled in for Steel Panther on a Friday. The line moved, first round acquired, and the crew staked out a vantage point. Just below us sat a row of empty, comfy couches—$300 to occupy, including a bottle and mixers, said the courteous guard. Negotiations ensued; the number slid to $150 with a $100 bar tab. Tempting, but with two in our group off the sauce, we passed. The show delivered what Panther fans expect: tight musicianship, big hooks, and a torrent of banter. At times the patter ran long and the backing tracks felt a bit too sampled, but the room’s sound held up—clear vocals, punchy guitars, and a mix that didn’t punish the ears. One gripe: drink specials. A bathroom placard promised $6 24oz Bud Lights on Fridays. Having just paid $11 for 24oz Coors Light, I pivoted and ordered three Buds, only to be rung up $33. The bartender said the sign meant 12oz cans. If that’s the case, spell it out; bathroom advertising shouldn’t require translation. Verdict: a solid venue with smart sightlines and sound, but watch the upsell and read the fine print. GA works fine; VIP feels like paying for furniture anyway.

Terrible grooming experience. I dropped my chow off at 10:30 and he wasn’t even touched by 3:30. When they finally rushed the cut, he came back with abrasions all over his skin. This place clearly can’t handle their volume and quality suffers. Truly unprofessional, careless, and unacceptable. I would not recommend this business to anyone, ever.

I keep returning to The Liberty hoping my opinion will improve, but each visit lands around “meh.” I’ve been here for pub crawls, beer tastings, and a handful of business lunches and dinners. I’ve sampled the famous truffle chips, the more famous burger, and several appetizers. While I understand the appeal—central location, ample parking, a solid beer list, and consistently decent service—the food remains just okay. Nothing stands out as memorable or craveworthy, and the overall experience rarely rises above average. It’s the kind of spot that works when convenience matters more than character. For now, The Liberty stays in my so-so column, though I haven’t given up on it entirely just yet.

Taqueria Los Angeles: A Hole-in-the-Wall That Misses the Mark On the strength of glowing Yelp reviews, my wife and I visited this humble, hole-in-the-wall spot on a Saturday night around 7:15. The empty dining room didn’t deter us; we ordered three tacos—chicken, fish, and steak—and chicken enchiladas to go. The food was ready in about ten minutes, and we headed home optimistic. Service was quick. Unfortunately, the meal underwhelmed. The chips and salsa were the highlight, crisp and lively, but the proteins disappointed: the chicken and steak were slightly overcooked, and the tacos leaned bland despite acceptable seasoning. The enchiladas were serviceable yet forgettable, and the beans tasted like they came straight from a can. Flavors felt safe rather than vibrant, and nothing truly stood out. I want to root for small, independent spots, but I can’t recommend this one over local stalwarts like Carolina’s. The food is inexpensive, but it tastes that way. Perhaps other menu items shine, yet this first impression makes a return visit unlikely. I wish Taqueria Los Angeles the best, but for now, I’ll look elsewhere.

Disappointing visit. At 6pm, only one server/cashier handled the dinner rush, causing waits and confusion. Communication issues with the cashier led to ordering errors. Management should staff and train better. I left frustrated and won’t return soon.

Worst Trader Joe's ever! Never coming back here! I stopped by this Trader Joe’s while I was in the neighborhood, and it turned into one of the most frustrating grocery runs I’ve had in a long time. The store felt unusually cramped, and the aisles were packed, making it difficult to maneuver or grab items without constantly sidestepping. Many shoppers lingered mid-aisle debating choices, which only amplified the congestion. Whether it’s the layout or the timing, the crowd flow seemed unmanaged, and the experience lacked the easy, upbeat rhythm I’ve come to expect from other locations. The checkout sealed the impression. I picked up a single six-pack and approached the register with my ID ready. While verifying age is standard, the cashier’s tone came off as suspicious and brusque. She scrutinized my ID longer than usual and offered none of the warm, conversational energy that typically defines Trader Joe’s service. It felt more like an interrogation than a routine check, and the interaction left me feeling unwelcome. To be fair, not everything was negative. A team member at the sample station was friendly and engaging, offering a sausage and mustard pairing that was genuinely tasty. We chatted briefly, and the “surprisingly good” mustard was a highlight in an otherwise disappointing visit. Overall, this location didn’t deliver the charm, efficiency, or hospitality that makes Trader Joe’s a go-to elsewhere. Between the congested aisles and curt checkout, it fell short of expectations. I hope management takes a hard look at crowd flow and customer service training, because a few adjustments could transform the experience. For now, I’ll stick to other stores. One star, saved by a great sample and a kind employee.
Doughy crust, scant toppings, disappointing quality. Never ordering Papa John’s again. Truly yuck and overpriced.

I love my gym..... but only at certain times of the day. The biggest drawback is the parking lot during peak hours—think Christmas shopping chaos, all year long. If you’re aiming for a stress-free entry, avoid the 5:00–10:00 rush and go in the early afternoon. Once you’re inside, though, it’s a different story: this place is huge, efficient, and designed to get you moving as soon as you’ve checked in and breezed past the sales offices. It’s a true two-story fitness center with a smart layout. Downstairs hosts a juice bar/deli where you can grab workout snacks, full meals, or recovery drinks and actually sit and enjoy them. The women’s gym is a great space to go hard without self-consciousness, and the main free-weight area is unapologetically built for grunts, gains, and focus. Add a lap pool and steam rooms for the perfect workout-plus-recovery combo. Locker rooms are expansive, with showers, lockers, and changing areas—basically everything you need to transition in and out comfortably. Upstairs is where the energy really spikes. The class lineup is fun and varied: Zumba, hot hula fitness, yoga, and yes—stretching, which is much tougher than it sounds. Beyond classes, there are plenty of machines for both light and heavy lifting, a dedicated stretching area with mats and those mysterious spiderweb-like stations, and rows of treadmills, bikes, and ellipticals. It does get crowded, but I’ve never failed to find a machine, even if it’s next to someone drenched from their own hustle. Bonus points for entertainment: a giant wall of TVs runs different channels, and most cardio machines have personal screens to keep your mind off the sweat. There’s a daycare with camera monitoring, which is convenient, though I’m not a fan that anyone with TV access can view the feed. Limiting visibility to parents—via key card or secure access—would feel safer. That said, friends who use the daycare are happy with the staff and services. A final perk: an indoor track wraps around the top floor, offering a change of pace from the machines. And they frequently roll out appealing sign-up deals—think $5 enrollments or promotions for women. Bottom line: an outstanding gym with serious amenities and smart programming, best enjoyed outside peak hours. Fix the parking and tighten daycare viewing policies, and it’s almost perfect.

Most of my extended family was going to Dr. Mohan...no longer. After years of trusting Dr. Mohan’s practice, my family is moving on. Scheduling is needlessly difficult, and when you’re seriously ill, the lack of follow-up is alarming. There’s no easy channel to reach the doctor with a quick question; twice I called and never received a call back. Other practices offer secure text messaging and respond promptly—this office does not. Attempting to reschedule an appointment during a serious illness went nowhere. Staff interactions have been rude, and crucial details get mishandled, including booking my CT scan at the wrong location, wasting time and adding stress. There are no automatic reminders for annual physicals, so preventive care slips through the cracks. We expect competence, compassion, and basic communication; this practice consistently fell short. Overall, the service was poor and deeply disappointing. Never again.

With new management in place, I decided to give this Korean BBQ spot another shot, and I’m glad I did. The all-you-can-eat concept is smartly executed: meats are brought to your table fresh rather than languishing in a buffet. Quality has improved noticeably. During a solo lunch, I sampled four buffet selections—marinated beef kalbi, thin-sliced pork belly, shrimp, and squid. The kalbi was flavorful and tender, the pork belly nicely fatty and crisp when grilled, and the squid pleasantly chewy with a clean taste. The only miss was the shrimp, which tasted soft and oddly delicate, almost malnourished. Still, at $15.99 per person all day, even at dinner, the value is hard to beat. I’ve returned three times since, and while the dining room has been quiet, the consistent quality keeps drawing me back. For affordable, fresh-served AYCE Korean BBQ, this spot deserves another look.
Smart Style’s Walmart location makes haircuts convenient and affordable. I’ve visited many times for cuts and styling, and the results are consistently great—never disappointed, friendly staff.

This Just Hit the Spot I stopped in for a light meal and chose a seat at the bar, where the bartender suggested a cocktail that paired perfectly. The $8 Tom Kha Chicken soup was generously sized, with bright, balanced flavors—comforting yet lively—and could have been a meal on its own. The Spicy Papaya Salad truly delivered heat: crunchy, zesty, and addictive, with a lime-fish sauce punch that built until tears signaled surrender. Friendly atmosphere, attentive bar service, and strong value seal the deal. I’ll be back for more Thai favorites—maybe medium spice next time. The cocktail was balanced and refreshing too.

I’ve visited this Pita Jungle countless times, and one thing keeps pulling me back: the berry iced tea mixed with lemonade. If I could rate the place on that drink alone, it’d be a 5+++—you should absolutely try it; it will rock your world. Food-wise, I like what I usually order, but the broader menu rarely inspires me to branch out. The offerings just aren’t quite what I’m looking for. Credit where it’s due: the roasted red pepper hummus and grilled chicken are consistently great. I’ve also enjoyed the spinach quesadilla and tzatziki. Beyond those highlights, both food and service tend to be squarely mediocre. Still, I come here often. It’s a dependable stop for a healthy meal, and I prefer supporting a local business over the many chain restaurants nearby. If you go, start with that berry tea-lemonade, add hummus, and keep expectations measured for everything else. The atmosphere is casual and lively, but wait times and attentiveness can be hit-or-miss during peak hours on weekends here too.

Haifa Restaurant catered an event I attended, and the experience was deeply disappointing. The hors d’oeuvres were extremely good, raising expectations, but the main courses were barely edible. To make matters worse, everything was served on paper plates with plastic cutlery—unsuitable for food that needed real utensils. I didn’t visit the restaurant itself, so I can only speak to their catering, which fell far short of standards.

Playboy Club/Moon at the Palms offers a spacious alternative to the hyper-trendy spots on the Strip. The Playboy Club itself is roomy, with two bars and brighter lighting than Moon — a welcome change if you want to see your surroundings. Table minimums regularly hit $50–$100 depending on the night, so casual visitors may prefer to skip the seats and roam. There’s a small area in the back where dancing is allowed, though it tends to attract only a handful of people before most migrate upstairs to Moon. The biggest drawback is the scene: this duo is no longer the hottest ticket in town, and its off-Strip location means a longer, pricier cab ride unless you’re staying at the Palms. The crowd skews less “trendy and gorgeous” than the headliner clubs, which can be a plus for comfort but a minus if you crave that high-glam atmosphere. Logistics can be rough at closing time. With the elevator as the only way in and out, departures bottleneck into a slow queue. If you leave when everyone else does, expect 30 minutes or more of waiting among impatient, intoxicated patrons. Plan your exit strategically to preserve the night’s good vibes.

After eight mostly dry days in Florida, stumbling upon this quirky tequila bar in the heart of Phoenix Sky Harbor’s C terminal felt like an oasis—only this mirage didn’t disappear. Two double gin and tonics in, with time to spare before my next flight, I found exactly what every traveler hopes for: quick, friendly service, generous pours, and unexpectedly excellent food. The nachos were standout—crisp chips, ample cheese, balanced toppings, and just the right kick—comfort food done with care. The bartender kept an effortless rhythm, attentive without being pushy, and had me on a seamless re-up that matched the pace of a relaxed layover. Atmosphere is lively yet easygoing, prices fair for an airport, and the vibe singular. I’d return in a heartbeat. Damned. Fine.

This spot is consistently packed, likely due to its location across from The Palms, so expect crowds and a busy vibe. Service is efficient. My only concern is the frequent loitering in the parking lot during evenings, which can feel unsafe. I’d appreciate more security or staff presence outside to discourage harassment and ensure guests feel comfortable safely coming and going.

A Gluten-Free Promise Broken: A Friday Night Fiasco As someone newly navigating a gluten-free life, I’m always grateful when a restaurant claims to cater to customers with allergies. That promise carries weight—especially when you plan a Friday night around it. I placed an online order several hours in advance for two veggie pizzas: one gluten-free for me and one traditional for my niece. I don’t live nearby, but I was willing to make the drive. I even left early to run a few errands on the way, confident that a simple pick-up would cap off the evening. The restaurant was easy to spot—small footprint, modern décor—and initially gave off the right vibe. But things went sideways the moment I identified myself. The employee, who didn’t introduce himself and wore no name tag, told me they were out of gluten-free pizzas and could make both traditionally instead. For anyone living with a medical need or serious sensitivity, this response is more than tone-deaf; it signals a fundamental misunderstanding of why gluten-free options exist in the first place. When I asked how this could happen after placing my order hours ahead, I was told they’d tried to call me. A quick check of my phone showed a missed call four minutes before my scheduled pick-up time. Four minutes. By then, I was essentially in their parking lot. The restaurant had ample time—more than two hours—to notify me and potentially save a long, hungry drive. At minimum, that’s poor planning. At worst, it’s a breach of trust that puts customers with dietary restrictions in a difficult position. Running out of a specialty item happens, but businesses that position themselves as allergy-friendly must manage inventory with extra care and communicate proactively. That means honest systems for tracking supply, contacting customers as soon as a problem is known, and offering real solutions. Staff also need training on food allergies, cross-contamination, and empathetic customer service. A simple introduction, a sincere apology, and a meaningful alternative—refunds processed immediately, a credit for a future visit, or help locating a suitable option nearby—would have gone a long way. None of that was offered. Instead, I left hungry, frustrated, and disappointed, feeling that their promise to serve gluten-free diners was more marketing than mission. Reliability is non-negotiable for customers with dietary needs. If you advertise gluten-free options, you must be able to fulfill them, especially when orders are placed well in advance. The takeaway: educate staff, tighten supply ordering, build a buffer of gluten-free crusts, confirm and reconfirm special orders, and reach out early—far earlier than four minutes before pick-up. I wish I could say this was an isolated misstep redeemed by thoughtful service, but it wasn’t. Based on this experience, I can’t recommend this spot to anyone relying on gluten-free options. If I could give less than one star, I would.

Having lived in Hawaii for years, this spot hits the mark—authentic Hawaiian fast food with all the classics and a few extras. Tasty, inexpensive, and generously portioned. It’s exactly like I remember. Quick, satisfying, and highly recommended for a nostalgic bite.

Good Food, ok quality Fish, Atmosphere could use some help and they need to clean the establishment better. Menus had sticky residue and the table wasn’t very clean, which felt questionable. While the flavors were decent, the sushi was packed with rice—clearly a filler tactic for an all-you-can-eat spot. Reduce the rice and improve cleanliness, and this place could earn 3 or even 4 stars. Until then, the food can’t overcome the hygiene issues and heavy fillers. For now, it’s a 2-star experience.

OK, here’s the deal: skip PV Mall’s food court—go to Julio G’s. When lunchtime hits at PV Mall, Paradise Bakery may seem like the only decent option, but variety awaits just across Tatum at Julio G’s. Expect complimentary, plentiful, tasty chips and salsa that keep coming. The menu covers all the Mexican standards at reasonable prices. Nothing I’ve had screams “must-order,” but everything is reliably good, and service is friendly and efficient. Be warned: portions are huge. I’ve never finished an entrée—possibly because I demolish two baskets of chips before the plate lands. For a satisfying, no-frills Mexican meal near the mall, Julio G’s is an easy, wallet-friendly upgrade.

We had a lovely first trip to St. Francis, where food, service, and atmosphere strike a perfect balance—upscale yet casual, never overbearing, even down to the valet. For a bachelorette dinner, The Vig might suit better with its broader menu and more party-forward vibe. Back to St. Francis: our Cioppino and hanger steak were spot-on, flavorful and expertly prepared. It’s a great neighborhood spot with refined comfort. We’ll definitely return and gladly recommend it for relaxed, high-quality dining.

Battling a miserable cold, I popped in for a quick juice before tackling Walmart. I ordered the Citrus Kick, and the friendly staffer suggested adding vitamin C and zinc to help me feel better. Her kindness and thoughtful recommendation made my day. Great service, delicious boost, and genuine care—exactly what you want from a juice spot.

I ordered two items for carry-out on 7/28/2013. I was very disappointed in the quality of my food. I requested a grilled chicken quesadilla with just chicken and cheese, and a ground beef taco with beef and cheese only. Both came wrong. The quesadilla was shredded chicken swimming in liquid, with unwanted tomatoes and onions. The taco arrived with lettuce, and the beef was burnt. I took one bite of each and tossed them. The chips were stale, and the salsa tasted bland and anything but fresh. Altogether, it felt like a careless rush job and a complete waste of $15.

Totally what you would expect from Bobby Flay! We’ve been for dinner before—excellent—and this time aimed for a 1 pm Saturday lunch, pleasantly surprised by the brunch menu. Complimentary bread basket: awesome. The shrimp corn tamale featured four plump shrimp on an open tamale with a sauce of pure deliciousness; a must-order starter. Goat cheese dip was yummy. Pear iced tea, served with simple syrup, was refreshing, though the pear note was faint. Striped bass was nicely cooked, but the corn side and sauces were just okay. Service was attentive and good overall, and friendly too.

Solid Value at Sahara’s NASCAR Cafe On two recent visits—first in November 2010 and again in early December—the prime rib special at the NASCAR Cafe delivered exactly what I wanted: a hearty slice of prime rib with mixed vegetables and, on the latest visit, surprisingly good mashed potatoes. At $9.99, it’s a strong value, but note you’ll need a Club Sahara card to get the discount. I also tried the fish and chips back in September or October 2010, and they were good as well. The atmosphere is casual and no-frills, and beers can run pricey—$6 for a Guinness—so consider playing a bar slot machine for comped drinks or grabbing a $1 beer before you head in. The cafe’s location next to $1 blackjack and other Sahara attractions is a plus, making it an easy, convenient stop. I don’t usually visit other Strip casinos; Sahara is my go-to, partly because my wife and I were married there in 2006. For straightforward comfort food at a fair price, this cafe fits the bill: consistent plates, satisfying sides, and a budget-friendly special that feels like a throwback. If you value affordability over ambiance, the NASCAR Cafe is a dependable choice at Sahara.

I have mixed thoughts on this place. We went in with high expectations, having heard it’s the spot where everyone goes, and on atmosphere alone it delivers. The energy is electric, the crowd thick, and the overall vibe a blast. Beach balls sailing overhead add a playful touch, and the setup—with clear tables designed for dancing—leans into the party spirit. The pool itself is on the shallow side, which isn’t ideal, but it doesn’t ruin the fun. Where things falter is in the rulebook and the way it’s enforced. Right off the bat, our friend was denied entry for wearing a tank top and had to shell out $30 for a basic hotel shirt just to get in, while my sleeveless shirt somehow passed muster. That kind of inconsistency sets a frustrating tone. Then came the no-bag policy at the pool area, which meant paying another $20 for a locker. It’s not the end of the world, but it feels like nickel-and-diming when you’re already paying for entry and on-site prices. Inside, staff were strict about drinks being kept out of the water, a rule that seems more symbolic than practical given the reality of a packed pool on a party day. It’s hard not to question what’s gained by policing a few spilled sips when public pools inevitably have their own hygiene challenges. The dress code enforcement continued with a guest in a European-style speedo being told to buy longer shorts. While they’re within their rights to set standards, the heavy-handed approach detracts from what’s otherwise a carefree environment. Despite all this, we still had a great time. The location and atmosphere are top-tier for daytime partying, and if you want a high-energy pool scene with plenty of people-watching and music, this place nails it. Prices are what you’d expect—think $10 for a domestic beer—so budget accordingly. Ultimately, the strict rules and uneven enforcement keep it from being perfect. If they eased up a bit, borrowed the more relaxed approach of spots like Ditch Fridays at the Palms, and focused on guest experience over regulation, it would be an easy five-star destination. As it stands, go for the vibe and be ready to play by the book.

Located next to Ross in the shopping center at Charleston and Rainbow, this spot surprised me in the best way. It’s not a fancy sit‐down restaurant, but the food does all the talking: delicious aromas, better flavors, and generous portions. Service is fast, the staff are friendly, and the open kitchen looks spotless. I grabbed the $24 dinner deal—two entrée plates, two egg rolls, two crab rangoons, fried rice, and egg drop soup. Everything hit the spot, though the egg rolls were the only miss. Still, the value and taste easily outshine Panda Express. I’ll definitely be back—especially for their lunch specials running until 4.

We are fortunate to live just a couple moments away, but after one visit I’d happily drive across town for this food. My wife and I wandered in on a Saturday afternoon for a glass of wine, hoping for a few small bites. The kitchen hadn’t opened yet, so we settled at the bar to sip and learn about the place. Within minutes, the chef appeared with a dish of briny, fragrant olives; we asked for some bread, and the owner pulled up a chair. What followed was an unhurried, generous hour of conversation and hospitality that felt more like being welcomed into a friend’s home than dropping by a neighborhood spot. We booked a table for Monday dinner on the spot—and we’re glad we did. A crisp salad set the tone. My wife’s mussels arrived in a shimmering wine sauce, impeccably seasoned, perfect for dunking that same addictive bread and its lush garlic butter. My Steak au Poivre was a standout: deeply seared, tender to the core, peppery and richly sauced without overpowering the beef. The rack of lamb, charred just right and rosy within, was equally memorable; the one bite my wife shared was revelatory. Between the gracious service and the confident, heartfelt cooking, this is a reservation you’ll soon need to plan months ahead. Go now.

Average overall. The place looks great, with stylish decor, but prices feel inflated—likely to cover the ambiance. Lunch runs $15–$20 per person for a burger, fries, and a soda, which seems steep. I’d consider returning occasionally, but not often, given the overall cost-to-value balance.

I recently joined and I’m impressed so far. The staff is friendly, attentive, and helpful, creating a welcoming atmosphere. My gripe is the limited number of stationary bikes; they’re always in use, which is tough because my doctor recommends them for my hip. Despite that, the facility feels supportive and well-run. If they add more bikes, it’d be perfect. Overall, I’d recommend it.

After admiring a coworker’s gorgeous hair, I asked for her stylist—Jonny—and I’ve been a loyal client for four years. Jonny consistently delivers flawless cuts, color, and styling, listens carefully, and makes hair look and feel amazing. I’ve referred many friends, and he never disappoints, every time. Professional, talented, and reliable, Jonny is my go-to hair magician.

Nothing Bundt Cakes delivers irresistibly moist, tender cakes that melt in your mouth. Sample the wide range of flavors by ordering a dozen of the bite-sized Bundtinis—available only by the dozen. The medium and large cakes are equally delicious, perfect for parties, gifts, or indulgent treats.

New to the area, we’ve found this spot a solid go-to. The casual, laid-back sports bar vibe works even when we bring the kids. Wings are the standout—especially the boneless, strip-style ones. Service has been reliably good on every visit, and the Tuesday and Thursday specials make it easy on the wallet. Overall, a friendly, tasty, family-friendly choice for us.

When in Vegas, you gotta do it right and Mastro's is well...doing it right. Mastro's Ocean Club, the seafood-forward sibling of the famed steakhouse chain, delivers a stellar experience in the Crystals shopping center at CityCenter. Our group of nine scored seats in the signature treehouse, an unforgettable setting. I ordered the bone-in ribeye, impeccably cooked, and sampled the Chilean sea bass, buttery and delicate. The sides had serious swagger; the wasabi mashed potatoes stole the show. Service was polished, pacing spot-on, and the vibe upscale yet lively without being stuffy. For a celebratory night out or a splurge-worthy meal, Mastro's nails it. Highly recommend.
Love their in-house craft brews! The IPA was inexpensive and delicious, the food stellar, and fried pickles the best I’ve ever had. Great value, flavor.

While visiting Tempe, I ate here twice and was blown away by the Cincinnati chili 5-way—absolutely amazing. Service was solid and friendly. Highly recommend for tasty comfort food and a relaxing environment perfect for casual meals.

Came here with my Fiance because we were staying at the hotel and we saw great reviews. Our experience was..... ok? We started in the bar for happy hour, and that was the high point. The bartender turned out solid cocktails, and the small bites set a promising tone: a rich, deeply savory French onion soup with a cheese pull, and juicy sliders that balanced char and sweetness. If the rest of the night had stayed at that level, this would be an easy recommendation. Once seated in the main dining room, the momentum faded. We ordered pork chops, a Caesar salad, and a side of seasoned fries. The fries never arrived—and no one seemed to notice—so we let it go. The Caesar felt like form over function: three whole leaves dotted with dressing and cheese, more deconstruction than salad. I just wanted a classic bowl, not a concept. As for the pork chop, it was competent but forgettable—cooked fine, seasoned lightly, nothing that lingers. Dessert doubled down on the hit-or-miss theme. The chocolate sampler sounded fun but landed awkwardly: a chocolate mousse studded with popcorn that didn’t mesh, a chocolate cake pop so dry we left it, and a churro with chocolate sauce that was simple and good. I ordered a coffee with dessert; it showed up after we’d finished, so I sent it back. For a venue that leans fancy and commands elevated prices, execution matters. Remember the sides. Time the coffee. Let the salad be a salad. With a few fixes, it could match its reviews; as is, it’s uneven.

I am NOT a Senior Citizen yet and I love this place. This place makes me feel right at home. The staff is genuinely friendly, portions are generous, and drink prices are refreshingly fair. I’ve enjoyed everything from hearty breakfasts to standout liver and onions—always tasty and well-prepared. Best of all, the menu respects your wallet, with real value in every dish. Other spots could learn from their professionalism and fairness. Many thanks to a team that keeps quality high while keeping costs reasonable.

I used to work here, and I still come back for favorites: hot and sour soup, yakisoba noodles, orange chicken, red curry, and Mongolian-style beef. Happy hour is a steal for appetizers—get the wings and calamari and ask for a side of salad dressing for dipping; it’s unexpectedly perfect. Saturday lunches are just $5 for any dish and include a salad. Expect slower service then, since the kitchen juggles dine-in and to-go orders. Otherwise, food comes out quickly. Consistently tasty, great value, and an easy go-to local spot.

I've been there twice and it's a good place to go on a nice date. I prefer the places that are more casual or they have their own thing going on, but I won't hold that against The Cheesecake Factory. As you’d expect, cheesecake is the headline act, and it delivers. Slices are oversized, rich, and absolutely shareable—finishing one solo is a feat. On our latest visit, we chose the Chocolate Chip Cookie Dough cheesecake, packed with generous chunks of cookie dough and crowned with swirls of whipped cream. It was indulgent, well-balanced, and exactly the kind of dessert that makes their name make sense. Before dessert, there was a humorous mix-up: I ordered water and an Old Fashioned, and our server asked how I wanted it cooked—turns out The Old Fashioned is also a burger on the menu. Missed opportunity not to pair the cocktail with its namesake burger, but I went with Renee’s Special instead: a turkey sandwich, the soup of the day (clam chowder), and a house salad. The combo was satisfying and thoughtfully portioned. The clam chowder was comforting, the salad fresh, and the turkey sandwich flavorful, though the sourdough crust was tougher than I prefer. Not stale, just a bit too firm. The Old Fashioned cocktail itself was well made and complemented the meal nicely. The overall atmosphere leans lively and polished, which works for a date night, though it’s not the intimate, tucked-away vibe some might prefer. One downside: the tables are placed quite close together. Conversation carries easily, and you may feel as though you’re sharing space with the neighboring party. It didn’t ruin the evening, but it did chip away at the sense of privacy. Portions across the board lean generous, and the menu is encyclopedic. It’s the kind of place where everyone can find something, though you may spend a moment navigating the options. Splitting dessert is both sensible and fun. Service was cordial and efficient, and despite the initial confusion, our server kept things on track. The crowd skewed family-friendly during our visit, and like many busy restaurants today, screens were out in force, which can be a minor distraction depending on your tolerance. All told, The Cheesecake Factory succeeds at what it promises: a broad menu, polished chain-restaurant comfort, and standout desserts. I’d happily return for another date night—ideally snagging a table with a bit more breathing room—and I’d still recommend sharing a slice to finish. It’s a strong four-star experience, with a half-step to five if the seating felt less crowded.

Title: Ok, blunt and to the point I’ve lived in Phoenix for 17 months and genuinely love this city—its sunshine, energy, and pride. But my low rating hinges on a single, stubborn problem around Chase Field: rampant ticket scalping. Walking 100 feet from my parking garage means being bombarded by sellers shouting to buy their likely illegal tickets. State and city rules say these vendors should be confined to a designated spot off venue property. In reality, they roam freely, pulling people out of ticket lines and dragging them across the street, all in plain view of police. It’s chaotic, aggressive, and frankly embarrassing for a city that hosts visitors from everywhere. Beyond the unpleasant experience, it undercuts venue revenue and erodes trust in local enforcement. I’ve contacted my councilwoman and the city; so far, crickets. Phoenix can do better: enforce the law, corral the scalpers, and restore a safe, welcoming environment around our sports hubs. Clean it up, Phoenix—this is fixable, and it matters. Visitors deserve better now.

Living in LA, I’ve come to accept a hard truth: there’s no Raising Cane’s in California. When I lived in Denver, I practically camped out at the Fort Collins Cane’s, and that craving never left. So I did what any devoted chicken-finger fan would do—I drove four hours to Las Vegas for the box combo. Thanks, Friday traffic, for turning a three-hour jaunt into a six-hour odyssey. Silver lining: I’m dating someone in the area, so Cane’s runs now come with bonus quality time. I’m writing this mid-bite into my three-strip combo, and yes, I grabbed an extra Cane’s sauce I didn’t really need. Over-prepared? Happily. Yesterday, I nearly broke my streak, detouring to the Chic-fil-A in Upland because those are just as scarce around LA. And honestly, I don’t feel guilty about it. Both spots scratch the same itch, each with its own charms: Chic-fil-A’s tender chicken, waffle fries, side salad, and tart lemonade; Cane’s juicy strips, crinkle-cut fries, garlicky Texas toast, and sweet tea. They’re cousins in comfort food, different vibes, same satisfaction. Ultimately, it’s the ritual of the trek—the anticipation, the rarity—that makes the meal taste better. If you’ve got the time and the appetite, do yourself a favor: point your car toward Cane’s, queue up a playlist, and make a mini adventure out of it. Get some Cane’s in your belly. ASAP. You won’t regret the detour.

Having stayed at the Luxor before with a decent experience, I returned expecting the same—only to be thoroughly disappointed. We booked a suite advertised with an in-room Jacuzzi, but what we found was essentially a deep bathtub with jets that didn’t deliver a spa-like feel. The room’s condition was the bigger issue: curtains were visibly stained, the sort of set-in discoloration that suggests long-neglected spills, and there was a conspicuous hole in the wall, as if a fixture or safe had been removed and never repaired. Adding to the discomfort, I woke up with five spider bites on my arm. Amenities were surprisingly sparse for a “suite.” There was no refrigerator, coffee maker, hair dryer, or even a remote control for the TV. Overall cleanliness felt subpar, and the maintenance lapses created a sense of neglect that overshadowed any novelty of staying in the pyramid. Price is the only mitigating factor—we paid around $50 for a midweek night—but even at that rate, the experience didn’t feel like a bargain. I’ve stayed in budget motels that were in better shape. If you’re considering the Luxor, I’d strongly recommend avoiding the pyramid rooms unless you’re prepared to accept these issues. Front-desk assistance did not resolve our concerns.

Visiting the Starbucks inside the casino, my fiancé beelined for his beloved—if pricey—latte, ringing up at $6.75. As we approached the counter, I got a tickle in my throat and politely asked for a small cup of water, not a bottle, just a sip. The barista said it would cost $1. Charging for tap water felt petty, so I declined and grabbed a free cup on the casino floor instead. Beyond that, prices seemed inflated across the board: cakes I usually see at $2.25 were listed at $4.00. I understand casino markups, but the nickel-and-diming dampens the experience. If you’re set on Starbucks here, be prepared to pay a premium—and maybe make sure you’re winning at the tables before you order. Service felt transactional rather than hospitable overall.

Hmmm honestly? I've had better. We arrived as a group of four at 4:30 p.m., tossed our name on the list around five after waiting in line, and didn’t sit until 3.5 hours later. The upside: the pizzas are undeniably delicious—fresh ingredients, blistered crusts, balanced toppings—and the room hums with that coveted, top‐notch ambiance. The downside: service felt blasé, bordering on indifferent, as if attentiveness were optional in such a famous spot. We expected a wait, but this stretched patience past novelty. Oddly, our favorite part of the night was next door: drinks flowing, strangers bonding, everyone riding the shared anticipation of hearing their name called. Pizzeria Bianco remains an experience, a local legend with a great story, and worth trying once if you love pizza pilgrimages. Next time, though, I’ll skip the marathon queue and the shrug of service in favor of pleasant, non‐notorious comforts of Classic Italian Pizza. Sometimes the best pie is the one you enjoy hot—without hype.

Downtown Henderson isn’t the trendiest pocket of southern Nevada, and that’s part of its charm. It avoids the overrated, overpriced, and overcrowded scene, giving nearby residents a genuine sense of home. The Coffee House embodies that spirit. From the moment you step inside, it feels distinct from both indie spots and the corporate sameness of Starbucks or Coffee Bean, with a vibe that is warm and unmistakably local. As an avid coffee-shop goer, I seek out cafés for everything—schoolwork, business meetings, catching up with friends, or slipping into quiet solitude with a good book. I came to The Coffee House not knowing what to expect, and left delighted. My first visit was inviting, the kind of experience that reminds you why cozy, quaint cafés are worth finding. Owner Don greeted me at the door, calm, collected. You can tell he loves his work and treats the shop like an extension of his home. Unsure what to order, I appreciated his thoughtful questions and guidance. Rather than pushing whatever’s popular, he tailored recommendations to my tastes, a simple gesture that set the tone for the visit. Affordability is another standout. A large flavored macchiato costs less than five dollars—prices that undercut big chains without compromising quality. The space is comfortably sized, with plenty of tables, inviting reading chairs, and a window-facing bar with stools. Outdoor seating adds a sunny option on beautiful days, and the layout encourages both productivity and lingering conversation. Art lines the walls, and flyers spotlight local happenings; the shop doubles as a hub for community life. Locals supporting locals isn’t just a slogan here—it’s part of the atmosphere. Perhaps the most remarkable thing is the transportive feel: being there hardly seems like Henderson or Las Vegas. It’s unique, grounded, and refreshingly unpretentious. For a relaxed environment, thoughtful service, and consistently good coffee, The Coffee House is well worth a visit. It’s the kind of neighborhood café that makes you want to return, whether for an hour of work or a slow afternoon of savoring. Whether you’re a student hunting for dependable Wi‐Fi, a freelancer chasing focus, or a neighbor stopping in for a chat, you’ll find space, fair prices, and a drink matched to your palate. Sometimes, the best cafés are the ones that feel like home.

Excellent! This is now our go-to Mexican food restaurant. Every meal brings awesome chips and salsa; at dinner, add a side of exceptional beans.
