Total disappointment, especially from The Mirage, which I value. As a frequent Mirage guest and a fan of CPK in New York, I stopped in for a late-night takeout snack and hit a wall of indifference. The line was long, which I can forgive at that hour. What I can’t excuse is the service. The man with white sideburns who took my order was curt from the start—darting in and out, avoiding eye contact, and never cracking a smile. He pulled me aside to order, then walked off mid-sentence as I asked whether I could sit while waiting, leaving me stranded under a hundred stares. Not the Vegas hospitality The Mirage is known for. When my food was ready, he dropped the check and change without a thank-you and handed over a box. No bag. No basics. Dude, where’s my bag? For a brand I’ve trusted and a resort I respect, this was a letdown. Do better, Mirage CPK.

So far, I've been to this restaurant on three occasions: a brunch, a dinner and drinks with girlfriends. Holder has become a reliable go-to for me, especially for daytime and dinner plans. My first visit was a brunch for a mini class reunion, and the team couldn’t have been kinder. They handled late arrivals and no-shows with patience, kept our table relaxed, and never rushed us. The standout sips and bites set the tone: a rich, clearly not-from-powder hot chocolate; thick, perfectly crispy bacon; eggs that stayed warm and well-cooked; and generous refills of coffee and tea. It all added up to a satisfying meal at a very reasonable price point. Dinner confirmed the kitchen’s finesse and the front-of-house’s flexibility. We were a party of six with a reservation, including a lactose-intolerant diner, and staff took the time to consult the kitchen and navigate modifications without a fuss. My lobster ravioli with truffle and butter oil was beautifully executed—silky, aromatic, and indulgent—though the portion leaned small, as is often the case with richer pastas. I was still peckish and happily nibbled on some excellent fries from a friend’s plate. Dessert was a triumph: classic profiteroles with ice cream that hit all the right notes. I can’t speak to the final bill that night, but the experience felt polished. For Valentine’s Day drinks with girlfriends, the vibe was lively if a bit chaotic on the reservation front. We were told they weren’t taking bookings, only to be asked about a reservation on arrival. Still, we snagged a bar table with a fun view of date-night energy. The drink list is broad and compelling, though pricing is firmly on the high side. Service was brisk; appetizers, less inspiring. Two drinks and a shared entrée topped $20 for me. Bottom line: Holder shines for brunch and dinner—great service, well-executed classics, and a strong wine list. For drinks alone, consider your budget or look elsewhere.

I stayed at the hotel and tried both breakfast and lunch. Breakfast was a mixed bag: my french toast consisted of two battered slices—real maple syrup was a welcome touch—but the portion was small and the dish unremarkable. My partner’s egg white omelet fared better, accompanied by toast and potatoes, all well prepared. Lunch, unfortunately, was disappointing. The French onion soup was so salty it turned bitter, and the Caesar salad with a chicken breast tasted dominated by artificial lemon, with the chicken dried out and flavorless. The saving grace was the hot bread with fresh butter. Throughout, the atmosphere was pleasant and the service attentive, but based on the meals, dining here is worth skipping.

title: This should be called the porn hotel. Several of us were staying here for business. We came to the conclusion over lunch that this is less than desirable for a business traveller hotel, unless you are a porn producer. We visited for a work trip and were struck by the hotel’s pervasive darkness: dim bulbs everywhere, shadowy corridors, and moody rooms. The studio-style layout centers the bed in the middle, which might suit those seeking a theatrical, 360-degree feel, but it’s impractical for business travelers who need clear zoning and easy navigation. Finding the bathroom in low light is a hassle, and the closet is tucked away so discreetly it feels like an afterthought. Music pumps through common spaces at high volume, with a pulsing, club-like soundtrack that makes conversation and calls difficult. Combined, these choices create a distinctly adult-film vibe rather than a professional environment. If the aim is to court business guests, brighter lighting, quieter public areas, and more functional room plans would help tremendously. Alternatively, if the brand is intent on that retro, provocative theme, they could lean all the way in with playful touches—think 1970s-style mustaches on the bell staff and open-collar shirts with a relaxed, vintage flourish. As it stands, the hotel’s ambience is bold but misaligned with the needs of corporate travelers, who typically value clarity, comfort, and calm over theatrics. Consider practicality over mood lighting.

Probably one of the fewest Japanese restaurants that are decent in AZ. This spot isn’t phenomenal, but it’s about as good as it gets. Prices are fair, and the sushi holds up. The dining room gets tight and crowded when busy, so don’t expect a really relaxing dinner—better for catching up with friends.

Uhhhh, not a mile long..... not even close. This mall isn’t the mile-long behemoth some hype suggests, but its funky U-shaped layout can be surprisingly disorienting. It took a map, three gals, and 15 minutes just to track down H&M. Beyond the quirky navigation, it’s your standard, dependable mall—nothing groundbreaking, yet perfectly fine for killing time after dinner with a leisurely stroll. Stores are familiar, selection adequate, and yes, I still managed to buy something. If you’re nearby and need an easy indoor wander, it does the trick.

Locals have a cheeky nickname for this Denny’s, but the experience is standard-issue. There’s little reason to seek it out unless you’re already in Downtown Phoenix—say, after an event—when its proximity and late hours make it convenient. It’s the classic Denny’s draw: open late, reliably cheap, good for friends on tight budgets. Beyond that, there’s nothing special to warrant a detour. If you’ve got a neighborhood Denny’s, go there; otherwise, consider other options.

We’re longtime PF Chang’s fans, but this Strip location disappointed. Our usual hot and sour soup arrived scant on broth and overloaded with vegetables, we felt like we were chewing our soup. When we asked for a fix, the server said it couldn’t be changed because it’s prepared in large batches and “all the same.” The other two dishes were acceptable, but the overall experience fell short, especially for such a prominent venue.

Mmmmm delicious pizza at a great price. Stopped in while in town and was impressed from start to finish. Ordering is simple: choose your pie, pay, and swing back in 10–15 minutes for hot, bubbly goodness. I grabbed a medium 14-inch split half pepperoni, half mushroom for $9.10 ($7.50 plus $1.60 for toppings), and it was ready right after a quick walk. We snagged a seat outside—perfect spot to watch the world go by—and dug in. Ingredients were notably fresh, the cheese creamy and flavorful, and the crust nicely crisp without being too hard. They keep the menu focused on what they do best: pies, hoagies, and calzones. Excellent value, friendly efficiency, and consistently tasty slices. I’ll definitely be back for another.

Fresh yet forgettable sums up my recent visit to Baja Fresh. I ordered the mango chipotle chicken salad without the shell; it was fine, but the chicken portion felt tiny—maybe 2.5 ounces. The menu is surprisingly difficult to navigate if you’re watching calories: unless you choose a shell-less salad or a single taco, most items are 700+ calories. A veggie burrito clocks in at around 800. It’s been a long time since I last went, and this visit reminded me why. Decent ingredients, underwhelming value. I won’t be returning. Pricing and portions disappoint.

French food and I have a longstanding love affair. It’s my perfect way to dine: meat aplenty, but in demure, carefully considered portions—think a petite steak mignon, a silken duck leg confit, or a teasing sliver of foie gras. So when Blythe R of LunchQuest floated The Grain Store for lunch, I didn’t hesitate. The set lunch is a steal at £12.50 for two courses, especially when A La Carte mains hover around £23. On value alone, this kitchen signals confidence and generosity. My salmon starter arrived like a whisper: small, pristine, and utterly divine—less a course than a promise. It did exactly what a starter should: sharpen anticipation without dulling hunger. The risotto that followed was its glorious counterpoint, a bowl as generous as it was aromatic. As the steam rose, so did the white wine perfume, paving the way for plump wild mushrooms to do their woodland dance. Cheese threaded through the rice invisibly, present on the palate but never cloying or gluey. Blythe, who knows a good risotto when one lands, declared it excellent; I could barely finish it, yet finish it I did. Daytime ambiance is relaxed, with service that’s friendly, polite, and happily unobtrusive. The soundtrack leaned oddly toward Paolo Nutini—a quirk rather than a flaw—but the room itself feels date-ready, especially after dark. I’m already plotting a return by night to explore the full menu; I just need the right excuse. The Grain Store has that rare balance of value, craft, and restraint that keeps you thinking about the next visit even as you put down your fork. It all feels distinctly, delightfully French. The Grain Store, j’adore. Mais oui.

Title: I really only come here for work reasons. There was a conference being held here so I was forced to go, because I generally stay away from this hotel. I’ll give credit where it’s due: the rooms I’ve seen are gorgeous—sleek, stylish, and the kind of “divine” that inspires Instagram envy. But luxury without hospitality is just a stage set, and that’s where this property loses me every time. I can’t enjoy sleeping under the same roof where some of the most consistent rudeness I’ve encountered in Vegas seems to happen. Take a simple lost-and-found moment. I misplaced my keys; they were turned in—great. Yet the security manager proceeded to quiz me three separate times to describe them, each round more condescending than the last. Keys are keys; there’s only so much nuance to offer. Instead of feeling relieved, I felt talked down to, as if being a stressed guest needing help made me an inconvenience. The tone read less “we’ve got you” and more “prove you belong here.” Then there was the bar encounter, which sealed it. Standing at the counter, payment at the ready, I was treated like I was invisible—literally looked through—only for the bartender to spring into action for someone who stepped up behind me. It wasn’t about the tab; it was about being acknowledged. When a property is drenched in cash flow, perhaps a few top-shelf orders don’t matter. But for guests, being ignored matters a lot. The paradox is painful: a beautifully curated environment with a service culture that too often feels aloof, passive-aggressive, or indifferent. Hospitality should make you feel seen, welcomed, and valued—baseline, not a bonus. Until the attitude matches the aesthetics, I’ll continue to visit only when work demands it and spend my leisure dollars elsewhere. If you’re here for the scene and the rooms alone, you’ll likely be dazzled. If you need warmth, grace, and attentive care, look beyond the gloss. I don’t need perfection, but I do need love—and I haven’t felt it here.

My overall rating for this place is a "meh". Staff felt indifferent and unhelpful. Signage was lacking, making navigation frustrating. Patience seemed scarce, and customer service lacked warmth. Overall, a forgettable experience—serviceable, but far from inviting, memorable.

The food was good The food was good, but the service was shockingly inattentive. We were celebrating my wife’s birthday and hadn’t even reached the halfway point of our meal when the server dropped off the bill, without asking about dessert. She told us to use the table kiosk to pay and that we could order desserts there, but then never returned to check on us—no offer of napkins, no drink refills, no follow-up of any kind. It felt rushed and impersonal, more like fast food than a sit-down restaurant. With so many dining choices, basic hospitality matters. If staff are too busy to provide service, customers won’t return. Based on this experience, I’d recommend trying somewhere else.

One of Arizona’s original gastropubs, this cozy, small venue delivers standout beer and even better food. Traditional British comfort staples—shepherd’s pie, oggies, and hearty pasties—share the menu with flavorful twists like an excellent tikka masala. While dessert pasties don’t quite hit the mark, nearly everything else impresses. The atmosphere is intimate and comfortable, though limited seating makes it best for pairs or trios rather than large groups. Service is friendly and eclectic; expect servers with tattoos and piercings, which suits the pub’s character. The music skews away from classic English tunes, and somber coal miner photos lend a slightly heavy vibe, but overall this spot remains a must-visit for elevated pub fare and pints on tap.

One of my all time favorite spots! Descending into the basement bar at this beloved spot feels like entering a secret sanctuary: low-lit and fire-warmed, with easygoing music, comfortable bar stools, attentive service, and a convivial crowd. It’s the kind of room that turns a casual drop-in into a lingering evening. Regulars swear by the reverse happy hour, where $5 wines and $5 small plates make grazing irresistible. Don’t miss the tri-color roasted pepper bruschetta. Truth be told, the value extends beyond the HH menu. The Rokerij salad is a minor marvel—a luxurious wedge made even better with smoked turkey—and the bar pours a proper gin and tonic, complete with a generous measure and a 4.5-ounce bottle of Fever-Tree tonic. If HH isn’t your mood, brunch satisfies, and dinner can be downright celebratory. On a recent Sunday, a party of six enjoyed standout service (kudos to Jamie) and lucked into a special of spice-forward green chile stew alongside half-off bottles of wine. Plates shone across the table: succulent smoked turkey, green chile pork enchiladas courtesy of Richardson’s, and a top sirloin one diner declared the best she’d ever had. Warm, welcoming, and consistently delicious, this place rewards both loyalty and curiosity. If you skip it, you’re missing out.

I went here at 6pm on a Friday night to meet up with some friends This spot used to be a go-to after work because if you arrived before 6pm, they’d hand you a free bottle and mixers—an undeniably fun perk. Lately, though, it’s pivoted toward a high-end cocktail identity, which I was genuinely excited to try. Unfortunately, the reality fell short. I grabbed a seat at the bar and tried to catch the bartender’s eye for a solid 15 minutes. No luck. He was absorbed with a group of older gentlemen in suits who seemed intent on coaching him through their orders, insisting on adjustments and more alcohol after barely tasting (or just inspecting) their drinks. The bartender himself came off a bit spacy, repeatedly reaching for tequila when vodka was requested, pausing to stare at bottle labels for long stretches, and moving painfully slowly. The whole scene was oddly tense and, frankly, awkward. After being ignored long enough, I relocated to the lounge and waited for a cocktail server; she appeared only after my friends arrived. I ordered the Devil’s Whiskers, the Last Word, and a French 75—three gin classics I love. At $7 during happy hour, they were reasonably good, but nothing that stood out against the standards set by great cocktail bars in San Francisco or New York. The value was there; the precision wasn’t. Service added another layer of confusion: the cocktail waitress quoted me the full price initially, then rang the happy hour price without explanation. When I tried to order a second drink while nearly finished with my first, she responded with, “What? You didn’t like it?”—a strange interaction that made pacing the evening even more awkward. Maybe this place shines later at night, and perhaps I caught an off hour. But the move toward “high-end” cocktails needs to be matched by attentive, competent service and a smoother bar experience. Decent drinks at a good price are undermined by slow execution, inconsistent attention, and odd customer interactions. Overall, I left disappointed—and hoping they tighten up the bar program and service to match the ambitions on the menu.

I came in today because I wanted to buy a new flavor for my vape. I almost walked past the place because I was expecting a different atmosphere, the interior looks like a tropical island! - NO JOKE. Walking in felt like stepping onto a beach, with a bright, tropical vibe that immediately set the tone. I was greeted by an associate, told him I wanted to browse, and he invited me over to take a look at my device. To my surprise, he pointed out that my vape was a knockoff of the Joyetech eGo C-Twist, explaining that authentic models have a logo on the bottom—mine didn’t. I was genuinely astonished and appreciated the honesty. He was juggling another customer, so he asked a different associate to help me, and that handoff was seamless. The second associate was friendly, patient, and ready to field all my questions. I came for flavors, and he guided me through options he thought I’d like. I sampled a few, and while the selection was decent, the flavors didn’t pop the way they have at other shops. That said, this store clearly prioritizes customer service, and I get the sense they’re committed to improving. Part of the issue might be the tester setup: the tips felt extremely small, which made it hard to get a full sense of the taste. I kept wondering if larger tester tips would deliver a better, more accurate profile. In the end, I settled on menthol. As I headed out, I noticed the seating: no comfy couch area, just a round table with a few chairs in the corner. It’s functional, but not really a place to linger or relax. Maybe that’s intentional, but it was a slight letdown. Overall, I’m giving the store 3 stars. I rarely hand out 5s unless a business truly blows me away. Starting at 4 stars: minus one for meh flavors and no-bueno tester tips, minus one for the limited seating, plus one for phenomenal customer service and the standout atmosphere. With a better tasting experience and a more inviting seating area, this spot could easily climb. I’ll update my review after my next purchase.

I've been to this restaurant multiple times, but after this last experience, I am never going back. Having had both dine-in and takeout experiences here before, I walked in with my mother and grandmother expecting a solid, reliable meal. Unfortunately, what followed was a string of delays and missteps that turned a casual dinner into a lesson in how not to run a service shift. We were seated promptly and ordered an appetizer, but then waited roughly 20 minutes just to place our entrée order. The dining room wasn’t busy—four occupied tables by my count—but the staff seemed overwhelmed by a crush of takeout orders. With three to four servers on the floor and a manager present, it was surprising to see such visible disarray. Our appetizer didn’t arrive until 10–20 minutes after we’d ordered our meals, and the entrées took another 20–25 minutes beyond that. When we checked in about the delay, our server explained that the kitchen was backed up with takeout. As someone who has worked in restaurants, I understand balancing channels, but dine-in guests shouldn’t feel secondary to to-go tickets. The low point was a serious error with my entrée. I ordered the vegetarian squash curry, a dish I’ve enjoyed here before. What arrived looked off, and despite the server’s initial assurance, it turned out to be mango curry with chicken. Only after I pointed out the mistake did she acknowledge the mix-up. Between the kitchen’s pace and the lack of verification on a clearly marked vegetarian item, confidence waned fast. Compounding everything, we had to ask multiple times for water refills, and the overall attentiveness never recovered. Mistakes happen, but communication, ticket management, and basic table maintenance are nonnegotiable. I’ve previously left this restaurant satisfied. This time, the combination of slow service, misprioritized takeout, and a significant order error was enough to end my repeat visits. Dine-in guests deserve better.

This is my favorite place to dine every time I go to Vegas. Grand Lux Cafe is my go-to whenever I’m in Las Vegas, thanks to its prime locations inside both The Venetian and The Palazzo. There’s also a Grand Lux at the Beverly Center in Los Angeles for those who can’t wait until the next Vegas trip. While the food quality holds up in L.A., the service and overall atmosphere in Vegas feel a notch above—more polished, more energetic, and unmistakably indulgent. Start with the Grilled Pork Chops: a porterhouse-cut, glazed to a shimmering finish and served with mashed sweet potatoes, seasonal vegetables, and the restaurant’s own chutney. The meat is remarkably tender, and the glaze has that perfect sweet-savory balance that keeps you reaching for another bite. For something with a kick, the Crispy Caramel Chicken is a standout. Bite-sized, batter-crisped chicken bathed in a spicy Thai caramel sauce arrives tangled with mushrooms, onions, red chile peppers, garlic, and ginger, alongside a mound of rice. It’s craveable comfort with a playful heat—an instant favorite introduced to me by a friend who knows her way around a menu. If you’re drawn to bold, layered flavors, the Indochine Shrimp and Chicken is an absolute must. This fusion of Chinese and Indian influences brings together jumbo shrimp, tender chicken, onions, and sweet ginger in a vibrant sauce of curry, plum wine, and a touch of cream. Sun-dried cherries and apricots on top add a bright, unexpected accent that makes each forkful pop. I’ve heard nothing but praise for the Wiener Schnitzel—Austrian-style veal medallions with mashed potatoes and braised red cabbage—and it’s high on my list for next time. Dessert is where Grand Lux truly flexes. Beyond the full lineup of Cheesecake Factory cheesecakes, the Crème Brûlée Duo delivers silky perfection in classic vanilla and deep chocolate beneath a delicate sugar crust. And don’t skip the warm New Orleans Beignets with three sauces—generous enough to share with two to four people. Next time you’re in Vegas, make Grand Lux Cafe your first stop.

A great idea! Personal karaoke booths? Embarrass yourself with no one watching? Don’t forget the liquid courage! Private karaoke rooms rented by the hour might be the best invention since the mic itself: all the fun, none of the stage fright. This spot nails the formula with a huge song library that makes it easy to jump from classics to current hits, plus a menu of bites and beverages to keep the party rolling. I visited for a 12-year-old’s birthday, so I skipped some of the more adventurous dishes—think Buldogi pizza and spicy beef noodle soup—but the lineup suggests a kitchen that’s willing to play. And if all else fails, pair a round of fried crowd-pleasers with a cocktail or two and you’re golden. Even as someone who couldn’t carry a tune in a bucket, I had a blast cheering on the brave souls in our group. It’s a welcoming, low-pressure way to cut loose with friends. I’m already plotting my return—ready to grab the mic and happily wreck a few eardrums.

DO NOT TRUST THIS PEPBOYS! I went in after my car overheated and shut down mid-trip home. Before I could finish explaining, the man behind the counter instantly declared it was a blown head gasket and quoted roughly $2,000. Wanting to be sure, I authorized their $40 diagnostic. Two hours later, the same person called to reaffirm the head-gasket diagnosis and push me to schedule the repair. Instead, I declined and had a family member at an automotive shop take a look. The true issue was a cracked thermostat housing, which was fixed for about $200, parts and labor. When we called Pep Boys to ask how their block test supposedly proved a blown head gasket, the desk representative was curt and insisted he stood by “his mechanic’s” conclusion—even though he was the one who made the expensive call over the counter without even opening the hood. This experience felt less like careful troubleshooting and more like rushing to the priciest explanation. It wasn’t an isolated concern, either. Several friends have shared similar stories, including one who went in for a routine oil change and left with brake pads loose—a scary and unacceptable outcome. Based on what I experienced and what others have reported, I cannot recommend this location. The service struck me as careless, the communication dismissive, and the diagnoses questionable. If your vehicle has a problem, get a second opinion, demand thorough testing, and don’t be pressured into high-dollar repairs without clear evidence. My advice: steer clear of this Pep Boys.

Ordered online for carryout; they’d run out of pepperoni. Waited 25 minutes past pickup time with no discount, apology, or compensation. Frustrating and unprofessional. Not a way to treat customers or earn repeat business.

It was a hotel. The staff was friendly and seemed genuinely eager to accommodate, and the property was impressively clean from the lobby to the breakfast room to our guest room. Our room was simple yet spacious—lots of floor space, decent storage—and the blackout-style blinds kept the sun at bay. The bed was comfortable enough, though my girlfriend struggled to find a pillow she liked. The TV worked without fuss, and the complimentary Wi‐Fi, while reliable, was notably slow. Breakfast is free but unremarkable. Offerings rotate slightly day to day, which is appreciated, yet items were often understocked and the quality hovered around typical continental standards. The standout was biscuits and gravy, available only once during our stay. Otherwise, expect breads and bagels, a modest fruit selection, cereals, oatmeal, and a single wafflemaker that takes its time. Amenities include an outdoor pool we didn’t use and a compact fitness room with four cardio machines and a Bowflex‐style weight station—no free weights. The hotel sits on the outskirts of town, so convenience depends on your plans. For us, heading to Talking Stick for baseball, the location worked well, with quick highway access into Scottsdale proper and Phoenix. Overall, it didn’t wow us, but it didn’t disappoint. Clean facilities, courteous staff, and fair value balanced by a mediocre breakfast and sluggish Wi‐Fi. Solid for a straightforward stay if your priorities are location and cleanliness over deluxe amenities. We’d gladly stay again.
Great food and great staff! Service is fast and consistent, with reasonable prices for generous portions. I love this place and will be back.

I kept hearing about this establishment as a great breakfast spot, and didn't want to go to a watered down version of it with locations located throughout various casinos on the strip. So, we opted for the one about 6 miles off the strip. Don’t let the drive scare you off. The route is lined with vacant storefronts, and the destination sits across from a CarMax next to a vampire-themed club (yes, really), but push through the scenery and you’ll be rewarded. We rolled in around 8:30 a.m. on a Saturday, following the sage advice to arrive before 10, and found the dining room pleasantly quiet. The ambiance is mellow, the soundtrack easy, and the staff couldn’t have been warmer—menus landed the moment we sat, and waters were poured without prompting. The menu is a showstopper, vaulting well beyond standard breakfast fare into a realm of playful, hearty, and occasionally audacious combinations. Plenty of dishes elicited an audible “ooo” and “ahh,” but with a long outdoor day in Utah ahead, we aimed for fuel over novelty. I chose the Original HH Benedicts, while my husband went for the Tractor Driver Combo. The benedicts are an event: a crispy, hand-hammered pork tenderloin layered with market yellow tomatoes, spinach, and a rich barbecue cream, then crowned with scrambled eggs. All of this arrives perched on a massive biscuit with a side of mashed potatoes—more a topographical model than a plate, complete with a rosemary sprig standing like a tiny tree in your personal Red Rock canyon. Cutting into it means cleaving through five or six distinct strata, each adding texture and comfort. As a hollandaise loyalist, I was skeptical, but the barbecue cream works—smoky, silky, and unexpectedly perfect with the pork. It’s the kind of entrée two could easily split, though I managed about 75% solo in the name of hiking carbs. The Tractor Driver Combo is straightforward by comparison but no less dramatic in scale: a pancake roughly the size of a pothole, flanked by eggs and bacon. My husband is a pancake guy, and even he tapped out halfway to leave room for the eggs and bacon. Classic flavors, solid execution, and a portion that borders on comical—come ready. Portions here embody the excess that American breakfasts are famous (or infamous) for. If Man vs. Food needed a set, this would be it. Plan to share, or arrive hungry enough to take on the challenge. I’m already eyeing the chicken and waffles for a return visit, though that one will absolutely be a shared affair. Prices match the scale and the enjoyment: you get quality, creativity, and a mountain of food. Pair that with genuinely friendly service and a chill vibe, and it’s easy to call this spot legit. Arrive early, bring an appetite, and don’t be deterred by the drive—this off-strip original is worth the trek.

Eileen (I think that’s her name) was wonderful, and I absolutely love my dress. I also ordered two flower girl dresses and an ivory veil to match; be aware their ivory is very soft and reads almost white—great for true-white gowns, but not a match for gold or champagne tones. The shopping experience was pleasant, but I strongly recommend skipping their in-house alterations contracted through bridalxoxo. The seamstress I met was rude and quoted $400 for a simple one-point bustle and a 3/4-inch hem, then said she’d only steam my dress because of how much I’d be paying. That felt unreasonable and off-putting. In short: buy your dress here, but take it elsewhere for tailoring. Fit for a Bride provided far better service and value.

Returning to Binion’s after two decades was disheartening. Half the casino appeared shuttered, the energy muted, and the back lobby hawked bargain bin tee shirts on sad display. The once vibrant landmark felt tired, diminished, and struggling. Nostalgia met neglect, making our family meal feel more like a farewell than a reunion. I hope management revives its spirit, soon.

Dropped in for Sunday breakfast after hearing the buzz, my wife and I found the ordering setup a touch confusing at first. Once a friendly cashier walked us through it, the rest flowed. The dining room felt a bit free-for-all, but even at 10:30 a.m. we snagged seats quickly. The payoff was the food: my Commuter Sandwich—egg, bacon, and tomato stacked on a fresh-baked English muffin—was bright, salty, and satisfyingly fresh. My wife’s chicken sandwich delivered the same crisp, juicy appeal. I added a specialty latte that leaned sweet but still tasted great. The vibe is trendy and energetic; the music was on the loud side, yet we still relaxed and were in and out in under 45 minutes. Minor quirks aside, we’d happily return. Portions were fair and prices reasonable.

A great little find, this funky, fresh deli is tucked inside a shared space and serves playful, steamed bagel sandwiches with names like The Tonya Harding and the Federline. The steam treatment makes everything taste downright magical. I loved the Southend, paired with a crisp, tangy cucumber salad. Plenty of seating and an artsy, picnic-style vibe make it easy to linger. Casual, quick, and affordable, it’s a perfect lunch spot you’ll want to revisit—and bring friends.

I was extremely excited to finally visit China Wing, which to my knowledge is the closest place to me where Korean food is served. China Wing looks like it used to be a Long John Silver or similar fast food joint. To make it work, the Korean owners serve a range of American fast-food staples alongside a full Korean menu. You want the Korean menu, which features detailed descriptions and photos of most dishes—an inviting, low-stress touch for first-timers. On our visit, everything we ordered impressed: a crispy, savory seafood and scallion pancake; silky, sesame-kissed japchae; tender BBQ pork; and a comforting bibimbap, my personal favorite. The one letdown was the banchan selection. Typically, Korean meals come with several small side dishes, and here we received only two—tasty kimchi and crunchy pickled radish. In Atlanta, I’m used to four or five varieties, sometimes more. Still, given how flavorful the mains were, and how satisfying the banchan we did receive tasted, it’s hard to complain too loudly. The meal scratched my Korean-food itch and then some. China Wing’s hybrid concept and approachable menu make it a welcome addition for anyone curious about Korean cuisine in the area. I look forward to returning and exploring more of the menu, and I’m eager to check out other Korean spots around Charlotte. Super G Mart and Cho Wan Garden are next on my list. Where have you had Korean food in Charlotte? Recommendations are welcome. I’ll be back soon.

Good place for breakfast, but be prepared for a line—mine took about 30 minutes. I used the $39.99 buffet card, arrived late morning, and was seated closer to lunch. Desserts were a highlight, though the overall selection felt limited compared to other Vegas buffets. Small space, decent quality, and a pleasant experience overall. Enjoyable visit.

Delicious but on a pricey side of things. I chose this spot on the strength of other Yelp reviews and was greeted by a lively atmosphere, friendly staff, and a menu for adventurous eaters. Tapas lean pricey, but if you’re a foodie, the creativity and quality justify the cost. This is not a meat-and-potatoes destination; bring friends who enjoy bold flavors. I ordered the tuna tartare ($19) and crab cakes (around $13), both beautifully executed—fresh, balanced, and well-portioned. Cocktails sounded great but were steep, so we passed. One misstep: my friend’s fish ceviche skewed too citrus-forward and fell flat. Credit to our server, who offered candid guidance on standout dishes and ones to skip, which made the experience feel curated rather than upsold. Despite the ceviche, my overall meal was excellent. For curious palates and date-night vibes, it’s a recommended splurge.

Fresh from Seattle, we sought out Floyd's after reading glowing reviews, and it lived up to the buzz. Tucked away and a bit tricky to locate—our GPS kept sending us into the next mall—it's worth the small scavenger hunt. The room is compact, lively, and staffed by friendly, attentive servers. Though they don't take reservations, both visits we were seated quickly despite a full house. The chicken piccata was a standout: bright, tender, and perfectly executed. Salads are crisp, generously portioned, and ideal for sharing. Wine is offered by the glass only; our server wasn't sure about corkage, but the by-the-glass lineup satisfied. With well-prepared dishes, fair pricing, and a fun, bustling vibe, Floyd's delivers strong value. Once you find it, you'll want to return—we certainly will. Service remained upbeat throughout both meals.

Paris Las Vegas delivers solid value if you’re not chasing opulence. Our room was decent—clean and comfortable, but nothing fancy—which matched the great rate we scored. The real standout is the pool. It’s enormous, so even on busy days there’s space to spread out and actually relax. A live DJ spins by the water, lending a lively, unmistakable Vegas party vibe without feeling overwhelming. Best of all, the pool sits right beside the Eiffel Tower replica, creating a striking, only-in-Vegas backdrop for sunning and selfies alike. For an affordable stay with a fantastic pool scene, I’d happily book again—especially if the price is right.

Went to get dim sum with my classmates. Wasn't expecting anything comparable in SGV but service is much better and the food was good enough to not say bad things about this restaurant. However, it's very pricy compared to LA. My frd got a to go fried shrimp paste balls, 3 pieces and there goes her $5. Can't say how this compares to other dim sum places in Vegas since this is the only one I've been to. But overall, it's a good experience except for its prices of the dishes Went for dim sum with classmates and came away pleasantly surprised. I wasn’t expecting anything close to SGV, yet the service here was noticeably better—attentive and efficient. The food was solid, with flavors that satisfied, if not dazzled. Pricing, however, is steep compared to LA: my friend’s to-go order of three fried shrimp paste balls cost $5, which felt high for the portion. I can’t compare it to other Vegas dim sum spots since this is the only one I’ve tried, but overall it’s a good experience—just be ready for higher prices.

For the $18 ticket price, this aquarium was way smaller than I expected. At $18 a ticket, this aquarium underwhelms on size and scope. We rushed through exhibits expecting bigger showcases around the corner, only to hit the exit and wonder where the rest was. My 4- and 3-year-old nieces loved it—though the neighboring monorail wowed them just as much. Highlights include a serene jellyfish display and a hands-on stingray pool, but little else feels essential. Service didn’t elevate the visit either; an attendant chatted about the Lakers instead of engaging guests about the piranhas. If you’re nearby and need a short, kid-friendly diversion, it’s a fine, low-stress stop. Otherwise, save your time and money for a larger aquarium—or enjoy the hotel pool instead.

I'm usually not a fan of cake-based donuts—they’re too filling and heavy—but Crémy’s are an exception. Their donuts are outrageously good: moist, rich, and bursting with flavor, though a touch too sweet for my palate. Even so, they’re worth the indulgence. And if the fabled donut burger makes a comeback on the menu, do yourself a favor and order it. It sounds wild and a little wrong, but the sweet-savory mashup is unforgettable. Your taste buds will thank you, even if your conscience won’t.

FRAUD & DECEIT! AVOID PAYLESS - THEY WILL CHEAT YOU! After reading numerous Yelp reviews and experiencing it firsthand, I will never rent from Payless again. I rent cars frequently and, at the counter, I explicitly declined all optional insurance because I carry personal coverage. I initialed every required spot to refuse add-ons, and my printed agreement reflected no insurance. Three days later, when I returned the vehicle, I was stunned to find an extra ~$100 charged for insurance and “roadside service” I did not knowingly accept. In my view, the counter process is confusing at best and deceptive at worst, and customer service felt more interested in defending the charges than fixing them. Getting a refund proved an uphill battle, with policies and fine print used as a shield instead of a solution. If you still choose to rent here, scrutinize your contract line by line. Watch for the trap: after five initials to decline insurance, a sixth initial can authorize roadside service. This experience felt like bait-and-switch, and I won’t be back.

I went in with high expectations after glowing reviews, but left disappointed. The meal was very average—honestly, Denny’s would be just as good. The fried okra arrived bland, lacking any seasoning. The waffle was fine, but the chicken breasts were dry and flavorless. Even the sweet tea skewed oddly fruity rather than sweet. The chili tasted canned, with hot sauce simply dumped in. On the positive side, everything was served hot, and service was brisk. However, our check came fast and included items we never ordered. Prices felt steep: $37 for two at lunch without cocktails. After this experience, I don’t plan to return. Value and accuracy were disappointing overall.

Food 4 Less has been my dependable, one-stop grocery destination for years, covering everything from pantry staples to toiletries. I appreciate its broad selection, especially the diverse ethnic offerings, which makes shopping easy and interesting. Another plus: I don’t have to drive farther to a big-box store like Walmart for personal-care items, since this location stocks most of what I need. Compared with nearby markets, prices are consistently reasonable—you really do get solid value—and overall quality is reliably good. The notable exception is produce, which can be hit-or-miss, but most other departments deliver. The only persistent drawback is the parking lot, where solicitation is common and often from the same individuals; it can make arrivals and departures uncomfortable. Inside, though, the store remains well-priced, well-stocked, and convenient, which keeps me coming back despite that nuisance.

Amazing carpet cleaning—affordable, efficient, and friendly. They revived my carpets, giving them a new lease of life. Highly recommended for anyone needing refresh. I’ll use their services again. Excellent service overall.

Ok, I really like this spot. If you’re chasing the frostiest beers in Las Vegas, this is your place: mugs arrive so cold a delicate sheet of ice clings to the rim and blooms across the surface—big kudos. The kitchen is reliably solid, with tacos as the standout. My chicken tacos, glazed in teriyaki and brightened with pineapple, balanced sweet and savory beautifully and were genuinely tasty. The only thing holding it back from a perfect five stars is the ambiance; the room can feel a bit lifeless at times. Still, don’t let that deter you—come for the food, stay for an icy cold one.

Seemed very tame this year, but it's kinda nice to not walk into a festival/pride event without overextending my jaw tendons for the next six months. The drinks were good tho. This year’s event felt low-key and welcoming. A relaxed, family vibe drew many community members who don’t usually attend the flashier pride festivities. Drinks were good, and conversation came easy without the sensory overload. The only downbeat moment was stopping by the Human Rights Campaign booth, where staff noted limited funding to oppose Prop 102—a sobering reminder amid an otherwise pleasant day.

I ordered one of the sushi boats, and the sushi tasted like supermarket sushi. The boat itself was $26. They were probably one of the worst tasting sushi I've had in my entire life..... Fish was far from fresh, and the rice was definitely not sushi rice. My boyfriend liked their ribeye steak though so that was fine. Service was great. Just avoid their sushi at all cost..... Paid $26 for a sushi boat and regretted it. The fish tasted far from fresh, the rice wasn’t proper sushi rice, and the overall flavor resembled supermarket sushi—among the worst I’ve had. Thankfully, my boyfriend’s ribeye was tasty, and the service was attentive and friendly. If you go, avoid the sushi at all costs and stick to other items; your wallet and taste buds will be much happier.

I so wanted to give this a better review, and there are a lot of good things about this place, but recent changes have dulled what once made it special. Since last summer, management has implemented some controversial shifts, and you can feel the strain as they try to keep up with increased customer demand. Happy hour used to be the star attraction: a broad, well-executed menu of Italian bites and solid drinks at genuinely attractive prices. Lately, though, those prices have climbed—nearly doubled in some cases—and small but meaningful amenities have disappeared. It’s the restaurant equivalent of noticing your cereal costs more and the box has shrunk. That’s not a great feeling for loyal regulars. Take the zuppa di clams. It was once a standout—briny, garlicky, kissed with white wine—and came with Italian bread perfect for sopping up the broth. Now the bread is an upcharge, the portion feels smaller, and my last bowl arrived with rubbery, overly salty clams. When a signature dish slips, it’s hard not to wonder what else has changed behind the scenes. Ambiance has never been this spot’s strong suit. The layout is wide open, with tightly spaced tables and little in the way of intimate or elegant seating. When the food was excellent and priced right, the cafeteria-style setup felt intentional and even charming in its simplicity. With prices inflated and quality uneven, that same setting starts to feel more like a compromise than a choice. I genuinely hope they course-correct. When this place opened, it was a breath of fresh air—a dependable, delicious option that didn’t ask you to overthink or overspend. Scottsdale diners have plenty of alternatives, and this particular location has seen more than a few concepts come and go. If management listens to feedback and restores value and consistency, there’s still a path back to what made it great. For now, though, there’s not as much to love here as there once was.

Bankok Balcony never disappoints me. Bangkok Balcony never disappoints. I’ve been there a few times, and it consistently lives up to my expectations. We frequently visit Silk Elephant too, and taste-wise they’re quite comparable, especially when it comes to their curries. My go-tos are the red curry, pad Thai, and Thai fried rice. Recently, we tried the fried fish in chili sauce; at $18 it’s a bit pricey, but the fish was beautifully cooked—tender, flavorful, and absolutely delicious. I’m also a big fan of their Thai iced tea. The seating is comfortable, and the ambience strikes a nice balance between trendy and casual. Overall, a reliably good Thai spot in Squirrel Hill.

Yum, Yum, Yum—need I say more? The Napoleon, lobster tail, and cannoli are irresistible; choosing is impossible, so I get them all. I tried the gelato last visit and have had better—save the $5 and pick a pastry. The baba ricotta is fantastic, truly.

Craving burgers, we arrived just before the Friday lunch rush and ordered two regular burgers cooked pink, one vegan burger, and truffle fries. Both beef burgers arrived so undercooked they were inedible; the vegan patty was cold. Even after sending them back, the fixes disappointed. Service then crawled to a halt. Deeply disappointed—won’t return.

Alpha Phi Sigma Bowling Social vs. Criminal Justice Club We set out to stage a friendly, competitive bowling challenge—Alpha Phi Sigma versus the Criminal Justice Club—only to be stymied before the first frame. By 7:15 p.m., every lane at the Gold Coast was tied up with league play, and despite a cashier’s offer to call The Orleans, we decided not to relocate. It was an immediate reminder that this place is popular with leagues and that calling ahead isn’t just smart; it’s essential. The Gold Coast Bowling Center is exactly what you’d expect from the Gold Coast: sprawling, dated, and aching for renovation. There are about 70 lanes, plus a pro shop, cafe, full bar, and a kids zone arcade. The pro shop can service your bowling balls, which is convenient for regulars and league bowlers. The cafe leans divey, serving slices of pizza, hot dogs, fries, nachos with bagged cheese, chips, and fountain drinks—basic fuel at budget prices. The bar is the designated smoking area, and it feels like it; expect a haze and a crowd coasting toward closing time. Bartenders were fine but clearly counting down the minutes. No obvious happy hour specials, but prices were reasonable: around $4 for a glass of wine and a little over $3 for a bottle of Heineken. Practical touches abound, even if they’re not glamorous. There are plenty of lockers likely available to league members for a monthly fee. Forgot your socks? A vending machine has you covered for $3 or $4. House balls are plentiful, with a wide range of weights, colors, and hole sizes, and shoes are available with game purchase. Staff sprays disinfectant in the rentals after each use, but if you’re squeamish about shared shoes, that detail only goes so far. Technology isn’t the strong point. The monitors at each lane are crying out for an upgrade, though their worn look does match the overall old, slightly grungy vibe of the venue. On the plus side, the lanes themselves are smoke-free—just steer clear of the bar if you’re sensitive. Service is hit-or-miss. One staffer was friendly; the rest felt grouchy and checked out. Don’t come for hospitality. Do come for value: it’s an inexpensive spot to gather a group and have fun, provided you plan ahead. Before you haul a crowd over, call to confirm league schedules and lane availability—or be prepared to pivot to another nearby alley. For price and nostalgia, the Gold Coast delivers. For polish and service, look elsewhere.

I am not sure why so many of these are going out of business, but this was a solid lunch. This spot delivered a solid lunch. The new chicken sandwich, layered with pepper jack and Ortega green chiles, shines on parmesan sourdough that’s genuinely excellent. Generous avocado adds richness. Fries, however, fell flat—forgettable and underwhelming. Service was friendly and impressively quick, smoothing the rough edges. For straightforward, satisfying flavors and speed, it’s worth a visit, even if not every bite excels overall.

This was my second time at Encore Beach Club, and enjoyed it both times. We had a day bed for my friend's bachelorette party and was well worth it. Huge and clean pool, great DJs and music, food and alcohol were good, staff was great! Can't wait to come back in June! Encore Beach Club continues to impress. Our daybed for a bachelorette was worth every penny—comfortable, shaded, and perfectly situated. The pool is huge and spotless, DJs keep the energy high, and drinks and food hit the spot. Staff were attentive and friendly throughout. Already counting down to our June return. Can't wait.

If I was only rating based on the beef noodle stew (which comes in both normal and spicy variety), I would have definitely given this place 5 stars. Only reason I brought it down to four was because the cold dishes we ordered on the side were atrocious. It was so evidently clear that they sat in the fridge for ages that I preferred to leave them untouched. This unmarked spot—look for the Pig mascot from Journey to the West—hides a bowl of beef noodle stew worth seeking out. The broth is deeply layered, fragrant with spices and herbs, and the spicy version turns that complexity into a bold, satisfying kick without overwhelming the palate. Tender beef, toothsome noodles, and an aromatic heat make it a standout comfort dish that lingers in the best way. If your craving is centered on beef noodle stew, you’ll struggle to find a more rewarding bowl. Unfortunately, the cold side dishes were a stark contrast: clumped together like an ice block, clearly long-refrigerated, and needing a fork to pry apart because chopsticks were too flimsy for the job. Stick to the stew—especially spicy—and you’ll leave happy.

Endroit charmant et bien situé en bordure du canal Lachine, avec une jolie petite terrasse offrant une vue sur l’eau et de superbes couchers de soleil. Le personnel est sympathique et le service, correct. Côté menu, certains items paraissent trop chers au regard de la qualité et des ingrédients. Ma salade repas à 9,00 $ n’était pas mauvaise, mais composée d’éléments très basiques (laitue, tomate, fromage râpé) dont le coût semble minime. En revanche, le gaspacho était incroyablement délicieux et vaut le détour. J’y retournerai volontiers, mais je ferai une croix sur les salades. L’ambiance reste très agréable, globalement.

Seeking shelter from a rainy Edinburgh morning, we ducked into Deacon’s House for breakfast. The setting is charming, steeped in the lore of the Deacon—once a respected cabinetmaker with a decidedly darker side—and the space retains the feel of a historic workshop. Service was friendly enough, and the coffee was a pleasant surprise: robust, well-balanced, and just what a dreich day calls for. The standard breakfast, however, missed the mark. Eggs arrived scrambled but strangely watery, as if they’d been held too long or undercooked; bacon and sausage were passable but lacked the crispness and snap that make a classic fry-up sing. Everything was edible, but only just, and the plate felt more functional than satisfying. In a city where it can oddly be difficult to find a truly great morning fry-up, this one didn’t change the narrative. Go for a warm cup and the atmospheric backstory; look elsewhere if you’re chasing a standout breakfast.
Great, family-owned barbershop offering excellent cuts at affordable prices. Spotlessly clean, friendly service, and welcoming atmosphere. I'll definitely return and recommend.

I have been twice, once with friends and once with family. Each visit left me disappointed. Service was consistently slow, and staff bordered on rude—whether it’s an attempt at “Italian attitude” or just indifference, it doesn’t land. Drinks took 10 minutes to arrive, noodles came out cold, and a pizza took an unforgivable 45 minutes. The biggest letdown, however, is how unfriendly the place feels toward families. Serving chicken fingers without ketchup is baffling, and there were no crayons, paper, dough, or any simple activities to keep kids occupied. In Ocotillo, most restaurants welcome children with coloring sheets or word searches; this spot stands out for ignoring that norm. I gave them a second chance because we’re always hunting for great pizza, but the experience didn’t improve. If this restaurant wants to thrive, it needs to step up: faster, warmer service, hot food served promptly, and thoughtful touches for families. Until then, I’ll look elsewhere for good pizza and a welcoming atmosphere. That’s a real missed opportunity.

If you’re craving fish tacos, this spot delivers fast. Come Tuesdays after 2:30 p.m. for half off their classic fish taco, but do remind the cashier—the register didn’t automatically apply mine, and I paid $8. The shrimp verde taco is flavorful; I’d order it on corn tortillas for better texture. They’re promoting a langostino burrito that sounds tempting, yet the fish tacos remain the reliable stars: generous, crispy, and satisfying. Service is surprisingly friendly, and this location feels a touch more formal than the usual grab-and-go, making it a pleasant place to sit, snack, and cure a taco craving.

My first visit delivered a respectable lunch. The sandwich was genuinely delicious—well-balanced and satisfying—while the tomato basil bisque was smooth and enjoyable. Nothing dazzled, but nothing disappointed either. It’s the kind of spot where you’ll get a good, dependable meal without the afterthought cravings. Solid value for a casual bite, but not a destination meal—an overall experience.

I haven’t had much Caribbean food, so I decided to try this neighborhood spot and leaned on the server’s recommendation: coconut curry shrimp and scallops with white rice and plantains, plus a side of jerk wings. The coconut curry was quite tasty—distinct from the Indian-style coconut curries I’ve had—and the shrimp were cooked nicely. The standout was the scallops, seared just right and wonderfully tender. Where the dish fell short was balance and value. The portion was dominated by peppers and onions, with relatively few shrimp and scallops. Everything tasted good, but for a seafood entrée priced in the mid-teens, I expected more actual seafood. As it was, the plate felt a bit padded with vegetables, echoing other reviews that mention it being over-priced for what you get. The jerk wings delivered big flavor: smoky, aromatic, and an explosive heat in the sauce. They were enjoyable, yet ultimately too spicy for me to order again, though heat seekers will likely love them. Service was friendly and helpful, and I appreciated the guidance in navigating the menu. I’m interested in returning to try the lunch buffet, but the timing doesn’t line up well with my schedule. Overall, a flavorful introduction to Caribbean fare with room for improvement on portion value and consistency.

I always seem to crave a gyro when The Greek Isles is closed, which tells you how much this place has its hooks in me. When I time my cravings right, it’s my first choice for takeout. I haven’t dined in yet, but I’ve devoured plenty of to-go orders, and nothing calms the savage beast like their slow-cooked meats wrapped in a pillowy pita. One day I’ll make it in early enough to sit down and soak in the uniquely decorated space that still feels proudly mom-and-pop. Until then, I’m sticking with the killer food that keeps me coming back. If you’re like me and once you find “the thing” nothing else will do, this is that spot. Do yourself a favor: go Greek.

I can't recommend her enough—sweet, skilled, and delivers what you want After moving to the neighborhood, a quick Google search led me to her chair—and after that first visit, I knew I’d found my stylist. She’s a joy to work with: friendly, attentive, and responsive. Scheduling is effortless via text or call, and she gets back promptly. I wear a very short pixie cut—the kind that can go wrong fast—and she nails it. She checks in at each step, making sure I’m comfortable with length, shape, and texture. The result is polished, flattering, and easy to maintain. She’s truly sweet, talented, and reliable. I recommend her without hesitation to anyone in Las Vegas.

The idea of a bar with a pool is a great idea. However Spanish Fly could do better. Spanish Fly nails the poolside bar idea in theory, but execution differs day to night. On two visits, the nighttime no-swimming rule pushed everyone onto the narrow deck, turning simple circulation into an obstacle course. It feels crowded, and walking around the pool is tricky when you have to hug the edges. The pool itself looks great, which makes the restriction disappointing. Daytime is better. The menu is impressively large with plenty of food options, and the drink list has range. I’m glad they kept the ginormous cocktails Drift made famous—still fun and shareable. The vibe leans tattoo-forward; it can feel like you need a tribal sleeve to fit in. The place gets packed, so without a day bed or cabana, arrive early to claim a spot. Food and drinks are okay but a bit overpriced for what you get, and service was just okay. Overall, Spanish Fly is a solid spot for people-watching, best enjoyed during the day, and more frustrating at night.

Beehiv delivered a straightforward midweek pub experience. The bartender corrected my “beer” inquiry with a firm “we only carry ales,” which set a slightly awkward tone, but service remained competent. The fish and chips were fine—crispy batter, decent portion—while the mushy peas landed in the “good, not great” zone. Atmosphere on a Wednesday was unsurprisingly subdued; still, about a third to half of the tables were occupied, more than neighboring spots that night. Beehiv isn’t a destination for revelatory food or craft tap exploration, but if you’re nearby and craving classic pub staples, it gets the job done without fuss. Solid, if unspectacular. Prices are reasonable and portions satisfy for most appetites.

Walking in, they played a Kenny Loggins track that instantly transported me back to Memphis ’87. Kenny lit up the stage, and meeting him afterward proved he’s as genuine as his music—passionate, warm, real. That same spirit echoed here: friendly staff, good vibes, and a soundtrack that hits the heart. Simple, memorable, worth returning again soon.

For a man who claims to love Panang curry as much as I do, how on earth did I resist their special of softshell crab panang curry? I can totally see why this place has gotten the high reviews, it's cozy, the service is good, and they even have an elderly Thai woman working in the kitchen (can't get much more authentic than that)! Walking into this warmly lit, cozy dining room, I immediately understood the high marks: friendly servers, a hum of conversation, and the charming sight of an elderly Thai cook at the wok promised comfort and authenticity. I nearly ordered the softshell crab Panang curry special—catnip for a Panang devotee—but let the menu talk me into the “signature” mixed seafood Pad Thai. The regret set in as soon as the plate landed. The seafood didn’t look or smell promising, and the shrimp were, frankly, inedible. A pungent, off-putting note scared me away from the rest of the large white “seafood” chunks. It’s a shame, because the baseline flavors were otherwise in the right neighborhood: tamarind tang, a hint of sweetness, springy noodles, crisp bean sprouts. Unfortunately, my medium spice request delivered zero heat, leaving the dish flat instead of lively. Despite that misfire, I’d return. The room has heart, the service is solid, and I’m convinced the kitchen can shine—especially with the Panang curry, which I’ll order next time. My advice: skip the mixed seafood Pad Thai and lean into the curries or a simpler noodle plate with chicken or tofu. There’s clearly a good restaurant here; it just needs better seafood sourcing and a bolder hand with spice. Prices felt fair and portions generous, adding to the appeal.

Everyone in Vegas, local or traveler, should make time for Monta Ramen. I’m a notoriously hard grader—most of my Yelp reviews land at three stars, with a rare four—but Monta earns a full five. Plan to arrive right at opening if you want to skip a wait; the shop isn’t in the most prominent spot in the center, and lines form fast. Service is efficient: our bowls arrived in about ten minutes. Order the specialty tonkotsu ramen. The noodles, while packaged, are springy and satisfying, and the roasted pork—thinly sliced yet tender and deeply seasoned—melts into the broth. Toppings of mushrooms, bamboo shoots, and green onion bring texture and brightness, but the true star is the soup stock: rich, silky, and remarkably well-balanced, the kind of broth that ties every element together and keeps you sipping to the last drop. At $7, the price feels exactly right—excellent value without cutting corners. For those comparing, Sora Ramen is the closest contender. Sora offers thicker meat, a bit more broth, and slightly more generous toppings, but Monta’s noodles and, crucially, its soup stock are superior; the overall experience sits on a different level. Subsequent visits confirmed the first impression. On my second trip, the mini mentaiko bowl was a savory, satisfying side. By the third visit, the consistency remained impressive. In a city overflowing with options, Monta Ramen stands out—and stands up—every single time. Highly, highly recommended indeed.

Grossly over priced! Extremely slow and incompetent. I visited Sambalatte for a simple tea and a basic coffee, expecting prompt service at a neighborhood café. Instead, I encountered disorganization and indifference. The manager informed us they were out of brewed coffee, offered my girlfriend a half cup to sip, and promised a fresh pour when the new pot finished. That promise evaporated. She repeatedly walked past us at the end of the counter as we waited, even while staff cranked out half a dozen specialty drinks for other guests. When we finally stopped her to ask about the coffee, she looked baffled, as if we were interrupting, and offered neither apology nor explanation. Eventually, a cup appeared—handed over without a word—and we were left with the impression that basic hospitality is optional here. My tea was fine, but nothing special, and the prices felt steep for such inattentive service. If remembering a simple coffee order is this hard for management, something is seriously off. This was my first and last visit. Sambalatte may shine at crafting complex drinks, but it failed spectacularly at the fundamentals: attentiveness, communication, and value. For a reliable cup and respectful service, I’ll stick with Starbucks or Panera. Cafés should make guests feel welcome, not invisible and overcharged. Consider other options nearby.

I just returned from my first trip to Las Vegas, and on my first night there, I knew I wanted to check out China Poblano. (Having gone to school in DC, I'm familiar with Jose Andres and his great food.) With my friends' flight landing after mine, I slipped into a solo seat at the bar around 8:30 on a Saturday night. Service was attentive and warm without hovering, impressive given the crowd. Food arrived promptly yet never felt rushed. The Arrachera con Salsa Molcajete was the star: tender, deeply seasoned steak bathed in a smoky, vibrant sauce. At my server's suggestion, I ordered a side of fresh, house-made tortillas and happily assembled DIY fajitas: simple, perfect, and satisfying. I paired it with a sea salt margarita; unusually foamy, but refreshing. China Poblano delivers on Jose Andres' reputation for inventive, flavor-forward cooking and an engaging experience. My only hesitation is value. Portions lean toward small plates designed for sharing, and costs add up faster than you might expect, especially if you're sampling across the menu. I left pleased and well fed, but with a bill that felt a touch steep. Four stars, with enthusiasm.

Pretty good price for a hotel room right next to the Las Vegas strip. Only paid $70 a night and stayed here for a week. Perfect for a family of six. Got the 2 bedroom one. Kitchen has everything we need. Spacious rooms, living room had a pull out bed under the couch, and downstairs you could get complimentary popcorn, dvd movies, books, and coffee maybe even more. This property offers impressive value and space just off the Strip, without the constant casino bustle. At $70 per night for a week, it’s a budget-friendly choice that doesn’t skimp on comfort. The two-bedroom suite easily accommodated our family of six, thanks to a convenient pull-out bed in the living room. A full kitchen with cookware and utensils made it simple to prepare meals, and the rooms felt clean and generously sized. Downstairs amenities were a pleasant surprise: complimentary popcorn, DVDs, books, and coffee gave the stay a welcoming, family-oriented touch. The main drawback during our August 6 visit was the construction directly in front of the hotel, which eliminated self-parking and made valet mandatory. Unfortunately, the valet service became the most frustrating part of the trip. Vehicle retrieval times were extremely long—one evening took about 1 hour and 20 minutes even after calling ahead. Additionally, staff interactions with our car felt intrusive, with settings adjusted and controls touched before we had even stepped out, undermining trust. While construction can explain some delays, the overall service did not feel responsive or respectful and noticeably disrupted our plans. If you’re visiting while construction continues, budget extra time for the valet and keep your valuables with you. For families seeking space and convenience near the Strip, the rooms and price are excellent. With improved valet operations or the return of self-parking, this would be an easy five-star stay; as is, the accommodation shines, but the valet issues hold it back.

I arrived excited and left satisfied, if not awestruck. The standout was the dedicated gluten-free menu—such a relief compared with the usual “let me check with the kitchen.” Unfortunately, our seating dampened the glow: despite a reservation we were placed beside the bus station while a prime window table sat empty throughout the meal. Service, however, was exemplary—attentive without hovering. Wines by the glass were enjoyable but, as others note, priced a notch too high. The food was very good across the board. My spaghetti with tomatoes and basil, often hailed as “amazing,” was fresh and comforting, though no better than the version I make at home. The creamy polenta with mushrooms made a terrific starter, and the rest of the table was pleased with their plates. Dessert stole the show: a flourless chocolate cake my husband practically inhaled, complete with closed eyes and blissful murmurs. Overall, a solid choice with room for small tweaks.

I didn't have the highest of expectations for the Luxor, but it failed to even meet the bar that had been set so low. My friend and I checked in around 1 a.m. on a Friday night/Saturday morning, and the process was straightforward enough. We went straight to bed, thinking we’d judge the place in the light of day. Unfortunately, morning brought a much different picture. When I stepped into the bathroom, the floor was wet. Assuming someone had showered, I asked my friend; they hadn’t. A second look revealed the source: water was dripping from the light fixture above. A leak like that is not just inconvenient—it’s a safety concern. We called the front desk and were told an engineer would come up to fix it. After an hour of waiting without a visit or update, we called again. This time, the solution was to switch rooms, but the catch was that we had to go down to the desk to retrieve new keys. My friend went, and the experience there made a bad situation worse. The clerk was curt and unapologetic, offering no acknowledgment of the disruption or the hazard we’d reported. We weren’t nitpicking; the bathroom floor was soaked within minutes. We weren’t asking to be waited on hand and foot, just hoping for basic courtesy and prompt attention. Leaks happen. What shouldn’t happen is indifference. The lack of empathy and the dismissive tone from the staff turned a fixable problem into a frustrating stay. Sincerity and a simple “we’re sorry” would have gone a long way. Given the poor response and attitude, it’s difficult to recommend the Luxor. Even with low expectations, guests deserve safety, responsiveness, and respect—none of which were meaningfully provided here.

WORST SERVICE IN HISTORY at the Scottsdale location I love their food, but the disrespect and incompetence make it not worth it. Servers botch my order every visit—how is sausage over bacon hard? Staff ignore customers walking in, leave them waiting, then eventually seat them or casually announce they’re closed. The chaos is consistent, unprofessional, and exhausting. Until management fixes training and basic courtesy, I’ll never return. Do not eat at Over Easy Scottsdale.

Super cute lounge with a playful twist: I heard you can write on the couches and see it pop up on the walls. The ladies’ special was a hit—free pink vodka, yes please! We danced for about thirty minutes, soaked in the vibe, then hopped to another club. It’s an ideal spot to kick off the night, especially if you snag the drink specials. Before you go, snap photos out front with the big REVOLUTION letters—they’re Insta-ready and memorable.

Lord, please bring one of these to New York! This spot serves awesome, top-notch sandwiches: smaller in size, but perfectly paired with the best, velvety tomato soup I’ve had. Quality is high, flavors pop, and prices are refreshingly reasonable, especially by Las Vegas standards.

Our neighborhood coffee house is a gem—spotless, friendly, and ultra-convenient with a speedy drive-thru. Consistently great drinks and service. My only gripe: popularity leads to sell-outs, especially during holidays. Stock up more; we’d hate to miss favorites.

Everyday Noodles was a breath of fresh air for me, coming from a city with very very few authentic AND delicious Chinese restaurants. Aside from one miss—the minced pork noodles, which oddly tasted like liver—our table was thrilled. The potstickers were fantastic, arriving fused together in a crisp, golden raft straight from the pan. My won ton noodles packed real heat (finally!), and a friend’s cold sesame noodles with chicken stole the show: a bright peanut-lime dressing that clung to springy noodles and tender chicken. The highlight, though, is the spectacle. They make the noodles right in front of you, and when the kitchen ran out, two noodle-makers stepped up, thumping huge ropes of dough on the counter like culinary drummers. It’s dinner and entertainment in one, with quality that justifies the buzz. For fresh, hand-pulled noodles and lively flavors, Everyday Noodles delivers—and then some.

Chose this place to get out of the insane crowds in this horrible airport and sit down to eat. I ordered a BBQ chicken with bacon dish that was just okay—heavy, a bit greasy, and forgettable. My SO’s sandwich was adequate but nothing special. Most items felt microwaved or pre-packaged, and the iced tea machine was out of order, which didn’t help. On the plus side, service was friendly and attentive. Prices were predictably steep, but that’s airport dining. Overall, a convenient but underwhelming stop.

While never understanding the whole cake pop and cupcake trend that seems to be growing, I do enjoy a cupcake on occasion. They are a nice treat in a small package. Mind Over Batter seems to have perfected the cupcake. I knew about this place before because I used to work with one of the owners at a previous job, but did not decide to check it out until I purchased a groupon. Mind Over Batter makes a compelling case for the cupcake’s enduring appeal. Spurred by a Groupon, I finally stopped in and, between my husband and me, sampled at least eight flavors. Across the board, the cakes were impressively moist, the flavors well-defined, and the presentation inviting without feeling gimmicky. It’s evident the bakers care about texture, balance, and freshness. My standout is the Pink Cadillac: a strawberry cupcake capped with buttercream that tastes like peak-season berries. The cake is tender and fragrant, and the frosting—while rich—delivers that nostalgic strawberry shortcake vibe. I prefer a lighter hand with frosting because it can skew sugary; for me, half as much would be perfect. Even so, this cupcake is one I could eat every day without complaint. Close behind is the toasted coconut: lush white cake, creamy frosting, and a crown of nutty, crisp flakes that add contrast and aroma. I find myself practically drooling just thinking about it. My husband’s favorites are the Reese with a spoon and red velvet. The former marries chocolate cake with peanut butter frosting and a sprinkle of chocolate-peanut butter candies—decadent without being cloying. The red velvet is classic, with that subtle cocoa note and a balanced tang that keeps it from feeling heavy. Not every flavor hit my personal sweet spot; chocolate chips in the chocolate batter aren’t for me, though others might enjoy the extra texture. Pricing feels fair compared to similar bakeries: under $3 per cupcake and less than $2.50 per cake pop. The cake pops are fun but, for my palate, the frosting is too sweet; I’ve only tried them once. Beyond the pastries, the value of supporting a local business owned by genuinely great people matters, and Mind Over Batter makes that choice easy. If indulgence has consequences—hello, tighter pants—this is the kind of place worth returning to once the scale resets. Next on my list is the lemon cupcake, which looks bright and irresistible. Until then, Mind Over Batter remains my go-to for a small, perfect treat.

Stopped by the store with some friends while walking the strip. It's very attractive with all the colors that you're drawn to go inside. On a stroll down the strip, we wandered into this candy boutique, lured by its rainbow glow and glossy displays. The merch is eye-catching—blinged-out $25 lollipops with plastic caps to save for later, novelty designs, and celebrity-themed options; I liked the Kim Kardashian one. The caramel apple decorations were stunning, almost too pretty to eat. Prices felt steep, and the vibe leaned more showcase than snack stop. Customer service was okay; the staff didn’t have the warmth you’d expect in a candy shop. I’m not sure I’d buy anything here, but as a quick pop-in for photos and window-shopping, it’s a cool place.

Arriving for Saturday brunch on a wave of hype, this buffet’s first impression certainly dazzles: the decor is gorgeous, polished, and inviting. But once past the aesthetics, the experience settles into something far more familiar—competent, occasionally good, yet rarely distinctive compared to other average Strip buffets. Expectations ran high, and while there were highlights, they didn’t consistently rise to the premium price or the buzz surrounding the venue. Made-to-order tacos were arguably the coolest feature, but the perpetual line dampened the appeal. For anyone spoiled by Southern California’s abundant, excellent Mexican food, the execution here feels more novelty than standout. The meat spread promised more: a generous variety of sausages, whole hens, smoked brisket, and pork ribs. The brisket delivered on flavor, but the ribs on this visit were noticeably overcooked, with a rubbery texture that undercut the selection’s potential. To their credit, service shined; the attentive server clocked the uneaten ribs and politely asked what went wrong, demonstrating genuine care. Surprisingly, the Asian section stole the show. Delicate xiao long bao, comforting blackened chicken soup, and a trio of noodle options—pho, tonkatsu ramen, and udon—offered breadth and warmth. Kalbi appeared without its natural partner, kimchi, but the stir-fries and Chinese BBQ brought energy: peking duck, char siu pork, and BBQ pork ribs were welcome sights. The sushi, however, landed squarely in the “meh” category: serviceable, not memorable. Away from the hot stations, a salami and cheese spread was intriguing, though not the first thing most crave at a buffet. The beverage program proved a bright spot, with genuinely fresh-squeezed juices; two bottles of vibrant carrot juice were a highlight. The raw bar disappointed: signature oysters were absent, replaced by mussels. Desserts felt standard Vegas buffet fare. Hopes for custom crepes and macarons went unmet, though the gelato case offered playful, well-executed flavors—balsamic fig, chili mango, blood orange, and baklava stood out as inventive and enjoyable. Overall, this is a good Vegas buffet, just not the best—and not particularly unique. For the price, it lacks the distinctiveness found at Wicked Spoon, which was $10 cheaper that day. For broader variety, Carnival World Buffet at Rio remains a solid alternative. A small perk: Total Rewards cardholders get a dollar off per buffet purchase.

Man I had a hard time deciding how many stars to give this place. We actually stumbled onto it by accident after striking out at another spot in the same strip mall. What caught my eye was a window plastered with “Best of Vegas” stickers—a promising sign, though a closer look revealed those accolades were a bit dated. Still, optimism won out and we headed in for a late breakfast. Service is where this place really shines. We were greeted immediately and made to feel welcome from the start. Our server was genuinely friendly, and the drink runner was even more personable. The standout moment came when our 1-year-old started getting fussy and, without prompting, they brought over some crackers to tide her over. That kind of attentiveness is gold for parents and the surest way to earn a generous tip. It set a warm tone and made us want to like everything else even more.
