The food, however, didn’t quite keep pace with the hospitality. I ordered the Jamm’s omelet, which comes with steak and a sauce. I wasn’t expecting filet mignon for breakfast, but the steak resembled the thin, processed freezer-aisle kind and tasted about as exciting. The sauce couldn’t rescue it, and at around $10, it felt like a miss on both flavor and value. On the brighter side, the pot bread was excellent—warm, airy, and satisfying—and easily the best bite on the table. My wife’s French toast earned a thumbs-up for being nicely done and flavorful. Our daughter stuck to simple eggs and toast, which were fine. When the check landed, it hovered around $30 for the three of us—a price that stung a bit given the uneven experience. The room carries a comfortable, old-school breakfast-and-lunch vibe that suggests it was once a neighborhood favorite. And maybe, at one time, it truly lived up to those “Best of” decals. Today, it feels like the scene has moved on, with newer breakfast spots raising the bar. Bottom line: come for the warm, family-friendly service and consider sticking to crowd-pleasers like the pot bread and French toast. Skip the steak-heavy omelets. With so many breakfast options in town, this one’s worth a visit for the hospitality—but the kitchen needs to catch up to make it a must-return. Cheers.
Delivery arrived 20 minutes early; food was mediocre overall—nothing remarkable, yet still personally slightly better than Big Wa’s offerings.

A little overwhelming compared to what I was expecting Part bakery, part sit-down café, this Colombian spot packs more into a small footprint than you’d think—and that abundance is both its charm and its challenge. The bakery cases brim with sweets, cakes, and breads; even after an early afternoon rush had clearly thinned the selection, there were still plenty of goodies to tempt. A compact freezer adds to the take-home appeal with empanadas, fry-ready doughs, and cheese-filled dough “fingers” whose official name escaped me, but whose promise did not. Beyond the glass cases, the eat-in side reads like a full-fledged restaurant. A wall menu leans hearty at breakfast and generous at lunch, with daily specials scrawled on a whiteboard. One such special—tamales—derailed my careful pre-planning. Freshly made but not yet ready to eat, they required cooking at home. To tide me over, I grabbed a beef empanada from the warmer perched by the register, a dangerously placed siren if ever there was one. The woman at the counter, surprised I only wanted one, pointed me toward the communal condiment station. She was right: the sauces were outstanding, including a verdant number reminiscent of the green jalapeño sauce at Pio Pio. Back home, I discovered the tamales are Colombian-sized—translation: huge. One was more than enough. After about 20 minutes of boiling, the pork version emerged fragrant and fantastic, banana-leaf aroma mingling with a savory, casserole-like masa packed with sliced potatoes, carrots, peas, and richly seasoned meat. It was one of the most satisfying tamales I’ve had in a long time. The only drawback was a sizable bone-in piece tucked inside—perhaps customary, but jarring as a three-inch inedible surprise in an otherwise soft, comforting dish. Service here is brisk but friendly, with helpful nudges that enhance the experience—like the gentle insistence on sauces, which truly elevate everything they touch. The overall vibe is casual and bustling, a neighborhood place where impulse meets appetite. I’ll be back to graze deeper across the menu and to work my way through the breads—if only as vehicles for those excellent condiments. Go with an appetite, some patience for the special items that require finishing at home, and a willingness to be pleasantly overwhelmed. It’s absolutely worth checking out.

Deserves the Big "O" Award Las Vegas has no shortage of dining destinations, but San Marco just claimed my new favorite table. The vibe hits that sweet spot between casual and polished, with relaxed outdoor seating that invites lingering and prime people-watching. I went with a group of friends and nibbled my way through the menu, and while we sampled plenty, a few standouts made the night unforgettable. Start with the Fried Pizza Dough. Curiously shaped strips arrive golden and warm, with a perfect chewy bite, scattered with shaved cheese and a gentle shake of pepper flakes. It’s simple, unfussy, and wildly addictive—the kind of thing you pass around the table and still wish you’d ordered two. Next up, the Caprese Salad. Thick slices of ripe tomato under a cloud of soft, almost oozy mozzarella is a study in freshness and restraint. The balance of acid and cream had us negotiating for the last bite; it’s a classic done right. The showstopper, though, is the Braised Pork Shoulder. A hefty, tender slab arrives lacquered in a bright apple reduction, with cool cucumber for contrast. It’s melt-in-your-mouth good—comforting and refined at once. Don’t sleep on the sides: the Fried Smashed Potatoes—little red potatoes crushed, crisped at the edges, and dusted with a salty, slightly spicy kick—are instantly habit-forming. Zucchini sautéed in butter and garlic delivers pure, simple satisfaction. A few misses: the plain pizza feels unnecessary in a city brimming with slices; the butternut squash appetizer reads a touch too floral; and the pasta margherita DOC leans heavy on salt. Service is warm without hovering, and the overall atmosphere stays chill while feeling special—ideal for a long conversation under the Vegas sky. San Marco is the kind of place that makes you plot your next trip before you’ve paid the bill. Order smart, share generously, and prepare to be smitten.

I walked in optimistic—the menu reads like a modern crowd-pleaser—but the kitchen never matched the promise. Nothing was inedible, yet the prices demanded finesse that simply wasn’t there. The roasted cauliflower arrived unpleasantly firm, lacking the tender char you expect. My grilled pineapple was served cold; staff explained they grill it and refrigerate it, which defeats the point. My dad’s burger looked and tasted like chain-restaurant fare, and the crab cakes were forgettable, neither crisp nor luxurious. Service didn’t redeem things. Our server was friendly but inattentive and slow; something as basic as butter for the bread basket took ages to appear, though the bread itself was surprisingly good. The atmosphere tries hard to be trendy, but mismatched serve ware and tables clash with shifting ambient lights that cycle from purple to blue to green, creating a nightclub vibe more than a cohesive dining room. With the value off and the execution uneven, Luma feels like it’s playing dress-up rather than delivering a memorable meal. I wouldn’t return or recommend it to friends.

B&B is normally one of my favorite restaurants. Over five prior visits, I’d sampled nearly everything on the menu and rarely left disappointed. While I’d seen mixed reviews citing burnt or overly salty dishes, my experiences had been consistently pleasant—until last Friday. This visit was a shock. The gnocchi, once my go-to, arrived so salty it was inedible. The mint love letters, a dish I had previously enjoyed, were unrecognizable and frankly gross. Even the bread was different and served cold. We were a party of five and had ordered five pastas with the intent to share, inspired by Mario’s oft-repeated notion that food is meant to be passed around. The Venetian’s own write-up of B&B celebrates that convivial style. Unfortunately, our server reacted with condescension, spoke down to us, and refused to provide side plates or a serving spoon so everyone could have a taste. The tone made us feel like we were bothersome rather than welcome. Adding insult to injury, we discovered that a mandatory gratuity applies to groups of five, which might explain why the server seemed indifferent to providing good service. I normally tip generously, often above 20 percent, but being forced to reward rudeness left a sour taste that matched the food’s seasoning. I was embarrassed to have recommended B&B to my companions, and it pains me to say that I most likely won’t return. Consistency matters, and when a beloved spot delivers cold bread, oversalted pasta, and dismissive service, trust erodes quickly. B&B has the potential to shine—it has before—but management needs to address quality control in the kitchen and empower staff to support the family-style experience the restaurant itself promotes. Until then, I’ll seek my pasta elsewhere. I hope leadership listens, retrains the team, and restores the flavors that once made B&B special again soon.

Excellent course conditions and a smart, enjoyable layout make this track a joy to play. Unfortunately, the experience is undermined by the pro shop’s abysmal customer service. Staff were unfriendly and unhelpful—more like surly gatekeepers than hosts—draining the fun before tee-off. Fix the front-of-house attitude, and this would be a top-tier destination for locals and visiting golfers alike.

Second visit in a year and likely my last by choice. Our table of four had a mixed experience: the osso buco landed squarely in average territory, and the cod special was overly pungent—thankfully tempered by a bright microgreens salad. Highlights did shine: the stone crab was genuinely delicious, and the lobster mac and cheese remained as rich and satisfying as I remembered. Service, however, lagged. Waters sat empty, dishes lingered, and no one checked on flavors or satisfaction beyond our primary server. Overall, a few hits overshadowed by service missteps.

Our first Indian dining experience was delightful. Staff guided us through the menu with patience and smart recommendations. Every dish was flavorful and satisfying. We left impressed and will return for more authentic Indian cuisine.

Over the years, I’ve visited the MTCCC numerous times and it consistently delivers a wonderful experience. Staff are unfailingly friendly and helpful, ready to guide you to the right meeting room or banquet hall. Catering has been excellent at every event, and when drinks are served, prices are reasonable. My only gripe is the parking ramp—an elaborate maze that begs for a slice of cheese at the exit.

Title: Excellent First Lunch with Gorgeous Golf Course Views Our first lunch here was excellent. The patio’s sweeping view of the golf course set a relaxing tone. We shared a burger cooked perfectly to order, and the staff thoughtfully split the burger and fries. Service was warm and attentive, and prices were reasonable. A delightful spot we’re eager to revisit.

For years, my wife and I have relied on Specialty Luggage downtown, and it remains our first stop for travel gear. The staff—especially Matthew—consistently take time to understand our needs, compare options, and recommend the best fit. Their honesty is refreshing: if they don’t have an item, they say so and try to source it; more often than not, if it isn’t on their shelves, it probably doesn’t exist. We’ve purchased multiple suitcases and countless accessories, all of excellent quality that has held up trip after trip. When repairs were needed, they handled them quickly and cheerfully, and in any gray areas around warranty coverage, they gave us the benefit of the doubt. Prices are reasonable, and the personalized guidance beats anything we’ve experienced with online retailers. It’s worth visiting even without a specific purchase in mind; you’ll learn a ton about current travel solutions, and we’ve discovered clever products we didn’t know existed. The store is also a fantastic source of holiday gifts, thanks to a diverse, well-curated selection. Specialty Luggage pairs expertise with integrity, and that combination keeps us coming back always.

Hey it was nothing great but the price was right. My wife and I stopped in on our last night in Vegas, and for the price it delivered a decent night out. They were generous with drinks—lots of free shots—but the alcohol quality raised eyebrows. My gin and tonic tasted like rubbing alcohol, and the whiskey sour was overly sweet. Still, bartenders vary, and the younger guy and girl were genuinely friendly. They even helped me snag the open-bar price during ladies’ night, which kept the tab low. Service was quick and upbeat, and a real DJ added energy, making it feel more like a party. If you’re expecting craft cocktails or elevated dining, rethink it. Come for cheap drinks, solid service, and music, not a gourmet meal. Despite mediocre booze, we had fun and would return if we stayed at the Flamingo again. To everyone going here to eat—what were you thinking?

Place is nice enough, and the ambience is pleasant, but I didn’t come to eat the ambience. We ordered a variety of dishes—pho, bún, and another noodle dish—and everything tasted surprisingly bland. Even the fish sauce seemed watered down, which was disappointing. Service was slow, though the servers themselves were kind and attentive. The restaurant wasn’t busy, yet our food and requests took far too long. Basics were missing: no utensils, no napkins, and no condiments like hoisin or sriracha set on the tables, which is standard at most Vietnamese spots. The standout was the coffee jello for dessert; it was genuinely enjoyable. This place is close to home, but I’d rather drive a bit farther to Pho Chandler, where the food consistently delivers.

We visited to kick off a bachelor party before a night out, and from the moment the elevator doors closed, the experience felt special. The ride up is a fitting prelude to a room with jaw-dropping decor and panoramic views; you come here for the atmosphere first and foremost. The food isn’t bad, but apps hover around $30 and entrees around $50, so value is a question. The lounge’s no-cover policy before 10 draws a more casual crowd; later it leans upscale. Service hit all the right notes: attentive, friendly, and efficient, with a generous $12 Chivas pour arriving quickly. The bread basket offered a nice, warm assortment, though the hard butter was better than the peanut butter pairing, which didn’t quite land. Among starters, the foie gras with apple was a decent, thick-cut rendition that pleased a first-timer. The standout surprise was the gnocchi with morels—silky, earthy, and far from bland, it was the most memorable dish of the night. Mains were competent but rarely transcendent. The bison tenderloin came with a peppercorn sauce and felt straightforward rather than special. A special of beef tenderloin with foie gras and truffle leaned on luxe ingredients but delivered an experience that was merely good. Seared tuna was exactly that—seared tuna—fine but forgettable. The rack of lamb was prepared well yet lacked the flair to justify a $50-plus tag. Another beef tenderloin seemed oddly priced considering its simplicity. Halibut was on the bland side, salvaged by the richness of foie gras and truffle sauce. Sides and extras highlighted the value gap. Elbow pasta with Gruyere and ham was comforting and well-made, but mac and cheese isn’t why you splurge at a destination restaurant. Forked potatoes were an expensive miss. The cake service for our group—slicing and adding ice cream—ran $7 per person, which felt steep for a dessert they didn’t make. As a venue, it’s excellent for celebrations: the elevator ride, design, and skyline views make it memorable, and the lounge is a fun place to linger after dinner. But if your priority is standout food at this price point, Las Vegas offers better options. Come to soak up the scene and mark a special occasion; go elsewhere when your night is all about the plate.

After sampling countless steakhouses, I found Prime to be a study in contrasts: an undeniably romantic setting with polished service, yet culinary execution that rarely rises above solid. The room radiates that “special night out” feeling—dim lighting, plush finishes, and a front-row view of the Bellagio fountains—so you walk in feeling dressed up even if you aren’t. Prices match the ambiance, but at this tier, value becomes the question, especially when comparisons to Craft or SW inevitably come to mind. I appreciated Prime’s sauces presented on the side, a thoughtful touch that lets you steer the flavor. Unfortunately, one of the four—the miso-mustard—never arrived. Of the set, the soy–rice wine sauce was the standout, with a whisper of garlic that paired nicely with the meat. The steak itself was high quality and properly cooked, but it didn’t distinguish itself from competitors. If you regularly order the Porterhouse at Mastro’s, you’ll recognize the experience, and you’ll likely pay less there. Where Prime does step ahead is with its sides. The truffle-laced mac and cheese is indulgent without being heavy, with unmistakable layers of truffle aroma and flavor. The mashed potatoes are velvety and seasoned with restraint, both superior to similar sides I’ve had at SW. Service was excellent from start to finish. A welcome surprise: our brought-in bottle of wine wasn’t charged a corkage fee, which is typically around $50, and the gesture set a friendly tone. Desserts, however, landed in the “fine” category—agreeable but not compelling. If you’re in Las Vegas and want a glamorous date-night backdrop, Prime delivers on atmosphere in spades and the fountain view is a genuine plus. For pure steakhouse excellence, though, Craft remains my top pick, with better value and more consistent culinary distinction. Still, if ambience and the classic Vegas spectacle matter more than chasing the absolute best cut, Prime will satisfy for most diners overall.

Let’s be clear: Erin’s bills itself as Irish, but functions more as an Irish-themed restaurant than a true pub. If you’re expecting a snug bar with a gastro-pub menu, you may be surprised. Think large, Olive Garden–style footprint and a sprawling menu that nods to Ireland alongside familiar American comforts—pastas, salads, burgers, and shareable appetizers. On our visit, we split scotch eggs, fried cheese curds, and a house salad, pairing them with a couple of brews. The scotch eggs and curds delivered: crisp exteriors, satisfying seasoning, and served hot. Service was friendly and efficient, with dishes arriving promptly. Where Erin’s stumbles is consistency. While most plates were average-to-good, the salad arrived with roughly a third of the lettuce limp and wilted, undercutting the experience. With fresher greens and tighter quality control, Erin’s would land higher. As is, it’s a decent, broad-appeal option.

After a couple’s photo shoot at Lake Las Vegas, my husband and I stumbled into this Mexican spot we’d never heard of, and left wondering why it isn’t better known. Despite some head-scratching Yelp critiques, our experience was overwhelmingly positive. We were seated on the patio just as the sun was melting into the horizon and a cool breeze rolled in. A staff member lit the fire feature, and a jazz band began to set up—instant atmosphere. The chips and salsa were fresh and snappy, our server was attentive without hovering, and we didn’t wait long for our entrees. Everything we ordered was well-seasoned and satisfying. My sangria was one of the best I’ve had—bright, fruity, and not overly sweet—and they even carried my husband’s favorite beer, Bohemia, which earned instant points. Service stayed smooth until the end, when closing out the check took far too long. That lag is the lone blemish on an otherwise delightful evening. Still, the combination of a relaxed patio, live music vibes, drinks, and tasty Mexican fare makes this a place I’d return to—even from North Las Vegas.

My sister and I dined here a while back and had a pretty satisfying meal. The atmosphere is unforgettable, with thousands of goldfish surrounding you, creating a playful, serene vibe. She ordered the tomato and egg flower soup—fine, but nothing special—while we both chose the eggplant noodles. Those were delicious, though skimpy on sauce; we’d have enjoyed them more with a richer coating. Unfortunately, service lagged, and our server was nowhere to be found until we finished, so we couldn’t request extra. Overall, it’s a solid lunch spot with decent prices for Las Vegas, especially inside Caesars. I’d return and ask for extra sauce upfront.

Attentive service set the tone for a memorable meal. The wedding soup and café salads were spot-on, and the warm, fluffy bread with olive oil was irresistible. House-made ravioli shone with a vibrant, fresh tomato sauce. My husband enjoyed the creamy chicken Alfredo, though grilled chicken would have elevated it further. Despite that minor note, plates were cleaned, smiles were had, and we’re already planning a return visit.

Sidelines walks a tightrope between cozy neighborhood haunt and buzzy, trend-forward bar—and, to its credit, it balances both identities better than most. The headline attraction is the wings: crisp, sauced just right, and every bit deserving of their reputation. But the sleeper strength is the beer program, with a thoughtfully curated craft lineup and staff who actually know their hops and styles. Service steers you toward smart pours without the hard sell. My lone caveat is price: a tab can creep up fast, especially if you skip domestics. Still, it’s a compelling stop for wings and brews.

On my self-styled “Showgirls” diet of brown rice, vegetables, and Evian, I was delighted to find all that—and some tasty chicken—at Neo Tokyo. We dropped in for lunch and were impressed by how fresh everything tasted and how affordable it was. The lunch special, just $6.50, even included a crisp spring roll. Service was upbeat and helpful; the staffer offered spot-on recommendations without a hint of pushiness. I don’t frequent this neighborhood, but if I’m nearby again, Neo Tokyo will be an easy repeat. A value for quick, satisfying Asian fare.

This review is actually from a friends stay. He had us up in the room for a little drinking party. Now he had got a groupon deal for this place. Without basically getting these rooms at half price, I would definitely stay elsewhere. I’m writing based on a friend’s stay. We visited his room for a small drinking get-together, and he’d booked via a Groupon at roughly half price. At that discounted rate, the value was acceptable; without it, I’d look elsewhere. The property felt dated and carried a lingering odor in common areas. The room itself wasn’t terrible—clean enough and functional—but Vegas offers far more modern options at comparable prices. For just a little more, you can stay on the Strip or just off it at places like the Rio, with fresher rooms and better amenities. This hotel makes sense only on high-occupancy weekends when rates skyrocket and you have a deep discount. Otherwise, there’s no compelling reason to choose it over newer, better-located alternatives. Service seemed average at best.

Stopped in here for a drink with friends, and had a great time. The bartender was super friendly, and signing up for a players card scored $20 in free play. Hot, fresh pizza and wings hit the spot. Nothing extravagant, but clean, welcoming, and reliably good service and food.

Few years ago I was there before. It was good with lots of choices and appropriate quality. This time, for the Sunday morning champagne brunch, it was a disappointment—nearly bad. The empty entrance should have been a warning, but we paid and went in. Our server was genuinely kind and attentive, promptly delivering champagne and soft drinks. Unfortunately, the food fell far short: limited selection, uninspired presentation, and quality that simply didn’t measure up. I tried the staples—prime rib, lamb, and ham—and each was not just average, but decidedly below. At roughly $30 or more, this brunch doesn’t justify the price, even for hotel guests. Save your money and seek out better options nearby; there are definitely superior brunches that offer value, variety, and taste.

I visited this Thai spot with a friend on a quiet evening, and we were the only diners. The server was friendly and seated us quickly, but the food disappointed. I ordered drunken noodles at medium spice, and they arrived lukewarm around the edges, as if they had been sitting. The dish lacked heat and, more importantly, flavor; the noodles tasted flat, with no depth from herbs, chilies, or wok char. For $10, I expect bold, balanced seasoning and a fresh, hot plate, especially when the kitchen isn’t busy. While the interior is undeniably cute—cozy decor and a clean, welcoming space—the ambiance can’t compensate for underwhelming cooking. In an area with better, cheaper Thai options, this meal didn’t justify the price. With more attention to spice and freshness, it could improve significantly overall.

I’ve visited Flancer’s in Gilbert three times and recently tried the Mesa location, hoping to see what all the rave reviews are about. Proximity kept me coming back, but the food hasn’t clicked for me. On my latest visit, I asked the server for the standout item and went with the roast beef sandwich. It was fine, nothing memorable, and my wife’s salad felt equally ordinary. Service was pleasant, but the flavors never rose above average. For sandwiches, I’d rather go to Crackers, and for pizza, Vito’s consistently delivers a better, more satisfying experience.

Great food and ambience make this one of Willy Street's best restaurants. Our large group was warmly accommodated, with attentive service and seamless coordination. Dishes were delicious and beautifully presented. It's equally perfect for an intimate romantic date—welcoming, stylish, and memorable.

Tasty Bites, Awkward “Lounge,” and Sticker Shock at Happy Hour We visited for happy hour and immediately hit a snag: the discount only applies if you sit at the bar or in the “lounge.” We opted for the lounge, which felt more like a waiting area with a few small tables—awkward for a meal, but we pressed on because we came for the food. The mojito was excellent—bright, minty, and balanced. Oysters were $5 apiece; we ordered two. Pricey compared to spots that offer half-dozens or dozens for better value, but they were fresh and beautifully presented. Our first plates arrived quickly. After that, service lagged while our server juggled bar duties, leaving a 10–15 minute gap before she returned. Her kindness and confidence—remembering our sizable order without hesitation—softened the delay. Food quality was strong across the board, but portions felt skimpy for the price. The yellowtail with jalapeño, a personal favorite I order everywhere, came with only two pieces, where other sushi bars usually serve more. It was clean, delicate, and delicious, yet it left me wanting another round. Overall, this is a spot for solid flavors and excellent cocktails, best experienced at the bar to secure the happy hour and smoother service. Expect polished presentation and quality ingredients, but be prepared for small portions and higher prices that may not match the setting. Value seekers should watch specials and ask about portions.

My latest visit to this burger spot was, unfortunately, a masterclass in how not to treat customers. We were a party of five; two arrived early and, with no host in sight, we sat ourselves and told a staffer the rest were coming. The response was a scolding and a forced “time out” while we were lectured for not being a complete party. When more friends arrived and we asked to be seated, the manager refused, despite several open tables and no visible wait. What turned an irritating policy into a deal-breaker was the tone: needlessly confrontational and dismissive. Instead of problem-solving, the staff escalated, making it clear our business wasn’t welcome. Dining out shouldn’t feel like an argument, and certainly not one that even hints at taking things outside. In a time when hospitality should shine, the arrogance on display was baffling. There were no apologies, just a taunting, dare-you vibe that soured what should have been an easy night out. Even setting service aside, the food doesn’t redeem it. On past visits, the burgers were greasy and undersized—the kind you need napkins for long after the check arrives. The scene, once laid-back years ago, now feels more posturing than substance, and the tight parking only adds friction. Bottom line: I won’t be back and can’t recommend it. If you want a friendly meal without drama, head to The Dish or anywhere that values guests over rigid rules and attitude.

I really dig their 8th Street Ale, and the kitchen delivers equally impressive flavors. The calamari arrives as tender steak-cut sticks instead of the usual rings and tentacles, paired with standout sauces that elevate each bite. The pork adobado was another home run—savory, succulent, and perfectly seasoned. This spot is a bit of a drive for me, but every visit proves it’s unequivocally worth the miles.

Disclaimer: This is the most critical review I've ever written. I am conscious of the negative aspect of internet culture that allows people to make unduly harsh comments at a high rate. With that in mind, these are my honest feelings about my stay. From the moment we arrived, subtlety was replaced by a wall of 80s hair metal blasting at concert volume. The soundtrack was inescapable—hallways, elevators, common areas—so our room became the only refuge. The hotel’s design doubles down on the theme, even lining corridors with actual drum cymbals. Predictably, late-night revelers treated them like instruments, and our ninth floor turned into a parade of amateur John Bonhams thundering their way back to bed. Sleep was further sabotaged by a blinking smoke detector positioned directly above the headboard. With lights off and blackout curtains drawn, the pulsing LED created an involuntary mini light show—more irritating than immersive—and made it hard to fully darken the room. Service underscored the chaos. Guest Services required five separate calls before an engineer finally arrived to address our air-conditioning issues. The overall staffing vibe skewed toward laissez-faire: lots of band tees, lots of valet jackets, not many steadying hands. Raising concerns felt like inviting a shrug and a “sucks, bro,” rather than a resolution. Finding a peaceful corner proved just as elusive. Unless you’re willing to pay for the spa, there’s no designated quiet space to decompress. The pool scene leaned heavily into party mode—energetic and loud—more spring-break than serene retreat, which won’t suit travelers seeking relaxation. The food didn’t redeem the experience. Dishes tasted mass-produced and overly sauced, the culinary equivalent of turning up the volume to hide a lack of finesse. It’s sustenance, not satisfaction. To be fair, the bed was soft and comfortable. Unfortunately, that singular comfort couldn’t offset the cumulative noise, light, and service frustrations. If you miss the social chaos of a freshman dorm—and crave a full-throttle hair-metal aesthetic—this hotel might hit your sweet spot. If you value sleep, attentive service, and calm spaces, consider booking elsewhere.

If you’re craving some of the best-tasting Mexican food in the Phoenix area, this modest, no-frills spot delivers. The food arrives fast and consistently delicious, and in 16 years of visits I’ve never experienced bad service. My go-to is the #10: two chili burritos with rice and beans, though they’ll happily swap in any burrito on the combo. Chips are thin and crisp, the non-chunky salsa is fantastic, and there’s beer plus a solid margarita if you want a drink with your meal. Many people order takeout, but the flavors shine brightest fresh at the restaurant. It’s not fancy or large—just reliably great Mexican comfort food done right, every single time.

Scheduled me and my two kids. Appt at 9 am. Didn't see the first of us until 10am. Didn't let me escort my daughter (teen) but did let me escort my son (at about 10:30am). They were disorganized and behind schedule. My daughter said the doctor/dentist wasn't personable—didn't explain things to her. She said the hygienist was nice though. Same dentist seemed like he wanted to get my son in for more X-rays, saying he might be missing an adult tooth under a baby molar. But after he left, the assistant took us back and did a full pano X-ray, and it showed he wasn’t missing that tooth. Odd that the dentist wasn’t willing to do it right then and instead wanted us to make another appointment. They also did a fluoride treatment on my daughter without asking me first. It was $17, which I paid, but consent should come before any add-ons. I never got seen at all because we had to leave by noon; in total, it took 2.5 hours to see only two out of three of us. They use Dr. Jeffrey Kootman on Thursdays. He extracted my wisdom teeth years ago, and based on that experience, I would never let him treat me or my kids again. Overall, very disappointed. If you have Total Dental insurance, be aware that finding a good in-network dentist can be difficult, and this visit is an example of what you may encounter.

Cheapest Gas Near the South Strip—with Unexpected People Watching If you’re looking for low prices on fuel near the south end of the Strip, this station reliably comes through. The convenience store is a solid bonus, stocking basics like drinks, snacks, and a few travel necessities so you can grab what you need and go. What truly sets this place apart is the slice-of-life scene on weekend mornings. Stop by between 7 and 9 a.m. and you’ll catch an entertaining cross-section of late-night Las Vegas wrapping up their shifts. Think bold outfits, distinctive tattoos, and that unmistakable Vegas energy—free people watching that rivals an airport concourse. Bring a coffee, respect everyone’s space, and enjoy the moment. Pro tip: It gets very busy. Approaches are tight, and the forecourt fills quickly, so pull in cautiously and watch for merging cars. Pumps are clean, payment is straightforward, and they accept all major credit cards. Lines move fairly fast, but expect a brief wait during peak times. Lighting is good, staff are efficient, and essentials like window squeegees and air are available. Bottom line: A typical gas station done right—fast, affordable, and convenient—with an unexpected dash of Vegas atmosphere if you swing by on a weekend morning.

So disappointed! I went in for a solo lunch and asked to sit at the sushi bar—being pregnant, I thought it would be comfortable, quick, and a good spot to see how the food was handled. I opted for the all-you-can-eat option and immediately hit a snag: a 30-minute wait for my appetizer, gyoza. Throughout, the chefs at the bar never greeted me or acknowledged me with any warmth, which felt odd given that bar seating usually comes with at least a friendly hello. One chef made a silly comment as soon as I sat down, and from that moment I had the sense I’d picked the wrong place. From four different rolls I tried, only the Maniac Roll stood out—spicy, clean flavors, and no cloying sweet sauce or imitation crab. Everything else was a letdown. The Monster Roll fell apart piece by piece the moment I tried to lift it, and most of the rolls were unattractive and tasted overwhelmingly of super sweet sauces and overly sweet crabmeat. The overall impression was muddled, sugary, and careless. Service was polite but both slow and confused. I never received a water refill despite the long wait times, and the pacing was frustrating: each order took 25–35 minutes, and the check added another 20 minutes at the end. My entire visit stretched to about an hour and a half, far longer than it should have for a casual lunch. What bothered me most was the sense of uneven treatment. Management and the sushi chefs seemed to fawn over well-dressed, photogenic guests while everyone else—myself included—felt overlooked. I don’t think diners should have to dress up to be treated with basic respect. In the end, the only redeeming feature was the option to order half portions, which made trying different items less of a commitment. Still, I wouldn’t return. For better quality sushi and genuinely attentive service, I’d rather drive to 808 Sushi, which isn’t fancy but delivers where it counts. This visit was the worst dining experience I’ve had in a long time.

I'm not sure why this place got such high ratings but what I experienced was not even close to 4 stars. I ordered the rib eye, which looked promising when it arrived, but it had almost no flavor. After a week of solid steaks in Death Valley, I expected this one to be the standout; I was wrong. Everyone at our table reached for the salt shaker, and several shakes barely helped. It seemed as if the kitchen forgot to season the meat at all. My baked potato side was good, though that’s hard to mess up. For a restaurant so highly rated, the bland, underseasoned steak was a disappointment.

After a late night out, there are only a couple things that can motivate me to roll out of bed — Sunrise Cafe being one of them. Sunrise Cafe is a standout for anyone who craves a genuinely vegetable-forward breakfast. In a world of carb-heavy brunch menus, this place treats produce like a star, weaving fresh veggies into many main entrées without sacrificing flavor or heartiness. The omelettes deserve special mention: while the Garden of Eden is a tempting option for health enthusiasts, it borders on veg-overload even for dedicated vegetable fans. The Davezilla, however, strikes a satisfying balance — still wholesome, but with enough spice to keep things lively and far from bland. Beyond eggs, the create-your-own salad is consistently excellent, crisp, and customizable, making it a reliable choice whether you’re refueling or keeping things light. And then there’s the signature muffin, a table-stopping moment every time it arrives piping hot. Friends rave about it so relentlessly that it might be time I finally cave and order one myself. Expect a short wait if you arrive late, but it’s rarely unreasonable. Outdoor seating adds charm on sunny days, and the sweet touch of a mini treasure chest for kids shows thoughtfulness and a sense of fun. Overall, I love this place. I have yet to find a breakfast spot that tops it.

What a great dive. If you don't know to look for it, you'll drive right past. Tucked away, this Charlotte staple proves that true comfort doesn’t need polish. I’ve become loyal to the vegetarian chili and its chili mac variation—steaming, hearty, and exactly what you crave on a cold day when you need quick satisfaction without the slow-cooker wait. Portions are generous, prices friendly, and the flavors reliable enough to become an old faithful. Service is straightforward and efficient: your check lands as soon as the food arrives, and you head to the register by the kitchen to settle up. Bring cash if you prefer to tip the server directly, or expect a small extra charge when using a card. It’s an old-school rhythm that suits the place. The ambiance? A dive, happily and intentionally. No frills, just a lived-in charm and regulars who call it theirs. While the menu reportedly hides other gems, I’m content to stick with what I love. Try it once to say you’ve been; return because your heart—and hunger—insist.

Nachdem Schottland 1998 in einem Referendum ein teilweise eigenständiges Parlament bekommen hat – Pàrlamaid na h-Alba für die gälisch Bewanderten – brauchte man ein Gebäude. 2004 war es dann soweit. Eingeweiht wurde es durch Queen Elisabeth am 9.10. Von außen ist das Parlamentsgebäude eine mutige, fast skulpturale Architektur, die mit ihren geschwungenen Linien an ein Schiff erinnert und sicher nicht jedem gefällt. Umso angenehmer ist die Erfahrung als Besucher: Kein bürokratischer Hürdenlauf wie beim Deutschen Bundestag, sondern ein freundliches „Hello“ am Polizisten und hinein zur Sicherheitsschleuse – Flughafenstandard, schnell und unkompliziert. Direkt danach öffnet sich die helle Eingangshalle. Mitarbeitende begrüßen einen, fragen nach dem Anliegen, reichen einen Plan und erklären die klaren Foto-Regeln: alles ist erlaubt, außer das Porträt der Queen und der Plenarsaal nach 11 Uhr, wenn die Sitzungen beginnen. Weil es schon 10:30 war, ging es für mich gleich auf die Besucherterrasse – perfekter Ort für Fotos und einen ersten Blick auf das Herz der Demokratie. Besonders positiv: Man kann ohne große Umstände einer Plenarsitzung beiwohnen und das politische Geschehen live verfolgen. Diese Offenheit, Transparenz und Zugänglichkeit sind beeindruckend. So lob’ ich mir gelebte Demokratie: einfach vorbeikommen, hinschauen, mitreden. Ein Besuch lohnt sich jederzeit.

Restaurant Week is usually my favorite excuse to revisit familiar spots and try new menus, so we joined another couple for dinner with high hopes. We opted for an indoor table and kicked things off with drinks. My Palm Refresh—vodka with muddled basil and citrus—lived up to its name: bright, clean, and genuinely refreshing. Unfortunately, the evening’s hospitality hiccup arrived early. When we asked our server for the Restaurant Week menu, he seemed baffled and oddly combative, repeatedly asking what we were talking about. It created an awkward moment that was only resolved when a different staff member immediately understood and brought the correct menus. No apology followed, and the service never recovered from that rocky start—confused, argumentative, and inattentive despite our attempts to lighten the mood. We ordered the Restaurant Week prix fixe and added a Calamari Fritti to share. The portion was generous, but the calamari didn’t taste fresh and lacked seasoning; even the accompanying marinara was underwhelming. First courses were uneven. The lobster bisque carried decent lobster flavor, but it leaned aggressively salty and needed balance. The roasted beet and goat cheese salad had pleasant, sweet beets, but the arugula was over-dressed to the point of droop, and the goat cheese lacked tang or creaminess to pull the dish together. For mains, I chose the single-cut filet mignon with goat cheese whipped potatoes and a wild mushroom and black truffle demi. The accompaniments shined: the potatoes were luscious and well seasoned, and the demi added a savory earthiness without being heavy. The steak, though, missed the mark—overcooked well past the requested medium-rare, dry, and surprisingly short on flavor. On the other side of the table, the chicken Parmigiana split the difference. The linguine marinara was spot-on—perfectly al dente with a simple, bright sauce and fresh basil—while the chicken itself fell flat, lacking the crisp, juicy payoff you expect from the classic. Dessert was the evening’s redemption. The New York–style cheesecake was excellent: light yet structured, with a terrific crumbly crust and a bright berry compote that cut the richness without overpowering it. The key lime pie was equally successful—balanced rather than bracingly tart, sporting the same stellar crust, and lifted by another well-judged berry compote. Overall, portions are undeniably generous and the desserts alone could tempt a return. But the core experience—service clarity and the consistent execution of savory dishes—needs attention. If a restaurant participates in a high-visibility event like Restaurant Week, every server should be briefed to avoid confusion at the table. And in the kitchen, fresher fry work, lighter dressing, proper seasoning, and accurate temperatures would go a long way. As it stands, with stronger Italian options like Ferraro’s and better steakhouses nearby, I’d rather pay a bit more for reliably better food and service.

We walked into this restaurant hopeful, but the experience unraveled within minutes. The hostess led us toward a bar hightop, dropped menus without a word, turned her back, and walked away. We took the adjacent table and waited as staff clustered at the front chatting—four servers and the hostess—with several more strolling past us without even a nod. Despite a visibly idle floor, not one person approached to greet us, offer water, or confirm our seating. The atmosphere felt unmanaged and unwelcoming, with a young staff and no oversight. After an extended wait, we decided to leave. As we exited, we explained why to the hostess and a server at the door; their response—“we must not have heard you”—sealed it. Man oh man, this was disappointing. We won’t be back, and we won’t be giving them a second chance.

So in love with Cost Plus for stationery, home decor, wine, kitchen gadgets, and non-perishable international snacks—my go-to for stocking stuffers and the rare spot where I can find something for guys and gals alike. I popped into this location for a change from my usual Camelback & 18th Street store and it delivered the same treasure-hunt charm. For coworker gifts, I scooped up mini wines and single-serve shortbread cookies; vintage-bottle sodas will be a hit chilling on ice for Christmas Day. I also snagged a sturdy mug for my uncle and a whimsical lobster pâté for his stocking, plus beautifully wrapped gourmet soaps and a festive Christmas dish towel for my mom. While browsing, an associate checked in and offered help, which I appreciated. Checkout moved fairly quickly, though the cashier seemed overwhelmed by my cartload of goodies—understandable given the tiny counter space. A backup would have helped when the line started to grow; perhaps Kim could have called another cashier sooner. Still, the selection, value, and gift-ready finds make this store a holiday lifesaver and a year-round favorite. I’ll definitely be back, happily.

As a self-professed shabu shabu fanatic, I was thrilled to see this spot open not far from home. I’d visited the space back when it was Match, so the layout felt familiar, but the current incarnation makes a striking first impression. The interior is modern and sleek, with barbecue-ready tables and Asian-inspired decor anchored by an eye-catching upside-down boat as the focal point. There’s also a private room, a nice touch for group gatherings. Overall, the venue radiates potential. We arrived during their Happy Hour and couldn’t resist the $2 boba. For dinner, we opted for the shabu shabu hot pot, and their approach stood out. You choose two broths—we went with Coconut Milk and Spicy Chinese—then head to a bank of refrigerators to pick your vegetables, meats, mushrooms, and more. Everything is individually packaged, fresh-looking, and priced so you pay only for what you take. I love this level of control and customization. We both selected beef and cracked an egg into the simmering broths for richness. Flavor-wise, both bases delivered: the Coconut Milk broth was silky, aromatic, and my personal favorite, while the Spicy Chinese broth had a satisfyingly assertive kick that my husband preferred. The ingredients cooked up beautifully and felt high quality. The only miss was the boba. At $2 it’s a deal, but the pearls weren’t cooked properly, which dulled the experience. Service, on the other hand, was warm and attentive—granted, we were one of just two couples there at the time. With a LivingSocial deal in hand, I’m already planning a return visit. Dial in the boba, keep the broths this good, and this modern shabu shabu spot could easily become a neighborhood favorite.

I’ve lunched at Sidewinders at least twice a week for over a year, and it still never gets old. The Spicy Italian Combo is my go-to—flavor-packed and affordable. The staff is consistently fun and friendly, adding to the experience. If you’re craving great subs, this place beats every other spot in town, hands down.

First time here, and I’m not sure I’ll return. In a district with limited standout dining, this spot is pretty good. I ordered the Chicken Pita and it was tasty—the chicken was moist and the fresh greens were a highlight. All pitas come with fries, which is a nice touch. That said, I prefer Pita Pit’s build-your-own approach and customization. Pricewise, this felt a bit steep; for a dollar more, you can get a Mediterranean restaurant experience with table service. Solid, but not compelling enough to become a go-to spot.

My husband works near Tom’s Thumb and insisted I try it. After several lunches and a cookie for our little guy each visit, I’m smitten. This cozy spot delivers OUTSTANDING customer service, a welcoming, country feel, and a treasure trove of unique items to buy. It’s the best establishment I’ve visited—warm, friendly, and consistently delightful. Thank you, Tom’s Thumb, for making every visit memorable and delicious.

Addictive Tong Mein at Wah Kee Down the Street Living nearby, I’ve fallen hard for Wah Kee’s assorted Tong Mein noodle soups. Each steaming bowl is a customizable mix of beef, pork, ginger, scallions, and your choice of dumplings—wonton or gyoza—anchored by a generous mound of thin, stringy noodles and a satisfying broth. Portions are big enough that one soup plus an appetizer or two easily feeds two, yet we often order a bowl per person to satisfy strong cravings. The menu is extensive, but I rarely stray from the Tong Mein because it’s consistently excellent and comforting. If you’re seeking standard Americanized “junk” Chinese fare, look elsewhere; come here for the soup. It’s simple, hearty, and addictive.

Had a wonderful dinner here while on a work trip. I booked a reservation online before flying in, which was incredibly convenient. Staying in Old Montreal, I loved that the restaurant was just around the corner. The ambiance is warm, and the live music adds a charming touch to the evening. The food was good and affordable for the area. I ordered the catch of the day—simple, fresh, and what I wanted. Service was friendly. I’d happily return and recommend it.

Oh dear. I was totally underwhelmed by the customer service and quality of food here that I really can't even justify an'A-OK', although based on the surroundings it is probably more of a two-and-a-half star rating. With family visiting from Ireland over the weekend—his sister, mum, and grandmother—we chose this spot for its postcard-perfect views and classic Edinburgh setting. On those counts, it delivered. For just under £30, we ordered five cakes and five coffees, a fair price for a treat in the city. Unfortunately, the experience unraveled immediately. At the counter, staff couldn’t say what flavors the cakes were, and our questions seemed more annoyance than opportunity to help. We defaulted to safe choices—scones, caramel shortbread—because guessing didn’t feel worth the eye-rolls. Seated, we discovered the scones arrived without jam or cream. Off he went to ask, only to wait five minutes while the till attendant chatted and hugged friends. The eventual “solution” was a token splash of pouring cream and a shrug: no jam available. When drinks finally reached the table, one coffee was not only scorching but contained a floating fly. The replacement did come, but so slowly that the rest of us were nearly finished by its arrival. A free coffee card served as the apology. Appreciated, yes, but for a grand old name like Jenners, you expect sharper service, product knowledge, and the simple basics of hospitality. It’s a shame, because the deli shelves were full of tempting goods and the view truly is stunning. On balance, the surroundings suggest a middling two-and-a-half star experience, yet the service and quality tip it downward. Edinburgh has many spots marrying charm with competence; until this one does the same—train staff, mind the details, and prioritize guests—I won’t be rushing back.

My Husband and I were here a couple of weeks ago. It was 8:00pm on a Friday night and the place was pretty empty, maybe two or three tables were occupied. We came with another couple and started with several margaritas, a combination platter, and a side of guajillo mashed potatoes, then moved on to a mix of tacos. I had my eye on the Camarones a la Diabla and the Fresh Lobster tacos. The shrimp arrived blazing hot—so fiery that the heat overwhelmed the other flavors, even for someone who usually likes serious spice. By contrast, the lobster with jicama tasted muted and a bit lackluster, missing the pop you hope for in a premium taco. On the brighter side, the tequila list is strong, and the Cucumber Margarita was cool, crisp, and genuinely refreshing. Pricing landed higher than expected: with the combo platter, four margaritas, and a couple of beers, the tab came to just over $80 per couple. We might return when a margarita craving hits, but for food, we’d hope for better balance between bold and bland.

It was definitely worth checking out this buffet, but the Wicked Spoon is over-hyped for sure. It’s not bad by any means. I appreciated the sleek food presentations and many of the desserts—cute touches like the tiny metal milk carton for coffee cream made me smile. I visited for Sunday brunch around noon; at about $36 per person, the price feels reasonable. Lines were manageable. Still, the spread lacked several items I expect at a standout Vegas buffet: no crab legs, limited sushi, and an emphasis on cheaper proteins. Sausages were generic, the roast beef tough, the Korean galbi under-seasoned, and the Chinese dishes overly salty. Despite these misses, the ambiance and some sweets redeem the experience. I might return to try dinner, hoping for a broader selection and better execution.

This is where good cars go to die. And your wallet. I stopped into Tire Works a couple months ago because it was close to home and I assumed a simple fix wouldn’t turn into a saga. The clerk tried to sign me up for a store-only credit card. When I said I have enough credit cards, he rolled his eyes. I’d recently had an oil change elsewhere and was told I might need a new radiator cap. I’m not mechanically inclined, so I went in expecting an inexpensive cap and a quick exit. Instead, I was told I needed a new alternator and a laundry list of other repairs—plus the cap. I decided to get a second opinion. At O’Reilly Auto Parts, I explained the situation and walked out with a new radiator cap for about eight bucks. My car has been fine since. I’ll be sticking with my usual mechanic, and I’ll review them soon. Save yourself time, money, and frustration—get a second opinion before agreeing to major work here.

What a gem! Visiting town for two nights, we lucked into Harry’s on night one and loved it so much we returned the next evening. We started with an assortment of appetizers—duck wings, fried brie, and sliders—and were blown away. The duck wings were so incredible we immediately ordered a second round, and the portions across the board were generous. On night two, we sampled the signature burger, a flavorful blend of meats, and the surf-and-turf pairing: a 6 oz ribeye with a crab cake. The crab cake was outstanding—hands down the best I’ve had, and I’m a crab cake connoisseur. The bar impressed, too, with a thoughtful selection of beer and wine and a welcoming vibe. Harry’s delivers big flavors and value. This is a must-visit.

This was our first visit, and after seeing the commercials we were excited to try it. A crowd out the door meant a 30-minute wait to be seated, which was reasonable. Service was the bright spot: our waiter was friendly and attentive, deserving a bonus star. Unfortunately, the food didn’t live up to the hype. Most of it tasted like cafeteria fare, with the salad bar the only decent offering—and even there, I’d steer clear of the shrimp topping. Quality control seems to be the restaurant’s Achilles’ heel. Several fried items had a strange, lingering aftertaste, and when we asked, we learned that all fried foods share the same fryers and oil. That practice left a pervasive, fishy note across anything breaded or fried. The steak appears to be the marquee attraction; when we left, the line stretched to the dessert bar. Ironically, the steak was okay—far from memorable. In the end, this feels like a place people visit for variety and volume rather than flavor. If you value taste over quantity, you may want to look elsewhere.

Discovered a welcome addition to downtown Mesa last week and returned for a Thursday lunch with a party of four. The lunch specials are very reasonably priced and portions generous. Appetizer and soup were unexpected highlights—fresh and flavorful. Service was gracious, attentive without overbearing. Overall, excellent value and a pleasant experience. I’ll definitely be back soon, with friends and family.

Hidden off the Strip, this tiny spot serves Southern BBQ bliss. A surprising find in the middle of the desert, it channels the Deep South—smoky, tender meats crowned with a spicy, flavorful sauce, and sides that hit every note. Portions are generous, but you’ll wish your stomach were bigger to keep savoring. I’ll definitely swing back before leaving town; this gem is worth a repeat visit again soon, for sure.

I went back to TT Roadhouse last night for the $1-off Ska Brewing Wednesdays, and it reminded me why I love this spot. My husband happily downed three pints of Decadent, and just when we thought we’d call it a night, Elise queued up Ghost Ship. The impromptu screening sparked nostalgic memories and a lively chat with Elise, a fellow movie buff. Where else can you sip solid craft beer on tap, watch a cult flick, and actually talk about it? TT Roadhouse nails that laid-back, living-room vibe. For great pours, great films, and better conversation, it beats any theater.

I had a strange experience coming here. Something I wouldn't expect from a high class restaurant. I visited as a weekday walk-in in February and checked in upstairs. As I arrived, another guest exited the dining room asking to change seats; the host told me I was set and asked me to wait by the elevators. Over the next 20 minutes, several guests—presumably with reservations—were greeted and seated while I remained parked in the corridor. When the host finally looked my way, they asked, “Do you need help? Oh, no wait, you ate already.” I clarified that I had checked in earlier and was still waiting. To their credit, they apologized, searched the system, and seemed unsure what had gone wrong. I even offered that the earlier seat-change request might have distracted the check-in process. In a bid to make amends, they made a point of securing me a “good seat” by the window—ironically, a view of the very hotel where I was staying and had already admired several times. The view was lovely all the same, but seconds after I sat, a server dropped a plate and retrieved only the larger shards. I ordered a glass of wine, the lobster bisque, and steak and lobster. The bisque was divine in flavor, though the lobster pieces were oddly inconsistent in temperature—some warm, some cool. The steak and lobster entrée, however, was spot on. Service missteps continued to pile up. My water glass sat empty throughout the meal. A different server broke a wine glass nearby, again collecting only the big pieces and leaving me uneasy about smaller fragments underfoot. The team in my section—three servers—frequently called to each other across different levels of the restaurant, their voices carrying and disrupting what should have been a serene atmosphere. When I slowed down, a server asked if I was finished; I said yes, expecting to be offered a box. Instead, my plate—still holding a fair amount of food—was whisked away without a word. As I waited for the check, my waiter dropped a cloche at another table. The food and view delivered on the promise of a high-end experience. Unfortunately, the front-of-house execution—seating confusion, inattentive hydration, loud floor communication, incomplete cleanup, and premature clearing—felt careless and left me uneasy. For a restaurant of this caliber, that gap was hard to overlook.

This is a fun place to go if you don't have to pay any cover, which usually runs around $25 on weekends. Otherwise, save your money and go somewhere else. Suggestion: Tao for the clubbers, Caramel for the loungers, and Body English for the small venuers. As hotel guests, we skipped the admission and that made all the difference. Inside, the strategy is simple: find a go-to bartender, tip generously, and you’ll likely see drinks comped and rules relaxed. Our crew ended up with whipped cream and a cup full of cherries—no questions asked. The vibe, however, isn’t what it used to be. Rumjungle once felt like the IT spot; now the crowd leans heavy on bachelor parties, men well into their forties, and groups of girls out for a loud night. The guy-to-girl ratio felt off, and the overall scene skewed more wannabe than wow. Music and energy are fine, and the convenience for hotel guests—an elevator ride away—can turn an average night into a fun one. Still, if you’re paying a weekend cover, there are better options. We landed at three stars: no cover, free drinks, easy trip home.

Situated across from the MGM sportsbook, this sports bar hits the sweet spot for a quick beer and bite before or after placing a bet. Expect a lively crowd, especially on football Saturdays and Sundays, when snagging a table for a large group can be tough; early birds will fare better at the ample bar seating. The menu leans classic and uncomplicated—think reliable wings and solid burgers. Stray much beyond that and you may be underwhelmed. Game-day specials help the tab go down easier, with shot-and-beer combos a popular pick. Beer fans will find a respectable tap list alongside the usual domestic bottles. Screens are everywhere, sightlines are strong, and the atmosphere is built for watching multiple games without fuss. It’s not aiming to be memorable cuisine or a craft-beer temple, but as a convenient, energetic spot to chill and follow the action, it does its job well.

Five girlfriends and I chose this restaurant as the kickoff for a girls’ night out mostly for the promise of that postcard view of Mt. Washington, the fun of riding the incline, and a bill that seemed gentler than its Grandview Avenue neighbors. Unfortunately, the old adage proved true: you get what you pay for. The restaurant feels uncertain about its identity. It aspires to polish—white linen tablecloths and tiny lamp fixtures at each table—but offers little ambiance beyond the sweeping look at downtown Pittsburgh. The skyline ends up doing most of the heavy lifting; the room itself feels more set-decorated than atmospheric. That same uncertainty shows up on the plate. The menu is oddly split between try-at-fancy entrées and casual choices like sandwiches and wraps—fine for lunch, less compelling in a dinner setting. Given its steakhouse lineage, a tighter focus on seafood, pasta, and steaks would make more sense. I don’t eat steak, so if it was listed, I would have skimmed right past it, but the overall selection felt small—maybe 15 to 20 items. A limited menu isn’t a flaw if every dish is dialed in; here, it reads like a compromise. No one at our table loved their meal. The food wasn’t disastrous, just forgettable—a smattering of middling choices rather than a confident, well-executed lineup. Service was personable yet stretched. Our server was friendly and clearly wanted to do right by us, but he seemed overworked, which is puzzling in a space that isn’t particularly large. Drinks took longer than they should have. We had to ask for the complimentary bread we noticed on neighboring tables. As dusk fell, we even asked to have our tabletop lamp lit—only to learn there wasn’t a candle inside it at all; the lamps are essentially props. To his credit, he handled bumps gracefully. He swapped out a glass of wine one friend disliked for a better pick with no fuss. And when he overheard another friend struggling to cut her tuna steak with a butter knife—something that shouldn’t require a knife—he offered to have the kitchen remake it and took back the overcooked portion so they could see the issue. There’s plenty to like about the setting. The patio and windows frame the city beautifully, and the incline ride bookends the evening with a bit of romance. But beyond the view, the restaurant hasn’t defined itself. The ambiance feels staged, the menu lacks focus, and the execution hovers at average. With a more disciplined menu and better support for the staff, the experience could match the setting. For now, I wouldn’t rush back for dinner. If I’m in the area, I’d stop for drinks on the outside patio to soak in the skyline—and head elsewhere for a meal worth savoring.

Some cute and affordable stuff. The selection is solid for basics and trendy finds, and prices suit a quick wardrobe refresh. Staff are friendly and attentive—sometimes too attentive. Constant hovering and repeated pitches for a membership discount card feel pushy. I’d prefer browsing in peace and grabbing a new top or cheap shorts.

What can I say?! The best hookah place in Vegas by far!!! Food, service, and music are spot-on, true tens across the board. The hookah is so good I bought one to take home. Backed by a wall of five-star reviews, this lounge is a sure bet. Recommended.

I have always loved having fish in my home, and an aquarium has been a calming, therapeutic presence. Research suggests watching fish and marine life can lower stress, ease tension, and increase attention and relaxation, and while I don’t seek those benefits, I’ve always been drawn to the beauty of aquatic worlds. This store caters to that passion with a comprehensive selection: air pumps, filters, aquariums in multiple sizes, decor, and all the maintenance essentials. You’ll find fish food and medicines, plus a range of species including turtles, parrot fish, plecos, and goldfish—favorites of mine. The turtles are particularly striking, coming in different colors, and there are baby turtles on display that are a delight to watch. For saltwater enthusiasts, the coral offerings are impressive. The “Open Brain” coral shows gorgeous purplish-red and green tones, and the “Torch” coral gently undulates, adding hypnotic movement. Many more corals and clams are available, and everything looks clean and consistently cared for by the attentive staff. Customer service is a strong suit here. Staff members are helpful and ready to answer questions or guide you to the right product. The shop carries the scent of aquatic life without being overpowering. Three accessible, well-lit rows of display aquariums make browsing easy and enjoyable. As with any living creatures, costs vary depending on what you choose to bring home. The store is open Monday–Friday from 10:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m., and Saturday–Sunday from 11:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.

I used to work in downtown Tempe, and one of the highlights of my week was sneaking off with my boss to this Thai spot—at least once, sometimes twice. Even though I’m now within walking distance of LGO, Radio, and Chelsea’s (with Deluxe just a short drive away), I still miss this place for one reason above all: the curry. Let’s get the caveats out of the way. The atmosphere isn’t much to write home about, and the service can be spotty. That said, they offer to-go, which instantly solves both issues if you’re grabbing lunch for the office or heading back home. If you’re dining in at lunch, time it right—either get there early or go late. Hit it at high noon and you’ll likely wait, sometimes outside. The Thai iced tea is reliably good. Lunch specials are well priced and come with an egg roll and either soup or salad, which they seem to rotate with the seasons. I’ve noticed the egg roll presentation can change—on one visit there was corn—but it’s generally satisfying for a set lunch. The pad thai leans nutty and balanced, the kind you happily finish every bite of. I wish they offered a green mango salad with dried shrimp, but they more than make up for it with their Thai basil, a signature dish that’s an excellent fallback if you’re not in a curry mood. But truly, come for the curries. I’m not a yellow curry devotee (those potatoes), but the red curry, the sweet nut curry (also red), and especially the green curry are phenomenal. The green stands in a class of its own—lush, aromatic, and deeply satisfying. Choose your protein—tofu, chicken, beef, pork, or shrimp—and you’re set. I favor tofu or shrimp, but chicken and pork both shine. Bonus: TOPS Liquors sits in the same plaza, with a stellar beer selection—worthy of its own visit.

A couple of friends and I went to Bamboo Club on Tuesday, January 7 for happy hour. I visited Bamboo Club for happy hour with two friends on Tuesday, January 7, and we sat at the bar. The bartender greeted us promptly and took our drink and appetizer orders. Our first round of drinks and the initial appetizers arrived quickly. But when another friend joined us and we ordered a second appetizer, things went downhill. After about twenty minutes, we checked in; the bartender apologized and said the delay was his fault. By then our original appetizers were gone, so we ordered yet another. A runner eventually dropped off the delayed appetizer followed closely by the second one, but didn’t clear the two empty plates we had deliberately moved to the edge of the table. Despite the restaurant being fairly empty, the bar was busy, and the bartender seemed overwhelmed. The staff delivering food were neither friendly nor attentive, and there was little interest in bussing dirty dishes or checking on guests. It was a decent night to catch up, but the service made the experience frustrating. Based on other reviews I read afterward, poor service seems to be a pattern at this location. I won’t be rushing back unless management addresses staffing and training issues.

This place is AMAZING!! I visited Canyon Ranch Spa during a day-pass special and, for just $30, had unlimited in-and-out access to the facilities all day. I didn’t even book any services because the amenities alone were more than enough to fill an entire day. I ended up staying for about six blissful hours and could have lingered even longer. The standout feature for me was the jacuzzi—honestly, the best I’ve ever experienced. In the center, “volcano” jets bubble up in a gentle eruption that’s perfect for tired feet; you just sit, lift your feet, and melt into the sensation. There are also two ergonomic spots where you can recline so comfortably that your body stays immersed while your neck and head remain just above the water. Add in the tiny, precisely placed jets that deliver a soft, full-body massage, and it’s pure heaven. I drifted so close to sleep more than once. Beyond the tub, the thermal and relaxation zones make it easy to lose track of time. I rotated through rooms that range from hot (sauna) to invigoratingly cold (igloo), plus spaces designed simply for rest. My favorite was the herbal aromatherapy room—warm but not stifling, with fragrant stone “aroma rocks” that cleared my sinuses and left me breathing easy. After each room, I stepped under the rain showers with their three settings, and each rinse came with a playful sequence of lights and sounds. It’s a quirky touch, but genuinely fun and refreshing. The Wave Room deserves a special mention. Picture the most comfortable recliner imaginable, set in a quiet, serene environment that hushes the mind. I don’t usually nap, yet I nodded off there, lulled by the calm. For the value, ambiance, and thoughtful design of every space, this was one of the most relaxing spa experiences I’ve ever had. Canyon Ranch Spa nails the art of unwinding, and that $30 day pass felt like a luxury steal. I’m absolutely going back—next time I might even try the services, but honestly, the facilities are a destination in themselves.

Mostly a hang out place for students. It is a Student Union. If you’re looking for a central campus hub to meet friends, kill time between classes, or run quick errands, this Student Union delivers, but temper your expectations about food quality and noise. The ground-floor food court is a familiar lineup—pizza, Subway, Starbucks, salad, Panda Express, Taco Bell, Jamba Juice, plus a small snack shop—with a sushi spot, Sushic, replacing Burger Studio. Variety isn’t the issue; consistency is. Most options taste serviceable at best, and better meals await across the street in the surrounding plazas. Crowds swell between class blocks, and the building gets very loud. Greek life has staked out the space by the main doors and staircase, so expect a lively scene there most days. As a services hub, though, the first floor shines: information desk, game room, US Bank, RebelCard, Kaplan, a handy postal kiosk for small items, and a surprisingly clutch DMV kiosk. Two Bank of America ATMs and a US Bank ATM add to the convenience. Upstairs, the second floor caters to studying and student leadership, with three lounge rooms, a computer room, multiple meeting rooms, and a ballroom. Recognized student organizations can book meeting space for free, making it a vital resource. The third floor houses offices—including SUES, CSUN/OCED, the main RebelCard office—and the Source Room, a well-stocked supply center for student orgs. Bottom line: as a social and services center, this Union works. For a quiet spot or a great meal, head off-site. Peak-hour lines and crowds can be hectic.

I tried the Max Burger and left impressed. This Certified Angus Beef patty comes loaded with cheddar, crisp bacon, sautéed mushrooms and onions, and—most impressively—tender roasted short ribs, with fries on the side. Short ribs on a burger sound over-the-top, but here they add deep, beefy richness without overwhelming the sandwich. I wished I’d added avocado, but even without it, this was one of the best, juiciest burgers I’ve had. The portion is huge; I couldn’t finish. Service lagged, and our friendly server never brought bread, but I’d gladly return for another Max Burger again soon.

Beware of this location, says one frustrated customer. Staff were polite enough to allow a last‐minute arrival right at closing, but minutes later allegedly refused service, citing a cracked radiator and dripping fluid. According to the reviewer, the fluid was from a recent fill and the van was otherwise fine. Citing liability concerns, the shop declined to work on the vehicle. The customer then visited their trusted mechanic, who reportedly found nothing wrong. Feeling misled and inconvenienced, the reviewer vows never to return and wishes they could assign zero stars, urging others to think twice before choosing this place.

This Starbucks is one of my Charlotte favorites. Spacious and inviting, it offers plenty of tables, comfy chairs, and generous outdoor seating, making it ideal for meeting clients, tackling homework, or settling in with a book. I’ve spent hours here, happily people-watching while enjoying the reliable free Wi‐Fi and relaxed atmosphere. Baristas keep the vibe friendly, and there’s room to spread out. The only downside is the parking: be extremely careful and read every sign. Towing is common in the lot, and it can feel like tow trucks are waiting for missteps. Park smart and enjoy.

Logan’s Roadhouse Is a Total Waste of Money Logan’s Roadhouse left me disappointed and frustrated. I can grill a better steak at home while enjoying a clean, comfortable setting instead of the grungy, budget vibe here. Whenever family picks this over Chili’s, I brace myself. The advertised “high quality” steaks arrived tough, bland, and unpleasant, and the sides tasted generic. Between my brother and me, we’ve eaten enough truly great steaks to know the difference; Logan’s doesn’t come close. Service swings from indifferent to slow, and the value simply isn’t there. Short and simple: don’t waste your money. If you like low-budget steak, this might be your place. I’ll spend a bit more for a real steak at a real steakhouse.
Best ramen in Las Vegas! Packed, so arrive at 11:30 when doors open. Rich broth, springy noodles, and amazing potstickers. Friendly service. Great spot—highly recommend for very satisfying bowls.
Fantastic yogurt with amazing toppings; the Oatmeal Cookie flavor is irresistible. Absolutely worth a North Scottsdale trip!

It's Denny's—don't expect gourmet or a flawless veggie burger. The real issue here is Scottsdale's entitlement; if you want fine dining, go elsewhere. My meal arrived quickly, the waitress was attentive, and everything matched what a budget-friendly diner promises. No frills, decent food, efficient service. Good job, Denny's; exactly what I expected.

I can't believe this show got such high ratings! As someone who isn’t a die-hard Beatles fan, I went in with tempered expectations—but I’ve been won over by other tribute shows before. The venue’s circular seating is a clear plus: sightlines are strong from nearly anywhere, and being mid-way up offered a pleasing, aerial perspective. Attendance at the Saturday 9:30 performance was light enough that the usher encouraged seat upgrades after the start, which was a considerate touch. Unfortunately, the production itself didn’t meet the hype. Aside from a single standout scene, the rest felt flat, unevenly paced, and emotionally distant. At 90 minutes, it dragged considerably; I kept checking the time.

At the Fashion Show Mall food court, Panda Express delivers exactly what you want from a mall standby: food that’s freshly wok-cooked, hot, and reliably tasty. The sticker shock, however, is real. Prices skew tourist-high; a three-item plate with a small soda rang up to a jaw-dropping $14, which blurs the line between quick bite and sit-down check. Service was functional but stingy on hospitality—staff balked at offering a sample of a new dish, treating a simple request like an oddity. There is one notable perk: self-serve fountain drinks with free refills, a rarity among neighboring stalls. If you buy the small soda, you can refill to your heart’s content—Pepsi products only—though pounding multiple cups of Diet Pepsi to justify the spend may not be everyone’s idea of value. Bottom line: dependable flavors and sizzling freshness earn Panda Express a spot in your food-court rotation, but prepare to pay premium prices for what is, ultimately, fast-casual Chinese at this location.

Was good, but underwhelming overall. I went searching for the “best burger in Las Vegas” and thought I’d found it—turns out, not here. Thankfully I didn’t pay, or I’d be annoyed. Bright spot: my first-ever snails, tasty, which nudged the rating up notch.

Clear Sound, Smooth Entry, and One Minor Hiccup at Comerica Theater The Comerica Theater in downtown Phoenix proved an excellent venue for the Arctic Monkeys, even at full 5,000-seat capacity. My sister and I were in the third seating section behind the pit, yet the sound was crisp and the sightlines strong. There weren’t any big screens showing close-ups that night, but the mix and lighting made it easy to stay engaged without them. Operations were a standout. Security and ticketing moved briskly, so we were inside with minimal waiting, and the show started on time and flowed without a hitch. Seats were comfortable, aisles clear, and staff helpful. One frustration: my sister was refused service at one bar because she had a vertical ID, despite the card clearly showing she’s over 21. Minutes later, another bar served her without issue. It’s unclear whether this was a venue policy or a single employee’s misinterpretation, but training or posted guidance would help. Overall, Comerica Theater delivered a well-run concert experience with strong acoustics and good visibility, even from farther back. I’d happily return the next time I’m in Phoenix.

I've been here on 3 separate occasions and have been seen by 3 different techs. After three visits, I’ve come to see this spot as a reliable, busy neighborhood salon where the experience can vary slightly with the technician—but the basics are solid.
