On my first visit, a male tech delivered a good pedicure with a massage that hit the right pressure. The only hiccup was his insistence on repositioning my elbows during the manicure. It was specific and distracting. Visit two was the standout. Tricia worked quickly without cutting corners and seemed like a perfectionist. The proof was in the wear: my nails lasted nearly five weeks with no lifting, even through house painting and spring cleaning. If I were rating the salon solely on that appointment, it would be five stars. On my third visit, I called hoping for Tricia, but she was off on Sunday—good for her. I walked in and was paired with Ivy, who was cheerful throughout. The pedicure massage this time was on the lighter side, and the finished nail thickness was a touch more than I prefer, but the service was still good. The space itself is what you’d expect from a modern nail salon: clean, decorated, and outfitted with two TVs. There are plenty of manicure and pedicure stations—around 10 or so each—and a polish selection (I usually bring my own for toes, but they have options). They’re often busy, yet waits rarely exceed about 10 minutes. Bottom line: a convenient, well-run salon with consistent fundamentals. For the best experience, book ahead and request your preferred tech—especially Tricia—though walk-ins are generally treated efficiently and kindly.

I'm giving 2 stars just because the food is decent. The food here is decent, which is the only reason I’m giving two stars. Unfortunately, the service is consistently rude. On my last two takeout orders, I asked for soy sauce and utensils and was met with a sigh and visible annoyance. Being busy isn’t the customer’s fault; hire enough help. I tried again to see if it was an off day—afraid not. For friendlier service, better prices, and genuine care, go to Siamese Kitchen at 43rd and Olive. Sweet front staff, owner-cook, and no disappointment.

First of all, I only when there to see my Dr. who had moved over there from my old Dr.'s office. Something got mixed up with the appointment time and I had to reschedule. Instead of setting me up with my DR. they had me see the nurse practitioner the next day, she is not a Dr. anyway she could not help me because she did not know enough about the issue I went to see my Dr. for. She told me she would not charge me for the visit because of that. However she set me up to come back for some blood work. I came back two weeks later and they wanted to do some extensive physical I opted for the blood test only since that was all I needed. I WAS charged for the first visit, and never did see my Dr. Then I was informed that my Dr. had either left, or was sick and could not see me and there was no other Dr. that could help me with my issue Getting my lab results sent to my former doctor turned into an ordeal. I spoke with three different people; twice I was assured the results would be forwarded, yet nothing happened. Only Amber in billing finally resolved it—she discovered I needed to sign a release, a detail the previous two staff members failed to mention. Without Amber’s intervention, my paid-for test results, which indicated something wasn’t right, would likely have remained unsent. I will be seeing my former, qualified doctor on Monday and will not be returning to WFP. This experience highlighted poor communication, inadequate care coordination, and billing inconsistencies—exactly the opposite of what patients need during sensitive health issues. It was a disappointing, avoidable experience that eroded my trust.

Their Vanilla swirl can never go wrong!!!! Every visit is anchored by their perfect vanilla swirl—silky, rich, and consistently delightful. I recently added a buttery, flaky croissant to my order, and it’s another standout. The staff elevates the experience: attentive, patient, and never pushy, giving plenty of time to browse. I’m excited to return and explore more of the menu, confident it will keep exceeding expectations.

Delivery arrived in about an hour as expected, but the order was riddled with mistakes. Spring rolls had turkey despite my request, peanut sauce portion was tiny, and the #17 was served with chicken instead of shrimp, missing mung beans. Overall, a very disappointing experience.

Pretty neat place! I volunteered here on 7/3/14 packing nutrient meals for children in need. Our group finished 21 boxes, 38 bags each, thanks to a highly organized operation with clear, friendly guidance. Upbeat music kept the energy high, making the shift fly by. Rewarding, efficient, and genuinely fun—can’t wait to come back and volunteer again soon.

Treasure Island has shed its campy, pirate-themed, family persona for a sleeker, sexier vibe—and it works. The pool, while smaller than typical resort standards, compensates with upbeat, loud music and a lively atmosphere. Rooms are clean, remodeled, and anchored by pillow-top beds that feel like heaven. Service impressed: at check-in, I was offered a higher-floor room with a view at the same rate, and a third bed was provided at no extra charge. For travelers seeking energy, comfort, and thoughtful touches without breaking the bank, TI is a compelling choice on the Strip.

It is rare for me to give a restaurant such a low rating, but service is central to the dining experience. I visited with two coworkers for after‐work drinks and sashimi, arriving at 6:00 p.m. to an empty dining room. Staff were clustered near the entrance, waiting for anyone to walk in. After we sat, a waitress asked about drinks. I requested a Chambord martini; she said she’d check, walked to the man at the cash register, asked, and then disappeared to clean tables. She never returned. Ten minutes later, the cashier finally approached to take our drink order. When I repeated the Chambord request, he said he doubted they had any. Meanwhile, we still had no water, no menus, no acknowledgement beyond that brief exchange. Nearly fifteen minutes passed without so much as a glass of water. At that point, we decided to say “sayounara” and leave. It’s disappointing to encounter such inattention, especially as we were the only guests in the room. Even basic hospitality—prompt water service, communication, and follow‐through—would have changed the tone. Sadly, we never made it to the sashimi that night, unfortunately.

This spot earns five stars for its friendly, attentive staff who remember regulars and keep things spotless. Every dish I’ve tried is delicious, with plenty of satisfying vegetarian options. The spice level is flavorful yet gentle, perfect for someone who isn’t into heat. I visit often and plan to return again and again, for years to come—unless I move!

I enjoyed a good margarita, and the Machaca tacos were fantastic. My brother raved about the ahi tacos; I tried them and thought they were good, not great. The salsa was too mild for my taste, but the staff brought a hotter option that hit the spot. You can quickly become addicted to the chips and salsa. The atmosphere has a nice urban feel, with a spacious, open dining room. I especially liked the bar—stylish and inviting. Ole’ indeed.

I’ve been purchasing from Cheap Joes for over two years as a Minneapolis-based artist constantly hunting for good prices on supplies. Ordering online has been straightforward, and in general their pricing is competitive and shipping times average. However, a recent experience with a $500 Artograph projector exposed weaknesses in their order handling and communication. I received the projector with a faulty fan and called immediately. To their credit, the representative was helpful and assured me a replacement would be sent, along with a packing slip to return the defective unit. I was told it would ship Friday and arrive the following week. That initial interaction left me reasonably satisfied, even though I was disappointed not to use the projector that day. The problems started when no tracking number ever arrived. The next Wednesday, I used their live chat to check status and learned the projector hadn’t shipped at all because the previous agent hadn’t recorded my approval to proceed with the replacement. I was told it would finally go out that day, with tracking to follow, and should arrive the next week. What stood out was the absence of any apology and the cascading delay that ultimately pushed back my studio work by three weeks. This episode suggests Cheap Joes can be unorganized and slow to acknowledge inconvenience, even while maintaining attractive prices. I’ll continue buying from them, but only for items I don’t need immediately. If you choose to order time-sensitive gear, build in extra buffer, confirm that approvals are documented, and insist on receiving tracking promptly. For non-urgent supplies, the savings may still make Cheap Joes worthwhile. For critical equipment, consider alternatives with tighter logistics and more proactive customer care. Communication and follow-through need improvement to match their pricing consistency.

Holy moly, you guys. Talk about AMAZING FOOD! Gah, I am still salivating over this meal and it's been 4 days! As self-professed Bobby Flay fans, we earmarked one of our two Vegas nights for Mesa Grill, and our first visit proved why his name carries weight. Even before the first bite, the experience kicked off smoothly: with a 7 pm reservation, we arrived early and were seated right away. Our table in the back was tight and close to neighbors, but once the food started arriving, any seating quibbles faded into the background. Cocktails set a confident tone. My grapefruit vodka concoction was bright and refreshing, but the Hendrick’s-and-cucumber option my husband ordered was the clear star—crisp, aromatic, and balanced in a way that made mine feel merely good by comparison. Then came the starters, and that’s where Mesa hit its stride. The tiger prawn tamale was the kind of plate that makes you reconsider what a tamale can be: tender shrimp, a sweet masa dotted with juicy corn kernels, and a sauce so luxurious and perfectly spiced we could have eaten it on everything. The smoked chicken quesadilla was satisfying and hearty, but it couldn’t eclipse the tamale’s show-stopping presence. A bread basket followed, delighting with variety. The standout was an incredible corn muffin—sweet, moist, and sadly, singular. Jalapeño cheese bread added a pleasant kick, while a raisin-walnut slice felt like an odd inclusion for the Southwestern theme, though my husband enjoyed it. Round two of drinks introduced our only real hiccup. Our server enthusiastically pushed a particular margarita, overriding my husband’s wish for a custom pour with his favorite tequila. When my husband asked for it on the rocks, it arrived up; the replacement was correct but just okay. The pushiness, while well-intentioned, detracted from the otherwise seamless service. Let customers order what they want—especially when they know their preferences. Any lingering annoyance vanished with the entrée. We shared the seared scallops, and they were impeccable: deeply caramelized on the outside, buttery within, and seasoned to a tee. The accompanying grits were everything grits should be—creamy, rich, and comforting—elevated without losing their soul. Dessert sealed the deal. The toasted coconut cake was transcendent: impossibly moist, layered with true coconut flavor, and the kind of slice that lingers in your memory long after the trip ends. The ambiance leans a bit casual for the price point, but it’s pleasant and relaxed. Service was attentive overall, marred only by the drink detour. Still, Mesa Grill delivered the best food we had in Vegas, hands down. We left thrilled, full, and already plotting a return. Get the tiger prawn tamale, don’t skip the scallops, and save room for that coconut cake.
Love this place! Varied menu, tasty food, and quick, friendly service. I eat here at least once a month—always reliable and welcoming.

St. Patrick’s Day: Eight people at the bar and four bartenders, yet I waited 10 minutes for service. Put down phones, focus on guests, earn the tip. Efficiency and attentiveness matter on nights like this.

When the first location opened on Indian School, the food was impressive, largely thanks to the owner in the kitchen. Since expanding to multiple spots, quality has slipped. My biscuits and gravy were barely edible—so salty it was shocking. The menu leans heavily toward sugary breakfast items, which isn’t my preference. I’ve heard the chocolate chip pancakes are a standout, but overall the shift from chef-driven roots to a broader operation has dulled the experience.

Das Ettlinger Tor Karlsruhe hat sich zum pulsierenden Herz der Fächerstadt entwickelt und bietet Shopping mit echtem Weltstadtflair. Der architektonisch beeindruckende Boulevard lebt von Licht, Transparenz und eleganten Linien. Auf drei Ebenen eröffnen lichtdurchflutete, glasüberdachte Galerien rund 37.000 Quadratmeter Verkaufsfläche. Hier warten 130 Fachgeschäfte mit einer überwältigenden Vielfalt: Mode, Trends und Accessoires, Kosmetik, Beauty und Wellness, Literatur und Unterhaltungselektronik, bekannte Marken und gefragte Labels. Ergänzt wird das Angebot von einladenden Restaurants, Cafés und Bars, die zum Verweilen einladen. Dank der zentralen Lage, direkter Anbindung über die Kriegstraße/B10 und 900 Parkplätzen ist das Center aus allen Richtungen komfortabel erreichbar. Service und Sauberkeit sind vorbildlich. Fazit: Ein „5‐Sterne“‐Kauftempel, der Karlsruhe ein gehobenes Einkaufsniveau und ein urbanes Erlebnis beschert.

I Only Rated It One Star Because I Had To—Otherwise, Zero There’s one bright spot here: the owner. When a battery I’d purchased a week earlier failed, he swapped it out immediately—no hassle, no pushback. That kind of accountability matters. Unfortunately, nearly every other aspect of my experience fell flat. Interactions with several staff members were consistently curt and unhelpful. Asking basic questions or requesting to sample more than one e-juice flavor seemed to be treated as an inconvenience rather than a normal part of choosing a product. For a shop built around taste-driven purchases, that tone sets the wrong expectation. Worse, the house juices are wildly inconsistent. The flavor I sampled in-store did not resemble what I brought home—so different that it felt like a bait-and-switch, even if unintentional. This wasn’t an isolated incident for me, and a number of friends who vape report the same thing: a flavor can be enjoyable one week and markedly different the next. That level of variability undermines trust and makes repeat purchases feel like a gamble. With tighter quality control on mixing and more attentive customer service—plus a clear policy for addressing mismatched flavors—this shop could be solid. As it stands, apart from the owner’s professionalism, I can’t recommend it. A disappointing, one-star experience.

Just like Morris' review..... The wonderful smell of barbecue greeted us at Tennessee Grill, raising hopes on a quick stop between Sedona and the Phoenix airport. Unfortunately, the experience didn’t match the aroma. Service was surprisingly slow despite a not-too-crowded dining room—maybe a big takeout order caused the delay. My tuna sandwich was just fair, and they were out of potato chips. My buddy’s chicken wrap was equally forgettable, nothing special. It’s a shame, because the owner and servers were genuinely friendly, which made leaving a critical note harder. For us, it was a first visit and likely the last.

I recently visited this nail salon with my mom and had mixed experiences. The gentleman who did my manicure and pedicure delivered fantastic French tips on both fingers and toes. He air-brushed my hands, resulting in clean, neat lines, and despite some difficulty understanding him, we communicated enough to achieve exactly what I wanted. Unfortunately, my mom’s simple solid color application fell short. There were small specks and smudges of polish left on the skin around her nails, which looked unprofessional, and she was placed under a UV lamp to dry—with the lamp switched off. The salon itself appeared fairly clean. Overall, skilled artistry for designs, but inconsistent basic polishing and attention to detail overall.

This was my first time going to a Ramen house, but I was lucky enough to have a Japanese friend with me. Stepping into this ramen house as a first-timer felt easy, thanks to an English-friendly menu and helpful staff. The menu highlights three regional miso broths: Kome Miso from Hokkaido offers a full-bodied, hearty base; Shiro Miso from Kyoto leans fruity and natural; Mame Miso from Nagoya ends with a pleasing bitterness. Choose a pre-set bowl and then customize with as many toppings as you like. I ordered the Kome Miso #4 Spicy Ramen. The pork was tender and flavorful, and the bowl felt balanced, though the heat was gentler than expected. Next time, I’d pick the extra-spicy add-on to turn up the kick. I also tried the fried chicken and fried shrimp, and both were standouts—crisp, juicy, and great for dipping into the broth. If you add just one topping, make it the fried chicken; it pairs beautifully with almost any bowl. Don’t hesitate to visit solo: the staff speaks English, the menu is straightforward, and the flavors are worth exploring. Use these tips, trust your palate, and enjoy a satisfying ramen experience.

Went to Texaz on a whim wanting some steak and we were thoroughly disappointed. Went to Texaz on a whim craving steak and left disappointed. My T-bone arrived small, grey, and unseared, with a filet portion barely the size of a JFK half dollar. My friend opted for the grilled shrimp instead of fried; one was raw and the rest were tiny—hardly worth the $16 price tag. On the plus side, the staff was friendly, and the potato wedges and biscuits were solid. Unfortunately, the kitchen missed the mark. Two stars, and I can’t recommend this spot.

They started out great, attentive, then somewhere along the way service spiraled down. Was steered in wrong direction and am now facing a high dollar repair. Towards the end keeping an appointment was becoming difficult, keeping up on service didn't even seem like a concern. Many opinions vary on pool maintenance so I took their opinion only to realize maybe their is a difference between adding chemicals and skimming a pool, and exactly knowing how to care for a pool and extending its lifespan. They began strong—attentive, responsive, and seemingly knowledgeable. Over time, appointments slipped, follow-through lagged, and service quality spiraled. Worse, I was steered in the wrong direction, and now face a high-dollar repair that might have been avoided with proper guidance. I learned there’s a big difference between tossing in chemicals and truly understanding pool care that extends equipment lifespan. Opinions abound in pool maintenance, but expertise matters. If consistency and reliable advice are priorities for you, proceed cautiously and demand clear explanations and accountability.

After a few years away from Star Nails due to bad service, I gave them another chance. I used to get consistently great pedicures, but one rushed, 30-minute session made me stop going. This time, the pedicure itself was fine, yet the polish application was sloppy; one nail was so poorly done I had to completely redo it at home. For $35, I expect clean, careful polish and a finished look that lasts. I shouldn’t have to fix mistakes after leaving a salon. I’m not convinced they prioritize quality anymore, which is disappointing. With so many nail salons nearby, I may choose elsewhere.

Rooftop Gem with Great Drinks and Comfort Eats I've been here several times, and the beer and wine are excellent. The rooftop seating is a highlight. I've tried the wings, tater tots, sausage platter, and hummus; each was fantastic. Pricing is reasonable, and happy hour deals are solid. Though they've only been open a month and are still ironing out a few kinks, the staff’s enthusiasm shines. I recommend stopping by once; I can’t wait to explore more of the menu.

Six-sample craft beer flights are the star here, making exploration both fun and low-risk. Instead of committing to a full pint that might miss your palate, you can sample three unfamiliar styles and then circle back to three trusted favorites to land the session on a high note. The menu mirrors that spirit of variety. Wings arrive with sauce on the side—an interesting twist that invites customization. A salad proved fresh and tasty, though a bit light for the price, especially when it matches the wings. The standout bite was the Sweet Potato Tacos, more akin to empanadas, crisp and comforting with a bright pesto dipping sauce. As a longtime Southwestern eater, I wished for a bottle of house hot sauce or a signature table spice to add heat. The room runs loud at the moment, but the open floor plan and generous windows promise a lively, all-season spot once the acoustics are dialed in. Set squarely in the Evans Churchill district, it’s perfectly placed for a casual pint before or after a neighborhood pub crawl. For curious drinkers and grazers, this is a welcome addition. Expect to linger, compare notes, and discover a new go-to without buyer’s remorse here.

Been going to Juan's for over 10 years. It is family owned, they are great people but don't expect them to be gregarious, they seem somewhat shy. This family-owned spot has been my go-to for a decade, serving comforting Mexican fare with a humble charm. The salsa is fresh, bright, and house-made—not the canned stuff some claim—though the chips can be hit-or-miss, occasionally not hot or crisp. Standouts include the chimichanga and carne asada tacos, generous, flavorful, and paired with simple yet satisfying beans and rice. The value is outstanding: it’s hard to find this quality and quantity for under eight dollars anywhere else. Cleanliness is impeccable, with consistently top marks from county health inspections. Expect lunchtime and Friday-night crowds, a clear sign of its popularity, and you’ll often spot local police eating here, too—a dependable indicator of a beloved neighborhood restaurant.

This is a good shop to visit that is not too far out from the city centre and well worth looking into if you are passing. The fish on offer here offers both good quality and reasonable pricing, which is as much as you can really ask for. Conveniently located just beyond the city centre, this fishmonger delivers on freshness and value. The counters are tidy, the turnover seems brisk, and the staples—salmon, cod, haddock, and the like—look inviting and are priced sensibly. My main quibble is with the way prices are displayed solely in pounds. While it’s common in the trade, many shoppers think in kilos, and having to convert on the fly can be awkward. A dual display would be a small effort for the shop and a big help for customers, sparing us the mental arithmetic and making comparisons clearer. Even so, you do feel you’re getting a fair amount for your money, broadly in line with other reputable fishmongers. Staff are welcoming and easy to chat with as they weigh your order and sort your change. The brief banter adds a pleasant human touch to the visit. I’ll admit I sometimes struggle with certain accents, so my contribution can trend toward nods and smiles, but the warmth comes through regardless. The selection leans conservative—solid classics rather than adventurous variety. Most will be satisfied, but if you enjoy exploring lesser-seen species or specialty cuts, you may find the range a bit limited. That said, for dependable basics, fair pricing, and friendly service, this is a nice fishmonger to have nearby and a worthwhile stop when you’re passing through.

Some artisans seem blessed with a magic touch; Tracy’s happens to be dipped in chocolate. As warm and welcoming as her confections, she turns simple ingredients into fresh, melt-in-your-mouth bliss. I’ve chased her sweets across the Valley—from Citizen Public House and Arcadia Farms Market Place to Smeeks and the Downtown Phoenix Public Market—and they’re consistently excellent. Beyond those spots, she crafts made-to-order treats from her public kitchen, which means personalized boxes of joy are just an email away. Her silky caramels and snappy chocolates shine, and the desserts are downright irresistible. Feeling bold? Try the bacon pecan brittle: a cheeky mash-up of salty, smoky, and sweet that somehow lands perfectly. With fair prices and quality that never wavers, Tracy’s shop is my go-to for gifts and gatherings. I’m already earmarking a holiday haul—and maybe a little stash just for me.

I’ve been a loyal customer here for years, but today’s eyebrow wax was a nightmare. A new technician handled my brows, and I didn’t catch her name. My eyebrows came out completely uneven—one is super thin—and I’m genuinely embarrassed. Worse, she ripped skin below my brow; it bled, which has never happened to me here before. This was a shocking decline in quality and safety. I left upset and disappointed, and I can’t recommend getting waxed here anymore. I won’t be returning after this experience.

Good but not that great. We opted for the tasting menu in the so-called Swan Court, paying an extra $10 for swans peering through the window—an upsell that felt silly in the dark. A request to split a wine pairing was curtly dismissed, a surprising hard no given many restaurants accommodate it. The meal opened with a trio of amuses: a bacon-wrapped scallop that was fine, the others forgettable. Ironically, the standout of the night was the house-cured bacon served alongside the beef—astonishingly crisp without greasiness, with our server detailing their meticulous process of curing and slow-cooking between absorbent sheets. Unfortunately, the “duo of beef” was uneven: a flat-iron cut arrived dry and overdone, dulling what should have been a highlight. Dessert brought a playful trio of sorbets with a guessing game; two were easy enough, while a pomegranate-cherry stumped us—pleasant, if hardly memorable. We left very full yet without the sense of wonder a great tasting menu should deliver. For context, L’Atelier de Joel Robuchon—pricier, yes—has left us dazzled on past visits; this experience simply didn’t approach that level. Service oscillated between informative (on the bacon) and dismissive (on the pairing), lacking the warmth and polish we expect at this price point. My brother previously raved about the service here, but we didn’t see it. Between the awkward upsell, uneven execution, and uninspired hospitality, I wouldn’t return and would point friends toward stronger options in town. There were good moments, but not enough to justify the hype—or the check.

On the hunt for something new, inspired by a binge of travel shows, I set out to find blood sausage and pirozhki. The pirozhki mission fizzled—too many places closed—but I remembered a small shop up the street and took a chance. A quick call brought a rare flash of luck: they answered, and yes, they had blutwurst. A short drive later, I stepped into a tiny, cool space with one or two customers and a lively hum of German floating through the room. It was charming and a bit disorienting—like stumbling into a corner of Berlin—but the cultural immersion added character. One gripe: three staffers were in the back smoking and chatting, while one person up front was helping another customer. I waited a good 10–15 minutes before someone emerged to assist. Also, bring cash or plan to spend at least $10; they won’t run a card for less. Service, once it started, was warm and efficient. The woman who helped me quickly packed exactly what I wanted: blutwurst and kasseler, a smoked pork chop. I’d had kasseler before and figured it would be a reliable lunch if the blood sausage turned out to be an acquired taste. Back home, I grilled both to a satisfying, toasty finish. The pork chop was solid—smoky and familiar, more comfort than revelation. The blutwurst, however, was a revelation. Deep and dark, it delivered a rich, layered flavor with an earthy backbone and a pronounced maltiness from barley that gave it structure and intrigue. There’s a subtle iron-tinged complexity, rounded and savory rather than metallic, with a pleasing snap to the casing and a lush, almost pâté-like interior. As Anthony Bourdain might have said, it’s a standout among tube-shaped foods—elevated, rustic, and utterly craveable. Despite the wait and the card minimum, this shop proved worth the detour. If you’re adventurous or simply curious about German specialties, bring a little patience and some cash. You’ll be rewarded with honest, traditional flavors and a sense of place that’s hard to find elsewhere. I’ll be back—for more blutwurst, and maybe another run at pirozhki.

We ordered our "getting ready" food for our wedding day from Jason's Deli because of all the rave reviews from The Knot Las Vegas message board. Well, those reviews were all correct. Jason's Deli is really awesome. For couples assembling a calm, well-fed start to their wedding morning, Jason’s Deli stands out. It was easy to place platters for 12. A quick phone call a couple days before secured the order and payment, and day-of service exceeded expectations. Despite a shooting that shut down the Las Vegas Strip and snarled traffic across the freeways, our delivery driver was exceptional. He called every 15 minutes with location updates, turning what could have been a stressful delay into a reassuring countdown. When he arrived, he didn’t just drop at the door—he brought the trays straight to our suite with a friendly smile. The food itself impressed: breakfast sandwiches arrived warm, the fruit was crisp and fresh, and even the coffee stayed hot in its jug. Everything tasted great, fueling our wedding party during hair, makeup, and final touches—and keeping this bride far from bridezilla territory. Jason’s Deli delivered reliability, hospitality, and value when it mattered most. From ordering to delivery, the experience was smooth, thoughtful, and delicious. We’ll wholeheartedly recommend them to every bride planning a Las Vegas wedding. Viva Jason’s Deli indeed!

Early Dinner at Toby Keith’s My husband and I stopped in for an early Saturday dinner and were pleasantly surprised. Despite seeing mixed reviews, our experience was smooth from start to finish. Our waitress was genuinely attentive; drinks were refilled without asking, and check-ins felt timely, not intrusive. The food was decent, classic pub fare prepared well, with satisfying portions. The atmosphere matched the meal: casual, comfortable, and upbeat without being loud. We’re curious to return in the evening for live music, which could elevate the vibe even more.

They’re closed on Mondays, so plan accordingly; our first attempt to dine here was thwarted. On a weekend dinner for two, service was welcoming and efficient, with attentive pacing and friendly staff. The Baked Scallop Roll doesn’t win on looks—picture a creamy slop atop a California roll—but it absolutely delivers on flavor. While scallop is scarce and mushrooms dominate, the blend of mayo, scallop, mushrooms, and soy sauce creates a rich, savory bite I’d order again. At $12.95, it feels pricey for the amount of scallop, yet it remains a standout I’d still recommend. The Salmon Salad Roll is a lighter counterpoint: no rice, just finely cut cucumber wrapping generous chunks of salmon. It’s delicately assembled and impressive, though I personally prefer the indulgent taste of the baked scallop roll. Not everything hits. The Unagi-don arrived dry—the eel lacked its usual luscious glaze, and the rice didn’t help—making it a dish I wouldn’t order again. The Chicken Udon Soup fares better. The broth is flavorful and comforting, with a healthy mix of onions, mushrooms, and broccoli. The chicken was a bit tough, but the overall bowl satisfied. In sum, friendly service and memorable rolls make this spot worth a visit—just skip Monday and the unagi-don. Expect clean presentation, fair portions, and a menu with thoughtful variety. We’ll be back.

Visited this salon for the first time for both a pedicure and manicure, and unfortunately the experience was disappointing. The technician did a poor job; the next day my toenail polish peeled because it hadn’t dried properly. They did fix it, but four days later the gel and polish on my fingernail lifted, requiring another visit. When I returned, the technician was curt, and while attempting to repair the manicure, she nicked my skin. I paid $56 for both services, which felt like a waste given the quality and attitude. I won’t be back and can’t recommend this place based on my experience.

Ordering through the restaurant’s site via Eat24 was seamless, and delivery was impressively fast—definitely a strong start. Our House Lo Mein was decent, and the kitchen honored our request to omit celery and mushrooms, though they also skipped the baby corn, which was disappointing. The Wonton soup was the clear miss: rubbery, off-tasting dumplings that we couldn’t finish. Fried shrimp arrived soggy, suggesting they’d sat too long; steamed dumplings were doughy but passable. Ironically, the fortune cookies ended up being the highlight of a $30 order. If you can drive, consider a higher-rated spot; if you’re sticking with delivery, choose carefully. From this experience, rice and noodle dishes seem like the safest bets, while appetizers and soup may be hit-or-miss. Service was polite, but quality varied across the menu.

Come for the ambiance, NOT the food! Capo’s nails the mobster vibe: a speakeasy-style entrance, dim lighting, and a vintage soundtrack that makes your first visit feel like stepping into a noir film. As an experience, it’s undeniably fun and perfect for a Vegas story. Unfortunately, the culinary side doesn’t live up to the show. The food is just okay—think bland pastas, overcooked entrées, and forgettable appetizers—and the prices seem geared more toward sustaining the theme than reflecting quality on the plate. Service was mixed on our last visit: our server was genuinely kind and attentive, but the bar staff was brusque and borderline rude, souring the mood with slow pours and snarky attitudes. If you’re hungry and hoping for a standout meal to savor, this isn’t the spot. If you’re hunting for atmosphere and a memorable tale, Capo’s will deliver—though what you might remember most is how mediocre the food was and how much you paid for it. After a couple visits, I’m not sure I’ll be back; I’ve had my fill of Vegas stories.

Hidden at the back of Stonecrest, in a storefront facing Regal Cinemas, Kabob Grill delivers the kind of quality Mediterranean fare that keeps cravings alive. On a recent Tuesday, my tahini-and-falafel fix brought Casey and me back, and—as usual—we left fat and happy. The room is classy without pretense: tasteful décor, lighting, and a casual, relaxing vibe. Though the dining area is smaller than most, comfort isn’t compromised; conversation flows easily, there’s never a din, and I almost always spot families alongside couples enjoying a laid‐back meal. Menu highlights abound. The grilled kafta kabobs—spiced ground beef, smoky and tender—are standouts, as is the succulent grilled lamb kabob. My latest favorite is the lamb kabob pita: a warm, overstuffed wrap packed with hommos, hearty lamb chunks, and tangy pickled vegetables. For sides, don’t miss the creamy baba ghannouj, crisp falafel, and the addictive potato harra. Service is consistently excellent. The team here is unfailingly friendly and attentive without hovering, adding to the restaurant’s easy charm. For those 18 and older, there’s hookah available on the patio—a mellow finish to a satisfying meal. In Ballantyne/South Charlotte, Kabob Grill is a must‐try.

Thanks to Groupon I Didn’t Have to Pay Full Price for This Mess! I went to this salon hoping for a simple haircut and deep conditioning, and left wishing I’d chosen anywhere else—and anyone but Josh. The visit started promising: the receptionist was welcoming, offered me a drink, the music was upbeat, the space looked clean and well cared for, and I even appreciated the posted reminder asking people not to bring children unless they’re there for services. Once I sat in Josh’s chair, the experience went downhill fast. His conversation was focused almost entirely on chatting with coworkers, not on me or my hair, and the overall tone felt unprofessional. Communication was minimal, yet the appointment dragged to nearly two hours for what should have been routine services. I have naturally curly hair. Josh cut it while curly, then decided to straighten it—against my stated preference—because he said he needed to “make sure it was even.” In my many years of haircuts, no one has ever had to chop curly, then straighten, then cut again. When I questioned the approach, his response was a dismissive “ha ha, I know what I’m doing, I do this shit all day,” which did nothing to inspire confidence. Worse, he burned my scalp twice with the straightener, turning an already frustrating session into a painful one. Thanks to Groupon, I didn’t pay full price for this mess, but a discount doesn’t excuse poor service and careless technique. I won’t be returning to Josh, and this experience makes me hesitant about the salon overall. That said, the environment and front-desk hospitality were solid, and other stylists here seem to have strong reviews. If you go, book with one of the well-reviewed women and steer clear of Josh. Choose wisely and protect your curls.

As an educated buyer, I appreciate the occasional gems at Lee’s. The selection can be impressive, with bottles that carry real age you won’t find at Total Wine, which focuses almost exclusively on recent releases. However, Lee’s size seems to compromise quality control. I’ve seen too many white wines and rosés lingering well past their prime—sometimes browned—still on the shelf, and returns can be inconsistent. Staff knowledge is hit-or-miss; less-informed shoppers risk being guided toward whatever inventory needs to move rather than what suits their palate. If you know your producers, vintages, and storage caveats, you can score excellent deals. If you don’t, shop carefully. Lee’s rewards the informed and can frustrate the casual buyer. Proceed with eyes open.

BEST. THAI. FOOD. IN. VEGAS. I’ve tried countless spots and remain a tough Thai critic, but this place wins. I crave the fried spinach salad, the curries are consistently great, and the drunken noodles are my favorite. If only it were closer—please open more locations!

The Bellagio impresses with room sizes that feel larger than remembered—genuinely spacious and comfortable. Despite the property’s age, the hotel has consistently invested in smart renovations, preserving its signature elegance while updating essentials. That commitment shows: the public spaces and guest rooms look fresh, refined, and far from a 15-year-old footprint. Perhaps most telling, the Bellagio continues to attract its longtime clientele, a testament to reliable service, quality finishes, and an enduring, upscale Vegas experience.

This has got to be the worst Wendy's I've ever been to. Disappointing from start to finish. The value menu felt anything but: while many fast-food spots keep items in the $1–$2 range, this location’s lowest price was $1.50 and most hovered around $2.50, undermining the idea of “value.” Despite having one person ahead of me, the service dragged on painfully, suggesting staffing problems. When a quick meal costs more and takes longer than it should, there’s little incentive to return. I’ll look elsewhere.

The good: Our waiter provided excellent service and the food was very tasty. The lobster won tons were amazing. There’s a tale of two venues here: the dining room that delivers and the door that derails. At the table, our server was exceptional—attentive, personable, and on top of every detail. Courses arrived at a good pace, drinks were spot-on, and the kitchen showed real finesse. The standout was the lobster won tons: delicate, richly flavored, and perfectly balanced, the kind of dish you remember and want to return for. If the review were about food and service alone, this would be a strong recommendation. Unfortunately, the experience was bookended by a front-of-house gauntlet that took the shine off the night. Despite having a dinner reservation, we explained it to four different bouncers before being allowed to bypass the line, only to be met by a hostess who was brusque and inflexible about seating the party until every guest was present—even with one person en route from a delayed flight. We agreed to sit without her, yet our table wasn’t ready, and we waited at the bar for about 30 minutes with a pager. Meanwhile, a bouncer repeatedly flashed a flashlight at us, ordering “you can’t stand there,” which felt needless and unwelcoming. After an expensive meal—over a hundred dollars per person on dinner and wine—we expected smoother access to the nightclub. Instead, we were told we needed to pay a cover and join the long corridor queue like anyone else, unless we had a “line pass” from our waiter. We hadn’t been advised of this, and the policy felt confusing and punitive to diners. If you plan to transition to the club, proactively ask your server for a line pass before you finish dinner. Otherwise, consider taking your night elsewhere. Mix offered excellent food, stellar service, and thoughtful hospitality—our waiter there even escorted us into the lounge. Between the two, the kitchen here impresses, but the door policies may leave you wishing you’d gone with the smoother option.

This is such an awesome gym! Sitan Gym has become a beloved spot for our whole family. The scheduling is incredibly convenient, with kids’ classes running at the same time as adult sessions, so we can train together without juggling daycare. The facility is spotless and well maintained, and the atmosphere is welcoming from the moment you walk in. Every instructor is patient with beginners, deeply knowledgeable, and clearly passionate about their craft. They meet you where you are, push you safely, and celebrate your progress. I’ve never worked so hard, and I never expected to fall in love with Muay Thai—but I’m absolutely hooked. If you’ve been on the fence, stop waiting and head to Sitan Gym. You won’t regret it.

Really enjoyed this spot for both its food and quirky artwork and memorabilia. The banana and pumpkin breads were standout—moist, flavorful, and elevated by the butter. The omelette was solid, while the chicken-fried steak was just okay. Service was friendly and impressively fast. Would return.

I live nearby and decided to try this place—big mistake. This was the worst sushi I've had in ages. The rice was very dry, and the fish tasted like grade D. They seem to hide subpar cuts in their rolls. I’m kicking myself for going.

Weekend Stay in Vegas – Solid Value for $29 I stayed here last weekend and was surprised. After reading harsh reviews, I booked anyway because vegas.com had a $29 nightly deal, and it delivered value. The hotel isn’t fancy, but our room was clean on arrival and felt maintained. Parking was easy during the day; at night it can take a few minutes to find a spot, but you’ll get one. Check-in and check-out were straightforward and quick, with friendly staff. If you’re looking for budget lodging near the action and don’t need luxe amenities, this place works. I’d definitely return if they offer another great deal.

Cafe Diem’s menu reads like someone curated all my favorites from every kind of restaurant. Breakfast classics sit beside diner comfort, pub bites, and global staples like pad thai, bulgogi, loco moco, stir fry, bananas foster, crab cakes, and more. It’s the kind of variety that makes you excited to order. Unfortunately, the cooking didn’t match the promise. The french toast arrived soggy, with no caramelized, crusty edges. The sausage gravy skewed oddly sweet, and the regular iced tea had an off flavor that was hard to enjoy. The shoestring sweet potatoes were shaved so thin that frying turned them into crispy, oily toothpicks rather than satisfying fries. Service, though, was warm and welcoming; the owner and waiters were genuinely friendly and attentive. With such an ambitious, crowd-pleasing menu, a few tweaks in the kitchen could transform this spot into a must-visit. I’m rooting for improvements and hoping to make Cafe Diem a regular stop on future trips to Las Vegas.

I was referred to Gianni and ended up working with Jake, and both were fantastic. I’m not into tattoos and needed a small cover-up, so I was out of my comfort zone, but they made me feel at ease. Jake’s design exceeded my expectations. Professional, friendly, and talented—absolutely love this place. Truly recommend.

Wow. What a treat. I haven’t even tasted the food yet; this review is strictly about delivery. I ordered through Grubhub around 11:30 p.m.—late, yes, but still three hours before the posted closing time. The order arrived about twenty minutes earlier than the app’s estimate. Unfortunately, everything else about the experience erased that goodwill. The driver was curt on the phone upon arrival, and when he reached my door he literally shoved the bag into my hands. Part of the order slipped, hit the floor, and he simply said “ok” and walked away. No apology, no checking the spill, nothing. I had already tipped more than 20 percent on my card because I value service, especially at night, and I expected basic courtesy and care. I’ll admit I was having a terrible evening—I had to say goodbye to my cat—and I was just hoping for a simple, fuss-free pizza delivery. Even without my emotions running high, this behavior felt rude and unprofessional. Food might be great, but service matters. After this, I won’t be ordering here again. Management should train drivers on respect and handling.

For the price, Spice Market Buffet is hard to beat. During two recent stays at Planet Hollywood, I was pleasantly surprised by the quality and selection. Without breaking the bank at high-end buffets like Bellagio, Spice Market delivers real bang-for-your-buck value. Standout dishes included chilled crab legs, Mediterranean kabobs, pork loin, and a decadent French silk pie. Affordable, tasty, and satisfying—I'd happily return.

As a longtime admirer of Mon Ami Gabi, I’ve come to expect polished service and confidently executed bistro fare. That’s why my latest visit was such a letdown. From the outset, our server’s standoffish demeanor set an awkward tone - aloof where hospitality should feel warm. Unfortunately, the evening’s low point was the kitchen’s handling of a special: bacon-wrapped sea bass. Halfway through, I discovered the center was noticeably undercooked - not a translucent edge, but a substantial raw portion. After a quick check from my dining companions, I flagged our waiter, who did return the plate to have the fish finished. While the correction was appreciated, the damage was done; it’s hard to relax into a meal once trust in basic execution wavers. Mon Ami Gabi has, in my experience, delivered far better. That history makes this stumble more disappointing than infuriating. A refresher on service fundamentals - attentiveness, warmth, proactive problem-solving - along with tighter quality controls on specials would go a long way. Proper temp checks on thick cuts of fish and a more engaged recovery (a sincere apology, perhaps a comp or alternative dish) could have salvaged the evening. I hope this was an outlier. For now, my return is on hold, but not off the table entirely.

Once our go-to Thai spot, we ate here twice a month, but the past year has brought a slide in quality. It’s not just the entrees; even the once crazy-good spring roll dipping sauce has lost its punch. My heart is still with this place, yet I now stop by only occasionally. With new competition in S Chl, I sincerely hope they reclaim their former standards: fresh, balanced flavors and consistent execution, because when they’re on, this restaurant can be fantastic.

I have never been to Red Lobster up until this point in my life. I am 27. I never want to go back to Red Lobster ever again. Whisked away to Red Lobster for my brother’s birthday dinner, I went in with an open mind and left wishing we had chosen literally anywhere else. From the first bite, the kitchen’s heavy hand with salt dominated the experience. It felt like the food was engineered to suit an aggressively iodized palate, and subtlety never stood a chance. I ordered a shrimp duo featuring shrimp scampi and seafood-stuffed shrimp. Both missed the mark. The scampi arrived swimming in butter, more greasy than garlicky, and the stuffed shrimp lacked any memorable texture or flavor beyond salt and oil. My side salad came drowned in ranch—my mistake for not asking for it on the side—but the result was a limp, over-dressed afterthought. Even the famed Cheddar Bay Biscuits, a hallmark of the brand, were merely okay and oddly dry. Others at our table opted for lobster tails. I tasted a few bites: decent, but far from exceptional. To be fair, I’ve rarely had life-changing lobster, but I’m confident Red Lobster isn’t where I’ll find it. The bright spot was an appetizer plate from the build-your-own selection—clam strips and mozzarella sticks. Hard to mess up, and mostly fine. The clam strips satisfied that fried, briny craving; the mozzarella sticks could have used a bit more heat to achieve that ideal stretch. Service, to its credit, was a highlight. Our waitress was friendly, efficient, quick with refills, and kept things moving. Yet when we mentioned it was my brother’s birthday, nothing happened—no small gesture, no complimentary dessert, just silence. In a chain known for standardized hospitality, that stung. Bottom line: if I’m paying for seafood, I expect freshness, balance, and care. Here, everything felt blunt, salted into submission, and coated in butter. Red Lobster might suit those craving predictability, but for me, it’s a one-and-done. The atmosphere felt generic, the kind of nautical kitsch that aims for cozy but lands on dated, and the value proposition just didn’t align with the quality on the plate today.

I found this place on Yelp and decided to try it out From the moment you walk in, the setup is simple and welcoming: cash register up front, a bright yellow menu to the right, around twenty seats across six tables, and a modest salad bar reminiscent of Roberto’s. The menu mirrors Roberto’s in many ways but adds its own twists, including a full breakfast lineup for early birds. I ordered the chimichanga—a deep-fried burrito—and it hit the spot. Crisp exterior, flavorful filling, and, refreshingly, none of that watery, greasy runoff that dampens plates elsewhere. Cutting it open revealed a clean, well-crafted bite every time. Service was straightforward, prices felt fair, and the space, while compact, works well for a casual meal. I’m already eyeing the churros and a couple of other items for my next visit. This is a solid neighborhood find I’d happily return to.

This casino sits just off the Strip and offers a quieter gaming floor with an old-school vibe. For Pai Gow fans, there’s one $5 table—a rare find and a draw if you want to stretch your bankroll while sipping a cold Corona and playing a few relaxed hands. The drawback is capacity: when that lone $5 table fills up, options are limited to waiting or switching games. Another miss for me is the lack of Pai Gow insurance, a side option I like to play when my hands run cold. The property itself feels small and dated. It’s serviceable, but the décor leans old-fashioned, which isn’t my preference. I’ve visited several times and, aside from the usual wallet-lightening casinos are built for, the experiences were pleasant, if unremarkable. I haven’t stayed in the hotel, so I can’t speak to the rooms. Overall, this is an acceptable spot for a low-stakes Pai Gow session, but not a destination I’d prioritize over more modern casinos with more tables.

The Cheesy Bread Was Awesome Cheesy bread stole the show—gooey and perfect. Unfortunately, the pizza was a mess: cheese and sauce sliding everywhere, nowhere near Lou Malnati’s attention to detail. Friends praised the beer, and my root beer was solid. With execution this loose, I’m docking points despite highlights.

We had a BALL on this trip! From start to finish, this Boulder City zipline experience was unforgettable. The weather was perfect, and the excitement amped up when a Telemundo crew arrived to film an “extreme adventure” segment—so who knows, we might even catch ourselves on TV. What really set the day apart, though, were the guides. They were knowledgeable, helpful, and genuinely UBER fun, the kind of team that clearly loves what they do. There were no “let’s just get this done” vibes—only enthusiasm, safety, and great energy. They offered bottled water regularly and never rushed anyone, patiently waiting for those who needed a moment on the hike between platforms. Their dedication shone in one standout moment: a guest ignored instructions to secure personal items, and her hat took off on the very first line. Without hesitation, one guide climbed down steep, rocky terrain into the valley to retrieve it, while another later secured the hat properly to her pack. That level of care and effort is rare and speaks volumes about their commitment to guests. As for the ziplines themselves—awesome. We all wished they were longer and had a “reverse” button so we could do it over instantly, but alas, gravity only goes one way. Even so, each run delivered pure adrenaline and sweeping canyon views, with smooth operations, clear instructions, and gear that inspired confidence. Hitting speeds approaching 65 mph while zipping and weaving through desert canyons is a rush you won’t forget. If you’re visiting Vegas, living there, driving through, or even just daydreaming about it, do yourself a favor: book BC Flightlines online, head to Boulder City, sign in, suit up, and go. Bring a great crowd, a significant other, or fly solo—this adventure works for everyone. You will not regret it. It’s laughter, scenery, speed, and stellar service rolled into one. What are you still waiting for? Get moving!

Seated promptly but never approached by a server, even after we asked staff to send someone—frustrating and disappointing. However, the manager later apologized and offered to comp some food, clearly monitoring Yelp and taking feedback seriously. Appreciated the accountability. Because of that, we’re willing to return and give them another chance to earn our business.

Stopped in for curry goat with rice and peas and cabbage—tender, flavorful, and satisfying. I sampled my friend's brown stewed red snapper, which was equally delicious. They were out of plantains, but Kola Champagne, a sweet cream-soda-like drink, hit the spot. Service was fair; despite the bustle, staff managed the crowd well. Overall, a tasty, comforting Caribbean meal worth revisiting soon.

Visiting for my husband's Christmas party, we had a delightful first-time experience. The calamari was the best I've ever had, crispy and tender. We both ordered steaks; mine was slightly undercooked and needed a touch more salt, but still tasty. I sampled three martinis, with Southern Peach as the standout. The S'mores dessert was good, capping the festive evening.

The ice cream is good. This spot serves tasty ice cream. I haven’t tried the cupcakes at this location yet, but I loved them in LA and plan to sample them soon. I wish they served warm cookies—I hate them cold. Heard they offer a gluten-free cupcake, which is a big plus.

When my parents visited for the first time since our move from Chicago, fatigue turned dinner plans into a pizza night. My dad, late 60s, lifelong Chicagoan—South Side roots, nearly five decades on the North Side—knows his pizza. Chicago isn’t only deep dish; many of us swear by a proper, crispy, square-cut thin crust. Having tried the regular crust before, we ordered the medium crust with sausage and onion, easy on the cheese—an owner-favorite combo. The verdict: fantastic. My dad took one bite, looked up, and said, “Kid, you found yourself a great pizza joint out here.” That’s high praise from someone raised among neighborhood institutions where quality is the baseline. This place nails Chicago-style thin crust: balanced toppings, a restrained hand with cheese, well-seasoned sausage, and that essential crackly base that holds its own without flopping. The square cut isn’t a gimmick; it’s a way of eating. We start with the outer crust squares, working inward, saving the center pieces—those tender, crustless bites—for the next day. And yes, they’re best cold. We don’t reheat pizza. If you’re from Chicagoland and longing for the family-style spots you grew up with, or simply curious about the Chicago thin tradition, this is your spot. Skip the floppy pie-cut slices and embrace a style built for sharing, for conversation, for that satisfying crunch. Bravo to the team. The only thing my dad missed were the crinkle-cut fries and a side of garlic bread from his hometown haunts. No big deal—leaves more room for pizza. Consider us impressed, and consider this a new go-to when the craving hits. We’ll be back, and bringing fellow Chicago expats soon.

Awful! My dish was literally dripping with oil—like a bowl of hot olive oil with a few pasta pieces. Absolutely gross. The service was terrible, staff unfriendly, and the whole experience disappointing. I expected much better. Won’t be back and do not recommend.

Lori made me feel completely at ease as I took the plunge from super-long hair to a chic short cut. As a short-hair newbie who struggled to describe what I wanted, she asked smart, targeted questions, translated my vague ideas, and delivered an exciting, flattering look that felt instantly “me.” I came in first thing in the morning and the place was quiet, but even on busy days—when the waiting area can feel cramped—they move efficiently and get you finished quickly. Best of all, I’ve never needed an appointment. Friendly, intuitive service and reliable pace make this my go-to spot for stress-free cuts.

I ordered the sampler plate to share with coworkers and was really let down. For a brand-new spot, this felt careless. The buffalo tenders arrived soggy and limp, while the mozzarella bites and fried pickles were soft instead of crisp—overall pretty unappetizing. It should be easy to nail at least one item on a basic sampler, but nothing impressed. I work next door and wanted to become a regular, yet this first experience was disappointing. Hoping they tighten up execution soon.

I’ve visited several Black Angus locations, and this one stands out. The atmosphere works equally well for lunch and dinner—comfortable, lively, and welcoming. Service is consistently friendly and generally efficient, and I’m impressed that the manager regularly circulates, checks on guests, and even clears plates—a rare, hands-on touch that sets the tone for the team. Pricing is my only hesitation: a $29 steak feels steep, and tacking on an extra charge for a simple side like asparagus doesn’t sit quite right. Still, the quality keeps me coming back. The steaks are cooked perfectly, well-seasoned, and reliably delicious. Despite the price, I’ll definitely return with friends and family alike.

After a major storm destroyed my roof, garage door, HVAC, and trim, I faced the largest insurance claim of my life. Jared and his crew took charge, managed every detail, and delivered upgrades I truly loved. Four years later, while selling the house, I misplaced the contract buyers needed to verify the materials’ strong warranty. Jared stepped in again, tracked down the documentation, and saved the deal. Exceptional service, real professionalism, and genuine respect—this is the team you want on your side today.

Happy hour is awesome with great prices and generous pours. The hummus and quinoa balls are must-tries. Cozy, inviting ambiance, and staff are wonderfully friendly and polite. We especially love Haley—she’s beautiful, courteous, and always remembers our drinks. Highly recommend this spot.

Don't get alterations done once you purchase the suit! We ordered 12 suits for our bridal party, and the in-house alterations turned a simple hem into a fiasco. My fiancé’s pants came back with nearly six inches of fabric folded up inside the leg, making them bulky, heavy, and visibly misshapen. Staff admitted the job was botched and “fixed” it while we waited, but the result was worse: obvious holes in the fabric you could spot from across the room. We had to replace the pants entirely and took the new pair to a competent tailor elsewhere. To top it off, the suit wasn’t pressed when we picked it up; it looked like it had been lying on the floor. Between poor workmanship, dismissive attitude, and lack of quality control, this experience was unacceptable. Inspect thoroughly, skip their alterations, and be wary of the “big sale” pitch. Our trust is gone.

The portions are massive, so expect to share—and laugh—a lot. The messier the better, honestly; we spent half the time wiping spice dust off our faces and hands, but it’s part of the charm. The server was friendly but warned us about the “shell mountain” we’d create, and they weren’t joking. Between the crawfish and shrimp, we skipped dessert (the flavors were too satisfying). Pro tip: Bring extra clothes or wear something you don’t mind smelling like garlic-butter dreams for days. Also, the sides—like the corn and potatoes—are solid but get lost in the shrimp hype. Still, the vibe is electric, especially with a group. It’s not just a meal; it’s an experience. I’ll definitely return, gloves and all—this place has earned a permanent spot on my “must-visit” list. Worth every smelly, messy minute.

Here’s the continued review in approximately 197 words: What really grinds my gears is the lack of basic hospitality. The staff seems indifferent, like they’d rather text on their phones than help customers. I once stood at the counter for five minutes, unsure if I should grab a paper or just ask them for help. By the time I got my pesto pasta (which tasted like jarred sauce warmed up in a pan), my enthusiasm had flatlined. And don’t get me started on the “customize everything” approach—sure, you can swap mozzarella for goat cheese, add 10 kinds of greens, or pile on $5 worth of truffle oil, but why? It feels like performative effort, like they’re trying to pretend they’re a gourmet spot instead of just being a budget-friendly place. The second time I went, I asked for a simple margherita pizza. When it arrived, the cheese was rubbery, and the crust was undercooked on one side. I almost sent it back but figured, *why bother?* At least the prices are laughable—$9 for a “salad” with three slices of tomato and a handful of croutons. It’s the kind of place where you feel like you’re paying for the experience of being annoyed rather than the food. But hey, if you’re in a rush, hate decision-making, and enjoy eyeing crumpled menu papers like a scavenger hunt, by all means, go. Just don’t act surprised when your meal tastes like an afterthought. I’ve had better meals at gas stations—and faster ones, too.

The constant billing errors, unresponsive maintenance, and lack of accountability left me stressed and undervalued. When I raised concerns, I was met with excuses or silence. My monthly rent paid for neglect and poor management, not service. I’ve stayed in cheaper hotels with more respect. Save yourself the headache—avoid this place at all costs. It’s a toxic, money-draining nightmare.

Continued review: The inconsistency is frustrating—great food in one visit, questionable quality the next. While the staff’s friendliness is consistent, the chaotic vibe during my first trip (with staff arguing and police involved) made me question the restaurant’s management. Prices for sushi felt jarring compared to the budget-friendly appetizers, and the lack of freshness in the fish case was a red flag. The crunch roll was a bright spot, but not enough to justify the overall hit-or-miss vibe. I’d return for the appetizers in a pinch, but the stress of unpredictability might keep me away. They have potential but need more consistency in service, pricing, and food quality to earn a loyal customer like me.
The spicy Cajun seasoning balanced the sweetness of the lobster, and the crispy garlic fries provided the perfect salty contrast. Highly recommend this combo for a flavorful, satisfying meal!

The service definitely had some growing pains—our server was polite but overwhelmed, taking ages to refill our waters and respond to questions. At one point, we had to flag down a manager just to clarify our order for the Surf and Turf Roll (turns out it’s a sesame-crusted shrimp and filet mignon hand roll—creative, but the shrimp overshadowed the beef). Still, the food’s creativity and presentation kept things engaging. The Beef Carpaccio stood out most: paper-thin slices of raw beef with arugula, truffle oil, and shaved Parmesan, drizzled with a tangy balsamic reduction. It felt like a $30 taste of luxury, even if the Tuna Tartare veered slightly into “overseasoned with lime” territory. The ambiance is undeniably Instagram-worthy. The 16th-floor vantage point offers a front-row seat to the Strip’s chaos—neon hotels, the Eiffel Tower’s hourly light show, and the Fountains’ synchronized dancing—all framed by floor-to-ceiling windows. Even toward the back of the restaurant, the view felt like a $50 tax on the check. The bar area, though, is the star of the show: a sleek, glass-enclosed nook where the skyline blurs into the background as you sip on $16 cocktails. We skipped the menu (too tempting to splurge) and split a round of house sparkling wine, which paired nicely with the patio’s cool, breezy vibe. Would we return? Yes, but with reservations next time. While the food leans more “elegant snack fare” than “full-course meal,” the novelty of dining 16 stories up in a city where everything screams for attention is worth the splurge. If the kitchen refines its pacing and the service smooths out its kinks, Veloce could become a must-stop for Strip-view seekers—just don’t come expecting a casual, budget-friendly bite. Bring a date, a credit card, and a willingness to trade time with the staff for time with the city lights.

The entire experience was marred by poor communication and a lack of professionalism. When I was switched to Pat last-minute, there was no clear explanation of why the initial arrangement changed, nor was I offered any compensation for the inconvenience. The back of my haircut was so drastically different from what I requested that I left the chair feeling frustrated—especially since I had to later visit another barber to fix the uneven neckline. For $25 before tip, I expected at least basic accuracy and consistency, not a rushed job that required rework. Additionally, the fact that this place isn’t a licensed barber shop is concerning. Without proper licensing, there’s no guarantee of the staff’s training or adherence to hygiene and technical standards. It’s hard to justify the higher-than-average prices when the result is subpar and the service feels disorganized. The comparison to a chain like Sports Clips isn’t just about price—it’s about the expectation of at least a baseline level of skill and efficiency, which this establishment failed to meet. Overall, I wouldn’t recommend this salon to anyone seeking reliable service or quality results. Between the scheduling snafus, mismatched expectations, and uneven work, it’s not worth the risk or the cost. I’ll stick to barbers with proven track records and clear credentials—this place just isn’t worth the hassle.

Overall, Takumi exceeded my expectations for a budget-friendly sushi experience, though the word “budget” feels almost misleading in the best way. The combination of premium ingredients, skilled preparation, and thoughtful presentation made every bite memorable. I appreciated the servers’ attentiveness; they were eager to explain the menu’s nuances, like the difference between the toro and tuna selections, and even offered recommendations based on our preferences. The dining area was intimate yet lively, with soft lighting that complemented the focus on the food

The atmosphere was lively, which I expected in Vegas, but the over-the-top hype made everything feel underwhelming. The menu’s "premium" price tag didn’t justify the mediocre results—our $15 chicken strips were just breaded and bland, nothing special. While the tangy remoulade sauce was a nice touch, I couldn’t shake the feeling I could replicate this at home for half the cost. The sweet tea, though, was sweet and refreshing, and the portion sizes were generous for the price. But even with those small wins, the meal felt overhyped. If you’re craving greasy comfort food, maybe give it a shot. But for a place legendary among locals? I’ll stick to their recommendations for better eats. Honestly, unless the kids demand it, this won’t be my return trip. Just too much buzz for too little substance.

The employees were surprisingly friendly and helpful, which made browsing more pleasant. The store’s layout felt modern and easy to navigate, with clear signage for sales sections. Though I left without a purchase, the relaxed atmosphere and occasional discounts make this a place I’d revisit. Ross continues to impress with its mix of affordable, stylish finds—even if you’re just shopping for time.

The shoe department was a goldmine—Allen Edmonds loafers and oxfords lined up like treasures, with price tags slashed to unbeatable deals. The energy was electric, with crowds buzzing over finds, but the staff stayed helpful, guiding us to hidden steals. Even the accessories section shone: pocket squares, belts, and those Zegna ties felt like luxury grabs under $50. We left with a duffel bag full of staples, already planning how to justify another trip next year. Pro tip: Wear comfy shoes—it’s a lot of walking! But trust me, it’s worth it. Happy shopping! 🛍️

The ambiance is cozy yet vibrant, with a modern rustic feel that complements the upscale casual vibe. The staff is consistently friendly and attentive, offering helpful recommendations without being overbearing. As for consistency, every visit has delivered the same level of quality—fresh ingredients, creative flavor combinations, and generous portions. While the pricing is undeniably higher than your average burger joint, the ingredients justify the cost (kobe beef doesn’t come cheap!). Even the sides, like the crispy, herb-seasoned fries, feel thoughtfully crafted. I’ve also yet to experience a wait, which speaks volumes about its underrated accessibility in busy North Scottsdale. If you’re prioritizing a memorable, elevated burger experience over budget, this spot is a clear winner. The mediocre reviews? They just don’t align with my reality—stick around, and let the flavors do the convincing.

The ambiance was cozy, with string lights overhead and the fire pit adding a warm, inviting glow. Our server, Kenley, checked in frequently without being overbearing, ensuring our water and wine glasses were always full. The lettuce wraps, while decent, lacked the zing we hoped for—perhaps a touch of lime or spicy dipping sauce could elevate them. Still, the coconut shrimp stood out; their crispy coating balanced the sweetness, making them a highlight. The steak *flambe* was a showstopping main, cooked to perfection with a caramelized crust, while the apricot glaze on my pork chops veered too sweet and cloying for my taste, overshadowing the meat’s flavor. The generous portions meant we left satisfied, even after indulging in the rich, fudgy chocolate cake. While the location near the PGA store is convenient, we’ll aim for a weekday return to better savor the calm atmosphere. Overall, a solid choice for a relaxed evening meal—just skip the pork.

The "resort fee" debacle is just the start—every amenity feels like a chore. Housekeeping? A joke. We returned to our room to find trash untouched for two days and a bathroom that still smelled like the previous guest’s cologne. The front desk claimed they were “overwhelmed” by the holiday rush, but that’s no excuse for losing reservations or misplacing a pet’s vaccination records (yes, that happened). The breakfast buffet? A tired spread of lukewarm pastries and soggy waffles, served by staff who seemed more interested in their phones than guests. And don’t even think about asking for a coffee refill without a fight. The pet policy is a disaster—urine stains on the carpets, barking echoing through hallways, and staff shrugging when confronted. The only “service” here is the $50 charge to clean up after other guests’ messes. Meanwhile, the “premium” parking lot is a maze of potholes and dead-end alleys. In the end, we left relieved. The only thing this place delivers is sticker shock and stress. If you’re looking for a Scottsdale escape, book *far* away from this overpriced eyesore. Save your money—or better yet, save your sanity.

The service, while not overtly hostile, felt disinterested—hostesses slouched at the host stand, eyes glazed, as if they’d rather be anywhere but there. The “creepy” hollandaise? A thin, sun-yellow drizzle with a faint, off-putting metallic tang that made the broccoli feel less like a side and more like a science experiment. And don’t get me started on the fries—they were good, sure, *crisp* even, but the portion felt undersized for the $6 tab, especially when paired with that sad veg plate. If you’re a carnivore, maybe this spot’s got charm. But for anyone avoiding meat or dairy after 11 a.m.? This feels like a relic in more ways than one—clinging to outdated rules and skimpy offerings in a food scene that’s long since evolved. Across the parking lot, the taco truck at the center’s north end? Fresh, bold, and way cheaper. Even the gas station’s gourmet hot dog has more personality. I’ll give them the decor, the ambiance, the ghosts of ’70s diners past—but for actual sustenance, look elsewhere. You’ll eat better at a vending machine.

The cake’s cloying sweetness clashed with its rubbery texture, and the artificial chocolate flavor lingered like a bad memory. The cream cheese frosting, usually a redeeming quality, was bland and congealed. Each bite felt like a culinary crime, and I half-expected a bill for the experience. Truly, a masterpiece of disappointment.

Well, Dilworth’s baristas craft frothy, artful cups with locally roasted beans, but Starbucks’ mocha? That velvety chocolate swirl and instant gratification..... it’s a guilty pleasure. I’ll sip my ethical cappuccino, though—Dilworth’s worth the extra trip. Even if my wallet prefers the chain’s predictability. #FirstWorldProblems.

The service was friendly but rushed, which I can’t blame them for given the tiny space. Still, I expected better execution for a chain with decades of experience. The drink’s lack of creaminess made it feel cheap, and the $6+ price tag felt steep for a syrupy slush. I’ve had better fruit-infused drinks at gas stations. Skip this unless you’re desperate for a sugary pick-me-up—and even then, maybe bring a straw to mitigate the ice-chip texture. Not a fan of where DQ is headed with this menu shift.

The portions remain generous, but the prime rib lacked the juiciness of past visits, and sushi felt more mass-produced than fresh. Drinks are a highlight—coffee, beer, and wine flow freely without hidden fees. While Paris Buffet isn’t adventurous, its consistency makes it a default choice for families or those prioritizing convenience over culinary risk. Still, for $40+ per person, I’d expect more innovation or at least better value. Would return, but likely only as a backup when hunger outweighs pickiness.

When I first stumbled upon this bakery it was during my lunch hour and I was getting bored with my usual selections at Sack's next door, so, I decided to give it a try after reading a review of Essence on the Chowbella blog. Anywho, I was saddened that they no longer had any croissants and only a few macarons left, so, I ordered a Quiche Lorraine along with a side order of the Spanakopita. I guess I was in true hunger mode, and the smells wafting through the air of the baked goodies along with the lingering scent of the already gone croissants were making my tummy rumble far more than usual. So, maybe I had an expectation that the price I paid for a Quiche Lorraine at $7.95 would be satisfying to match my hungriness. Sadly this was not the case instead the Quiche turned out quite petit and somehow the portions were really meant for a light lunch. My first visit was marred by my expectations of the food and although quite good in itself with taste and quality ingredients it took awhile for me to come in for another visit until this morning. When Phoenix New Times, yelpers, and other food enthusiasts have simply raved about the croissants (both plain and chocolate), you know..... you just have to try it at least once. And I will tell you..... yes..... these croissants are close to perfect. So light, flaky, buttered goodness! I am not a croissant connoisseur at all—not even close—simply due to the fact that I am more of a pastry fan and would rather have cake, or some stuffed cheese pastry, more so than a croissant, but sometimes the hankering gets me that I need a cafe au lait with a croissant. And maybe I have a bias with my other croissant love at P. Croissant in South Tempe, but believe you me..... these croissants are heavenly. They are so scrumptious and buttery that every bite seems to have a layer of lightly buttered deliciousness, and it messes with your senses of how good this is. What sets them apart? For starters, the balance of texture is unmatched—the paper-thin, crisp layers crackle under your teeth, while the interior remains soft and airy, almost like a warm hug in

They refused to take responsibility or offer a free repair. The customer service was as terrible as their craftsmanship—rude, dismissive, and untrained. I’ve used them before without issues, but this was a disaster. Avoid at all costs; your precious items deserve far better care and attention. Find a jeweler who truly values your trust and memories.

The classic flavors felt disappointing and low-quality, but the novelty options like Samoa cookie—chocolaty and toasted coconut-rich—showcased the shop’s potential. Cookies and cream was creamy and balanced, with generous chunks, making it worth the splurge. While the Groupon helped stretch our spending, I’ll prioritize sampling next time. Their unique flavors clearly shine, but the basics need improvement. I’ll give them another shot, but stick to specialty picks!

The service was friendly, and the place had a cozy vibe, but the pizza left me wanting more balance. The crust could’ve used a bit more char for that perfect crisp-tender mix. I did appreciate the house-made mozzarella’s tangy freshness, though it couldn’t compete with the sauce’s dominance. BF went for the pepperoni, which had a nice kick, but he echoed my complaints about thin cheese coverage. Drinks were standard, and the small dessert menu (gelato, tiramisu) felt underwhelming. Still, with the city’s pizza rivalry heating up, Sola has potential—let’s see if they tweak their formula. I’ll give ’em another shot with a meatball sub or a white pie next time. For now, it’s a B- at best.

The inconsistency in service is frustrating, especially when the food and drinks are clearly worth celebrating.
