The steak was perfectly seared and tender, and the lobster was fresh and flavorful, complemented by the crispy fries. While the initial service was warm and attentive, we noticed a lull later on—when we remembered to request steak sauce, it took about 15 minutes for her to return with it. Still, the ambiance was cozy, with soft lighting and a stylish decor that enhanced the dining experience. The kitchen’s speed in getting our meals out was impressive, and every bite felt worth the wait. Despite the minor hiccups, the combination of delicious food and the staff’s overall friendliness left us eager to return. A few tweaks to service pacing would make this spot near-perfect.

The smell of fresh hay, manure, and curious livestock instantly transports you to a simpler time, and while the chaos of a school trip can be overwhelming, there’s a charm in watching wide-eyed children interact with goats, ducks, and even the occasional grumpy cow. The hands-on experiences—feeding the animals, petting their fuzzy faces, and watching piglets scuttle past—make it a place where both kids and adults reconnect with the wonder of rural life. I still laugh thinking about how my traumatic lamb encounter didn’t deter me from wanting to hold every animal that day, despite my classmates’ horrified protests. What stands out is the dedication of the staff. They’re patient, knowledgeable, and clearly passionate about making the farm accessible to everyone. From explaining the difference between sheep and lambs to helping someone coax a shy goat out of its pen, they create a warm, inclusive atmosphere. However, if you’re after a peaceful visit, avoid weekdays. The farm transforms into a bustling classroom hub, with groups jostling for space and squeals echoing across the fields. Weekends are quieter, perfect for wandering at your own pace and sneaking a treat at the tiny on-site café. Ultimately, this farm is a delightful reminder of childhood’s messy, unforgettable moments. Even that delinquent lamb can’t take away from the joy of seeing animals thrive in a place that clearly loves them. Just bring hand sanitizer—or maybe a towel. 4 stars, because some memories (and smells) linger longer than others.

The variety of fresh, hot dishes is unmatched—from sizzling steaks to vibrant sushi rolls. The salad bar boasts exotic ingredients, and desserts like cheesecake and churros are heavenly. Staff always offer warm greetings and prompt refills. Kids loved the playful atmosphere, too! Studio B exceeds expectations every time. Highly recommend for foodies seeking quality, variety, and a welcoming vibe. Can’t wait to return!

I waited 25 more minutes, but the staff ignored my repeated attempts to ask about my order. When I finally confronted the manager, they shrugged and said, “We’ll get to you.” Eventually, I gave up and left, still hungry. Poor communication and zero accountability ruined what could’ve been a decent experience. Will not return.

The Albondigas Soup ($7.25), which my son’s fiancée finally ordered, was a modest attempt at a classic—tender meatballs in a tomato-based broth with a touch of garlic and oregano. However, the soup lacked warmth in flavor, and the broth felt underseasoned, as though it were a side rather than a star. She noted it was “harmless,” but nothing more. The dessert, a side of Mexican Chocolate Cake ($4.50), was a sweet but unremarkable end to the meal. The cake was dry, with a chocolate flavor that leaned more toward bitterness than richness. What stood out most was the contrast between the restaurant’s popularity and the mediocrity of the food. The place was packed, buzzing with laughter and clinking glasses, yet the kitchen’s execution felt unrefined. My son, a self-proclaimed “foodie,” admitted he’d expected more from the hype. The portions were generous, and the prices seemed fair for the neighborhood, but quality and creativity were missing. Even the tortillas, supposedly homemade, had a store-bought texture—stiff and flavorless compared to the soft, corn-based alternatives we’ve enjoyed elsewhere. Frank & Fina’s might appeal to those craving casual, no-frills fare, but for diners seeking authentic depth or bold flavors, it’s a letdown. The team clearly has potential, but their approach feels safe, like they’re hedging between traditions without leaning into either. My advice? Skip the mains and stick to the Sangria—a rare highlight that actually delivers on promise. Otherwise, take the $11 you’d spend on the Al Pastor and opt for a street vendor’s al pastor taco instead. It’s riskier, but far more rewarding. In the end, I understand why my son and his partner enjoy the

The ambiance of Pyarr is another aspect worth mentioning, though it’s hard to evaluate fully based on a single visit. The dining area is bright and modern, with soft Indian music playing in the background, creating a relaxed yet slightly clinical vibe. The minimalist decor—a splash of color on the walls and a few traditional artifacts—lends a subtle cultural touch without overwhelming the space. While the setting is inviting, the restaurant’s quiet, almost deserted atmosphere during lunchtime felt at odds with the bustling energy one might associate with Indian dining. Still, the open layout made the sparse crowd feel less awkward, and the staff’s attentiveness kept the experience from feeling isolating. The pricing of the lunch buffet, at $12.99 per person, seemed reasonable for the amount of food available, though I question the value when the selection is so limited. The standout, of course, was the naan—light, fluffy, and perfectly charred at the edges, with just the right balance of tandoori flavor. It’s a small menu item, but it speaks volumes about the kitchen’s capabilities. I hope Pyarr channels that same attention to detail into expanding their hot offerings, particularly for vegetarians, who are already outnumbered by non-veg options in most Indian restaurants. A few more gravies, vegetable curries, or even pickled snacks could transform the buffet from underwhelming to enticing. I’m intrigued by the idea of returning for dinner to test their full menu. Would their biryani or tandoori dishes live up to the naan’s promise? Could their dessert section (a sad array of fruit and packaged sweets during lunch) evolve into something more inventive? Only time will tell. For now, Pyarr feels like a work in progress—a place with potential but lacking the consistency or confidence to fully capture its audience. If the team doubles down on improving the hot buffet selection, offering a few standout vegetarian dishes, and building on their strong service ethic, they might carve out a niche in Vegas’ competitive Indian restaurant scene. Until then, it’s a place I’ll keep an eye on, but one I can’t yet wholeheartedly recommend.

The key to “New York Style” Chinese food lies in its hybrid identity—a blend of Chinese regional traditions adapted to the cultural tapestry of the city itself. At **China-A-Go-Go**, the menu reflects this balance, offering dishes that cater to both classic Chinese sensibilities and the palate of a lifelong New Yorker. For instance, their **“real” lo-mein** uses hand-pulled noodles, chewy and elastic, tossed with smoky soy and garlic—unlike the slippery, overly sauced versions found at most local takeouts. The **chow mein** here is light yet deeply savory, with crisp, toasted noodles that anchor the dish without oil, a stark contrast to the greasy, soggy messes often masquerading as the dish elsewhere. The **egg rolls** are a revelation: massive, flour-dusted rolls filled with crisp cabbage, julienned carrots, and a whisper of Chinese sausage, golden from a proper frying technique that avoids sogginess. These aren’t the flimsy, microwave-reheated impostors you’ll find at chain spots. Dishes like **sweet and sour pork** lean into a tangy, vinegar-forward balance, avoiding the neon-red, ketchup-heavy glop common elsewhere. Even the **General Tso’s chicken** here has a nuanced sweetness, with a subtle numbing spice from Sichuan peppercorns—a nod to the diverse roots of New York’s Chinese community. What truly sets this place apart is the **family-style experience**. You’re handed oversized platters of **steamed dumplings**, **braised beef with broccoli**, and **seafood fried rice** meant to be shared, paired with warm, fluffy **jiaozi** and a house-made sesame noodle salad. The waitstaff, though not overtly formal, are attentive and passionate about explaining the origins of each dish

For a 1st timer I wanted to be honest but I hope to return to a better experience. Parking was tight. It was raining & waiting area was small & in the way of receptionist desk. We were told to move aside but there was nowhere to move. Wait staff were energetic & friendly. Very helpful with choosing the right meal! Lemonade was delish! Next time I will try it mixed with Koolade. Wait was ok for lunch time. One of 3 plates came & we were told tables were put in wrong order so other 2 plates would take a few min. Chicken wasn’t too flavorful but was perfectly cooked & juicy! Tasted great with the ranch. Waffle was tasty & crispy but soft inside! Food was hot. Plate was more than enough. Atmosphere was well spaced & not too busy on walls which I like. Will return! If not for mix up of tables & awkward wait area would’ve gotten 4 stars. The service ultimately improved as the meal progressed, with staff checking in regularly to ensure everything was satisfying. While the table mix-up was a minor inconvenience, the team handled it with apologetic humor, which helped ease any frustration. I appreciated the generous portion sizes and the attention to detail in plating, even if the chicken’s seasoning felt a bit restrained. The waffle’s contrast between a crunchy exterior and pillowy center was a standout, pairing nicely with the tangy ranch. Though the wait area left much to be desired—especially for rainy days—I’d give the restaurant the benefit of the doubt for future visits. With a few tweaks to logistics and a boost in flavor profiles, this could easily become a go-to spot for casual dining. The charm and friendliness of the team alone make me eager to return.

The lackluster experience continued with the service. Our server, despite being the “Mexican guy” mentioned in the update, seemed disengaged from the moment he approached our table. His demeanor was indifferent, and he barely acknowledged our complaints about the cold, underwhelming wings and the forgotten sauce. When we flagged the issues, he offered a perfunctory apology and vanished for 15 minutes, leaving us to fend for ourselves. When he finally returned, he handed over a meager discount coupon without eye contact or a genuine effort to make things right. It felt less like a gesture of goodwill and more like a chore to tick off a task. The ambiance, once a cozy, family-friendly vibe with the soft hum of conversation and clinking plates, now feels rushed and impersonal. Rocco’s has always been a place where the waitstaff remembered regulars by name, but tonight’s encounter felt transactional, as if we were just another number in a long line of diners. Even the decor seems faded compared to my memory—brighter colors dulled, the laughter of the past replaced by a hushed, almost uncomfortable energy. While I understand that restaurants evolve, the decline here is glaring. The food, once a highlight, now feels like an afterthought. For a place with such a rich legacy, this version of Rocco’s feels like a shadow of its former self. I’ll give them one more chance—perhaps a new chef or manager could turn things around—but if this is the standard now, I’ll have to admit it’s time to write this local favorite off. For now, I’ll stick to the memories and seek out the authenticity that once made this place special.

The wine list didn’t help matters—though the sommelier insisted on upselling a $120 bottle with a “charming backstory,” the pairing was indifferent at best. For the price, you expect a bit of care, but this felt like a rushed, half-hearted attempt at fine dining. Even the bar menu, which promised “small plates with flair,” offered nothing memorable: the “artisanal” flatbread was gummy, and the “house-made” pickles tasted store-bought. The atmosphere leaned into pretension without the polish to back it up—dim lighting clashed with garish wall art, and the clatter of dishes in the kitchen made conversation a chore. Meanwhile, the staff’s apathy was glaring. When we asked to split a dessert, our server shrugged and said, “We’ll do our best,” then vanished. (Spoiler: The cake didn’t split.) For all the red flags, the final insult was the receipt: a $50 tab for two overcooked shrimp, a brick of cake, and lukewarm coffee. You can’t fault a restaurant for being what it is, but there’s no excuse for charging this much for incompetence. If you’re in the mood for a meal that actually matches the price, there are a half-dozen better options within a mile. Save your money and your appetite—and trust that whatever’s censored on Yelp is worth the trouble.

The brewery’s pricing is refreshingly transparent—$5 for a flight is a steal considering the craftsmanship on display. Each beer tells a story, from the crisp Watermelon Ale to the bold Arizuma. While the hop-forward options like Camelback IPA and Hoppy Valley Ale might not convert lager lovers, they’re a haven for those who crave a punchy bitter finish. Fretzy’s American Hefeweizen stood out as a flawless blend of citrusy wheat and clove, a crowd-pleaser that begged to be paired with the pretzel basket (a $3 addition). The surprise star, though, was the Wheat Stalk Orange Hue Ale—a tangy, coconut-kissed wheat beer that balanced sweetness and zest perfectly. I left with a 22oz bottle, eager to savor it at home. The vibe here is casual, community-focused. The small menu of pretzels (gluten-free available) and the lack of kitchen amenities feel like a design choice rather than a shortcoming. It’s easy to see why folks bring in their own fries or sandwiches from nearby fast-casual spots like KFC—patrons often share a chicken leg while debating the merits of “Fretzy’s Unfiltered Ale” versus the more aggressive IPAs. For those seeking a laid-back, beer-forward experience, this spot nails it. The growler fill station is a bonus, letting you take home 64oz of local flavor for $15—a steal for beer enthusiasts. While the lineup leans heavier on ales than lagers or stouts, the diversity within the ale category alone is enough to satisfy most palettes. Pro tip: Ask the staff for their seasonal picks—some of the rare releases are worth the wait. Whether you’re a hophead, a malt lover, or just curious about local brews, this brewery’s got a glass for you.

The atmosphere here leans casual but carries a welcoming vibe, with a rustic, no-frills setup that prioritizes efficiency over pretension. The kitchen’s pace is brisk, and the plates—especially the seafood—arrive steaming and heaped generously. Presentation isn’t an art here, but the portion sizes more than compensate; a pound of crawfish or shrimp is no joke, and we left with ample leftovers for lunch the next day. The corn and potatoes, as advised, were a solid addition—tender, slightly smoky, and perfectly charred at the edges. They balanced the richness of the sauces well, though the sugary corn relish on the side was an odd choice that felt out of place. While the spice levels were hit-or-miss, the lack of extremes was a relief for our group. My partner, who avoids heat, enjoyed the medium garlic butter shrimp without incident, while the spicy Hot N Juicy crawfish provided a satisfying kick that lingered without becoming overwhelming. The extra spicy, however, felt like a marketing ploy—bright red sauce but minimal bite, more show than substance. Still, the crawfish themselves were consistently fresh and meaty, plucked from their shells with ease. The calamari, though, was a letdown. Oversalted and paired with a bland marinara, it felt like a filler item. I’d skip it and opt for the Cajun fries instead—golden, airy, and crisped to a perfect crunch. They arrived in a thick, crinkly stack, just the right texture to pair with the greasy seafood. For dessert, we split a slice of banana pudding (a $5 extra), which was sweet, creamy, and utterly indulgent, though not worth the splurge if you’re calorie-conscious. The low beer prices ($3 for quality domestics and imports) are a standout perk, especially for a place that doesn’t skimp on portion sizes. We sipped Heine

Despite the lack of lighter fare, there’s something comforting about the cozy, dimly lit vibe—it’s the kind of place where you can lose track of time sipping a hoppy IPA or a rich stout. The staff is friendly, and the bartenders are eager to chat about their favorite brews, which helps offset the menu’s meat-centric shortcomings. If you’re a carnivore, you’ll probably love it here, but if you’re dining with someone who’s not a fan of greasy, hearty fare, you’ll both end up eyeing the pretzel like it’s a lifeline. Still, for a night when you want to drown your sorrows (or celebrate) with beer and a side of communal meat obsession, it works. Just bring a salad to share and call it a balanced meal.

The more I think about it, the more the inconsistencies at Mez feel glaring. It’s one thing to enforce a dress code, but the way it was handled felt arbitrary and off-putting. My Dutch friend’s attire—clean, presentable, and certainly not disruptive—felt like a red line drawn in the sand for no real reason. Meanwhile, the bar’s tolerance for..... well, let’s say *unconventional* behavior, seemed to have no boundaries. If a place can’t apply its rules evenly, it loses all credibility. Back in the day, Mez had this cool, unpretentious energy. Sure, the cocktails were average, and the apps nothing to write home about, but the vibe was what drew people in—quirky, alive, a little unpredictable. Now, though, it feels like the charm has been replaced by a desperate, corporate formality. The security encounter last week wasn’t an isolated incident. I’ve seen other patrons turned away for similar reasons, and the once-bustling lounge now feels like a ghost town, even during peak hours. Watching staff loiter inside while the city thrived outside was surreal. It’s like they’ve forgotten how to engage with customers or keep the space relevant. Charlotte has evolved, and places like Mez need to keep pace—without losing their identity. Over-policed dress codes and half-empty rooms aren’t the answer. If you want to attract guests, focus on hospitality, not gatekeeping. I’ll stick to more welcoming spots that prioritize vibe over vanity. Mez used to be a Charlotte staple—it’s sad to see it slip into irrelevance. 2/5 stars, mostly for nostalgia’s sake.

Additionally, the museum’s collection of pre-Columbian artifacts was a standout—ceremonial masks and ancient tools offered a tangible connection to the ingenuity of indigenous cultures. The curation blends education and aesthetics, with detailed placards that contextualize each piece without overwhelming visitors. I appreciated the interactive digital guides, which provided deeper historical narratives and helped me grasp the symbolic language of the textiles and carvings. The museum also hosts rotating exhibits, and during my visit, a showcase on ancient Mesoamerican astronomy highlighted their advanced understanding of the cosmos. While the core collection is compact, the depth of storytelling kept me engaged. For those short on time, prioritize the permanent galleries; if you have an extra hour, the gift shop is a treasure trove of culturally rich, small-batch art supplies. A must for history buffs or anyone craving a slower, meaningful cultural detour in the midst of Vegas’ chaos! 😊

The entire system is a farce. Beyond the ridiculous delivery delays, clerical errors are rampant—mail misrouted, packages lost, and sensitive items left unattended in bins. The USPS’s refusal to modernize or train staff only compounds the chaos. Employees shrug off complaints as if their jobs don’t matter, while management drowns in bureaucracy. This isn’t just about one lazy carrier; it’s a culture of entitlement and apathy. Taxpayers subsidize this incompetence, yet the service crumbles. I’ve watched neighbors lose track of critical documents, bills, and even medical shipments—all because the USPS treats its role as a punchline. Privatization is often blamed, but the real issue is a lack of accountability. If a private company behaved this poorly, shareholders would revolt. Instead, USPS wields its government safety net to ignore consequences. Until there’s a drastic overhaul, this “service” will remain a punchline. Americans deserve better than a postal system that’s outdated, disorganized, and disgraceful. It’s time to demand leadership that prioritizes service over self-serving bureaucracy—or watch as our nation’s oldest public institution becomes its biggest liability.

The rest of the menu seemed less inspiring. We tried the "French Toast" ($12), which was overly sweet and drowned in syrup, leaving little room for the subtle flavors of the brioche. The café’s minimalistic décor—white linen, sleek chairs—felt out of place with the high-energy, no-nonsense service. While the staff moved quickly, their disengaged attitude made the experience feel transactional rather than memorable. For such a prestigious chef, the kitchen’s inconsistencies were surprising; my companion’s "Avocado Toast" arrived cold, and the bread was underproofed. Yet, the croissants remained a standout, their delicate layers and buttery aroma worth the price of admission alone. Still, at these prices, one expects consistency across the board. I’d return for a to-go croissant or a coffee break, but for a full meal? The risks outweigh the rewards—unless you’re a die-hard fan of Thomas Keller’s culinary universe.
The rice was mushy, the beans tasted like they’d been left out since

The service was equally terrible—waiters were dismissive and apathetic. The bland, soggy pasta was a far cry from the Mesa location’s excellence. We’ll never return. Save yourself the heartburn and dine elsewhere. This place is a ghost of its former self.

The service only compounded the disaster. Our server was perfunctory, jotting down orders without engaging us, and never checked in to gauge our experience—despite our plates sitting half-empty for over 45 minutes. When we flagged her down to request a refund or even a side of bread (we were *that* hungry), she shrugged and said, “It’s all we’ve got.” Meanwhile, the kitchen’s “specials” were being gobbled up by the couple at the next table, who raved about their “amazing” dishes. How a restaurant can serve two such divergent experiences under the same roof is beyond me. The ambiance, once lively during lunch, felt stifling at dinner—dim lighting casting shadows over our wilted, tasteless salads. My husband, a man who eats everything, pushed his plate aside and muttered, “This is like cooking from a bad recipe book.” We split a dessert on a whim, hoping for redemption, but the tiramisu was underbaked and soggy, like a failed science experiment. The bill? A staggering $150 for three meals we barely touched. For a place that prides itself on its “farm-to-table” ethos, the disconnect between the concept and execution was jarring. I’ve dined at mediocre and great restaurants, but this was something else entirely—a masterclass in how *not* to run a kitchen or a front-of-house team. If you’re in Vegas and see this spot, turn left or right. Your palate—and your wallet—will thank you. The lunch experience was clearly a fluke, and I’ll never understand how one restaurant can be both a gem and a landfill in the same week.

The rest of the night was a series of minor annoyances that compounded into a major letdown. After the show, we exited into a parking lot that felt like a war zone—crammed with tailgaters fighting over the last remaining spaces, all of them probably paying the $5 premium we did. I couldn’t help but laugh at the irony of “Cage the Elephant” being literal at this venue, with patrons caged in by absurd pricing and rules. The band, while competent, didn’t leave a lasting impression. Their energy seemed to wane under the weight of the oppressive atmosphere, and

The frustration only deepened when I returned to the dealership, expecting accountability. The staff insisted the finance team had “oversight” in calculating the trade-in’s value, but they offered no solution other than to shift the burden to me. I had already signed paperwork confirming the trade-in’s agreed-upon amount—how could there be an unexpected “difference”? They refused to absorb the cost, even after I explained how misleading this would look to my friends and family who’d already heard glowing reviews. It felt like a bait-and-switch: their initial friendliness eroded into cold bureaucracy. I walked out empty-handed, but more disillusioned. This isn’t just about money—it’s about respect. They exploited a clerical error to nickel-and-dime me, all while claiming empathy. I’ll never forget the smirk from the manager when I asked, “Is this how you’d want your business treated?” His silence said it all. Save your breath for better dealerships. This one’s all smoke and mirrors. #RichieWasRight.

**continued review:** Moving past the service quirk, the menu at The Cracked Egg is a treasure trove of breakfast classics with a few unexpected twists. Beyond the Eggs Benedict, I’ve tried their “Lighten Up Scramble,” which swaps traditional cheese for a zesty mix of spinach, tomatoes, and feta—refreshing and guilt-free! The portion sizes are generous, and while the prices aren’t cheap ($9.95 for benedict is standard for a brunch spot), the quality justifies it. That said, the coffee cakes are the real star here. Think cinnamon-rolled, buttery layers with a crumb topping so golden and crisp it’s borderline criminal. I ordered the lemon-blueberry one, and it was like a cloud of citrusy fluff—perfect with a side of their strong, slightly bitter house coffee. (Note: If you’re a latte lover, bring your own milk; the baristas here stick strictly to black coffee.) The health-focused options are a nice touch for those balancing indulgence with wellness. The “Garden Patch Omelette” is packed with kale, mushrooms, and roasted peppers, and you can opt for egg whites without feeling like you’re settling. Even the “low-fat scramble” doesn’t skimp on flavor—it’s herbed and bright,

The rotating selection of wines is impressive—there’s something for every palate, from bold reds to crisp whites, even a few unexpected natural or organic options. The tech-savvy vibe is infectious: each dispenser uses a sleek, touch-screen interface, and the LED lighting makes it feel like a futuristic wine lab. I love explaining how the system preserves the wine’s freshness (it’s nitrogen-sealed, by the way!) to curious friends. The staff is knowledgeable but laid-back, happy to guide you if you’re indecisive. And the food menu—simple, shareable plates like truffle fries or charcuterie—pairs perfectly without overshadowing the star of the show. It’s the kind of place where you can geek out over flavor profiles or just enjoy the playful, social energy. Even if you’re not a wine connoisseur, it’s a thrill to discover hidden gems at a fraction of the usual cost. Plus, the waitstaff’s humor adds to the fun—my favorite is the “wine flight of the brave” challenge with $100/glass bottles. A total win for wine novices and enthusiasts alike!

The wine list was thoughtfully curated, and the staff’s attention to detail made every course exceptional. Even the garlic knots were perfectly crisp. Portions are generous without being wasteful, and the atmosphere feels intimate yet lively. We’ll definitely return and have already recommended it to friends—delicious food, attentive service, and a vibe that makes you want to linger. A true gem!

The rest of the store is definitely a bright spot—shelves are neatly stocked, and the layout makes sense for quick trips. But every visit turns into a stress test just to parallel park in a space half the size of a cereal box. I’ve seen people U-turn three times trying to navigate the lot, and the 4-way stop gridlock feels like a meme come to life. It’s baffling how such a decent location gets ruined by basic courtesy issues. If you’re heading there on a Sunday afternoon, bring patience (and maybe a book). Otherwise, avoid peak hours or risk adding to the chaos. Target deserves better than being penalized for its parking lot’s Darwin Awards vibe.

The croissants, though buttery, are inconsistently flaky and priced higher than most bakeries. While their seasonal items occasionally shine, the lack of attention to detail undermines the premium price. I’d prefer paying less for reliably well-crafted treats or saving my money for the rare, sold-out bread. The potential is there, but execution and value feel mismatched.

The service was slow, with a 30-minute wait for our lukewarm dishes. Portions felt skimpy for the prices, which leaned toward the high end. The tea’s bitterness lingered, and the overly acidic vinaigrette left the pasta gummy and unappealing. While staff were polite, the menu lacked creativity, and the muted decor felt outdated. A meal here feels like an afterthought. Save your appetite—and your money—for better options. (2/10)

The Spiedino Di Mare was bursting with fresh, succulent shrimp and scallops, perfectly seared and kissed by garlic. The Cavatappi Amatriciana? A cozy twirl of pasta in a rich, peppery tomato sauce—comfort food at its finest. Our server, Mia, was attentive and even gifted a lemon sorbet to cleanse our palates between courses. Every bite felt like a hug from an old friend. The Blue Bell Ice Cream (I opted for the vanilla, because *of course*) was the cherry on top—a creamy, nostalgic punch that made me forget Vegas even exists. The ambiance is warm, with soft lighting and art that feels like a hidden European villa. Carrabba’s hasn’t just kept its charm; it’s elevated it. If you’re craving a meal that’s equal parts indulgent and heartfelt, this spot is still a gem. Don’t even *think* about leaving without dessert. 10/10, would moan again.

Here’s a continuation of your review, maintaining the tone and expanding on key points: --- If I had ordered the pizza myself, I would’ve requested less fennel and a crisper crust. The sweetness of the dough was unexpected—it almost clashed with the savory toppings. While the roasted red peppers added a smoky depth, the caramelized onions were underwhelming, lacking that golden-brown sweetness you typically get from slow-roasted onions. The Italian sausage was decent, but nothing special; it didn’t elevate the dish like, say, a garlic-heavy or spicy Calabrian sausage might have. Still, the pizza’s overall composition—thin base with a reasonable spread of cheese—was solid, and the price of $12.99 for a shared pie felt fair for the size. The citrus basil salad was a brighter highlight. The tangy dressing, which leaned heavily on lemon or orange juice (I couldn’t tell which), complemented the peppery arugula and crisp basil leaves. While one of us found it too acidic, I appreciated the refreshing contrast. The candied walnuts were a standout: sweet, crunchy, and generous in portion. A few more slivers of cucumber or shaved Parmesan might’ve rounded it out, but as it was, the salad felt fresh and light, a nice pairing with the heavier pizza. The wine, meanwhile, was forgettable. For $7 a glass, I expected something with more body or complexity. It tasted like a mass-produced merlot—smooth but lacking tannins or layers. Still, it didn’t ruin the meal, and the $14 for a small bottle (which held just two pours) felt slightly more justified for the group’s shared drinking pace. The staff’s approachability was a mixed bag. While the young register employee was cheerful and quick to answer questions, the lip piercings—a pair of large, dangling silver rings—were jarring. It’s a personal style choice, but I found them unprofessional for a front-of-house role. The kitchen staff, though unseen, clearly worked efficiently; our pizza arrived in under 10

While Chick FilA’s menu items are consistently good and the atmosphere pleasant, this location’s customer service is bafflingly subpar. The employees seemed utterly disengaged, prioritizing tasks like stacking cups or jotting down notes over assisting a line of hungry customers. Watching them chat idly while people left in frustration felt like witnessing a corporate nightmare. One worker even leisurely sipped a drink from the kitchen while I waited—how symbolic of their priorities! Even the drive-thru seemed neglected, with long pauses between orders and a lack of urgency. It’s as if they’ve forgotten the golden rule: *the customer is never wrong*. I get that fast food isn’t everyone’s dream job, but a team of seven people should *at least* manage a simple order, right? This isn’t a busy lunch rush—it’s mid-afternoon with half the staff “occupied.” Chick FilA’s reputation for warmth and efficiency should translate to every location, but here, it’s clearly missing. Between the glacial service and the indifference, I’ll take my business elsewhere. A great restaurant needs more than good food—it needs people who care. This one clearly doesn’t.

The staff at Quivey’s Grove consistently goes above and beyond, making every group feel welcome and well-cared for. From the moment we arrive, someone is there to greet us, guide us to our space, and ensure our needs are met. Their attention to detail—like accommodating dietary restrictions or adjusting seating arrangements—shows how seriously they take hosting groups. The food, while already high-quality, truly shines during holiday events, where the menu feels festive and thoughtfully curated. I’ve always been impressed by how they balance variety with a cohesive theme, whether it’s seasonal specials or their ever-popular apple crisp, which feels like a dessert made just for the occasion. Beyond the home and stable, the paddock is a hidden gem. In warmer months, it transforms into a charming outdoor space with string lights and picnic setups, perfect for celebrations or casual gatherings. The tunnel connecting the buildings isn’t just a novelty—it adds a fun, historic touch, and the wine cellar is a great place to sample their local vintages. Whether hosting a birthday, holiday party, or wedding, Quivey’s Grove offers a memorable blend of charm, comfort, and exceptional service. I’d highly recommend it for anyone planning a group event—they make every occasion feel special.

The atmosphere is welcoming, and the tranquil environment makes each class feel like a retreat. Whether you're a beginner or seasoned yogi, the instructors adapt the sessions to all levels. The variety of classes—from vinyasa to restorative—keeps it exciting. Plus, the Shadyside location is convenient. Highly recommend—mind, body, and soul find balance here! The studio also offers workshops and meditation sessions, enhancing the overall experience. Their cleanliness and attention to detail make every visit refreshing. It's not just a workout; it's a holistic wellness journey. I can't imagine my routine without it!

The restaurant’s no-frills, efficient setup is perfect for students or anyone craving a quick, flavorful meal without the hassle of waiting for a server. While the atmosphere is casual, the vibrancy of the menu and the enthusiastic energy of the staff make the dining experience feel lively and welcoming. I’ve noticed that even on busy days, the kitchen rarely falters, consistently delivering fresh, well-prepared dishes that hit all the right notes of spice, sweetness, and umami. For those hesitant to choose from the extensive menu, the staff’s friendly recommendations are spot-on—I’ve never regretted their suggestions, whether it was the *mapo tofu* (creamy, fiery, and packed with fermented bean paste) or the *pork belly*, which melts in your mouth while staying tender. The portions are generous for the price, and the *clams with black bean sauce* are a standout for seafood lovers, with the briny clams soaking up the bold, savory glaze. Even vegetarians have options, like the *eggplant with ground pork* (a meaty, savory stir-fry) or the *spicy fried chili chicken* (which, while not vegan, is a must-try for spicy food fans). The only downside is the short shelf life of the food in your to-go box—everything is so fresh and hot when you leave that you’ll want to eat it immediately. Since it’s a campus staple, it’s worth arriving early during peak hours to avoid long lines. But even if you’re waiting, the wait is never a chore, especially if you’re sharing stories with classmates or enjoying a complimentary cup of tea. For affordability, variety, and that *just-right* balance of convenience and flavor, this place is a campus gem—don’t miss it!

The portions were generous, but the menu felt repetitive. Prices matched the quality, though the dessert bar stole the show—creative flavors and a sweet-tooth paradise. Service was prompt, elevating the experience despite minor menu shortcomings.

Continuing the review: The rest of the menu was equally underwhelming. Most of the other dishes looked like they’d been reheated a dozen times—cold, limp, or just plain flavorless. The “premium” shrimp were rubbery, and the vegetables had a sad, overcooked texture that made me question their freshness. Even the dessert section, which I only half-heartedly explored, felt like an afterthought: the cake was dry, the gelato tasted like it came out of a box, and no one even offered to bring me a spoon for the chocolate fondue (I had to ask twice). What really stung, though, was the lack of basic hospitality. After the butter fiasco, I expected a server to check in, apologize, or at least acknowledge the mishap. Nope—just a cold “enjoy your meal” and radio silence. When I finally flagged someone down for the check, they stared at me like I was asking for the time. No thanks for the lamb chops. No “we’re sorry about the frozen crab.” Just a shrug and a “it’s on the self-service counter.” Bellagio might have its own issues, but at least it *tries* to make you feel valued. Here, it felt like we were just an inconvenience. The location’s decent, and the prices aren’t *insanely*

The rooms definitely felt like a step back in time—while the lobby screamed modern luxury, my room had beige carpeting that looked like it had been there since the 2000s, and the furniture was starting to creak. The mini-fridge and coffee maker were functional, but the lack of USB outlets was a bummer for a tech-savvy traveler. That said, the location’s perks made up for it! I loved exploring Old Town using the shuttle, and the 24/7 gym was a lifesaver after days of intense coursework. Plus, the nightly wine hour was the perfect way to unwind with new friends. Sure, the staff couldn’t fix the elevator issue, but their friendly attitude (especially the valets!) kept the stay light. If you’re prioritizing vibe and convenience over a room’s decor, this spot still wins. Arizona’s beauty and the hotel’s charm had me planning a return trip already—maybe next time they’ll upgrade the rooms!

I requested a manager’s apology, but they barely acknowledged the issue. The staff appeared disinterested, and the ambiance failed to deliver on its romantic promise. Don’t waste your time or money here—service is inconsistent, and quality is lacking. Save your celebration for a place that truly values its guests.

The burger was supposed to be "medium well," yet it was dripping with rawness—disgusting. The cashier rolled their eyes when I asked for a replacement, muttering about “customer complaints.” Even the soda tasted flat, like they’d been sitting out all day. I’ll stick to my freezer meals and save the cash. Save your appetite—and your wallet—for better options. This place is a fraud from the food to the service. Definitely not worth one star.

The selection is impressive, with everything from rare vinyl to retro video games. The cozy, retro atmosphere makes browsing a joy, and prices are often unbeatable. Whether you’re a collector or just exploring, there’s something here for everyone. Plus, the store’s passion for curating quality items shines through. Don’t miss their rotating specials—hidden gems await! A revitalized gem worth visiting again and again.

The continued review: What really stands out is how they treat you like a person, not just a number. I’ve had pharmacists remember specific details about my prescriptions—like when I was adjusting dosages or managing multiple medications—and they’d double-check with me to ensure everything was correct. It’s reassuring to know they’re paying attention, especially when navigating complex regimens. Another thing I appreciate is their willingness to go the extra mile. Once, when I couldn’t find a specific over-the-counter supplement, a technician spent 20 minutes helping me research alternatives that worked with my existing prescriptions. They even called a nearby store to confirm availability before I drove there. The attention to detail extends to the little things, too. The drive-through lane is always clean, organized, and well-stocked, and the staff uses a color-coded system to flag urgent pickups, which I’ve never seen at other places. I’ve also noticed they frequently offer helpful resources, like flu shot reminders, medication synchronization programs, and even occasional wellness checks to ensure I’m on track with my health goals. Honestly, in today’s world of fast-paced, impersonal service, it’s rare to find a place that combines efficiency with genuine care. They don’t just fill prescriptions; they build trust. I’ve recommended them to friends and family, and not once has someone come back complaining. Even when insurance companies throw roadblocks—like sudden formulary changes or denied claims—they treat it as *their* problem to solve, not mine. They’ll advocate, call providers, and sometimes even hold their breath (literally, I’ve seen it) while waiting for a call back from a rep who might just say “yes.” For anyone who’s ever dealt with the stress of medication errors, insurance headaches, or just the frustration of being ignored by a pharmacy, this is the kind of place that can restore your faith. They’ve earned my loyalty, and I won’t stop singing their praises until they’re the *closest* pharmacy to my house too.

The staff was friendly and efficient, even during the rush. Everything I tried was fresh and hot, especially the crispy fries and a warm apple pie that rounded out the meal perfectly. While it’s not a gourmet experience, the portion sizes and value make it hard to beat for late-night cravings. If you’re prioritizing convenience and affordability over culinary art, this spot nails it. Definitely my go-to for midnight munchies!

The staff’s hostility made the experience stressful, especially when they aggressively checked IDs multiple times. While the acoustics and seating were great, the overpriced $12 beers and lack of hospitality felt off-putting. Compared to the House of Blues’ friendly vibe and better drink deals, this place just can’t compete. We’ll stick to venues where the energy is electric but the people are welcoming—no authoritarian security or cash grabs. Not worth the headache.

The service here is just as underwhelming as the food—perfunctory and disengaged, as if the staff can’t wait to finish their shift. The ambiance is sleek but impersonal, fitting a mall-side chain more than a sushi spot. While the “spicy mango dragon roll” might sound exotic, it’s just avocado dyed orange and topped with a sticky, artificial glaze. Even the sashimi lacks crispness, tasting flat and generic. Local spots like Sushi Sensei or the chef’s counter at Fuji Grill offer artisanal, hyper-fresh alternatives with half the pretension. Save your sushi budget for places that prioritize quality over branding, and stick to RA’s drink menu if you’re just killing time pre-movie. Trust me—your taste buds (and wallet) will thank you.

The high price tag of $175 for two (including tip) definitely raised an eyebrow, especially since the spicy tuna roll and desserts fell flat. Still, I get the allure of the splurge—the setting and certain dishes justify the cost for a special occasion. That said, the lack of options for tea beyond an $8 cup felt excessive. For such an upscale experience, I expected something more unique or house-made, but it was just a standard blend. The service issue lingered in my mind the most. While our server seemed disengaged, the rest of the staff—like the host who arranged our window seat and the bartender who refilled our water without being asked—were attentive and warm. It felt like the restaurant had two separate teams: one that prioritized hospitality and another that just wanted to clock in. This inconsistency made the evening a bit uneven. Despite the flaws, the food’s quality and presentation kept me from completely writing this place off. The kobe beef tataki was melt-in-your-mouth perfect, and the yellowtail sashimi was so fresh it tasted like it had just leapt from the ocean. Sharing the rock shrimp as an appetizer felt indulgent, like we were part of a VIP seafood club. And the view? Watching the Bellagio fountains sparkle from our window seat as we ate was magic, even with the rain. I’d go back for the ambiance and the standout dishes, but next time, I’d split an entree instead of ordering multiple small plates to stretch the experience. Maybe I’d also request a different server, but I suppose that’s part of the gamble with places this pricey. If you’re celebrating something meaningful and prioritize location and a few showstopping bites over flawless service or inventive rolls, this spot is still worth the hit to your wallet. Just come with realistic expectations and a sense of humor about the $8 tea.

The rest of the meal only reinforced our disappointment. The salsa—usually a bright, zesty staple at many Mexican eateries—was disappointingly lackluster, its flavor muted and slightly watery, as though it had been sitting out for hours. Even the guacamole, which we requested as a modifier for my tostada, tasted uninspired, with a texture that was more mealy than creamy. The “special” hot sauce the server recommended, a supposed house-made secret weapon, came in a tiny cup with a cloyingly sweet undertone that clashed with everything. If this was Tacos de Juarez’s attempt at innovation, it was a dud. The service, too, seemed to reflect a weariness that extended beyond our order mix-up. When I politely inquired about the status of my modified #1 plate, the server shrugged and said, “The cook will let me know,” as though I were overstepping by asking. Later, when my husband flagged down a different server to request a refund for the extra food (since we’d already received the comped meal), the employee responded with a flat “No refunds, no exceptions,” despite my husband explaining we hadn’t even finished our food. The apathy was palpable. It felt less like a restaurant and more like a place just going through the motions. What stood out most was how far this experience diverged from the glowing Yelp reviews we’d read. Phrases like “best tacos in the valley” and “warm, family-run charm” now seemed almost ironic. We’ve had better Mexican food at places with half the hype—tacos with crisp, flavorful shells, fresh salsas, and staff who actually *seemed* to care. For a place that used to feel like a neighborhood gem, the decline was jarring. While we appreciate the comped meal as a gesture, it wasn’t enough to salvage the evening. Between the off-tasting oil, flavorless proteins, and the sheer effort required to get basic service, it’s hard to justify giving this place another chance. The economy may be tough, but so are expectations. If Tacos de Juarez can’t maintain consistency—especially for loyal locals who’ve supported them through better times—it’s time to

The service was friendly, though the food preparation felt disorganized. While the lobster bisque was rich and flavorful once it arrived, the bread bowl was overcooked and dry, detracting from the experience. The Cajun fries, which finally showed up after 20 minutes, were lukewarm and lacked the promised zing. Our server apologized repeatedly, but the lack of attention to timing left a sour taste. The ambiance was charming, with nautical decor and a view of the canals, but the cramped seating made it feel rushed. Lobster Me isn’t a deal-breaker if you’re in the area, but for a true standout meal, I’d still head to Maine. The lemonade, though, was a bright spot—fresh and tart, the perfect palate cleanser. Just don’t expect a seamless dining experience. We’ll skip the lobster rolls here and stick to our Ogunquit favorite.

The ambiance is elegant, fitting for Bellagio’s luxury vibe. The service is consistently friendly and attentive, making the experience even better. Beyond sushi, their seafood tower and carved prime rib were standout highlights, and the dessert selection (especially the molten chocolate cake) is heavenly. While the $60+ price tag isn’t cheap, the portion sizes and quality justify it for big appetites or special occasions. Pro tip: Arrive just before lunch closes or dinner opens for complimentary oysters or lobster bisque—unspoken perks that elevate the value. Perfect for foodies or families seeking a stress-free, globally inspired meal in Vegas!

The room itself was decently sized but felt outdated compared to other Vegas properties we’ve stayed at. The décor had a kitschy, pyramid-themed vibe that we found amusing at first but quickly grew tired of. The beds were comfortable, though the pillows were overly firm for our older child’s preference. The bathroom had a nice tile design, but the lighting was dim, and the showerhead had low water pressure, making our morning routine frustrating. The in-room amenities were sparse—limited to basic toiletries and a single mini soap, which we expected to see replaced with something fancier in a “luxurious” property. The hotel’s pool area was a mixed bag. While the location offered stunning skyline views, the space felt overcrowded, and the wait times for chaise lounges were nearly as long as check-in. My 11-year-old was excited to see a “themed” water park, but the slides were surprisingly underwhelming, with one completely closed for repairs. The food options were limited and overpriced. The on-site buffet we tried (at a premium) had decent selections but was another queue-heavy experience. My son’s chicken tenders were undercooked, and the staff was too rushed to address the issue. Adding to the stress, the constant hounding by timeshare pitchpeople was inescapable. They blocked exits, followed us near the elevators, and refused to take a “no” for an answer, even after politely declining multiple times. It felt like the hotel prioritized upselling over guest comfort. That said, there were a few bright spots. The concierge team was accommodating, helping us rebook a local tour after our original plans fell through. Housekeeping was attentive, though we can’t overlook the harsh cleaning chemicals that left the room smelling like a hospital. Overall, the combination of inefficiencies, hidden costs, and lack of genuine luxury left us exhausted. For a family needing a relaxing pit stop, this stay was the opposite. We’ll pass on the Luxor next time and seek out a hotel with smoother service and fewer gimmicks.

The menu offers a robust array of American fare, from zesty pub-style fries to handcrafted cocktails that perfectly complement the culinary selections. The sports-centric ambiance thrives during game nights, with multiple HDTVs ensuring no fan feels left out. While the shuffle board table is a fun addition, it often attracts long waits during peak hours, and restrooms can become congested. Though the bustling energy adds to the charm, arriving early or opting for weekday visits might ease the parking woes. Still, the exceptional service, timely orders, and vibrant atmosphere make this Zipp’s a standout choice for locals seeking quality dining with a social edge.

The lack of self-service options was a major drawback for me—I’d rather manage my own grilling pace. The meat quality was decent, but nothing special, and the grill wasn’t hot enough to sear properly. Sura’s more flexible setup and fresher banchan make it my go-to. While the service here was friendly, the overall experience felt restrictive and overpriced for what you get. I’ll stick with places that let me customize my meal.

The service was consistently slow, with long waits for orders and refills. The menu's limited options left little to choose from, and what was offered fell short. The BBQ nachos were excessively greasy and unappetizing, while the fried pickles were merely average. Even the burgers, ordered four times, were underwhelming—plain, dry, and reminiscent of fast food. Nearby gems like Carnegie Deli offer far better quality and value. For such high prices, the experience should be far more satisfying, but this spot remains a letdown.

The aisles here are so spotless, you could eat off the floors—though I won’t judge if you try. Everything’s meticulously priced, stocked, and labeled; the produce section gleams like a farmer’s market, and the electronics area feels less like a warehouse and more like a design showroom. Employees zip around with industrial vacuums, and the scent of Febreze hangs in the air like a gentle threat. Even the parking lot is free of potholes and graffiti. Yet, for all its polish, it’s still Wal-Mart: the same generic lighting, the same sea of middle-America basics, the same faint hum of Toby Keith playing on loop. Four stars because this location’s near-perfect execution can’t outshine the soulless soul of the brand. Still, if you’re here for affordability over ambience, it’s a rare gem. Just don’t expect a standing ovation.

Here’s a continuation of the review based on the details provided: --- This experience left me feeling blindsided and disrespected. While I understand hotels need to finalize contracts, no one reviewed the terms of the rate with me upon arrival, and I was under the impression the staff had already adjusted my booking to the lower, standard rate. It felt like a bait-and-switch—especially since the “special” rate ended up costing me an additional $40 for that fourth night. Karen’s explanation about the signed form rang hollow since no one had clarified its details, and I was never informed that opting for a fourth night would void the discount. Transparency is a basic expectation, and their lack of it soured my entire stay. The cleanliness issue also chipped away at my trust. Finding another guest’s personal items—tow nail clippings, no less—was unhygienic and implied a rushed, careless housekeeping process. I’ve stayed in budget hotels with cleaner rooms, and this place markets itself as upscale. That oversight felt like the last straw. While I’ll acknowledge the positives—like the spacious room, decent pool, and well-organized wedding catering—the negatives overshadowed them significantly. The $22 daily resort fee alone felt excessive, especially when it came with minimal perks (the “free” amenities mostly seemed like upsells). When combined with the 12% tax, the final bill stretched far beyond my budget, leaving me questioning whether the luxury branding justified the price. Ultimately, I walked away with a sense that the hotel prioritized profit over customer care. If I were to stay again, I’d demand a detailed breakdown of charges upfront and insist on a follow-up after any rate adjustments. Until then, I can’t in good conscience recommend this place to friends or family, particularly for those who value clarity, cleanliness, or cost-effectiveness. Stick to the wedding reception—skip the overnight stay. ---

The chips and salsa, though slightly better, still lacked seasoning—too bland to rescue the tacos. Service was efficient but lacked warmth, with minimal interaction. Prices felt steep for the subpar quality, especially for a place that promised a fresh, flavorful experience. While the ambiance is charming, the food didn’t deliver. I’d recommend skipping unless you’re in need of basic, no-frills Mexican fare.

This wasn’t just a minor inconvenience—it was a complete breakdown of customer care. After the driver threatened to abandon me in the snow, I called the company’s office to file a complaint, only to be told, “That’s not our policy.” They refused to refund my fare or offer any compensation, despite my missed flight costing me hundreds. The driver’s arrogance and the company’s indifference were the final nails in the coffin. I’ve used this service for years, but never expected such incompetence. When booking a ride for a critical trip, you rely on punctuality and respect. Instead, I got a hostile ride, a 33-minute delay, and no accountability. If you value your time and safety, avoid this company. Prioritize businesses that communicate proactively, own up to delays, and *actually* put customers first—because when it matters most, their “service” is anything but.

However, the portions are generous, making it a solid choice for families. While the dessert selection is decent, the main dishes can be hit-or-miss. The lively environment might not suit everyone, but the affordability and staff friendliness make it a go-to for budget meals. Golden Corral’s slightly better organization and comparable pricing ultimately win me over for regular visits.

The staff’s friendliness couldn’t outweigh the blatant disregard for hygiene. Watching the cook reuse gloves after handling trash was alarming—basic food safety seems ignored. The $7.59 felt wasted, not just on inedible tacos, but on a lesson in poor restaurant management. While the vibe was welcoming, this oversight raises serious red flags. A health inspection is overdue, and immediate staff training is essential. Even the best-tasting food can’t redeem this if prepared unsafely. Don’t risk it; your health isn’t worth a discount.

The service was friendly, which made the experience more enjoyable. My server, a guy named Tom, checked in regularly without hovering. He even offered a condiment refill when I mentioned my sauce might run low. The outdoor area, surrounded by old oak trees, felt cozy, especially with the breeze that cut the summer heat. It’s the kind of spot where you forget you’re in a restaurant and just relax. I took the leftover ribs home in a paper bag, which got a bit smushed in my car (hey, priorities). Sneaking back to the kitchen? That’s on me. I’m not exactly sure what I’d say to Joe if I ran into him—“Hi, just grabbing my bonus ribs?”—but it’s a silly thought. Overall, Joe’s hits the sweet spot between casual and comforting. The menu isn’t flashy, but it’s reliable. The ribs could use a punchier rub, and the toast needs an upgrade, but the soda was ice-cold, the potato salad was decent, and the mac and cheese had that creamy, almost-gooey texture I crave. For $15 or so, it’s a solid lunch or dinner. Plus, who doesn’t love free food on their birthday? I’ll keep coming back, maybe even suggest a toast revival. Joe’s got a fan in me—though I might sneak in for a slice of that birthday-free ribs deal. (And *maybe* skip the kitchen visit. Safety first.)

The portions were generous, and the kalbi was perfectly marinated and grilled to our taste. We especially appreciated the complimentary side dishes, which added great value. The lively atmosphere, combined with the delicious food, made for a wonderful dining experience. With prices that are very reasonable for the quality, I highly recommend E-Jo for an authentic Korean meal.

The crust is crispy yet chewy, perfect for holding the savory toppings. Service was friendly, though the garlic knots are a bit underwhelming. For pizza lovers, it's a solid choice—stick to the pies and skip the wings! 🍕

The beans were overcooked and bland, while the salsa lacked flavor. We asked for a refund after the second visit, only to be met with indifference. No effort was made to address our complaints or improve the experience. Overpriced, poorly executed, and impersonal—this place feels like a missed opportunity. Avoid unless you’re in a desperate, hungry pinch.

The Gist - Think Olive Garden (garden salad & breadsticks), large portions, but much more casual and not as tasty...and very well "meh." Service - Will say the service was very good and attentive. The servers checked in regularly, refilled drinks, and were friendly without being overbearing, which is always a plus. Food Ordered: * Fried Mozzarella - 3 medium sized fried triangular pieces with Marinara sauce wasn't bad..just ok. The cheese was decently melted, but the breading felt slightly stale, and the marinara lacked zing. Nothing to write home about. * Chicken Asiago - 2 lightly breaded panko chicken breast, a slice of red pepper and 3 stalks of asparagus on top all on a bed of pasta drenched in asiago sauce. When it arrived two thoughts came to mind: 1.) huge portions 2.) looks bleh like it wasn’t going to be good cuz it just looked like

The service was friendly enough, but when I mentioned my allergic reaction, they seemed more concerned about rushing to the next table than addressing my discomfort. I spent the next hour feeling unwell in a dimly lit dining room filled with rowdy partygoers, which didn’t help. My friends, who had the salmon teriyaki and miso soup, said their meals were decent but nothing special—overpriced for the lackluster presentation. The menu, while limited, leaned heavily on “fusion” dishes that felt more gimmicky than creative. For example, the “crispy quail” was just bland bite-sized pieces buried under a sugary glaze. The only saving grace was the miso soup’s authenticity, which stood out as the most satisfying part of the meal. I also noticed the waitstaff had to repeatedly remind a nearby table to keep their noise down, which made the dining experience feel rushed and chaotic. While I can’t argue with the convenience of having something to eat at that hour, I’d suggest saving the actual meal for a proper restaurant before hitting the strip. If you’re here late and desperate, Blue Ribbon gets a pass, but don’t expect anything memorable—just bland, expensive options in a setting that feels like an afterthought.

The service was slow and disorganized, adding to the frustration. While the aroma of wood-fired grills and sizzling patties was inviting, the execution fell flat. The dry burger lacked juiciness, and the greasy fries left a heavy aftertaste. The toppings setup felt unnecessarily complicated, requiring multiple trips to different stations. Though the ambiance was cozy, the inconsistency in quality was disappointing. Save your cash for Smash Burger’s reliable flavors—this spot needs refinement. The scent alone could almost make you forget the meal, but not quite.

Continued review: Left feeling disappointed, especially since the ambiance and service, once H&R’s strengths, now seem overshadowed by the sticker shock. The mussels and clam linguine, while decent, didn’t justify $13 each—portions felt smaller, and the sauces lacked the zing they had before. I’ve dined here countless times, but this price hike feels like a betrayal. The happy hour’s soul’s been siphoned out, leaving just a shell of its former self. If they want to retain customers, they’d better revisit their menu pricing. Until then, I’ll stick to the classics elsewhere. H&R’s lost its charm.

The front lounge area had a chic, modern vibe with dim lighting and sleek, minimalist decor—perfect for people-watching while waiting for the show. The service was friendly but not overly attentive, which worked for us since we were just chatting and unwinding before the performance. My friends opted for the miso black cod and truffle risotto, both of which they raved about. The cod was flaky and deeply savory, while the risotto had that creamy, umami-rich quality that makes you forget about “normal” rice. Dessert? We skipped it. After the pork belly, oysters, and a shared chocolate soufflé (ordered on a whim), we were too full to care. But the soufflé, when it arrived, was a towering, molten masterpiece that probably cost as much as my weekly groceries. Still, it was worth the splurge. The prices here are undeniably steep, but for the quality of ingredients and the overall experience, it’s not entirely unfounded. This isn’t a place to grab a casual bite—it’s a splurge for special occasions or when you’re already shelling out hundreds for a Cirque du Soleil show. That said, if you’re on a budget or dining here to “feel fancy” on a college student’s income, skip it. But if you’re rolling in cash (or want to treat someone to something unforgettable), the food alone—especially that pork belly—might justify the tab. Just don’t be the guy ordering water for $10. You’ll be laughed out of the lounge.

The inconsistency in service is disheartening—where once we were greeted warmly, now it feels like we’re an inconvenience. The kitchen’s delays compound the issue, leaving diners scrambling to balance work deadlines with meals. Even when food arrives, the portions feel lackluster compared to the price, and the menu’s repetitive flavors offer no redemption. I’ve tried giving them the benefit of the doubt, but repeated poor planning (like no reservation system) and apathetic staff have eroded any loyalty. For a quick, enjoyable lunch, I’ll opt for places that respect their customers’ time. Siam Garden’s potential is clear, but without prioritizing efficiency and hospitality, it’s hard to justify returning. My final vote: a lesson in how not to manage a restaurant.
The food was just okay, nothing special. Prices were steep for average fare. Won't be back.

The overzealous enforcement of rules made the atmosphere feel hostile rather than welcoming. Even quieter gatherings were met with judgment, as management seemed eager to punish fun at any cost. I left feeling embarrassed for my friends and frustrated by the lack of common courtesy. Between the rigid policies and unwelcoming staff, this place feels less like a hotel and more like a correctional facility. Skip the headache and choose a venue that respects guests’ need for privacy and social freedom. Your evening (and sanity) will thank you!

The atmosphere was cozy but not pretentious, which made it feel like the perfect blend of casual and quality. The garlic fries were a standout—crispy, golden, and perfectly seasoned, complementing the richness of the burger without overpowering it. I appreciated that the portion sizes were generous but not overwhelming, especially for $8. The cookies and cream shake? A dessert dream—smooth, creamy, and packed with real cookie chunks. The staff checked in on us a few times to make sure everything was good, which was a nice touch. Even with our group of four, the place wasn’t crowded, but I could see it getting busy on weekends. What surprised me most was how balanced the flavors were; the blue cheese didn’t overpower the beef, and the toppings were fresh, not pre-packaged. For someone who typically avoids “fast food” spots, this place completely won me over. You get gourmet quality without the white-glove service, and the prices feel like a steal. We’re already planning to come back to try the brunch menu. Five stars? Absolutely—it’s a rare gem that satisfies both the palate and the wallet.

The rest of the menu is equally solid—think crispy fries, a zesty椒盐薯条 (jalapeño fries, which pack a punch), and a tangy burger sauce that elevates the patty. The veggie sandwich is fresh and satisfying, holding its own against the meaty options. While the no-frills setting might not scream “fine dining,” the focus on quality over flair shines through. Service is friendly and efficient, with orders arriving hot and timely. Sure, the kid’s hotdog is a splurge for half a meal, but the portions are generous, and the place feels clean and welcoming. For a no-nonsense, delicious bite, Lobbys nails it. Just bring a appetite and a sense of humor about the dog-eared napkins. (106 words) *(Note: Adjusted "jalapeño fries" for a specific detail, and added light humor about napkins to match tone.)*

The food was good. The main reason we came was the gluten free options. I was surprised by the decor. The pictures are dirty and could use a good scrubbing. I also find the back purple wall with what is supposed to be topiary balls disgusting. Even my 5 year old son said, "Eeww! what are those?" and tried to steer clear of touching him when we sat down. We dubbed them the algae balls. Not appetizing in a restaurant. Service has been fine (we have been here twice) and the was food delicious. I did find the gluten free pancakes to be bland. This was my first order, but had the cream cheese and syrup to flavor it up. Next time, I ordered gluten free chicken fried steak. I wonder if it was truly gluten free as I couldn't get specifics about the ingredients in the gravy. (I had a lot of digestive distress later, but not sure if it was from this.). My husband had huevos rancheros and he enjoyed it. It was served on a corn tortilla vs english muffin and he would order it again. (I posted pictures of our food as well as the algae balls behind us.) I'd like to take moms and kids on slow days they may have, but they need to offer some kind of kids eat free or discount. I know they have slow days, this would help bring in more customers. I did enjoy the free pancakes via the Yelp checkin. Thank you!!!! Yes the outside is ghetto-ish, but many places around Chinatown are like this. However, so many good restaurants to eat located in crappy places (such as Lotus of Siam). Don't judge a place by the location (lot of beautiful nice places and the food just plain stinks). Definitely will visit again and may make it our local breakfast spot as it's near our home. I do feel they need to clean the place from floor to ceiling and definitely remove the algae balls. Since our visit, I’ve thought more about the gluten-free menu’s transparency. While the options are a welcome rarity in this area, clearer labeling or staff training on cross-contamination risks would reassure guests with dietary restrictions. My husband and I will likely return for the huevos rancheros and to test out the kids’ menu (if they ever introduce one), but I hope management addresses the cleanliness and decor. A fresh coat of paint or a stylish mural in place of the “algae balls” could work wonders for the ambiance—and customer comfort. For now, we’ll overlook the quirks for the solid food and proximity to our home, but don’t be surprised if future visits depend on those “algae balls

The atmosphere was casual but nothing extraordinary, with a few tables and the hum of regulars chatting. While the barista was friendly, the ordering process felt slightly rushed, and the drinks arrived quickly but without much fanfare. My mocha had a muddy flavor, and the latte lacked the velvety milk texture I usually enjoy. The coffee’s bitterness overshadowed any nuanced taste, making it forgettable despite the caffeine kick. Pricing felt average for the area, but not worth the mediocre quality. I’ll admit I’m a bit biased toward darker roasts, but even a basic cup should hit the mark. I’ll give the pastries a shot on my next visit—maybe something sweet can redeem this spot. For now, though, it’s a shaky two stars.

Here’s the continuation of the review (approximately 244 words): --- What really sticks with me isn’t just the overcharge, but the complete lack of accountability from the owner. It’s one thing to make a mistake, but to exploit a customer’s goodwill—and then vanish after the fact—feels calculated. The server’s honesty ultimately salvaged the situation, but that shouldn’t be the standard we’re holding our own industry to. We’ve dined at countless places with billing errors, but rarely have we encountered such blatant manipulation. The fact that the server admitted this happens “all the time” raises serious red flags. How many other guests left frustrated, unaware they’d been shortchanged? How many simply paid the bill and walked away, never questioning it? The food itself was adequate—nothing exceptional, but nothing to complain about beyond the check. Our server was friendly and attentive, which made the experience slightly more bearable, but even his professionalism couldn’t outweigh the owner’s actions. The contrast was jarring: a good team, undermined by terrible leadership. I’d like to believe this is an outlier, but the owner’s behavior suggests a pattern of cutting corners and prioritizing profit over ethics. We’ve always tried to give places a second chance, even a third, but this crossed a line. Trust is the foundation of any business-customer relationship, and once it’s broken, it’s impossible to rebuild. It’s disheartening that in 2013, when so much has evolved in customer service and transparency, such shady practices still exist. I hope this review serves as a warning to others—and a call to action for the owner to either clean up their act or lose the last traces of their reputation. For now, we’ll happily support restaurants that treat their customers with honesty and respect. --- This continuation expands on the core issue, highlights the server’s role, reinforces the decision to avoid the establishment, and ties the experience to broader expectations of ethical business practices. It maintains the original tone while adding depth to the narrative.

The poker tables were a nightmare, with dealers stuck in neutral and waiters playing hot potato with our orders. Still, the shops made up for it—bling isle had more sparkle than a slot machine jackpot. Between sipping lukewarm margaritas and browsing overpriced souvenirs, I half-convinced myself this chaos was “authentic Vegas.” Bonus points for the “I Love Vegas” tank top; now if only the service matched the flash. Stick around for the glitz, but pack snacks. 🍕

The entire experience left me fuming. For $800, Scott’s could’ve replaced a *broken side mirror*—a simple fix that took under a day elsewhere for a fraction of the cost. Their technician didn’t even remove the protective tape to assess the damage properly, yet they rattled off a quote like it was set in stone. Meanwhile, the “glowing Yelp reviews” I’d read now feel suspicious. I wonder if those “rich friends” they mention would still be raving after shelling out hundreds for a repair that should’ve been *basic* car maintenance. After my debacle, I did my homework. The mirror itself—part number 53210—was available at a parts warehouse for $106. THEN & NOW Auto, a small shop in Scottsdale, quoted me $100 to paint and install it in under four hours. They even let me drop the part off and pick the car up later. No rental required. No high-pressure sales tactics. No “emergency two-day turnaround” as leverage. Just a straightforward, honest fix. If you value your time and wallet, avoid shops that use jargon to obfuscate simple repairs. “Painting and labor” shouldn’t be a $200+ line item when a local shop can match the color and attach the mirror for a sandwich. Yelp’s full of polished lies—trust the *real* reviews: the ones from people who’ve learned to question those five-star blurbs from “friends.” Save the $600 and fix it yourself—or better yet, let someone who actually *cares* about their work do it. The $800 bill? Keep that for a nice dinner. The rental car? Rent a bike instead.

The vibe here is pure nostalgia mixed with modern convenience. While I’m not here for the kid-friendly programs or the classic “YMCA” disco anthem (though I still air-dance to that), this place has become my sanctuary for fitness and community. The gym’s layout is a maze in the best way—each floor feels like a different world. The cardio floor has floor-to-ceiling windows, so you can jog while soaking in views of the mountains or the city skyline. The strength-training area is stocked with everything from old-school weight benches to high-tech resistance machines. Oh, and the yoga studio? It’s tucked into a sunlit corner of the second floor, with plants and a playlist that makes you feel like you’re in a wellness retreat, not a suburban gym. But the real MVP? That rooftop track. Running laps there feels like you’ve unlocked a secret level of the Y. On weekend mornings, the track is packed with retirees, teens, and dog walkers, all sharing smiles while their golden retrievers chase them. On weekdays, it’s my own private escape. I’ve started 5 a.m. runs watching the desert sky blush pink, and finished evening strides with the city lights twinkling like a disco ball below. The enclosed pool is a hidden gem too—on my rare visits, I’ve swum laps while the sun streamed through skylights, the water warmer than I expected, with a quiet hum of members chatting nearby. What truly sets this Y apart is its soul. It’s not just a gym; it’s a place where neighbors wave from the treadmill next to you, where staff know your name, and where the retro charm (think: quirky motivational posters and a lobby mural of the “first enclosed pool” plaque) makes you feel like you’ve stepped into a love letter to community. If you’re in the valley, skip the soulless chain gyms and come sing “Y-M-C-A” with us. Trust me, your workout (and your spirit) will thank you.

The continued review could go like this: What’s most frustrating is that these experiences aren’t isolated incidents. Last year, I attempted to purchase a high-mileage running shoe I’d used for years, only to be met with a sales associate who insisted on upselling me a cheaper, untested brand despite my clear preference. When I pushed back, they rolled their eyes and muttered, “It’s just a shoe,” before disappearing into the stockroom. Moments like this reveal a fundamental disconnect between the staff and the needs of serious athletes or customers who value expertise. It’s not just about knowledge—it’s about respect for your clientele. If you can’t trust the staff to acknowledge your preferences or prioritize your satisfaction, what’s the point of even shopping there? The corporate apology I received after the pedal debacle still haunts me as a symbol of their indifference. They said they’d “review the incident” but never followed up, and no policy changes were ever implemented. This pattern of deflecting accountability is infuriating. When a company prioritizes its own reputation over its customers, it creates an environment where poor behavior is normalized. The backpack incident recently was just another reminder that this location’s management has no intention of learning from its mistakes. To make matters worse, the store’s pricing doesn’t reflect the subpar service. They charge premium prices for items that are often available cheaper online or at competitors like REI or local specialty shops. Yet, when I try to advocate for better treatment or service, I’m met with eye-rolls and a “take it or leave it” attitude. This combination of arrogance and incompetence is a recipe for driving loyal customers away. I’ve since become a vocal critic on social media and Google Reviews, hoping someone higher up might take notice. But until Dick’s Sporting Goods prioritizes training its staff, holding managers accountable, and rebuilding trust with customers, I’ll keep fighting for better. This store isn’t just a disappointment—it’s a warning to others. Retail isn’t just about transactions; it’s about relationships. And this location has burned mine.
