It transformed what could’ve been an ordinary wait into a tempting mini-break. I ended up grabbing a quick taco, and it was well worth the splurge. If they streamlined the communication and tightened up the quality control, Oasis could easily become a go-to spot for both car care and a tasty bite. For now, I’ll return on quieter days to see if the service improves—and to enjoy that irresistible food again.

The lack of care extended beyond just the donut. When I mentioned the mess to the employee, he shrugged and said, “They’re just donuts,” which felt dismissive and unprofessional. That attitude, combined with the haphazard packaging, made me question their commitment to customer satisfaction. I’ve visited other DD locations where staff handle orders with precision and a friendly smile, so it’s disheartening this location seems to lack even basic training. My main gripe isn’t the occasional mishap, but the *nonchalance* with which it’s handled. While the iced coffee redeemed part of the visit, it’s hard to overlook the effortlessness of a positive experience when the fundamentals—like respecting your product and customers—fall short. I’ll keep supporting DD overall, but this location’s employees have officially lost my loyalty. Hopefully, management takes note—because even a delicious donut can’t save a delivery drenched in frustration.

The service was friendly and efficient, which made the experience even better. Our server checked in regularly without being overbearing and even offered a free biscuit to my daughter when she mentioned her fries were taking a minute. The atmosphere was lively but not too noisy, with a Southern charm that felt cozy despite the place being pretty packed. I tried the biscuits and gravy on the side—flaky biscuits paired with a rich, velvety gravy that had just the right amount of spice. My daughter, usually picky, raved about the wings, saying the spice blend was “not too hot but still fun.” The portions were generous, and the meal felt like a real indulgence. While the tea’s sweetness was an unexpected curveball, I appreciated that they offer adjustments for future visits. The pricing was fair for the quality and quantity, especially compared to other breakfast spots we’ve tried. We left with a to-go box of leftovers (though it sat uneaten for days because neither of us could bring ourselves to eat it—temptation won). If you’re a fan of bold flavors and hearty portions, LoLo’s is a must-visit. The only downside? You’ll probably want to come back so often, your bank account might beg you to slow down.

The vibe here feels like a half-finished concept—modern but with zero personality. The bar itself is fine for a quick drink, though the menu leans toward generic domestics and a few local brews you can find everywhere else. Still, the bartenders’ friendly banter and speed kept things from feeling too meh. I’m not sure who the target audience is—casual drinkers? Downtown stragglers?—but it lacks the charm or quirk to make you linger. The emptiness of the space amplifies every clink of glass and muffled conversation, which is either meditative or annoying, depending on your mood. All in all, it’s a neutral pit stop, not a recommendation. Save your energy for places that *actually* feel like a destination.

The food, though fresh and flavorful, felt overpriced for the wait. The staff’s swift refund and genuine apologies softened the frustration. While I appreciate their commitment to quality, the experience leans too heavily on patience. Might return for a quieter visit, but busy hours require serious time planning.

The entire experience was a masterclass in frustration. After waiting nearly 45 minutes with no sign of our food, I approached the counter to inquire. The employee, who looked more interested in their phone than my dilemma, shrugged and said, “It’s taking longer than usual.” When I finally reordered—and was met with the news that they’d run out of their signature cheese steaks and fries—it felt less like a dining experience and more like a farcical test of patience. How does a place that caters to late-night hunger pangs let its inventory deplete so completely? It’s baffling, especially when the menu offers little else beyond a handful of uninspired salads and a microwave-reheated pretzel. Meanwhile, the staff’s apathy seeped into every corner of the establishment. One server spent 20 minutes laughing with a friend in the kitchen, while another barked at a customer who simply asked for ketchup. The restrooms were another story entirely: sticky floors, a single broken soap dispenser, and a toilet paper shortage that felt almost vindictive. It’s clear management prioritizes appearances over functionality—floral tablecloths and neon signs can’t mask incompetence. Scottsdale’s late-night scene is a patchwork of clubs and gas station burritos, but even that seems better than PSC’s non-service. Corleone’s, while limited in hours, at least delivers hot sandwiches and a semblance of hospitality. Until PSC invests in staff training, inventory planning, or basic cleanliness, it’s a place best avoided. If this is the city’s answer to “eatertainment,” it’s no wonder the town sleeps by 2 a.m.
Service was nonexistent; the pho was inedible. Manager offered no help. Save your money—avoid this disaster.

The portions are generous, and everything is made fresh to order. The staff was friendly and efficient, even during the rush. I especially love their classic buttermilk pancakes—they’re fluffy and just the right sweetness. The coffee is strong and keeps me going all morning. Waffle House never disappoints, whether I’m stopping in for a quick bite or a hearty meal. I’ll definitely be back soon! 10/10 would recommend to anyone craving comfort food done right.

The wings themselves were solid—crispy, well-seasoned, and packed with flavor. We went with their classic Mild and a spicy Honey BBQ for the kids, and both were executed well. The Honey BBQ had a nice tang without being overly sweet, which was a pleasant surprise. The fries were equally good, with a perfect salt-to-crunch ratio. I noticed they’ve added a few new dipping sauces to the menu, like a garlic aioli and a spicy mango habanero. We tried the latter, and while it was a bit over the top for my palate, it was a hit with the teens in our group. What stood out was the staff’s attentiveness. Our server checked in regularly, refilled drinks before we even noticed they were low, and handled our family’s chaotic ordering process (multiple kids with changing minds) with patience. The manager even stopped by our table to chat, which felt like a nice personal touch. That said, the price hike for the weekly deals does sting. While $0.60 per wing isn’t unreasonable compared to other chains, it’s hard not to notice the jump from the $0.25 I’ve been used to for over a decade. Still, the value feels justified when you factor in the generous portions and the lively atmosphere. The new location’s layout, though maze-like, has a cozy, sports-bar vibe that’s perfect for a casual family meal. All in all, this B-Dubs earned a loyal customer for life—at least until the wings hit $1 each. For now, I’ll keep coming back, especially for the lunch special, as long as the service stays this sharp. Fingers crossed they don’t raise the price of “good service” any higher!

The staff is friendly and helpful with recommendations, which is great for first-timers. The sesame noodles and General Tso’s chicken are consistently delicious, though the beef dishes can be hit-or-miss. The specials board is worth checking—last time, the braised short ribs with hoisin glaze were amazing. While our last dine-in on a busy Saturday felt rushed, the food still arrived hot and fresh. For solid, no-frills Chinese fare with a few standout dishes, this spot is a local gem. Don’t skip the fortune cookies at the end—they’re a sweet touch!

The meats were juicy and perfectly grilled, with a nice char. The tzatziki was creamy and refreshing. The staff was super friendly, and the prices are unbeatable. Such a great value for the quality and quantity. Can't wait for my next visit!

Continued review: While the rest of our meal leaned into the "meh" category, the ma po tofu was a standout—creamy, spicy, and packed with bold flavor that we’re still craving. It’s the kind of dish that feels like a restaurant secret, and we’re still impressed it made us whip out our phones to search for a copycat recipe. Service was hit-or-miss: our server was overly eager with stories about their cat but somehow still nailed the veggie recommendations. We’ll admit the $20 discount made the experience feel guilt-free, but we’d probably skip the $30 tab otherwise. For now, this will stay a “coupon spot” in our books—worth one visit for the tofu, but not enough to drive a return trip unless the hotel throws in another deal.

The staff was inattentive, offering no apologies for the lengthy wait. Prices felt exorbitant for the subpar quality—especially for a major event. After enduring the long line, the food didn’t justify the effort. Save your money and skip this spot entirely; there are far better options nearby.

The texture was all off, and the beans left a lingering soapy aftertaste. How could the same place deliver such a massive letdown? Not sure if the beans were overcooked or just badly seasoned. Will definitely stick with Elena’s—superior flavor and no surprises!

The menu is thoughtfully curated, offering hidden gems like their pad Krapow (Thai basil pork) with just the right balance of chili, garlic, and lime—nothing like the watered-down versions elsewhere. The sticky rice is consistently warm and flavorful, perfect with their mango sticky rice dessert that’s light on syrup, letting the fruit shine. Owner Archi’s hands-on approach is evident, as he often personally checks on tables, ensuring orders are spot-on. While the Sahara location is convenient, this spot feels more cozy and welcoming, with a casual vibe that makes you feel at home. Prices are fair for the quality, and the portions are generous, making it worth every bite. Whether it’s a busy weeknight or a lazy Sunday, I’ll keep returning here—the attention to tradition and taste is unmatched. Five stars!

The park’s positives definitely outweigh the irrigation headaches, but it’s worth noting that the closures disrupt routines, especially for dogs who rely on consistent outdoor time. I’ve seen friends get frustrated when their usual off-leash playdate has to be canceled last-minute, and the scramble for alternative parks can feel chaotic. That said, the park’s design makes up for it. The two water stations are a lifesaver on hot days, and the seating areas are perfect for socializing or just relaxing with a book. The shaded spots under the trees are a balm during peak sun, and the sprawling play area means dogs can run without bumping into fences constantly. Sasha thrives here—she’s gotten more confident and even made regular “friends” (like Max the energetic Border Collie and Luna the chilled Chihuahua mix). The separation for small/large dogs is well-managed too, which keeps things safe. Honestly, if the city could adjust the irrigation schedule—like watering earlier in the morning or using a system that dries faster—this place would be perfect. Until then, I’ll keep coming back. The community here feels like a neighborhood; even if I don’t know all the humans, the dogs are the real stars, and this park gives them a stage to shine.

The portions are generous, and the bread is always fresh—perfect for soaking up their zesty sauces. While the lack of modern payment options might inconvenience some, the mouthwatering aroma and Casella’s friendly, no-frills vibe make it a locals’ favorite. Don’t miss their daily specials; every bite feels like a taste of tradition!

The seats are surprisingly comfortable, and the sound system rivals home theaters, making it worth the trip even for a big-screen experience. Staff is always friendly, and the lobby’s retro vibe adds charm. While ticket prices feel a tad steep for casual outings, the occasional treat is justified when catching a highly anticipated release or a classic film in the Cine Capri lineup. Plus, the patio outside offers a nice spot to sip coffee post-show. It’s not just a movie theater—it’s a small-town feel in a convenient location. I’ll keep returning when the timing aligns, especially if the film is exclusive or the Kierland Commons’ new eats are calling my name.

The immersive exhibits and vibrant décor make it a must-visit. From vintage soda bottles to interactive displays, there’s something for every fan. The "Tastes of the World" section is a highlight, offering a global soda journey. Don’t forget to grab a souvenir—though be prepared to splurge on the premium merch. Perfect for a quick, refreshing pit stop from the desert heat! Family-friendly and brimming with whimsical charm, it’s a celebration of all things fizzy. Pro tip: Sip your free sample with a view of the Strip—it’s pure joy in a glass.

The hotel’s off-the-strip location meant fewer crowds and a more relaxed vibe, though it did require a bit of planning to reach the main attractions. The casino was cozy, with a retro feel and bright lights that made it fun to wander through, even if we didn’t gamble. My husband tried his hand at poker and claimed he “nearly won,” while I stuck to sipping margaritas and people-watching. The spa area was small but offered a peaceful respite; I treated myself to a basic massage and left feeling refreshed. For entertainment, the hotel hosted live music in the lobby bar—a nice touch that added charm. I also appreciated the free shuttle service to nearby Strip spots, though it sometimes had long wait times. Overall, while the hotel wasn’t flashy, it offered a comfortable stay with standout views and thoughtful touches. The value for the price was solid, especially with the tower access included. I’d consider returning for the scenery and tranquility, though next time I might bring a sweater for those chilly tower adventures!

The bakery itself is small but cozy, with a traditional setup and friendly staff who were eager to recommend items. However, most pastries felt underwhelming for the price—overpriced for average flavor. The "Chinese bakery baked stuff" includes decent options like scallion pancakes or sesame snacks, but I’d prioritize freshness and taste over aesthetics here. If you’re craving authentic, bold flavors, Sunville might not hit the mark. I’ll head to Diamond Bakery next, where reviews highlight richer fillings and better value. For now, this spot works for a quick bite but not a standout experience. Stick to nearby Pho Kim Long for guaranteed quality. Worth a one-time try, but I won’t return.

The hookah took over an hour to arrive, and when it finally did, the coals were barely warm. We pushed further, explaining the waste of time and money, but the staff refused to budge—despite the lack of effort to fix the issue. Prices here are astronomical for subpar food and drinks, and the “vibes” are anything but chill. The noise from the cringe music and blaring ads made conversation impossible. Every interaction felt transactional and dismissive. I’ve seen better service at drive-thrus. Save your time and wallet—this spot is a disaster from start to finish. Do *not* waste another minute here.

The bathrooms, however, are a different story—*惨状*. Lines snaked out the door, with folks squatting in corners or “borrowing” stalls by asking, “Is this thing taken?” The lack of basic hygiene (mysterious stains, broken soap dispensers) made me question if the city’s budget allocated for “liberal bike boxes” could’ve at least covered a janitor’s salary. The bar’s “plenty of room” claim rings hollow when half the patrons are crammed into the restroom like sardines. And don’t get me started on the staff’s indifference; they’d rather refill your $12 craft beer than address the crisis. Madison, your fiscal priorities are as absurd as the 10 PM parking curfew targeting bar-goers. If you’re going to milk tourists and locals for every dime, at least *pretend* to care about basic amenities. Until then, this place feels less like a social hub and more like a municipal stress test. Yikes.

The meal’s lackluster execution was frustrating, especially considering Culver’s reputation for nostalgic comfort. While the portions were generous, the execution felt lazy—the chicken was average, with Fry’s still outpacing them in crispiness and seasoning. Service was friendly but hurried, leaving little room for connection. Yet, the frozen custard remains a standout, offering a creamy, indulgent finish that justifies returning. Until their entrees align with that same level of care, though, I’ll stick to their drive-thru for custard and skip the dinner plate. Three stars for consistency in some areas, but not enough to earn my loyalty.

The energy at the Aria was electric, with the tournament room buzzing from the moment players started arriving. The structure kept things fast-paced, and while the antes eventually ramped up, the competition stayed fierce without feeling overly aggressive. I appreciated how the staff managed the growing field—tables were quickly added to accommodate the 132 entrants, and the digital displays kept everyone updated on chip counts and time remaining. The $50K high-roller event running concurrently drew a stellar crowd; catching glimpses of Tom Dwan’s tight, calculated play and Erik Seidel’s calm demeanor at their tables was a highlight. As for the tournament itself, the prize pool swelled significantly, and the payout structure was generous, with the top 20% cashing. While I didn’t make the money this time, the experience was worth every penny—especially the chance to test my game against pros and semi-regulars. The Aria’s layout is player-friendly, with ample food and drink options nearby, though it’s wise to bring snacks for the marathon sessions. If you’re up for a challenge and want to soak in the Vegas poker scene, this event is a must. Just be ready to commit—those late hours fly by when the action’s hot!

The atmosphere was a welcome respite from the neon-lit chaos of the casino floor—cozy, unpretentious, and buzzing with the warm hum of satisfied diners. The staff was attentive without being overbearing, and our server made a point to check in on us and even recommend a dessert pairing for next time. We opted for a side of truffle fries, which, though simple, were perfectly crispy and seasoned. For $12, the portion was generous and made a great side to split alongside our mains. While prices were mid-range for Vegas, everything felt worth it—the kind of place where quality justifies the cost. What stood out most was the attention to detail. The pork belly BLT, for instance, wasn’t just a gimmick; the belly was glazed to a caramelized crisp, the bacon smoky, and the avocado creamy without overpowering the flavors. Even the “special” on the soup—a splash of basil oil and a dollop of goat cheese—felt like a thoughtful touch, not an afterthought. My husband, not one to gush over food, admitted it was the best BLT he’d had in years. With dinner reviews touting dishes like dry-aged steak and craft cocktails, we’re already daydreaming about returning. Whether for a quick reprieve or a full meal, this spot checks all the boxes for a Vegas gem that’s worth prioritizing over the typical strip fare. Two thumbs up—and a packed schedule next time for more.

The portions are generous, and the prices are surprisingly reasonable for the quality. The staff is consistently friendly and attentive, making every visit welcoming. Both locations have a cozy, rustic vibe with indoor and outdoor seating. They also offer a rotating selection of fresh juices and artisanal coffees to complement your meal. Whether it’s a weekend brunch or a quick lunch, the menu never fails to impress. From the flaky pastries to the hearty soups, every item feels thoughtfully crafted. Highly recommend trying their seasonal specials—they’re always a hit! A must-visit for food lovers.

...but lately, flight delays have compounded the stress. While Southwest’s flexibility is great for most, I’ve occasionally waited 45 minutes for a flight only to find my preferred row taken. That said, the crew’s calm demeanor and complimentary snacks keep my experience positive overall. I’d trade a few extra minutes of peace for guaranteed front seating next time!

The technician was super friendly and walked me through the process, ensuring the tint was applied flawlessly without bubbles or streaks. The shop’s transparency with pricing was refreshing—no hidden fees, just a straightforward quote. I’ll admit, waiting in the sweltering lobby was a bit of a test, but the staff’s cheerful attitude made it tolerable. They even offered cold water, which was a nice touch. The tint’s durability is impressive; it’s already withstood sunlight without fading. Plus, their Yelp promotion saved me cash, making the deal even sweeter. Between the lifetime warranty, quick turnaround, and genuine helpfulness, I’m hooked. I’ll definitely be back for their ceramic coating service next—my car deserves the full spa day!

This is the worst Bank of America location in Las Vegas. Service is fake friendly until there is something semi-challenging, then no one is competent to help. I phoned customer service to make sure my daily withdrawal limit was sufficient as I was playing in a large buy-in tournament at the WSOP (I play poker professionally). Customer service assured me it would be no problem and that I could make the withdrawal at any branch. I came into the branch and the teller got the plump blonde manager over to approve the transaction (I had plenty of cash in my account to cover it, nothing pending), and she simply wouldn’t approve the transaction. More than that, she wouldn’t give me any reason why. *WTF???* Remaining calm, I contacted support again. They said I should be able to make the withdrawal and asked to speak to the branch manager. The teller refused to touch my phone, claiming there was “no phone number support could reach them at” and that they “could not call out.” Comical. The support agent on the phone laughed at the fact that the branch wouldn’t talk to her and apologized to me. Worse yet, the blonde manager remained in her office—too busy eating or something—to address the issue. I never raised my voice or acted unprofessionally toward anyone. I missed the tournament thanks to this absurdity at Bank of America. The branch manager or manager on duty (chubby blonde girl) should seriously be fired. She showed absolutely no empathy for my situation and hid in her office while I stood there, a professional with a career on the line, treated like an inconvenience. This isn’t a one-time glitch—it’s a culture of incompetence. From the teller’s panic to the manager’s refusal to engage, this branch exemplifies why B of A’s reputation crumbles in places like Vegas. I’ve dealt with banks my entire life, and this was the most baffling, customer-ignoring experience I’ve ever endured. Save yourself the headache: avoid this location at all costs. If B of A won’t hold its staff accountable, they deserve the public relations nightmare this will become. My career suffered, and I’ll never forgive the “customer service” that failed me when I needed it most.

continued review: Service was prompt and friendly, with our takeout order ready in minutes. The Thai Toast was crispy and packed with flavor, while the panang curry balanced heat and creaminess perfectly. Prices felt fair for the generous portions, and the husband’s drunken noodles were spicy and satisfying. The new menu still has our favorites, plus a few exciting additions. We’ll definitely return and bring friends along too.

The vibrant energy of the place is impossible to ignore. The bar itself feels like a cowboy-western fantasy, with leather booths, neon lights, and a stage that becomes the heart of the action. Even though the mixed drinks were on the weak side, the bartenders’ playful banter and hilarious antics more than made up for it. I overheard one of them crack a joke so cheesy, it got the whole crowd in stitches—pure entertainment. The drag queen’s performance was the standout for me; her bold confidence and over-the-top humor created a safe, inclusive space where everyone could be themselves. I’m not sure how she pulled it off, but she made my awkward first-time stage dance feel like a highlight of her set. While the 151 shot was an acquired taste (and a questionable choice), it added to the night’s wild charm. What truly stood out was the community vibe—no pretension, just people embracing the fun. The mix of hip-hop and potential country nights hints at a diverse playlist, and I can already picture myself swaying to twangy tunes in the future. Sure, the cocktails could use a stronger kick, but the combination of lively music, unforgettable characters, and zero-pressure socializing makes this spot a winner. I’ll definitely be back, cowboy hat and all.

The check-in process was a nightmare. I checked in early, gambled for 30 minutes, and was then summoned to the front of the line—only to wait another half-hour for a seat. As a buffet, I assumed service would be minimal, but no plates? Seriously? How does that even work? The food, however, was a bright spot: decent selection, fresh, and well-prepared, which made the wait somewhat tolerable. That said, the pricing felt exploitative. As a Total Rewards Platinum member, I received a $99 credit, yet still had to pay $30 for a “premium” upgrade? It’s baffling. Caesars has always delivered,

The new Bola Thai in Mesa has restored my faith in authentic Thai cuisine with its fresh ingredients, bold flavors, and attentive service. Every dish is bursting with traditional spices, and the menu offers exciting new twists on classics. If you're craving real Thai food, this is the place to go!

The lack of communication is maddening. When I finally received a voicemail (after weeks of silence), it was dismissive and automated, claiming my requested date was "unavailable"—despite no prior notice or flexibility offered. Their website remains stagnant, listing outdated promotions and contact details, which screams negligence. As a consumer, you deserve transparency, but this company treats customers like afterthoughts. I’m beyond frustrated that a $100 Groupon—purchased in good faith—has become a waste of resources. Their refusal to engage or resolve this reflects a complete disregard for accountability. I’ve since filed a dispute with Groupon and will pursue a refund through whatever means necessary. Save your time and money; this is not a business you want to support. Professionalism isn’t just about marketing—it’s about honoring commitments and respecting those who trust you. They’ve failed on every level.

The chaos and energy of the pool area are unmatched—think neon swimsuits, DJ towers by the water, and a crowd that’s 90% dressed for a red carpet. The music pumps, and even with the grossness of the pool, there’s a thrill in being part of the madness. That said, the "fun" comes at a cost. Food prices are just as insane as the drinks ($45 for a lukewarm chicken sandwich, which I now associate with trauma from my squeegee incident). The staff seems overwhelmed, but that’s Vegas for you—everyone’s there to party, not to care. I did meet some wild people by the tiki bars, though, and the sunset views over the pool deck are surprisingly nice when you’re not bleeding. Still, I’d recommend waterproof bandages, a high tolerance for chaos, and maybe a portable UV water tester. If you can ignore the reality TV vibes and the fact that your toes might be sharing a bath with strangers’ sunscreen and tears, it’s a memorable, if slightly delusional, way to spend a day. Just don’t trip on the steps—no one will catch you.

The drive alone felt like a small adventure, but the experience quickly deflated any anticipation. The menu boasted Caribbean-inspired dishes, which I assumed would resonate with my own culinary expertise—clearly, the kitchen lacked the same passion. My husband’s *lechon asado* was dry, the meat stringy and under-seasoned, while the rice and peas were bland, drowning in watered-down coconut flavor. The cold beans and rubbery, half-cooked plantains were the final strikes. I couldn’t shake the feeling that the chef was going through motions, not crafting a meal. The restaurant’s vibe was cozy, with colorful walls and a lively playlist, but the disorganization seeped through: mismatched silverware, a sticky table, and a host who seemed as disinterested as the kitchen staff. We lingered only to avoid wasting money, sipping lukewarm tea that tasted more like boiled water. The total? A hefty $35 for two uninspired plates. Potential? Absolutely. With better training, fresh ingredients, and attention to detail (like flattening plantains!), this place could thrive. But as it stands, it’s a missed opportunity. I’ll stick to my own kitchen—where the flavors are vibrant, the portions generous, and the satisfaction undeniable. Maybe a “break” *was* exactly what I needed..... from dining out.

The ambiance at Saffron only adds to its charm—soft, warm lighting and subtle Indian music create a cozy, inviting atmosphere without overwhelming the senses. The tables are spaced comfortably, and the staff ensures they’re cleared promptly, maintaining a spotless environment even during peak hours. This attention to detail extends to the layout itself: the buffet line is organized intuitively, with clear signage and a logical flow from appetizers to desserts, making the self-service process feel effortless rather than chaotic. While the chicken tikka masala and tomato soup stand out, the rest of the menu deserves equal praise. The biryanis are fragrant and layered with spices, the samosas crisp without being greasy, and the chutneys offer a refreshing tang that elevates every

As a loyal customer for over two decades, I expected better service. Spending 10 minutes studying the Note II, I anticipated basic courtesy—yet staff ignored me entirely. Meanwhile, newer customers were swiftly attended to, highlighting a clear lapse in professionalism. At 27, I’m not a “tech-savvy” demographic to be dismissed; I’m a paying customer deserving respect. The manager’s failure to intervene compounded the oversight. Poor training and apathy have no place in a Verizon store. This experience will undoubtedly impact my future interactions and loyalty. A brand built on reliability should ensure its people reflect those values. If this store can’t prioritize customers like me, it risks losing not just business, but trust entirely. Disappointing.
The cozy ambiance and attentive service elevate the experience. Try the spring rolls and mango sticky rice—flavors are vibrant, balanced, and unforgettable. Worth every bite!

The staff was attentive and friendly, which added to the pleasant stay. The hotel’s modern design and clean, well-maintained rooms created a welcoming atmosphere. While the restaurant’s prices felt steep for the limited menu, the complimentary bottled water and snacks in our room were a thoughtful touch. The glass-bottom pool, though enticing to glimpse from the street, seemed underutilized, and the gym/spa area lacked the energy of a more vibrant facility. Still, the hotel’s prime location—minutes from Old Montreal, shopping districts, and public transit—made exploring the city effortless. Despite the higher regular rate, the convenience, comfort, and the discounted Hotwire deal justified the cost for a short trip. I’d return for the peaceful stay and proximity to Montreal’s highlights, though I’d skip the hotel dining and opt for the nearby bistro scene instead. A solid choice for travelers seeking comfort without sacrificing location.

The staff was friendly and helpful. Clean bathrooms and modern amenities. Great value for the price. Close to attractions yet peaceful. Breakfast options nearby. Would highly recommend for a stress-free stay.

The conference facilities were underwhelming, with outdated audiovisual equipment and cramped seating that made networking difficult. While the spa and casino were nice to explore, the lack of nearby attractions forced us to rely heavily on the hotel’s limited offerings, which didn’t justify the premium price tag. Breakfast options were limited to a pricy, subpar buffet, and the pool area felt neglected with mismatched furniture and minimal shade. The constant elevator waits, combined with the key-card fumbles, added unnecessary stress after long days of meetings. For the cost, we felt we deserved more thoughtful touches—updated tech, better amenities, or at least more reliable access to our room. Nearby properties on the Strip, like The Cosmopolitan or Bellagio, offer modern comforts, seamless service, and vibrant energy at similar rates, making Red Rock feel outdated and inconvenient. Unless you’re desperate for a last-minute booking, it’s hard to justify staying here when so many superior options exist just minutes away.

The only thing redeeming about the evening was the mac and cheese itself, which had that creamy, just-right texture that makes you forget it’s technically a "kid’s dish." But even that was undermined by the way it was served—cold, in a shallow bowl, and drenched in so much water that the cheese resembled a lukewarm puddle. The soup, which was supposed to be rich and hearty, was similarly diluted and lukewarm, as if the kitchen had prioritized speed over quality. When I confronted the waiter about the phantom drinks on the check, he rolled his eyes, muttered something about "a mistake," and trudged to the register. To my shock, he returned with the same total. I pushed, pointing out the error again, and finally, he begrudgingly adjusted the charge—without an apology or even a shred of accountability. Meanwhile, the fly hovered near our breadsticks, and the gnat still clung to the table, as if mocking our discomfort. The worst part? By the time we finally left, we’d spent over $30 on subpar food, poor service, and a growing sense of indignation. Normally, I’d tip to cut through the noise, but not this time. I handed back the check with the exact amount owed, leaving zero cents for the man who treated us like a burden. This isn’t a one-off rant. Friends and family have had similar experiences—waiters who seem hostile, orders that vanish into the kitchen black hole, and a menu that never quite delivers on its promises. For a place that markets itself as "quaint" or "family-friendly," it feels disingenuous to nickel-and-dime customers while delivering slapdash service. I won’t be back. Nor will anyone who values food that’s edible, service that’s respectful, or a dining experience that doesn’t end in a bureaucratic nightmare over two phantom drinks. Save your money—or better yet, save your appetite for a restaurant that earns it.

The cozy, inviting atmosphere makes networking enjoyable. The staff is attentive and friendly, often remembering regulars’ orders. Pastries are flaky and fresh, and the menu offers healthy, hearty options. A must-visit for breakfast and connections!

**Continued Review:** What really stands out is the menu’s thoughtful balance between tradition and creativity. While staples like pad thai and curry shine, there are also unique offerings that make you pause and think, “I need to try that.” The group debated over sharing the mango sticky rice for dessert, and we’re so glad we did—it was a sweet, aromatic finale that

The rest of the meal wasn’t much better. While the fries were presented with a side of aioli, the greasy texture and under-seasoned salt left me unimpressed. The shake itself—a rich, vanilla-infused dessert drink—was pleasant enough, though overpriced for something that felt more like a gimmick than a standout offering. I couldn’t help but think of Umami Burger’s umami-laden creations, where every bite felt intentional and layered with flavor, versus Holsteins’ lackluster execution here. The atmosphere, while lively for a weekend spot, leaned chaotic. The open kitchen buzzed with energy, but the noise level made conversation difficult, and the tables felt cramped for the amount of traffic. More concerning was the inconsistent service: our waitress returned only sporadically, and when she did, she seemed distracted. When I mentioned the bland patty, she nodded politely but offered no apology or remedy, which left a sour taste (no pun intended). I’m not one to dismiss a place after a single visit, especially when the Yelp reviews are so polarizing. Maybe the Gold Standard isn’t their best bet for carnivores like me—perhaps I should’ve gone for their famed brisket or a different burger. Or maybe the kitchen was simply having an off day. Still, for a $20+ burger, I expect more than a dry, flavorless patty that feels like a $10 grocery-store imitation. I’ll give Holsteins another shot, ideally during a quieter time when the staff isn’t stretched thin. If they can deliver on the promise of their shakes, creativity in their toppings, and a commitment to quality over trends, they might earn those 4 stars. But for now, they’re a step below what I’d call a true standout—even if I’ll always have a soft spot for Umami Burger’s unmatched mastery.

The ambiance wasn’t much better. The lighting was harsh, and the decor leaned into a vague “farmhouse” aesthetic with exposed brick and generic art, which did little to elevate the energy. It felt like a casino buffet’s rejected twin, stripped of personality. Meanwhile, the menu’s pricing left me baffled. A simple Caesar salad ran $12, and the meatloaf tower (which, as noted, looked nothing like a tower) was $18. For that cost, I expected at least a hint of creativity or quality, but the dish was forgettable—neither rustic nor refined. The local sourcing angle, while commendable in theory, felt disingenuous. The “when available” caveat made it clear their commitment was seasonal at best. I asked about their “fresh herbs” and was told they’re sourced from a farm three states over in the winter—hardly local. It’s one thing to adapt, but the lack of transparency made it feel like marketing rather than ethics. Among my party, another person tried the “artisan” grilled cheese. It arrived with mediocre sourdough, lukewarm cheese, and a side of pickles that were brine-heavy and flavorless. “Artisan” here clearly meant “not worth the price hike.” Desserts fared no better. The chocolate cake was dry and under-seasoned, like a leftover from a different kitchen. In the end, Farm Cafe is the kind of

The shower had lukewarm water that fluctuated between icy and scalding. The bathroom floor was slippery and littered with hair. Staff shrugged off our complaints about mold, the broken heater, and the ashtray in a "non-smoking" room. Would never return—despite the 80’s TV, this was a disaster. Save money and stay elsewhere.

The food here is consistently stellar, and the vibe is cozy, with a counter-service setup that feels like a neighborhood secret. The crust on their personal pizzas is crispy on the edges but still chewy in the center, holding up perfectly to all the toppings. My Super Six pizza had a great balance—none of the meats felt overwhelming, and the veggies added a fresh, zesty kick. Wifey’s spinach special with ricotta was a flavor bomb; the creamy ricotta paired so well with the tangy marinara and earthy greens. Even the kids’ cheese ravioli was a hit, with tender pasta pockets and a rich, cheesy filling that even my picky daughter devoured. Prices are super reasonable for the quality, especially when you consider the half-off wine Wednesdays—it’s like a built-in date night perk. The staff is always friendly and efficient, even when the place is packed. Honestly, Spinatos checks every box: delicious food, top-notch service, and that rare charm of a no-frills spot that feels like a home-cooked meal. If you’re in the Valley craving pizza that actually tastes like it was made with love (and not a conveyor belt), skip the chain spots and sprint to Spinatos. Trust me, your taste buds will thank you—and don’t forget to grab a bottle of wine while you’re there!
After the owner’s outburst, the rest of the meal was ruined. Tension

The steak was overcooked, turning rubbery and devoid of flavor—utterly inedible. The $18 price tag felt like a mockery of the paltry serving. While the asparagus was merely adequate, the mashed potatoes were a sad attempt at comfort. My friends’ hearty, flavorful sandwiches at $9 each made my plate look like a joke. I left ravenous, questioning every life choice that led me to Crane Alley. If dining here is meant to be a “unique experience,” I’d recommend skipping the meal entirely and just paying for the privilege of being disappointed.

**Continued Review:** The rest of my meal was equally underwhelming. The tan tan mein, which should be a comforting blend of bold, savory, and spicy, was dominated by that strange creamy texture, as though coconut milk or heavy cream had been mistakenly added. Each spoonful felt heavy, almost cloying, rather than the light, umami-rich broth I’d expect from a dish rooted in Chinese-Sichuan tradition and popularized in Japan. The noodles themselves were slightly overcooked, slipping into a mushy state that clashed with the supposed authenticity of the dish. While some might argue creativity in reimagining classics, this felt less like innovation and more like a failure to understand the core identity of tan tan mein. The service didn’t improve. When I returned to the counter after my meal to ask about the gyoza, the same employee shrugged and said, “It’s not on the menu today,” as if the inconsistency were my fault. Meanwhile, the table that had interrupted my initial order received their sodas with a smile, while I was left to stew in my disappointment. The stark contrast in attention highlighted a lack of customer focus that overshadowed the otherwise cozy atmosphere. I can’t shake the frustration of this experience. For a place serving noodles, I expected at least basic reliability—having menu items available, staff trained to handle orders, and a commitment to the dishes’ traditional qualities. While the design and vibe initially gave me hope for

The store’s vibe is cozy and inviting, with shelves that overflow with charm. The magic section, with its flickering candles and mystical trinkets, feels like stepping into a fairy tale. While it’s clearly a haven for those into the new age scene, even skeptics might find quirky, conversation-starting items. Prices are reasonable, and the staff is friendly, happy to help you pick something unique. Whether you’re hunting for a gift or just love collecting oddities, The Bag Lady offers a delightful escape from the mundane. Just be warned: you might leave with more than you intended!

The restaurant’s ambiance was straightforward, with a no-frills layout that felt more like a casual eatery than a traditional sushi spot. While the lack of ambiance might not appeal to everyone, the friendly and attentive service compensated. Our server was apologetic about the construction, explaining the new location has been delayed due to permit issues, but still managed to keep the dining experience positive. The current setup, though functional, felt a bit cramped, with tables spaced closely together. Despite this, the staff moved efficiently, and we were served promptly. The portions were modest but reasonably priced, especially considering the early hour. The Japanese breakfast offered a nice balance of flavors and textures, with the grilled salmon being a standout—flaky and seasoned well. The fruit medley (oranges and cantaloupe) was a refreshing contrast to the savory elements, and the seaweed salad added a crisp, tangy bite. The fermented soybeans were an acquired taste for me, but my girlfriend found them intriguing. The green tea, served in a sleek ceramic cup, was perfectly brewed and a welcome addition. As for the deep-fried sweet tofu udon bowl, the tofu was light and airy, with a slight crunch, but the broth lacked the depth we’ve experienced elsewhere. It was serviceable but forgettable, though the simplicity fit the no-nonsense vibe of the place. If you’re an early riser craving a mix of traditional Japanese and American fare, this spot is worth a try—especially with the sushi option later in the day. However, the prolonged construction does raise concerns about the establishment’s commitment to its space. Still, the quality of the food and the cheerful service left us optimistic that once the new location opens, the experience could be even better. For now, we’ll return for the breakfast offerings but hope the construction wraps up soon to see what else Ichiban has to offer.

The event’s charm lies in its vibrant energy and the sheer joy of seeing dogs of all shapes and sizes—tiny Chihuahuas prancing alongside giant Great Danes, each vying for attention. The food stands serve up greasy but satisfying treats, and the kids’ activities (think face painting and photo booths with costumed pets) keep families entertained. The music, while not groundbreaking, adds to the festive vibe. Still, the focus often feels a bit scattered. While the adoption booths are heartwarming and the training tips from experts are helpful, the event could deepen its impact by incorporating interactive demonstrations. Imagine a stage for agility trials or a showcase of search-and-rescue dog work—these would add educational value and wow factor. The mention of cats, snakes, and rabbits in the “other pets” corner is a step toward inclusivity, but they’re relegated to a side stage. Expanding their presence—like a “pet spotlight” area for reptile handlers or rabbit agility—could make the event more universally appealing. Meanwhile, the lack of amenities for attendees and animals is a small oversight. A few strategically placed water stations and poop bag dispensers (beyond the scattered kiosks) would make navigating the crowd with furry friends easier. Financially, the event is donation-based, which is lovely in spirit, but as someone noted, a nominal $1 entry fee (matched with free food donations) could fund upgrades like shaded rest areas or waste management. That said, the organizers clearly care about community and compassion, and those values shine through. With a clearer mission—say, a balance of celebration, education

The portion sizes were generous, but that didn’t redeem the lackluster taste. The orange chicken’s glaze was watery and cloyingly sweet, with no balance of acidity or spice. The Hawaiian rice—basically saffron rice—was bland and lacked any distinct flavor, making the meal feel rushed and underwhelming. Even the side of sesame noodles we grabbed on a whim was oily and underseasoned. For the price, we expected fresh ingredients and decent execution, but this felt like reheated leftovers. The inconsistency between online hype and reality is baffling. Don’t let the star ratings fool you; this is subpar at best. I’ll stick to better-reviewed spots next time and won’t be giving this place another shot.

The delivery guy showed up, just pizza, no soda. I said that’s fine, but how do we resolve this? He said call the store, the shift leader Ramon can talk to me about it, and he wouldn’t mind driving it back out. So I called in, Ramon said, “Oh well it’s not on the order so...” I said, “But I ordered it, so can you have him bring it?” He replied, “You’re on the outskirts of our delivery area, so we can’t for just a soda, sorry.” I’ve worked in customer service, and I’ve never—*in all my life*, especially as a manager—seen someone handle a situation like that. They messed up, and the solution is just “Sorry, deal with it”? No apology. No effort. No empathy. “We’re slammed,” was not an excuse for their mistake. It was a dismissal. This isn’t about a *soda*. It’s about accountability. A soda costs $2.50. The customer service they squandered here is priceless. The delivery driver was even kind enough to offer a fix, but the moment it escalated to management, they shut it down. That’s not customer service—that’s a lesson in complacency. I’ve been a loyal customer for years. I’ve ordered late at night, on holidays, even when it was snowing. Their pizza has always been worth the wait..... *until today*. Now I’m left feeling like a problem to be solved, not a customer to be valued. Hungry Howie’s taught me that convenience without care is just a temporary fix. I’ll take my business—and my loyalty—to a place that *actually* believes in the promise of “service.” Maybe next time, the new girl will be paired with a manager who knows that the “H” in the logo stands for *humanity*. Until then..... goodbye. And don’t call me, Ramon.

The service is friendly enough, though often rushed, and the ambiance leans more “quaint” than cozy. While the menu offers some unique drink options, the pricing feels slightly inflated for the experience. On the plus side, the rustic decor and quiet corner location make it a decent spot for quick meetings or passing time. However, the lack of a loyal customer base (and my own reluctance to return) suggests the pros barely outweigh the cons. All things considered, it’s a passable pit stop—but not a destination worth championing.

The rooms are tiny and the decor feels like it hasn’t been updated since the early 2000s. Noise from the casino floor seeped through thin walls, making it hard to unwind. While the location is convenient for the Strip, there are far better options for the price. Skip this one for a modern stay—your wallet and sanity will thank you. (Yes, I’ll take the Cosmo over this any day. 😒)

The drinks here are equally worth the trip. RCT’s margaritas are bold and balanced—zesty lime upfront, with just the right kick of tequila and a hint of sweetness that doesn’t cloy. I also tried their hibiscus Michelada, which was refreshing and spicy, garnished with a lime wedge and a chili powder rim. For non-alcoholic options, they serve house-made aguas frescas (I recommend the mango-lime—it tasted like summer in a cup). Pairing tacos with drinks here feels like a fiesta, even if you’re just grabbing a quick bite after work. The atmosphere is lively but laid-back, with colorful murals, string lights, and the constant sizzle of the grill. The staff is friendly and knowledgeable, happy to explain menu quirks or suggest combos. Pro tip: Arrive during Happy Hour (4:30–6:30 PM) for half-price tacos—it’s a genius way to sample multiple kinds without breaking the bank. What truly sets RCT apart is its dedication to quality. The pork belly taco, for instance, isn’t just fatty and fall-off-the-bone tender; it’s glazed with a smoky chipotle-caramel sauce that sticks to every tortilla strand. Even the “lesser” pollo taco, while not transcendent, uses juicy, well-seasoned meat that’s far superior to the dry, flavorless chicken I’ve encountered at other fusion spots. My only gripe? The portions, while generous, aren’t shareable enough for a group of four unless you’re prepared to fight over the last bite of queso-drenched carnitas. Also, the menu leans heavily on familiar Mexican-American fusions, so adventurous eaters might crave something more experimental—like a taco with grilled pineapple and crema, or a dessert like churros. Still, RCT nails the core mission: delivering craveable, Instagram-worthy tacos that feel both nostalgic and new. If you’re a fan of bold flavors and the occasional culinary guilty pleasure, this place will hit all your buttons. And if you’re lucky, the chef might just sneak an extra spoonful of crema on your next order. *(Full disclosure: I returned three times in a week. My jeans suffered. My heart? Grateful.)*

Every detail of the visit felt thoughtfully handled. The technicians moved at a calm pace, spoke gently, and even adjusted their techniques to ensure my mother felt comfortable. The studio’s warm, inviting atmosphere made her feel at ease, and the staff went above and beyond—offering her water, soft music, and even a cozy blanket. Their professionalism and empathy truly set Elaine’s apart. I’ve taken friends and family since, and they’ve all raved about the experience. From the flawless nail art to the genuine care shown to every client, Elaine’s Nails isn’t just a salon—it’s a haven of kindness. I can’t thank them enough for making such a meaningful difference for my mom. You’ve earned lifelong loyal customers!

The service has always been warm and attentive, making each visit feel like coming home. The chefs’ dedication shines through—every dish is crafted with care and flavor that lingers. The festive ambiance during Christmas adds magic to our gatherings, with twinkling lights and a joyful vibe. My niece now counts down to our annual trip, eager to try the honey toast she calls “honey gold.” Even after a decade, there’s no sign of decline—Ichiza keeps surprising us with fresh twists on favorites. A true treasure in Vegas! Thank you for a decade of cherished memories and mouthwatering meals!

The service was friendly and efficient, which made the experience pleasant despite the lunch rush. The deli area felt cozy and bustling, with a variety of options that made decision-making fun. While the combo satisfied my hunger, I couldn’t shake the feeling it lacked standout flavor—think “competent” rather than “memorable.” My co-worker raved about the eggplant parmigiana’s crispy texture, though the oiliness hinted at a heavy hand with the fryer. For now, Panevino checks the box for a quick, no-fuss meal with decent value. However, I’m curious how the full restaurant menu stacks up—I’ll save room for that adventure next time. If you’re craving casual comfort food without breaking the bank, this spot works. Just don’t go expecting culinary fireworks.

The service was top-notch, with friendly staff who made our dining experience even better. Everything was perfectly cooked, from the tender filet to the rich, flavorful pork. Portions are generous, and the ambiance is chic yet cozy. Hard to pick a favorite, but the ahi nachos were a delightful start. Will definitely return on my next Vegas visit—this spot’s a gem!

The experience has become so depressing that we’re done trying to give this place the benefit of the doubt. The bartender’s dismissive attitude wasn’t an isolated incident—our server during dinner once left us waiting 20 minutes for water, and the hostess has made us wait in line despite having a reservation. Even the atmosphere feels hostile: the TVs’ lack of sports programming (a bar staple) and the staff’s indifference to customer needs scream neglect. We’ve spent hundreds here over the years, but loyalty means nothing when respect is absent. Buffalo Wild Wings might be the “lesser evil,” but honestly? *Any* place with better service feels like an upgrade. Save your time and money—this establishment prioritizes profit over people, and it’s clear they don’t value their patrons.

The menu offers a mix of classic bar fare and creative twists, like the zesty white pizza, which pairs perfectly with their signature margaritas or craft brews. TVs are strategically placed to ensure every guest gets a good view of the games, and the upbeat music keeps the energy high without overpowering conversation. Whether it’s a raucous night out or a relaxed evening, the 24/7 availability makes it easy to drop by any time. Regulars rave about the loyalty perks, while first-timers appreciate the warm welcome. From game day crowds to late-night hangs, Sierra Gold nails the balance of fun, flavor, and familiarity—proof that a neighborhood staple can still feel fresh and exciting.

The rest of our stay was marred by these interactions, leaving us feeling unsafe and unwelcome. Even simple moments, like relaxing by the pool or grabbing a drink at the bar, became tense because we were constantly aware of security’s hostility. One afternoon, my girlfriend was approached by a staff member while sipping a drink, accused of “loitering,” and told to “move along” despite being in a public area. I stepped in, and it escalated into a shouting match before management finally intervened—only to side with security and dismiss our complaints. What’s most frustrating is that we weren’t the only ones noticing this behavior. Overheard conversations at the pool and bar revealed other guests had faced similar treatment: a family was threatened with eviction for letting their kids play too loudly, and a couple was harassed for sitting in a “VIP-only” area (which wasn’t clearly marked). It’s clear this isn’t an isolated issue but a systemic failure in training and accountability. When we finally spoke to a front desk supervisor, they shrugged it off, claiming security “just did their job.” No apology, no offer to compensate for the trauma. How can a place pride itself on hospitality when its staff turns guests into suspects? The room was nice, the location convenient, but those positives mean nothing when basic respect is erased by fearmongering and misogyny. This isn’t just about one bad experience—it’s about a pattern of poor judgment and zero effort to improve. I’ve stayed at countless Vegas hotels, but none have left me so ashamed to associate with their brand. Save your money; there are far better places to celebrate than a hotel that treats its guests like criminals.

Continuing the review: "Tried to explain the 45-minute policy, but she shrugged and called me late. Forced to gate-check my bag, then rebooked to a later flight. Seats cramped, snacks nonexistent. Worst part? No apology. Spirit Airlines has no respect for customers—avoid like plague. Will never fly you again. Total waste of time, money, and patience. #NeverSpirit." *(54 words, emphasizing policy mishandling, added fees, poor amenities, and a lack of accountability while maintaining the angry tone.)*

What really stands out about Panera is its ability to balance casual dining with quality ingredients. While I focused on the You Pick Two deal, the menu offers so much more—everything from fresh-baked bread to hearty sandwiches and vibrant bowls. Even though I didn’t try the pastries this time, the irresistible aroma wafting through the dining area made me vow to return for their legendary cookies or cinnamon rolls. The portions are generous without being overwhelming, and the pricing feels fair for the quality, especially compared to other chain restaurants. I also appreciated the subtle details, like the soft lighting and the open, airy layout of the Steele Creek location. The seating is a mix of cozy booths and communal tables, which suits both solo diners and groups. The background music was just loud enough to keep the energy up without drowning out conversation. If you’re a fan of customization, Panera’s digital menu screens are a game-changer. You can tweak your order with dietary preferences—like swapping dressing or adding protein—all while watching your total adjust in real time. It’s a small touch, but it adds to the overall convenience. Since my lunch, I’ve been recommending Panera to coworkers and friends, especially for quick, stress-free meals. Whether you’re grabbing a bite between meetings or unwinding after work, the combination of great food, efficiency, and a welcoming vibe makes it a standout spot. I’ve already added Panera to my “regular rotation,” and I’m not alone—judging by the packed parking lot, this place clearly has a loyal following. Don’t just take my word for it: go try that broccoli and cheddar soup. You’ll thank me later!

The brunch menu here is a standout, offering a mix of classic Vegas fare with creative twists that keep things exciting. While the fried chicken benedict steals the show, their shrimp and grits are equally impressive—plump shrimp, silky grits, and a just-right amount of heat from the house-made jalapeño gravy. And let’s not forget the pancakes; they’re thick, fluffy, and come stacked with toppings like fresh berries or bacon, making them perfect for sharing (or not, if you’re not watching your indulgence). The drinks, while the bloody marys are a bit underwhelming, are saved by the enthusiastic bar staff who’ll happily suggest house specials. For $20, you get more than just food—you get a vibe. The bar area is lively, with big screens broadcasting sports and a crowd that’s equal parts tourists and locals trading stories over cocktails. It’s the kind of place where you can start with a mimosa, end up with a margarita, and leave full, happy, and not a penny over your self-imposed budget. Even the “upscale” hotel restaurants nearby seem to charge extra for ambiance that pales in comparison to the unapologetic fun here. My only gripe? The menu is so large, I’ve never left without wondering what I missed. But that’s part of the charm—Vegas isn’t about perfection, it’s about excess, and this spot delivers in spades. If you’re hunting for a meal that feels like a win, skip the souvenir shops and hit this spot instead. At the end of the day, when your hangover starts to kick in, you’ll be thanking yourself for the giant, delicious leftovers in the fridge—and the extra hour of sleep you bought with that second meal. 10/10 for value, 9.5/10 for style

What truly stung was the disconnect between the establishment’s pricing and the experience it delivered. The menu, already on the higher end, seemed to justify itself only if the food and service matched. Instead, we felt nickel-and-dimed at every turn. The $2.50 iced tea incident wasn’t just about the price—it was about the attitude it provoked. The manager’s defensiveness and dismissive tone (“This is a WINE BAR YOU KNOW”) felt condescending, as though we were unreasonable for expecting basic hospitality. It’s one thing to have niche pricing, but it’s another to alienate customers who are already paying a premium for the privilege. The seating arrangement compounded the frustration. Even with a half-empty restaurant, we were crammed into a table that felt more like a kitchen staging area than a dining spot. The lack of effort to accommodate a group of four—let alone the apparent disregard for basic comfort—suggested a lack of attentiveness that trickled down from management to staff. When my wife pointed out the ham in her “vegetarian” mac and cheese, the server shrugged it off as a “menu error” but offered no apology or replacement. The fact that a critical ingredient for dietary restrictions wasn’t flagged speaks volumes about their attention to detail. By the time we received the check, the experience had devolved into a cost-benefit analysis of whether the wine alone was worth the tab. We ordered two bottles of wine, which were decent but far from extraordinary—certainly not priced to justify the $60 mark. The appetizers had been the only highlight, but even they felt overpriced for what amounted to a modest charcuterie board. The final straw was the bill itself, which included a 20% gratuity despite the service being so lackluster that we wouldn’t have tipped that high otherwise. When I pointed this out, the manager insisted it was standard policy, but her insistence felt more like an excuse to avoid a discussion than a genuine effort to resolve the issue. In the end, the evening became a study in disappointment. For a place that markets itself as an upscale, curated experience, the execution felt unpolished and inconsiderate. If you’re looking for a casual bite or a place to sip wine with friends, there are far better options in the area. The Living Room and Postino, for instance, not only serve food that lives up to their prices but also treat guests with the respect and warmth that this wine bar conspicuously lacked. As for me, I’ll stick to bringing my own iced tea—and my expectations, far lower.

Continued review: Everything was fresh and well-prepared—crisp salad, tender grilled chicken. Vibrant, balanced flavors offered a healthier, satisfying twist on Southern classics. Generous portions made it a delightful, guilt-free meal.

The rest of the evening was a mix of cringe and charm. The “old Western town” vibe leaned heavily into kitschy aesthetics: creaky saloon doors, faux-rough-hewn wooden decor, and an overabundance of cowhide throw pillows. It all felt like a TV set someone forgot to pack away after filming a 1990s Disney Channel western. But for the kids running around (and parents taking Instagram photos with posed actors), it clearly hit the mark. The “actors” were the real highlight—impressive in their commitment to character. One “sheriff” lectured us about “maintaining order” while eating a cheeseburger, another “prostitute” gave deadpan, sassy responses to our friend’s absurd questions. It was the kind of campy, awkward humor that makes for a memorable night out if you’re in on the joke. That said, the place reeks of desperation to feel authentic. The rattlesnake appetizer, while unexpectedly tasty (and a conversation starter), couldn’t salvage the meal. The steak was overcooked, the sides generic, and the dessert menu limited to s’mores kitsch. Prices, though, were shockingly steep for what you got—$18 for a glass of wine in a cracked tumbler, anyone? Still, if you approach this place as a novelty over a fine dining experience, it’s..... tolerable. It’s the kind of spot that exists solely for tourists, families, and people who romanticize the Wild West without ever having read a real history book. All in all, I’d call it a “one-and-done” destination. Skip the food and opt for the cheapest drinks; focus on the theatrics, not the menu. If you’re here with kids, you’ll walk away with stories (and maybe a snake on the menu). If you’re here solo? Find a real bar and a real steakhouse. But hey, at least I didn’t have to explain why there’s no such thing as a mechanical bull in 1888..... my buddy still hasn’t figured that out.

The bread is undercooked and stale, crumbling more than providing structure. The "steak" is thinly sliced and flavorless, like chewy cardboard. Even the cheese feels like an afterthought—melted but bland, offering no richness to elevate the mess. Service is slow, with staff seeming disengaged, and the greasy, cramped environment does nothing to enhance the experience. For the prices they charge, you’d expect quality, but it’s clear Primantis relies on nostalgia and convenience, not culinary skill. I’ve had better hot dogs at gas stations. If you’re in Pittsburgh and crave a real cheesesteak, skip the tourist trap. Fatheads uses fresh, juicy beef, and Uncle Sam’s has a crispy, flavorful sandwich that actually stays intact. Primantis is a relic of a gimmick, and it’s time the hype died with it.

The rest of the stay only got worse. The bed was sagging in the middle, the sheets felt like sandpaper, and the bathroom had a musty smell I couldn’t shake. I tried reporting the TV issue to housekeeping, but they “would get back to me” and vanished. Meanwhile, the blaring static from the screen kept me up half the night—no volume button, just noise. To make matters worse, the AC was broken, so the room felt like a sauna. I begged for a room change, but they claimed “no vacancies” despite earlier lying about early check-in options. The next morning, I faced another ordeal at breakfast. The buffet was sparse, and the eggs tasted like they came from a can. When I asked for a refund, they laughed and said, “You paid for the room, so tough luck.” Every interaction with staff felt transactional and dismissive. Honestly, this place redefines “meh.” The “Vegas experience” they promised was nothing but a scam—overpriced, unclean, and utterly unreliable. Save your money and skip Harrahs. If I ever see a neon sign with their name again, I’ll cross the street. Worst. Trip. Ever. 💣🔥

The croquettes were a nice surprise—crispy, golden, and filled with a creamy, mildly spicy flavor that paired well with the tangy slaw on the side. The “spicy mayo bomb” was bold, balancing heat and creaminess perfectly. I’ll admit the pork and pineapple combo was a fun twist, though the pineapple’s sweetness didn’t fully complement the savory meat. Still, it had more moisture and depth than the chicken and pork tacos, which left me wanting. The dryness issue lingered, likely due to overcooking or under-seasoning. On the plus side, the industrial-chic design of the shipping-container-themed space made the meal feel unique and Instagram-worthy. I’ll return for the shrimp tacos and experiment with bolder salsa pairings next time—this place has potential, but the execution needs a little more oomph.

Here's a continuation of the review, maintaining the tone and expanding on the key points while keeping the word count in check: --- The rest of the menu didn’t fare much better. I ordered a side of their “Signature Slaw,” which tasted like it had been sitting under a heat lamp for hours—soggy, lifeless, and void of the tangy kick promised on the menu. The fries, while decently crispy, were over-salted and lacked any real seasoning. Honestly, it felt like someone just dumped ketchup in a cup and called it a day. The only thing redeemable was the chili, which was rich, smoky, and full of flavor—though even that couldn’t redeem the disaster that was my meal. Service was equally lackluster. Our server seemed disinterested, barely acknowledging our table beyond dropping off drinks. When I mentioned the hot dog’s alarming pop (which I half-expected to launch off the plate), they shrugged and said, “They’re all like that.” No apology, no offer to replace it. For a place that once had such a cult following, it felt like they’d checklisted “Vegas tourist trap” and called it a success. I get it—Vegas is all about spectacle, not sustenance. But to charge $18 for a hot dog that’s less “Nathan’s-style” and more “Nathan’s *nightmare*”? It’s a shame, because I still believe in Pink’s. Maybe this location is just a casualty of the Strip’s relentless grind. But if you’re a local or a fan, bring a friend and split the chili. If you *must* order a dog, do as I did: order it, snap a photo for the “experience,” and then..... well, let’s just say you’ll be grateful for the chili cheese fries. Trust me on this. Your taste buds—and your wallet—will thank you. This continuation mirrors the original’s frustration while adding specific critiques of other menu items and service, maintains the conversational tone, and reinforces the central warning while leaving a hint of hope for the brand’s potential.

The menu offered creative fajitas and spicy tacos, with generous portions that felt worth the price. Staff were attentive, even during the busy event. While the bathrooms were overcrowded and unclean, the vibrant atmosphere and flavorful dishes made up for it. Still, a quick cleanup during peak hours would elevate the experience. Would return for the food but suggest timing visits to avoid events like Glendale Glitters.

The entire process was seamless—Nelly was meticulous, explaining each step and adjusting the shape/color to match my preferences. The numbing was gentle, and she constantly checked in to ensure I felt at ease. The final result looks natural yet dramatic, with precise lines that pop without being overdone. It’s crazy how much time I save not applying eyeliner daily! Her attention to detail and genuine warmth make her a 5-star provider. I can’t wait to trust her with my eyebrows—they’ll look as stunning as these lashes! If you’re on the fence, don’t be. Nelly’s talent and kindness will blow you away. Book her—you won’t regret it! 🌟

The energy in the main room was electric, with lasers and strobes syncing perfectly to the DJ’s beats—every drop felt like a festival moment crammed into one sweaty floor. The crowd was a mix of seasoned clubbers and fashion-forward newcomers, all there for the same reason: to lose themselves in the music. While the admin line was a buzzkill (literally—patience wore thin after 9:45pm), once inside, the vibes shifted. Bartenders remembered names by midnight, and the bouncers even cracked jokes while checking IDs. The preview weekend’s bingo theme added a fun twist—winners scored free drinks, which made the $14 Bacardi cokes feel slightly less tragic. Sure, the prices will make you wince, but this isn’t a place for budgeting—it’s about splurging on a night where the music, the lights, and the crowd make you forget about the tab. Just stick to water (and your savings account) if you’re not ready to join the “crazy kids” betting their covers. Still, for a once-in-a-while blowout, it’s hard to beat the rush—and the 10/10 bass drops.

The salon was nearly empty, yet the staff ignored me, chatting among themselves instead. When the new customer—a man who’d just walked in—was prioritized, it felt like a slap in the face. No apology, no explanation. I’d paid for a basic service, but clearly, my time meant nothing to them. Terrible communication, worse customer service. Save yourself the frustration—skip Bebé Nails. If you value your time, go elsewhere. They’re not worth the headache.

The drink was a standard soda, but it was chilled and hit the spot, especially after the initial heat of the burger. While the chiles delivered a subtle warmth that built over time (not scorching, but enough to make you sit up a bit), I found myself savoring each bite—the juicy meat and gooey cheese balanced the tangy chiles perfectly. If I had one critique, it’s that the bun, while soft and slightly toasted, got a bit soggy from the sauce and melted cheese, but that’s more of a complaint about my own devouring pace than the burger itself. I also wish they’d added a touch of pickle or onion to brighten the flavor, though the simplicity let the chiles shine. All in all, it was a satisfying meal that reminded me why I’d loved Whataburgers back in the day. The combination of quality ingredients, quick service, and that signature Whataburger warmth (both in food and hospitality) made it worth the splurge. I’ll probably swing by again if I’m in the area—especially now that I’m curious about their legendary “add it all” burger. Just might bring a napkin or two..... and maybe a burn cream.

The service is efficient but unenthusiastic, and the ambiance feels generic—just a standard family-run eatery without any standout charm. While the bibimbap was adequately seasoned, the bulgogi lacked the caramelized richness I’ve come to expect. Portions are generous, but this doesn’t compensate for the overpriced, underwhelming flavors. I appreciate the availability of less common dishes like dakgangjeong (spicy chicken), but the execution often feels half-hearted. For a quick fix when cravings hit and I’m short on time, Korea Garden suffices. However, for a truly satisfying Korean meal, I’d rather make the hour drive to a neighboring city with better options. It’s a functional, forgettable spot—one that highlights how Pittsburgh’s Korean cuisine still has room to grow in both depth and authenticity.

The buffet’s variety didn’t disappoint—each dish felt thoughtfully prepared. The **mutton on bone** was a standout, rich and tender, with just the right amount of spices to highlight the meat’s natural flavor. Compared to other Indian places in town, their **curries** had a depth I rarely encounter, balancing heat and aroma without overpowering. The **tandoori chicken**, while slightly drier than I’d hoped, still hit the mark with its smoky, charred exterior and fresh herbs. I’m guessing the lunch rush hadn’t kicked in yet, so the plates were still steaming and vibrant. The **basmati rice with cashews and cranberries** was a surprising twist—sweet, nutty, and fragrant, a far cry from the usual basmati fare. My friend raved about the **mint chutney**, which paired perfectly with the tandoori. At $11–$12, it’s an unbeatable deal for the quality and portions. Plus, the servers’ warm, enthusiastic service (despite the thick Indian accent humor) added to the experience. I’m still not sure what changed from my last visit—maybe portion control or the timing—but this time, I left satisfied without the dreaded food coma. If you’re craving fresh, flavorful Indian food without breaking the bank, **Mint** is a must-try. I’ll definitely be back soon. 🌿

The service didn’t help either. Our server was disinterested, and the buffet staff seemed too overwhelmed to notice the seafood sitting under a heat lamp like it belonged in a museum. I half-expected to see “Do Not Touch” signs. For $15 a plate (which *felt* like $30 after seeing the state of the food), I expected better. My friend tried to defend the place, saying, “Maybe they’re having an off day,” but honestly? This isn’t a one-day fluke. The lack of consistency in the kitchen is alarming. I’ve had better luck with vending machine sushi. Buffets are supposed to be a gamble, sure, but this felt like someone said, “How hard can this be?” and left it at that. The menu variety was there, but execution is everything, and this place failed on *every* level. The fried fish and potatoes I actually enjoyed might as well have been a mercy mission to keep

The staff’s disorganization only added to the frustration—orders were taken haphazardly, and no one seemed to acknowledge the wait times. When our food finally arrived, the lukewarm temperature of the lechon (a dish that thrives on crispness) felt like the final insult. While the portion sizes were generous, the overwhelming greasiness left us feeling sluggish rather than satisfied. The $12 fried rice, though meaty, lacked balance, with adobo flavors drowned out by saltiness and oil. Even the lumpia, a highlight, was undermined by the glug of vinegar-based patis we needed to offset the greasy aftertaste. The restroom break during our wait revealed why the sewage smell lingered—pipes were exposed and unclean, and the air vents groaned with an oily haze. Yet, for all its flaws, DT’s isn’t entirely unworthy. The homemade lumpia, filled with a hearty mix of vegetables and pork, paired nicely with the tangy, umami-rich brown sauce, which might just be the best part of the entire meal. The prices remain tempting, especially for casual eats on a budget, but the experience is one of tolerance over enjoyment. If you do choose to stop by, plan for at least 90 minutes, even for small orders. While dine-in feels like a gamble, takeout might be preferable—though be prepared for inconsistency in quality. DT’s could be a decent option for a solo, no-frills lunch, but for anything beyond that, it’s hard to recommend. Stick to the lumpia and sauce, and leave the rest for those with a higher tolerance for culinary disappointment.

The service was friendly, but the overall vibe felt a bit rushed, like they were tending to bigger groups more. The sides were solid—mac and cheese was a standout—but the usual BBQ staples (coleslaw, beans) were forgettable. While the tri-tip’s smoky flavor shone, the rest of the menu felt like filler. At $40 a person, it’s fine for a casual meal if BBQ’s your thing, but for me, it’s just okay. Definitely hit or miss, but if you’re a sauce-slinger or a rib-lover, Lucille’s might just become your new happy place.

What really sets iPic apart is the seamless blend of luxury and convenience. The staff is attentive without being overbearing, always ready with a refill or a recommendation for the next movie or snack. Even the bathrooms are a step above typical theaters—clean, modern, and stocked with complimentary hand sanitizer and tissues. The lobby doubles as a chic lounge, perfect for pre-show drinks or post-film mingling, with a full bar serving craft cocktails that elevate the night further. For families or groups, the private dining pods are a game-changer.
